Proposed Natural Science Curriculum

Provisional proposal for grades 2–6. Model review is not teacher validation or Ministry approval. Misconceptions are diagnostic hypotheses; durations require classroom trials. The 160-hour scenario uses clock hours, not a verified official timetable.

Schedule status: rejected_before_scheduling. Coverage, balance and solver audit

Grade 2 · Grade 3 · Grade 4 · Grade 5 · Grade 6 ·

Grade 2

Matter

The unit begins with physical science, focusing on the observable and measurable properties of matter. Students start with qualitative descriptions (prop-qualitative) and move to quantitative measurements using tools (prop-measure-length, prop-compare-mass). This allows them to classify properties logically (prop-classify-quant-qual). They then explore specific material behaviors like malleability and chemical changes. In the second half, the focus shifts to life science. Students use their observation skills to distinguish living from non-living things (living-classify), identify defining biological qualities (living-qualities), and apply this by recording plant growth (living-germination) and analyzing responses to stimuli (living-stimuli). The progression moves from static properties of objects to dynamic processes of living organisms.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 6 planning weeks.

Physical and Chemical Properties of Matter

Students explore the physical world by observing, measuring, and classifying the properties of different materials. This foundational skill moves them from qualitative sensory observations to quantitative measurements using standard tools, and introduces basic chemical properties through observable changes.

describe organoleptic properties of everyday objects
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide students with a wooden block. Ask them to write down three words that describe how it looks, feels, and smells.
Expected response
The student lists three appropriate qualitative descriptors, such as 'brown', 'hard', and 'woody smell'.
Scoring rule
1 point for each valid qualitative property described, up to 3 points.
Mastery evidence
Students can accurately describe an object using at least three sensory properties (e.g., color, texture, smell).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think that 'property' only refers to who owns an object.; Students might confuse the material an object is made of with its sensory properties.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Characteristics of materials are formally called properties. · Source page 18 · paragraph p18-paragraph-8
measure length of objects in centimeters using a ruler
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Give students a printed line and a ruler. Ask them to measure the line and write the length in centimeters.
Expected response
The student writes the correct measurement (e.g., '12 cm') with the correct unit.
Scoring rule
Pass if the measurement is within 0.5 cm of the actual length and includes 'cm'.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly align a ruler and read the length of an object in centimeters.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may start measuring from the edge of the ruler instead of the zero mark.; Students might confuse centimeters with inches.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Rulers are used to measure lines and record values in centimeters. · Source page 11 · paragraph p11-paragraph-9
compare mass of two objects using a simple balance scale
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide a balance scale, an eraser, and a sharpener. Ask the student to place one in each cup and state which has more mass.
Expected response
The student identifies the object in the cup that goes down as having more mass.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly identifies the heavier object based on the balance scale's movement.
Mastery evidence
Students can use a balance scale to determine which of two objects has more mass.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students often believe that larger objects always have more mass than smaller objects.; Students may think the side of the balance that goes up is heavier.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • A balance scale can be used to compare the mass of everyday objects like an eraser and a sharpener. · Source page 12 · paragraph p12-paragraph-11
classify properties as qualitative or quantitative
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide a list of properties: 'red', '15 cm', 'heavy', '5 g'. Ask the student to sort them into 'Qualitative' and 'Quantitative' columns.
Expected response
Qualitative: red, heavy. Quantitative: 15 cm, 5 g.
Scoring rule
Pass if all four properties are sorted into the correct categories.
Mastery evidence
Students can distinguish between properties that are measured with numbers and those that are described with words.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think that any property involving a number (like '2 eyes') is a quantitative property of the material itself.
Local prerequisites
prop-qualitative, prop-measure-length, prop-compare-mass
Scientific support
  • Qualitative properties include descriptive terms like small or made of wood. · Source page 15 · paragraph p15-paragraph-7
identify malleability and ductility in common materials
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Show a picture of aluminum foil and a copper wire. Ask the student to label which shows malleability and which shows ductility.
Expected response
Aluminum foil is labeled malleability; copper wire is labeled ductility.
Scoring rule
Pass if both terms are correctly matched to the corresponding material form.
Mastery evidence
Students can recognize when a material is demonstrating malleability (flattening) or ductility (stretching into wires).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students might think all metals are equally easy to bend by hand.; Students may confuse breaking a material with deforming it.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Malleability is the property that allows materials to be formed into flat, thin objects. · Source page 27 · paragraph p27-paragraph-16
describe evidence of chemical properties through environmental exposure
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Show two images: a shiny metal gate and a rusty metal gate. Ask the student to decide if the material changed due to a physical or chemical property, and justify their choice.
Expected response
The student states it is a chemical property and justifies it by mentioning the color change or rust caused by the environment.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student selects chemical property and cites the color change or environmental exposure as evidence.
Mastery evidence
Students can explain that a change in color or the production of bubbles indicates a chemical property reacting to the environment.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think that a color change always means the object was painted.; Students might believe that rust is a type of dirt that can just be washed off.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Chemical properties are observed when materials are exposed to environmental factors. · Source page 31 · paragraph p31-paragraph-5

Characteristics of Living Things

This skill transitions students from observing inanimate matter to understanding biological life. They learn to differentiate living organisms from non-living objects by identifying specific biological processes (growth, reproduction, response to stimuli) through direct observation and structured recording.

classify entities as living or non-living based on observable traits
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide a list: dog, rock, tree, bicycle. Ask the student to sort them into 'Living' and 'Non-living' groups.
Expected response
Living: dog, tree. Non-living: rock, bicycle.
Scoring rule
Pass if all four items are placed in the correct categories.
Mastery evidence
Students can accurately sort a list of entities into living and non-living categories.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students often think that anything that moves (like a car or a robot) is alive.; Students may think plants are not alive because they do not move visibly like animals.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Objects in the environment can be categorized into living things and inert (non-living) things. · Source page 38 · paragraph p38-paragraph-5
identify essential qualities of living things (growth, reproduction, feeding)
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Ask the student to circle the four actions that all living things do from a list: grow, read, reproduce, feed, move, fly.
Expected response
The student circles grow, reproduce, feed, and move.
Scoring rule
Pass if exactly those four actions are circled.
Mastery evidence
Students can list the core biological functions that define a living organism, including movement.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students might believe that making noise is a requirement for being alive.
Local prerequisites
living-classify
Scientific support
  • Living things are distinguished by having a combination of qualities, including growth, movement, reproduction, and feeding, while non-living things may have some but not all of these qualities. · Source page 41 · paragraph p41-paragraph-4
record observable changes during seed germination
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide a worksheet with three blank boxes labeled Day 1, Day 3, and Day 5. Ask the student to draw the changes in a germinating bean seed based on their observations.
Expected response
Drawings show progression: a plain seed, a seed with a small root/sprout, and a seed with a larger sprout/small leaves.
Scoring rule
Pass if the drawings show a clear progression of growth over the three stages.
Mastery evidence
Students can document the sequential physical changes of a seed as it sprouts.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think seeds are non-living stones until they are put in soil.; Students might expect a full plant to appear overnight.
Local prerequisites
living-qualities
Scientific support
  • Seed germination involves observable changes in size, shape, and position over several days. · Source page 43 · paragraph p43-paragraph-5
describe bodily responses to environmental stimuli
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Ask the student to write what happens to their body when they run fast (internal stimulus) and what happens to their pupil when a light shines on it (external stimulus), explaining why these are responses.
Expected response
The student writes that they sweat/heart beats faster after running, and their pupil changes size in light, identifying both as responses to stimuli.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student identifies valid bodily changes (sweat/heartbeat for running, pupil change for light) and links them to the stimuli.
Mastery evidence
Students can link both internal and external environmental stimuli to corresponding bodily responses.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think sweating or a fast heartbeat means they are sick, rather than a normal response to exercise.; Students might not realize that light entering the eye is a stimulus.
Local prerequisites
living-qualities
Scientific support
  • Living bodies perceive and respond to phenomena occurring both internally and in the surrounding environment. · Source page 51 · paragraph p51-paragraph-5
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

act-teach-prop-qualitative · 60 min · teach

Introduce the concept of qualitative properties by showing a wooden block, a plastic cup, and a metal spoon. Guide students to describe how each looks, feels, and smells. Write their descriptive words on the board and explain that these are called properties.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally state at least two descriptive words for a given object.
Materials
wooden block, plastic cup, metal spoon, whiteboard, markers
Safety
Ensure objects have smooth edges to prevent splinters or cuts.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual word bank with symbols for colors, textures, and smells.
Time rationale
15 minutes for introduction, 30 minutes for guided group observation of three objects, 15 minutes for summarizing and recording vocabulary.

act-prac-prop-qualitative · 90 min · practice

Set up five observation stations with different everyday materials. Students rotate through the stations, observing the objects and recording three qualitative properties (color, texture, smell) for each in their notebooks.

Mastery criterion
Students record at least three accurate qualitative properties for each of the five objects.
Materials
cotton balls, rocks, rubber bands, cardboard, notebooks, pencils
Safety
Ensure rocks are clean and large enough not to be swallowed. Remind students to waft smells gently.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw their observations or use pre-printed checklists if writing is challenging.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 70 minutes for rotating through five stations (14 mins each), 10 minutes cleanup.

act-assess-prop-qualitative · 60 min · assessment

Provide each student with a wooden block. Ask them to independently write down three words that describe how it looks, feels, and smells on their assessment sheet.

Mastery criterion
The student lists three appropriate qualitative descriptors, such as brown, hard, and woody smell.
Materials
wooden blocks, assessment sheets, pencils
Safety
Ensure wooden blocks are sanded smooth.
Access and differentiation
Provide a scribe for students with severe dysgraphia, allowing them to dictate their three words.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup and instructions, 40 minutes for independent observation and writing, 10 minutes collection.

act-teach-prop-measure-length · 60 min · teach

Demonstrate how to use a ruler to measure length in centimeters. Show how to align the zero mark with the edge of the object. Measure a pencil and a book as a class, writing the results with the cm unit.

Mastery criterion
Students can correctly align the zero mark of a ruler with the edge of an object during guided practice.
Materials
rulers, pencils, books, whiteboard
Safety
Remind students not to bend plastic rulers to prevent snapping.
Access and differentiation
Use rulers with high-contrast markings and highlight the zero line with a permanent marker.
Time rationale
20 minutes demonstration, 30 minutes guided practice measuring two objects, 10 minutes review.

act-prac-prop-measure-length · 90 min · practice

Students work in pairs to measure the length of various printed images of local crops (maize leaves, sugarcane sticks) using a ruler. They record the measurements in centimeters in a structured table.

Mastery criterion
Students accurately measure and record the lengths of at least 8 images within 0.5 cm accuracy.
Materials
rulers, printed images of crops, recording tables, pencils
Safety
Ensure paper edges are smooth to avoid paper cuts.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn alignment lines on the images for students who struggle with positioning the ruler.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes measuring 10 different images, 15 minutes sharing results.

act-assess-prop-measure-length · 60 min · assessment

Give students a worksheet with five printed lines of varying lengths and a ruler. Ask them to measure each line and write the length in centimeters next to it.

Mastery criterion
The student writes the correct measurement within 0.5 cm of the actual length and includes cm for all five lines.
Materials
worksheets with printed lines, rulers, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Enlarge the printed lines and provide a magnified ruler for students with visual impairments.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent measurement, 10 minutes collection.

act-ret1-prop-measure-length · 45 min · retrieval

Students retrieve their rulers and measure the length of their own pencils and erasers, recording the values on a sticky note to place on a class chart.

Mastery criterion
Students independently align the ruler and read the correct centimeter value.
Materials
rulers, pencils, erasers, sticky notes, class chart
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Pair students to double-check each other's alignment before writing the final number.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup, 25 minutes measuring and charting, 10 minutes review of the chart.

act-ret2-prop-measure-length · 45 min · retrieval

Provide students with pieces of string of different lengths. They must measure the string in centimeters and order them from shortest to longest on their desks.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly measure and sequence the strings based on their centimeter length.
Materials
pre-cut strings, rulers
Safety
Ensure strings are not wrapped around fingers or necks.
Access and differentiation
Tape one end of the string to the desk to help students measure without the string moving.
Time rationale
10 minutes distribution, 25 minutes measuring and sorting, 10 minutes verification.

act-teach-prop-compare-mass · 60 min · teach

Introduce the balance scale. Demonstrate how placing objects in the cups causes the scale to tip. Show that the side that goes down has more mass. Compare an apple and a grape as a class.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally identify which side of the balance scale holds the object with more mass.
Materials
balance scale, apple, grape, whiteboard
Safety
Ensure the balance scale is stable on the table to prevent it from falling.
Access and differentiation
Use objects with drastically different masses for clear visual cues.
Time rationale
20 minutes introduction, 30 minutes guided demonstrations with various objects, 10 minutes summary.

act-prac-prop-compare-mass · 90 min · practice

Students work in small groups with a balance scale. They are given pairs of classroom items (e.g., marker vs crayon, scissors vs glue stick). They predict which has more mass, test it, and record the results.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify and record the heavier object for at least 5 pairs using the balance scale.
Materials
balance scales, markers, crayons, scissors, glue sticks, recording sheets
Safety
Instruct students to place objects gently into the balance cups to avoid breaking the scale.
Access and differentiation
Provide a recording sheet with pictures of the objects where students just circle the heavier one.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes group work testing 6 pairs of objects, 15 minutes cleanup and review.

act-assess-prop-compare-mass · 30 min · assessment

Conduct a whole-class demonstration using a balance scale. Place an eraser and a sharpener in the cups. Ask students to independently record on their worksheet which object has more mass based on which cup goes down.

Mastery criterion
The student correctly identifies the object in the cup that goes down as having more mass.
Materials
balance scale, erasers, sharpeners, worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a worksheet with pictures of the objects where students circle the heavier one.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup, 10 minutes teacher demonstration of 3 pairs, 10 minutes independent recording.

act-teach-prop-classify-quant-qual · 60 min · teach

Explain the difference between qualitative (words/senses) and quantitative (numbers/measurements) properties. Create a T-chart on the board and sort examples like red, 10 cm, heavy, and 5 grams as a class.

Mastery criterion
Students can explain that quantitative properties use numbers and qualitative properties use descriptive words.
Materials
whiteboard, markers, property cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use a magnifying glass icon for qualitative and a ruler icon for quantitative on the T-chart.
Time rationale
20 minutes direct instruction, 30 minutes interactive sorting on the board, 10 minutes summary.

act-prac-prop-classify-quant-qual · 90 min · practice

Students receive a deck of cards with various properties written and illustrated on them. In pairs, they must sort the cards into Qualitative and Quantitative piles, justifying their choices to each other.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly sort at least 15 out of 20 property cards and can justify one of each type.
Materials
decks of property cards, sorting mats
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the numbers on the quantitative cards in red to provide a visual scaffold.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes sorting and peer discussion, 15 minutes class review.

act-assess-prop-classify-quant-qual · 60 min · assessment

Provide a worksheet with a list of properties: red, 15 cm, heavy, 30 degrees. Ask the student to write them into Qualitative and Quantitative columns.

Mastery criterion
All four properties are sorted into the correct categories.
Materials
worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the properties aloud for students who struggle with reading comprehension.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.

act-teach-prop-malleability-ductility · 60 min · teach

Introduce malleability by flattening a piece of clay or foil, and ductility by showing a copper wire. Explain the definitions and have students repeat the terms while doing hand motions (pressing flat, pulling long).

Mastery criterion
Students can match the term malleability to flat objects and ductility to wires.
Materials
aluminum foil, copper wire, modeling clay
Safety
Ensure the ends of the copper wire are taped or blunted to prevent poking.
Access and differentiation
Use physical gestures consistently when saying the words to reinforce memory.
Time rationale
20 minutes introduction, 30 minutes passing around safe examples, 10 minutes vocabulary review.

act-prac-prop-malleability-ductility · 90 min · practice

Students explore stations with safe materials (foil, clay, pipe cleaners). They test if they can flatten them (malleability) or stretch them into wire shapes (ductility) and record their findings on a chart.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify which materials demonstrate malleability and which demonstrate ductility.
Materials
aluminum foil, modeling clay, pipe cleaners, recording charts
Safety
Monitor that students do not wrap pipe cleaners tightly around fingers.
Access and differentiation
Provide a chart with pictures of the materials and simple check boxes for flat or wire.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes station exploration, 15 minutes cleanup and sharing.

act-assess-prop-malleability-ductility · 60 min · assessment

Show a picture of aluminum foil and a copper wire on a worksheet. Ask the student to draw a line connecting the correct term (malleability or ductility) to the corresponding picture.

Mastery criterion
Both terms are correctly matched to the corresponding material form.
Materials
worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Include a small icon of a hammer next to malleability and a pulling hand next to ductility on the worksheet.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.

act-teach-prop-chemical-changes · 60 min · teach

Show a shiny iron nail and a rusty iron nail. Explain that the color change is evidence of a chemical property reacting to the environment (air/water). Discuss how this is different from just painting the nail.

Mastery criterion
Students can state that a color change like rust indicates a chemical property.
Materials
shiny nail, rusty nail in a sealed clear jar, whiteboard
Safety
Keep the rusty nail in a sealed clear plastic jar so students can observe it without touching rust.
Access and differentiation
Use a highly visual before-and-after poster of a rusting bicycle.
Time rationale
20 minutes observation, 30 minutes discussion on environmental exposure, 10 minutes summary.

act-prac-prop-chemical-changes · 90 min · practice

Students observe a teacher demonstration of baking soda and vinegar creating bubbles. They then look at pictures of cut apples turning brown and melting ice. They discuss in groups and write down which show chemical properties (bubbles, color change) and justify why.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the apple and the bubbles as chemical changes and justify it using evidence of color change or gas production.
Materials
baking soda, vinegar, clear cup, pictures of brown apples and melting ice, notebooks
Safety
Teacher conducts the vinegar/baking soda demonstration. Students wear safety goggles if close. No tasting.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters: 'I know it is a chemical property because I see...'
Time rationale
20 minutes demonstration, 50 minutes group analysis of pictures, 20 minutes class discussion.

act-assess-prop-chemical-changes · 60 min · assessment

Show two images on a worksheet: a shiny metal gate and a rusty metal gate. Ask the student to circle if the material changed due to a physical or chemical property, and write one sentence justifying their choice based on the color change.

Mastery criterion
The student selects chemical property and cites the color change or environmental exposure as evidence.
Materials
worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow oral justification for students who struggle with writing.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent writing, 10 minutes collection.

act-teach-living-classify · 60 min · teach

Introduce the concepts of living and non-living things. Discuss observable traits like needing food, growing, and moving on their own. Create a class chart sorting pictures of a cat, a rock, a tree, and a car.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally explain one reason why a cat is living and a rock is not.
Materials
picture cards, chart paper, markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use clear, unambiguous pictures (avoid tricky items like dormant seeds for the introduction).
Time rationale
20 minutes direct instruction, 30 minutes interactive chart building, 10 minutes review.

act-prac-living-classify · 90 min · practice

Simulate a nature walk using large posters of national protected areas around the room. Students walk around with a clipboard, finding hidden picture cards of entities (animals, plants, rocks, water) and sorting them into a living/non-living T-chart.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly classify at least 10 out of 12 hidden items into the correct categories.
Materials
posters of protected areas, hidden picture cards, clipboards, T-charts, pencils
Safety
Ensure the classroom is clear of tripping hazards during the walkaround.
Access and differentiation
Pair students so they can discuss their choices before writing them down.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes for the simulated nature walk and sorting, 15 minutes review.

act-assess-living-classify · 60 min · assessment

Provide a worksheet with a list of words and pictures: dog, rock, tree, bicycle. Ask the student to draw a line to sort them into Living and Non-living boxes.

Mastery criterion
All four items are placed in the correct categories.
Materials
worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Ensure pictures accompany all words for pre-readers.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.

act-ret1-living-classify · 45 min · retrieval

Give students old magazines. They must cut out two pictures of living things and two pictures of non-living things, and glue them onto a divided paper.

Mastery criterion
Students independently select and correctly categorize four images.
Materials
magazines, scissors, glue, divided paper
Safety
Use blunt-nosed safety scissors.
Access and differentiation
Pre-cut a selection of images for students with fine motor difficulties to choose from and glue.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 25 minutes cutting and gluing, 10 minutes sharing.

act-ret2-living-classify · 45 min · retrieval

Conduct a whiteboard relay. Call out an item (e.g., cloud, bird, volcano, grass). Students write L for living or N for non-living on their personal whiteboards and hold them up.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the category for 8 out of 10 called items.
Materials
personal whiteboards, dry erase markers, erasers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide L and N cards for students to hold up instead of writing.
Time rationale
10 minutes distribution, 25 minutes relay game, 10 minutes collection.

act-teach-living-qualities · 60 min · teach

Explicitly teach the essential qualities of living things: they grow, reproduce, move, and feed. Use a simple story of a puppy growing into a dog, eating food, moving around, and having puppies to illustrate these points.

Mastery criterion
Students can repeat the four essential qualities (grow, reproduce, move, feed) when prompted.
Materials
storyboard pictures of a dog's life cycle, whiteboard
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use hand gestures for each quality (e.g., hand moving up for grow, eating motion for feed).
Time rationale
20 minutes storytelling, 30 minutes discussing the qualities, 10 minutes vocabulary repetition.

act-prac-living-qualities · 90 min · practice

Students work in groups with a set of scenario cards (e.g., a caterpillar eating a leaf, a plant getting taller, a cat with kittens, a dog running). They must match each scenario to the correct quality (feed, grow, reproduce, move).

Mastery criterion
Groups correctly match all scenario cards to the corresponding biological quality.
Materials
scenario cards, category headers (Grow, Reproduce, Move, Feed)
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Include clear visual cues on the scenario cards.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes group matching activity, 15 minutes class review.

act-assess-living-qualities · 60 min · assessment

Provide a worksheet with a list of actions: grow, read, reproduce, feed, move, fly. Ask the student to circle the four actions that all living things do.

Mastery criterion
The student circles exactly grow, reproduce, move, and feed.
Materials
worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the words aloud for the class while they circle.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.

act-teach-living-germination · 60 min · teach

Explain the process of seed germination. Show a time-lapse video (if possible) or a series of large posters showing a seed sprouting roots, then a stem, then leaves. Set up a class demonstration of a bean in a clear cup with wet paper towels.

Mastery criterion
Students can describe the first thing that comes out of a seed (the root).
Materials
posters of germination, clear plastic cup, paper towels, bean seeds, water
Safety
Ensure students wash hands after handling seeds. Do not use chemically treated seeds.
Access and differentiation
Provide a physical 3D model of a germinating seed for tactile exploration.
Time rationale
20 minutes explaining the stages, 30 minutes setting up the class demonstration, 10 minutes summary.

act-prac-living-germination · 90 min · practice

Students are given a set of mixed-up picture cards showing the stages of maize germination. They must sequence them in the correct order from dry seed to small plant, and glue them into their notebooks.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly sequence the 4 stages of germination.
Materials
germination sequence cards, notebooks, glue, scissors
Safety
Use blunt-nosed safety scissors.
Access and differentiation
Number the backs of the cards so students can self-check their sequence.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes sequencing and gluing, 15 minutes peer review.

act-assess-living-germination · 60 min · assessment

Provide a worksheet with three blank boxes labeled Day 1, Day 3, and Day 5. Ask the student to draw the changes in a germinating bean seed based on what they learned.

Mastery criterion
Drawings show progression: a plain seed, a seed with a small root, and a seed with a larger sprout/leaves.
Materials
worksheets, pencils, crayons
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank (seed, root, leaf) for students to label their drawings if they wish.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes drawing, 10 minutes collection.

act-teach-living-stimuli · 60 min · teach

Introduce stimuli and responses. Have students jump in place for 2 minutes and notice their fast heartbeat (internal stimulus/response). Then, use a flashlight to show how a volunteer's pupil shrinks in light (external stimulus/response).

Mastery criterion
Students can identify that their fast heartbeat is a response to exercise and pupil change is a response to light.
Materials
open classroom space, whiteboard, flashlight
Safety
Ensure students have enough space to jump without hitting each other. Do not shine flashlight directly into eyes for prolonged periods.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to place a hand on their chest to physically feel the heartbeat change.
Time rationale
20 minutes physical activity and observation, 30 minutes discussion and mapping stimulus to response on the board, 10 minutes summary.

act-prac-living-stimuli · 90 min · practice

Students work in pairs to test mild stimuli. One student holds a cup of warm water, then cold water, and describes how their skin feels. Then they observe each other's eyes when covering and uncovering them to see pupil changes. They record the stimuli and responses.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly record at least two stimuli (temperature, light) and their corresponding bodily responses.
Materials
cups of warm water, cups of cold water, recording sheets
Safety
Ensure warm water is only lukewarm, not hot, to prevent burns.
Access and differentiation
Provide a matching worksheet where students draw a line from the stimulus picture to the response picture.
Time rationale
20 minutes instruction and safety rules, 50 minutes testing and recording, 20 minutes class discussion.

act-assess-living-stimuli · 60 min · assessment

Ask the student to write two sentences on a worksheet: what happens to their body when they run fast, and what happens to their eyes in bright light, explaining why these show responses to stimuli.

Mastery criterion
The student identifies valid bodily changes (sweat/heartbeat for running, pupil change for light) and links them to the stimuli.
Materials
worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence frames: 'When I run, my body _____. This is a response to _____.'
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 40 minutes independent writing, 10 minutes collection.

Limitations: The distinction between physical and chemical properties is highly simplified for Grade 2; complex chemical reactions are reduced to observable color changes or bubbling.; The definition of living things relies on macroscopic observable traits (growth, movement, feeding), which may oversimplify edge cases (e.g., dormant seeds, viruses).; Measurement tasks assume access to standardized tools (rulers, balances) which may require teacher calibration to ensure accuracy.; Germination timelines are idealized; actual seed growth depends heavily on local temperature and humidity, requiring teacher flexibility.

Energy

Students enter second grade with basic, intuitive observations of pushes, pulls, sunlight, and shadows. In this unit, they formalize these observations into distinct concepts of mechanical, electrical, and thermal energy, and explore the properties of light and color. This foundational vocabulary and observational practice prepares them for third grade, where they will study more complex energy transfers, the particulate nature of matter, and more advanced optical phenomena.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 6 planning weeks.

Energy Forms and Transformations

Students explore different forms of energy (mechanical, thermal, electrical) and how they manifest in everyday objects. This builds a foundational understanding that energy causes changes and can be transformed from one type to another.

predict the relative amount of water displaced by a sphere dropped from different heights
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Look at a diagram of two identical spheres, one held 20 cm above a cup of water and one held 60 cm above. Predict which sphere will cause more water to spill and explain why using evidence from class experiments.
Expected response
The sphere dropped from 60 cm will cause more water to spill because it has more energy from being higher up.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student selects the 60 cm sphere and mentions height or greater energy/impact as the reason.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately predicts that a higher drop results in more displaced water and justifies it using the concept of mechanical energy.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The height from which an object is dropped does not affect its impact energy.; Only the size of the object determines how much water splashes.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The energy of an object upon impact affects the amount of water displaced. · Source page 59 · paragraph p59-paragraph-3
predict the physical state of water after adding or removing thermal energy
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Read a short scenario: 'Maria leaves a bowl of ice cubes in the hot sun. What will happen to the ice, and what must she do if she wants to turn that water into a gas?' Write your prediction.
Expected response
The ice will melt into liquid water because of the sun's heat. To turn it into a gas, she needs to add even more heat (boil it).
Scoring rule
Pass if the student states the ice melts to liquid and that adding heat/boiling is required to create gas.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly predicts the state change and justifies it by referencing the addition or removal of heat.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Ice and water vapor are completely different substances than liquid water.; Cold is a substance that is added to water to make ice.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Changing liquid water into a gas (water vapor) requires a specific action (adding heat). · Source page 80 · paragraph p80-paragraph-5
select everyday objects that require electrical energy to function
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a worksheet with 10 images of household items (e.g., television, broom, mobile phone, book, fan), circle the ones that need electrical energy to work.
Expected response
The student circles the television, mobile phone, and fan.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correctly circled electrical device and 1 point for each correctly ignored non-electrical device. Mastery is 8/10 total points.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies at least 8 out of 10 electrical devices from a mixed set of images.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All objects that move require electricity.; Batteries do not provide electricity, only wall outlets do.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Everyday objects like televisions, radios, and mobile phones are common examples of devices students interact with that need energy. · Source page 61 · paragraph p61-paragraph-4
classify everyday materials as conductors or insulators of electricity
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Sort a list of materials (copper wire, plastic spoon, human body, rubber eraser, iron nail) into two columns: 'Conducts Electricity' and 'Blocks Electricity'.
Expected response
Conductors: copper wire, human body, iron nail. Insulators: plastic spoon, rubber eraser.
Scoring rule
1 point per correctly classified material. Pass requires 4/5 correct.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 given materials into conductors and insulators.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All metals are insulators.; The human body cannot conduct electricity.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Materials that allow electricity to pass through are called conductors, and the human body is an example of one. · Source page 66 · paragraph p66-paragraph-6
match everyday actions to their corresponding energy transformations
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Draw lines to connect the object (e.g., a fan plugged into a wall, a child sliding down a slide) to the correct energy change (e.g., electrical to mechanical, potential to kinetic).
Expected response
Fan connects to 'electrical to mechanical'. Slide connects to 'potential to kinetic'.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct match. Pass requires 3/4 correct matches.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly matches at least 3 out of 4 scenarios to their energy transformation.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Energy is used up and disappears completely.; An object can only have one type of energy forever.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Energy can be transformed from one type to another, such as the energy invested in pedaling converting into mechanical energy. · Source page 88 · paragraph p88-paragraph-3

Light and Color Interactions

Students investigate how light interacts with different materials and how colors are formed and used. This develops their observational skills and introduces basic optics concepts in a tangible way.

categorize materials based on whether they block light to form shadows or let light pass through
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a list of items (a thick book, a clear glass window, a wooden door, a piece of clear cellophane, a metal spoon), sort them into a table with two columns: 'Forms a dark shadow' and 'Lets light pass through'.
Expected response
Forms shadow: book, wooden door, metal spoon. Lets light pass: clear glass window, clear cellophane.
Scoring rule
1 point per correctly sorted item. Pass requires 4/5 correct.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 materials as light-blocking (opaque) or light-passing (transparent/translucent).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Shadows are objects themselves rather than the absence of light.; All clear objects let 100% of light through without any distortion.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Objects can be classified by whether they allow light to pass through or block it to form shadows. · Source page 94 · paragraph p94-paragraph-10
identify situations where white light is separated into multiple colors
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Look at a diagram showing a flashlight shining white light into a glass triangle (prism) and a rainbow coming out the other side. Circle the sentence that best describes what is happening: A) The glass paints the light. B) The light is broken into many colors. C) The light is blocked.
Expected response
The student circles option B (The light is broken into many colors).
Scoring rule
Pass if the correct option is selected.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies that white light can be broken down into multiple colors using a prism.
Diagnostic hypotheses
White light has no color.; Prisms add color to the light rather than separating existing colors.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Light can be decomposed into various colors. · Source page 91 · paragraph p91-paragraph-10
describe the purpose of combining subtractive colors in printing
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Answer the following question in one sentence: How do inkjet printers make pictures with many different colors if they only use a few ink colors?
Expected response
They combine or mix the subtractive colors to make all the other colors.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student mentions combining or mixing colors to get new ones.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly describes that mixing a few base colors allows printers to create many different colors.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Printers have hundreds of different ink cartridges for every single color.; Mixing all paint colors makes white.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Inkjet printers use the combination of subtractive colors to produce images of different colors. · Source page 98 · paragraph p98-paragraph-2
identify the meaning of specific colors used in environmental safety signs
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the color of the sign to its meaning: 1. Red sign with white letters. 2. Green sign with white letters. A) Emergency/Safe route. B) Stop/Danger.
Expected response
1 matches with B. 2 matches with A.
Scoring rule
Pass if both matches are correct.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly matches safety colors to their general meanings in a school or community context.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Sign colors are chosen just for decoration.; Red always means go.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Colors are necessary for signage, for example, green and white for emergency signs and red with white for stop signs. · Source page 95 · paragraph p95-paragraph-9
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-electrical-devices · 30 min · teach

Introduce electrical and non-electrical devices by showing a battery-operated toy car and a wooden push car. Discuss what makes each move. Show pictures of household items and sort them on the board into 'needs electricity' and 'does not need electricity'.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally identify which objects require batteries or a plug to function.
Materials
Battery-operated toy, Wooden toy, Picture cards of household items
Safety
Ensure battery compartments are screwed shut. Do not use devices that plug into the wall for this demonstration.
Access and differentiation
Provide physical objects instead of pictures for students who need tactile input.
Time rationale
10 minutes for the toy demonstration, 15 minutes for group sorting, 5 minutes for wrap-up.

prac1-electrical-devices · 90 min · practice

Students work in small groups to explore a 'mystery box' containing 20 different safe, unplugged everyday objects (e.g., hairbrush, remote control, book, flashlight, spoon, calculator). They must test or examine each object, discuss with their group, and sort them into two physical hoops labeled 'Electrical' and 'Non-Electrical'. They then draw their sorted groups in their science journals.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly sort at least 18 of the 20 objects and accurately record their findings.
Materials
Mystery boxes, 20 everyday objects per group, Hula hoops, Science journals
Safety
All electrical items must be battery-operated or completely unplugged with cords secured. No exposed wires.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist with images for students who struggle with drawing.
Time rationale
20 minutes for exploration, 40 minutes for sorting and discussion, 30 minutes for journaling.

assess-electrical-devices · 30 min · assessment

Students complete a worksheet with 10 images of household items (television, broom, mobile phone, book, fan, etc.). They must circle the ones that need electrical energy to work.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies at least 4 out of 5 electrical devices from a mixed set of images.
Materials
Assessment worksheet, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the names of the objects aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for independent completion.

teach-height-impact · 40 min · teach

Discuss amusement park rides like a slide (tobogán). Ask why sliding from a higher point makes you go faster. Demonstrate dropping a heavy plastic ball into a deep tray of flour from 10 cm and then from 50 cm. Discuss how the higher drop gave the ball more energy, creating a larger crater, just like starting higher on a slide gives more energy.

Mastery criterion
Students can state that the ball dropped from higher up made a bigger hole because it had more energy.
Materials
Heavy plastic ball, Deep tray, Flour, Ruler
Safety
Ensure students stand back so flour does not get in their eyes. Sweep up any spills immediately to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Use a brightly colored ball and dark sand instead of flour for better visual contrast.
Time rationale
15 minutes for demonstration, 15 minutes for discussion, 10 minutes for recording observations.

prac1-height-impact · 90 min · practice

Students work in pairs with a basin of water and a plastic block. They drop the block from 20 cm, 40 cm, and 60 cm, observing the splash. They use a large piece of chart paper behind the basin to mark how high the water splashed each time. They write a sentence concluding how height affects the splash.

Mastery criterion
Students accurately record that higher drops cause higher splashes and write a logical conclusion.
Materials
Basins of water, Plastic blocks, Chart paper, Markers, Rulers
Safety
Wipe up spilled water immediately to prevent slipping. Do not use glass objects.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters for the conclusion (e.g., 'When the block was higher, the splash was...').
Time rationale
20 minutes setup, 40 minutes experimenting and marking, 30 minutes writing conclusions and cleaning up.

prac2-height-impact · 90 min · practice

Students model volcanic rocks falling from different heights. Using a sand tray, they drop pumice stones from various measured heights and measure the width of the impact craters. They create a simple bar graph showing crater width versus drop height.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully measure the craters and create a bar graph showing a positive correlation between height and crater size.
Materials
Sand trays, Pumice stones, Rulers, Graph paper
Safety
Ensure sand is kept in the trays. Do not throw stones; only drop them straight down.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-labeled graph axes for students who need support with data organization.
Time rationale
30 minutes experimenting, 45 minutes graphing, 15 minutes sharing results.

ret1-height-impact · 30 min · retrieval

Flashback activity: Show students a picture of the flour tray experiment from the teach activity. Ask them to draw what the tray looked like after a 10 cm drop versus a 50 cm drop, and write one sentence explaining why they look different.

Mastery criterion
Students draw a larger crater for the 50 cm drop and mention height or energy in their explanation.
Materials
Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal explanations instead of written ones.
Time rationale
10 minutes drawing, 10 minutes writing, 10 minutes peer review.

ret2-height-impact · 30 min · retrieval

Read a short scenario: 'A coconut falls from a very tall tree, and another falls from a short tree. Which one will hit the sand with more energy?' Students must write their answer and justify it using evidence from past experiments.

Mastery criterion
Students select the tall tree coconut and justify it by referencing height and energy.
Materials
Scenario cards, Journals
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual diagram of the two trees.
Time rationale
10 minutes reading, 15 minutes writing, 5 minutes sharing.

assess-height-impact · 40 min · assessment

Look at a diagram of two identical spheres, one held 20 cm above a cup of water and one held 60 cm above. Predict which sphere will cause more water to spill and explain why using evidence from class experiments.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately predicts that a higher drop results in more displaced water and justifies it using the concept of mechanical energy.
Materials
Assessment diagram, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to dictate their explanation to the teacher.
Time rationale
10 minutes analyzing the diagram, 30 minutes writing the prediction and explanation.

teach-conductors-insulators · 30 min · teach

Build a simple circuit using a 1.5V AA battery, two wires, and a small LED bulb. Leave a gap in the wires. Test a metal paperclip to close the gap (light turns on) and a plastic spoon (light stays off). Introduce the terms conductor and insulator.

Mastery criterion
Students can define conductor as allowing electricity to pass and insulator as blocking it.
Materials
1.5V AA battery, Wires with alligator clips, Small LED bulb, Metal paperclip, Plastic spoon
Safety
Strictly use only 1.5V AA batteries. Never use wall outlets. Ensure wires do not short-circuit for long periods to prevent overheating.
Access and differentiation
Use a buzzer instead of an LED for visually impaired students.
Time rationale
15 minutes for demonstration, 15 minutes for vocabulary introduction and discussion.

prac1-conductors-insulators · 90 min · practice

Station rotation: Students use safe 1.5V battery circuits to test 10 different classroom objects (eraser, foil, copper wire, wooden block, etc.). They record their predictions and actual results in a T-chart labeled 'Conductors' and 'Insulators'.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly test and classify at least 8 out of 10 objects.
Materials
1.5V AA batteries, Wires, LED bulbs, 10 test objects per station, T-chart worksheets
Safety
Only use 1.5V batteries. Monitor groups to ensure they do not short the battery directly.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn T-charts with pictures of the objects to be tested.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 60 minutes testing at stations, 15 minutes reviewing results.

prac2-conductors-insulators · 90 min · practice

Students test various materials (rubber bands, cloth, foil, paper, paperclips) by placing them in a gap in a simple 1.5V battery circuit to see if the LED lights up. They categorize the materials as conductors or insulators based on whether they block or allow electricity to flow.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully test materials and correctly categorize them as conductors or insulators based on the LED lighting up.
Materials
Wires, 1.5V AA batteries, LED bulbs, Various materials (rubber, cloth, foil, paper)
Safety
Only use 1.5V batteries. Ensure students understand this is a model and real wall outlets or wires should never be touched.
Access and differentiation
Limit the material choices to two distinct options (one metal, one rubber) for students who need simplified decision-making.
Time rationale
20 minutes planning, 40 minutes testing, 30 minutes recording and presenting.

assess-conductors-insulators · 30 min · assessment

Sort a list of materials (copper wire, plastic spoon, human body, rubber eraser, iron nail) into two columns: 'Conducts Electricity' and 'Blocks Electricity'.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 given materials into conductors and insulators.
Materials
Assessment worksheet, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide physical samples of the materials for students to hold while taking the assessment.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent sorting.

teach-energy-transformations · 30 min · teach

Show a battery-operated fan turning on (electrical to mechanical) and a wind-up toy moving (potential to kinetic). Discuss how energy doesn't disappear but changes its job. Create a simple anchor chart with arrows showing the changes.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally describe that the battery makes the fan blades move.
Materials
Battery-operated fan, Wind-up toy, Chart paper, Markers
Safety
Ensure fan blades are soft or enclosed so fingers cannot be injured.
Access and differentiation
Use sound-making toys (electrical to sound) as an additional example for auditory learners.
Time rationale
15 minutes for demonstrations, 15 minutes for building the anchor chart together.

prac1-energy-transformations · 90 min · practice

Students play a matching card game in pairs. They must match a 'Before' card (e.g., a battery, a wound-up spring) with an 'After' card (e.g., a moving toy car, a spinning fan) and state the energy transformation out loud to their partner.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully match all pairs and articulate the transformation happening.
Materials
Sets of matching cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a reference sheet with the anchor chart for students to check their matches.
Time rationale
15 minutes explaining rules, 60 minutes playing the game, 15 minutes group review.

prac2-energy-transformations · 90 min · practice

Classroom scavenger hunt. Students walk around the room with a clipboard to find 5 objects that transform energy (e.g., pencil sharpener, clock, light switch). They draw the object and write what energy it uses and what it turns into.

Mastery criterion
Students identify at least 3 objects and correctly state their energy transformations.
Materials
Clipboards, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Instruct students not to touch wall outlets or switches without permission.
Access and differentiation
Pair students up so one can draw while the other writes.
Time rationale
15 minutes instructions, 50 minutes scavenger hunt, 25 minutes sharing findings.

assess-energy-transformations · 30 min · assessment

Draw lines to connect the object (e.g., a fan plugged into a wall, a child sliding down a slide) to the correct energy change (e.g., electrical to mechanical, potential to kinetic).

Mastery criterion
Student correctly matches at least 3 out of 4 scenarios to their energy transformation.
Materials
Assessment worksheet, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the scenarios aloud for students.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work.

teach-state-changes · 30 min · teach

Place an ice cube in a sealed plastic bag in a sunny window and another in a dark, cool closet. Ask students to predict what will happen. Check back later to see the melted ice. Discuss how adding heat changes solid to liquid, and conceptually discuss boiling water to make gas.

Mastery criterion
Students can explain that the sun's heat caused the ice to melt into liquid water.
Materials
Ice cubes, Plastic zip bags
Safety
Ensure bags are sealed tightly so water does not leak and cause slipping hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual diagram of solid -> liquid -> gas with heat arrows.
Time rationale
15 minutes initial setup and prediction, 15 minutes later for observation and discussion.

prac1-state-changes · 90 min · practice

Students create a 3-panel comic strip showing the journey of an ice cube. Panel 1: Solid ice. Panel 2: Heat is added (sun or stove), turning it to liquid. Panel 3: More heat is added, turning it to gas. They must write a sentence under each panel explaining the role of heat.

Mastery criterion
Students accurately depict the three states and correctly identify that adding heat causes the changes.
Materials
Comic strip templates, Crayons, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn panels where students only need to add the heat source and write the sentence.
Time rationale
15 minutes planning, 60 minutes drawing and writing, 15 minutes sharing comics.

prac2-state-changes · 90 min · practice

Using the water and sanitation context, students model how heat evaporates water. They place a small amount of water in a shallow dish under a warm desk lamp (representing the sun) and another dish in the shade. They observe and measure the water levels over the session, reasoning why the heated water 'disappears' into gas.

Mastery criterion
Students reason that the heat from the lamp caused the liquid water to turn into a gas.
Materials
Shallow dishes, Water, Desk lamps, Rulers
Safety
Ensure desk lamps are secure and cords are taped down. Do not let water touch the lamp bulb or plug.
Access and differentiation
Use colored water to make the water level easier to see.
Time rationale
20 minutes setup, 50 minutes observation and recording, 20 minutes concluding discussion.

assess-state-changes · 30 min · assessment

Read a short scenario: 'Maria leaves a bowl of ice cubes in the hot sun. What will happen to the ice, and what must she do if she wants to turn that water into a gas?' Write your prediction.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly predicts the state change and justifies it by referencing the addition or removal of heat.
Materials
Assessment paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw their prediction instead of writing it.
Time rationale
10 minutes reading, 20 minutes writing.

teach-light-transmission · 30 min · teach

Use a strong flashlight in a darkened room. Shine it through a clear glass cup, a piece of wax paper, and a thick book. Ask students to observe what happens to the light and the shadow on the wall behind each object. Introduce transparent, translucent, and opaque.

Mastery criterion
Students can identify which object makes a dark shadow and which lets light through.
Materials
Flashlight, Clear glass cup, Wax paper, Thick book
Safety
Do not shine the flashlight directly into anyone's eyes.
Access and differentiation
Use highly contrasting objects (very clear vs very dark) for clear visual distinction.
Time rationale
20 minutes demonstration, 10 minutes vocabulary discussion.

prac1-light-transmission · 90 min · practice

Students create a shadow puppet theater. They are given black cardboard (opaque) and colored tissue paper (translucent). They must design a puppet that has both a solid shadow body and glowing colored eyes/features. They test their puppets behind a sheet with a flashlight.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully combine opaque and translucent materials to create a functional shadow puppet.
Materials
Black cardboard, Colored tissue paper, Scissors, Glue, Popsicle sticks, Flashlights, White sheet
Safety
Monitor scissor use. Ensure flashlights are not shined in eyes.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-cut cardboard shapes for students with fine motor challenges.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 50 minutes building puppets, 25 minutes testing and performing.

ret1-light-transmission · 30 min · retrieval

Flashback activity: Provide a quick sorting tray with 5 small items (coin, clear plastic cup, wooden block, tissue paper, glass marble). Students must quickly sort them into 'Shadow Makers' and 'Light Passers' based on previous lessons.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly sort all 5 items based on memory of material properties.
Materials
Sorting trays, 5 small items per student
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Reduce the number of items to 3 for students who need a quicker task.
Time rationale
10 minutes sorting, 20 minutes discussing why they sorted them that way.

ret2-light-transmission · 30 min · retrieval

Read a scenario: 'We need to build a greenhouse to help plants grow. Should we use wood or clear plastic for the roof? Why?' Students write their answer recalling that plants need light to pass through.

Mastery criterion
Students select clear plastic and justify it by stating it lets light pass through.
Materials
Journals, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a picture of a greenhouse to help visualize the scenario.
Time rationale
10 minutes reading and thinking, 20 minutes writing.

assess-light-transmission · 30 min · assessment

Given a list of items (a thick book, a clear glass window, a wooden door, a piece of clear cellophane, a metal spoon), sort them into a table with two columns: 'Forms a dark shadow' and 'Lets light pass through'.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 materials as light-blocking (opaque) or light-passing (transparent/translucent).
Materials
Assessment worksheet, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide physical objects for the students to look at while taking the test.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent sorting.

teach-light-decomposition · 30 min · teach

In a dark room, shine a flashlight through a glass prism onto a white wall to create a rainbow. Discuss how the white light from the flashlight is actually made of many colors, and the prism breaks them apart.

Mastery criterion
Students can state that white light is made of many colors.
Materials
Flashlight, Glass prism, White wall or poster board
Safety
Do not shine the flashlight in eyes. Handle the glass prism carefully to avoid dropping and breaking it.
Access and differentiation
Use a larger prism or a water prism if the spectrum is hard to see.
Time rationale
15 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes discussion and drawing the observation.

prac1-light-decomposition · 90 min · practice

Students use old CDs and flashlights to explore light decomposition. They shine the light at the back of the CD at different angles to project rainbows onto paper. They trace the colors they see with crayons to document that white light breaks into multiple colors.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully project a spectrum and record the multiple colors that came from the white light.
Materials
Old CDs, Flashlights, White paper, Crayons
Safety
Ensure CDs do not have sharp cracked edges. No shining lights in eyes.
Access and differentiation
Tape the CD to the desk so students only have to manipulate the flashlight.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 50 minutes experimenting and tracing, 25 minutes sharing.

prac2-light-decomposition · 90 min · practice

Students create a 'rainbow spinner' (Newton's disc). They color a paper circle with the colors of the rainbow, attach it to a string, and spin it fast. They observe how the colors blend back together to look almost white, reinforcing that white light is a mix of colors.

Mastery criterion
Students observe and state that spinning the colors makes them look white, showing white light is made of colors.
Materials
Paper circles, Crayons, String, Scissors
Safety
Ensure students have enough space to spin their discs without hitting others.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-colored discs for students to just assemble and spin.
Time rationale
30 minutes coloring, 30 minutes assembling, 30 minutes spinning and discussing.

assess-light-decomposition · 30 min · assessment

Look at a diagram showing a flashlight shining white light into a glass triangle (prism) and a rainbow coming out the other side. Circle the sentence that best describes what is happening: A) The glass paints the light. B) The light is broken into many colors. C) The light is blocked.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies that white light can be broken down into multiple colors using a prism.
Materials
Assessment worksheet, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the options aloud.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work.

teach-subtractive-colors · 30 min · teach

Demonstrate mixing primary paint colors (cyan, magenta, yellow) in clear cups of water. Show how mixing two colors creates a new color (e.g., yellow and cyan make green). Explain that this is how printers make all the colors in a picture.

Mastery criterion
Students can state that mixing base colors creates new colors.
Materials
Clear cups, Water, Cyan, magenta, and yellow liquid watercolors or food coloring
Safety
Ensure students do not drink the colored water.
Access and differentiation
Use large, clear visuals of the color mixing process.
Time rationale
20 minutes demonstration, 10 minutes discussion about printers.

prac1-subtractive-colors · 90 min · practice

Students are given squares of cyan, magenta, and yellow cellophane. They hold them up to the light in pairs to see what new colors they can make by overlapping them. They record their findings by coloring in overlapping circles on a worksheet.

Mastery criterion
Students accurately record the new colors created by overlapping the subtractive primary colors.
Materials
Cyan, magenta, and yellow cellophane squares, Worksheets with overlapping circles, Crayons
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Tape the cellophane to cardboard frames to make them easier to hold.
Time rationale
15 minutes instruction, 50 minutes experimenting, 25 minutes recording.

prac2-subtractive-colors · 90 min · practice

Using the local crops context, students must paint a picture of a coffee plant (green leaves, red berries, brown stem) using ONLY cyan, magenta, and yellow paint. They must figure out how to mix the colors on their palette to get the colors they need for the plant.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully mix the primary colors to create green, red, and brown for their painting.
Materials
Paper, Paintbrushes, Cyan, magenta, and yellow paint, Palettes, Water cups
Safety
Use non-toxic, washable paints.
Access and differentiation
Provide a color mixing guide chart for students who struggle to remember combinations.
Time rationale
20 minutes planning and mixing practice, 50 minutes painting, 20 minutes cleanup and gallery walk.

assess-subtractive-colors · 30 min · assessment

Answer the following question in one sentence: How do inkjet printers make pictures with many different colors if they only use a few ink colors?

Mastery criterion
Student correctly describes that mixing a few base colors allows printers to create many different colors.
Materials
Assessment paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw a diagram of ink mixing instead of writing a sentence.
Time rationale
10 minutes reading the prompt, 20 minutes writing.

teach-color-safety · 30 min · teach

Show large images of local traffic signs (red stop sign) and school emergency exit signs (green). Discuss what the colors mean (red = stop/danger, green = safe/go). Ask students why it is important that everyone agrees on what these colors mean.

Mastery criterion
Students can identify red as danger/stop and green as safe/go.
Materials
Large printed images of safety signs
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide physical signs for students to hold.
Time rationale
15 minutes showing signs, 15 minutes discussion on importance.

prac1-color-safety · 90 min · practice

Students design a safety sign for a local public space (like a park or crosswalk). They must recall and use the correct color: red for a warning/danger sign or green for a safe area/route. They draw the sign and present it, stating the meaning of the color they used.

Mastery criterion
Students use the correct color for their sign's purpose and state its meaning during their presentation.
Materials
Paper, Markers, Crayons
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide templates of blank signs (circles, triangles, rectangles) to help start the drawing.
Time rationale
15 minutes brainstorming, 45 minutes drawing, 30 minutes presentations.

prac2-color-safety · 90 min · practice

Using the seismic risk context, students take a walk around the school to identify evacuation routes and safe zones. They return to the classroom and create a map of the room, using green markers to draw the safe evacuation path and red markers to mark dangerous areas (like heavy bookshelves).

Mastery criterion
Students correctly apply green for safe routes and red for hazards on their map.
Materials
Clipboards, Paper, Red and green markers
Safety
Ensure students walk calmly during the school tour.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-drawn outline of the classroom map.
Time rationale
30 minutes school walk, 45 minutes mapping, 15 minutes sharing maps.

assess-color-safety · 30 min · assessment

Match the color of the sign to its meaning: 1. Red sign with white letters. 2. Green sign with white letters. A) Emergency/Safe route. B) Stop/Danger.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly matches safety colors to their general meanings in a school or community context.
Materials
Assessment worksheet, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the options aloud.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent matching.

prac3-energy-transformations · 90 min · practice

Students build a simple sequence using safe classroom objects (e.g., a toy car rolling down a ramp to hit a bell). They draw their sequence and label the energy transformations happening at each step (e.g., potential to kinetic, kinetic to sound).

Mastery criterion
Students successfully build a sequence and correctly label at least two energy transformations.
Materials
Toy cars, Cardboard ramps, Small bells, Dominoes, Paper, Markers
Safety
Ensure objects used are safe and do not pose a projectile hazard.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-built sequence for students to observe and label if they struggle with building.
Time rationale
30 minutes building, 30 minutes drawing and labeling, 30 minutes sharing with the class.

Limitations: The textbook simplifies energy transformation, omitting the formal concept of the conservation of energy, which is appropriate for 2nd grade but requires careful teacher phrasing to avoid creating misconceptions.; Color mixing in the text blends additive (light) and subtractive (pigment) models without a rigorous scientific distinction; teachers must guide activities carefully to avoid confusion.; Safety constraints strictly prevent direct experimentation with mains electricity; all electrical concepts must be taught using safe, low-voltage battery-operated devices, simulations, or observational data.

Earth movements

The unit begins by establishing the Earth's internal movement (rotation) and its immediate, observable consequence: the day and night cycle. Once students grasp rotation and how it affects time measurement (hours, time zones), the progression expands outward to Earth's external movement (revolution) around the Sun. This larger scale introduces the concept of a year and global seasons. Finally, the unit grounds these global concepts in the local context, focusing on El Salvador's specific dry and rainy seasons and the environmental impacts associated with them.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 4 planning weeks.

Earth's Rotation and Time Measurement

Understanding Earth's rotation is fundamental to grasping the day-night cycle and how humans measure time. This skill moves students from concrete observations of day and night to the abstract concept of a spinning spherical Earth, using models to bridge the gap.

identify the imaginary axis of Earth's rotation using a physical model
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a foam ball and a plastic straw, assemble a model of the Earth and identify the imaginary axis.
Expected response
The student inserts the straw through the poles of the ball and states that the straw represents the imaginary line called the axis.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student correctly inserts the axis and identifies it; fails if they cannot identify where the axis goes.
Mastery evidence
Student successfully builds a model using a sphere and a stick, identifying the stick as the axis.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think the Earth's axis is a physical pole sticking out of the planet.; Students might believe the Sun moves around the Earth to create day and night.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Earth rotates on an imaginary axis passing from pole to pole. · Source page 115 · paragraph p115-paragraph-3
demonstrate the day and night cycle using a light source and a globe
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth, show why it is daytime in one country and nighttime in another.
Expected response
The student shines the flashlight on one side of the globe, points out that the lit side is experiencing day, and the dark side is experiencing night, then rotates the globe to switch them.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student correctly identifies the lit area as day and the shadowed area as night while rotating the globe; fails if they move the flashlight around the globe instead.
Mastery evidence
Student uses a flashlight and a spinning globe to show how only one half of the Earth is illuminated at a time.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think the Sun turns off at night.; Students might believe the Earth stops spinning sometimes.
Local prerequisites
m-rot-axis
Scientific support
  • Earth's rotation on its axis every 24 hours causes day and night. · Source page 113 · paragraph p113-paragraph-5
predict the apparent position of the Sun in the sky based on Earth's West-to-East rotation
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Based on the fact that Earth rotates from West to East, predict where you will see the Sun in the morning and explain why using your globe model.
Expected response
The student predicts the Sun will be seen in the East in the morning, demonstrating with the globe that the eastern side of a location rotates into the light first.
Scoring rule
Passes if the prediction is East and justified by the direction of the globe's rotation; fails if the prediction is incorrect or lacks evidence from the model.
Mastery evidence
Student logically deduces that because Earth spins West to East, the Sun appears first in the East.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think the Sun physically travels across the sky from East to West.
Local prerequisites
m-rot-daynight
Scientific support
  • Earth rotates West to East, causing the Sun to appear in the East in the morning and West in the evening. · Source page 115 · paragraph p115-paragraph-5
compare the time of day in different global locations using a time zone map
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Look at a simplified time zone map. If it is 12:00 PM (noon) in El Salvador, determine if it is earlier or later in a country located far to the East, like Spain, and explain why.
Expected response
The student states it is later in Spain because Spain is to the East and rotated into the sunlight before El Salvador.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student correctly identifies that eastern locations are ahead in time and justifies it; fails if they state the time is the same everywhere or cannot explain.
Mastery evidence
Student identifies that different regions have different times because the Sun hits them at different moments during rotation.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe it is the exact same time everywhere on Earth simultaneously.
Local prerequisites
m-rot-daynight
Scientific support
  • Different parts of the Earth experience different times of day simultaneously due to rotation. · Source page 107 · paragraph p107-paragraph-8

Earth's Revolution and Seasonal Changes

This skill expands the spatial scale from Earth's internal rotation to its orbit around the Sun. It connects the abstract concept of revolution to observable seasonal changes, specifically adapting the global four-season model to the local reality of El Salvador's dry and rainy seasons.

describe the Earth's revolution around the Sun and its 365-day duration
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
