Draw a diagram showing the Earth and the Sun. Draw an arrow to show the movement of revolution and label how long one complete movement takes.
Expected response
The student draws Earth in an orbital path around the Sun and labels the path with '365 days' or '1 year'.
Scoring rule
Passes if the drawing shows Earth circling the Sun and includes the correct duration; fails if it shows the Sun orbiting Earth or incorrect time.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately defines revolution as Earth's path around the Sun taking one year.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may confuse rotation (spinning) with revolution (orbiting).; Students might think a year is determined by the Moon.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Earth revolves around the Sun, completing one orbit in approximately 365 days. · Source page 118 · paragraph p118-paragraph-4
justify the addition of a day in a leap year using the exact duration of Earth's orbit
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain why we add an extra day to February every four years, using the exact time it takes Earth to orbit the Sun.
Expected response
The student states that Earth takes 365 days, 5 hours, and 49 minutes to orbit. After 4 years, those extra hours add up to almost 24 hours, which is one full day.
Scoring rule
Passes if the explanation connects the extra hours of the orbit to the accumulation of a new 24-hour day over four years; fails if the reasoning is missing.
Mastery evidence
Student explains that the extra hours from four orbits add up to one full day.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think leap years happen randomly.; Students might believe a normal year is exactly 365 days with no extra hours.
Local prerequisites
m-rev-orbit
Scientific support
  • A leap year occurs every 4 years because Earth's orbit takes 365 days, 5 hours, and 49 minutes. · Source page 127 · paragraph p127-paragraph-5
identify the dry and rainy seasons as the primary observable seasons in El Salvador
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Name the two main seasons that are most noticeable in El Salvador and describe one characteristic of each.
Expected response
The student names the dry season (época seca) and rainy season (época lluviosa), noting that one has little rain and the other has frequent rain.
Scoring rule
Passes if both local seasons are named correctly; fails if the student lists the standard four global seasons without distinguishing the local reality.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly names the dry and rainy seasons as the main climatic periods in their country.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe it snows in El Salvador during winter.; Students might think all countries experience the four seasons equally.
Local prerequisites
m-rev-orbit
Scientific support
  • In El Salvador, the four seasons are not felt with the same intensity; instead, the dry and rainy seasons are perceptible. · Source page 123 · paragraph p123-paragraph-7
relate extreme natural phenomena to the rainy season in vulnerable areas
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Read a short description of a landslide blocking a road. Decide during which season (dry or rainy) this is most likely to happen and justify your answer.
Expected response
The student decides it happens in the rainy season, justifying that intense rain softens the earth and causes rivers to rise rapidly or hillsides to collapse.
Scoring rule
Passes if the rainy season is selected and justified by the effects of intense water on the environment; fails if the wrong season is chosen or no logical link is made.
Mastery evidence
Student connects heavy rainfall during the rainy season to specific hazards like rapid river growth or landslides.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think floods happen randomly regardless of the season.; Students might believe all rain causes disasters.
Local prerequisites
m-rev-localseasons
Scientific support
  • Intense rain in vulnerable areas can cause natural disasters like floods and landslides. · Source page 125 · paragraph p125-paragraph-6
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

act-rot-axis-teach · 40 min · teach

Introduce the concept of Earth's axis by showing a foam ball and inserting a wooden skewer through its center. Explain that the skewer represents an imaginary line called the axis. Spin the ball to demonstrate rotation.

Mastery criterion
Students can point to the skewer and identify it as the model's axis, and describe that Earth spins on a similar imaginary line.
Materials
Foam balls, Wooden skewers, Markers
Safety
Ensure students handle wooden skewers carefully to avoid poking themselves or others. Skewers should have blunt ends if possible.
Access and differentiation
For students needing visual support, draw a bold line around the 'equator' of the foam ball so the spinning motion is more obvious.
Time rationale
10 minutes for introduction, 15 minutes for the teacher demonstration, and 15 minutes for guided student observation and Q&A.

act-rot-axis-prac1 · 40 min · practice

Students work in pairs to construct their own Earth models using a foam ball and a skewer. They must demonstrate the spinning motion to their partner and explain what the skewer represents.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully assemble the model and spin it in place rather than moving it in a circle.
Materials
Foam balls, Wooden skewers
Safety
Monitor the use of skewers closely. Students must remain seated while assembling and spinning their models.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-pierced foam balls for students who lack the fine motor strength to push the skewer through.
Time rationale
10 minutes for material distribution and instructions, 20 minutes for model construction and peer demonstration, 10 minutes for cleanup and review.

act-rot-axis-prac2 · 30 min · practice

Students are given various spherical objects (a plastic ball, a crumpled paper ball, a clay sphere) and must identify where the imaginary axis would be by drawing a line or placing a sticker on the 'poles'.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify opposite ends of the spheres as the poles where the imaginary axis would pass through.
Materials
Plastic balls, Paper, Clay, Stickers
Safety
Standard classroom safety. Ensure clay is not ingested.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use a physical stick to temporarily mark the axis before placing stickers if they struggle with the abstract concept.
Time rationale
10 minutes to explain the task, 15 minutes for hands-on identification with different objects, 5 minutes to share results.

act-rot-axis-prac3 · 40 min · practice

Students compare a spinning top to their Earth model. They spin the top on their desks and draw a diagram showing the imaginary axis of the top compared to the Earth model.

Mastery criterion
Students draw a vertical or slightly tilted line through the center of both the top and the Earth model in their diagrams.
Materials
Spinning tops, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Ensure tops are spun on flat surfaces and not thrown.
Access and differentiation
Provide a template with outlines of a top and Earth for students to draw the axis line on.
Time rationale
10 minutes for spinning tops, 20 minutes for drawing diagrams, 10 minutes for class discussion comparing the two.

act-rot-axis-assess · 30 min · assessment

Given a foam ball and a wooden skewer, assemble a model of the Earth and demonstrate its rotation, pointing out the imaginary axis to the teacher.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly inserts the axis and spins the model in place, stating the skewer is the imaginary axis.
Materials
Foam balls, Wooden skewers
Safety
Monitor skewer use during the assessment.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal explanation in place of physical assembly if a student has motor skill limitations.
Time rationale
5 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for individual assessments (rotating through students), 5 minutes for wrap-up.

act-rot-daynight-teach · 45 min · teach

Darken the room and use a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth. Shine the light on one side of the globe, explaining that the lit side is day and the dark side is night. Slowly rotate the globe to show the cycle.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally identify which side of the globe is experiencing day and which is experiencing night during the demonstration.
Materials
Flashlight, Globe
Safety
Ensure the room is not completely pitch black to prevent tripping. Do not shine the flashlight directly into students' eyes.
Access and differentiation
Place a bright sticker on El Salvador on the globe so students can easily track when their country moves from day to night.
Time rationale
10 minutes for room setup and introduction, 20 minutes for the demonstration and explanation, 15 minutes for student questions and guided observation.

act-rot-daynight-prac1 · 40 min · practice

In pairs, students use a small ball on a stick and a small flashlight. One student holds the 'Sun' steady while the other rotates the 'Earth', observing how the light hits the surface.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly rotate the ball in place while keeping the light source stationary, identifying day and night areas.
Materials
Small balls on sticks, Small flashlights
Safety
Instruct students not to shine flashlights in eyes.
Access and differentiation
Provide a stand for the flashlight if a student has difficulty holding it steady.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions and grouping, 20 minutes for hands-on practice, 10 minutes for role-swapping and cleanup.

act-rot-daynight-prac2 · 40 min · practice

Students are given a worksheet with a drawing of the Sun and the Earth. They must color the side of the Earth facing the Sun yellow (day) and the side facing away black or dark blue (night).

Mastery criterion
The half of the Earth facing the light source is colored brightly, and the opposite half is colored darkly.
Materials
Worksheets, Crayons or colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-shaded gradient on the Earth for students who need help understanding where the light stops.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instruction, 20 minutes for coloring and labeling, 10 minutes for peer review.

act-rot-daynight-assess · 40 min · assessment

Using a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth, show why it is daytime in one country and nighttime in another by rotating the globe.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies the lit area as day and the shadowed area as night while rotating the globe, keeping the flashlight still.
Materials
Flashlight, Globe
Safety
Do not shine flashlight in eyes.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to point to the areas while the teacher rotates the globe if they cannot manage both objects.
Time rationale
10 minutes for setup, 25 minutes for individual assessments, 5 minutes for wrap-up.

act-rot-daynight-ret1 · 20 min · retrieval

Teacher holds up a ball half-painted white and half-painted black. Teacher asks the class to point to the side experiencing 'day' and the side experiencing 'night'.

Mastery criterion
Students immediately and correctly identify the white side as day and the black side as night.
Materials
Half-painted ball (white/black)
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use tactile markers (smooth vs rough) on the ball for visually impaired students.
Time rationale
5 minutes for introduction, 10 minutes for rapid-fire questioning, 5 minutes for summary.

act-rot-daynight-ret2 · 20 min · retrieval

Students complete a quick matching card game where they match images of daytime activities with a picture of a sunlit globe, and nighttime activities with a shadowed globe.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly sort all activity cards to the corresponding day or night globe image.
Materials
Sorting cards with images
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use larger cards with high-contrast images.
Time rationale
5 minutes to distribute cards, 10 minutes for the sorting activity, 5 minutes to check answers.

act-rot-sunpath-teach · 40 min · teach

Explain that Earth rotates from West to East. Use a globe and a stationary light source to show how a specific point on the globe enters the light from the East first, making the Sun appear to rise in the East.

Mastery criterion
Students can state that the Sun appears in the East in the morning because of the direction Earth spins.
Materials
Globe, Stationary light source, Sticker
Safety
Do not shine light in eyes.
Access and differentiation
Place a small figure on the globe so students can visualize the perspective of a person standing on Earth.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explanation, 15 minutes for demonstration, 10 minutes for guided questions.

act-rot-sunpath-prac1 · 40 min · practice

Students use a small block (representing a building) on a piece of paper. Using a flashlight moving in an arc (to simulate the apparent motion caused by rotation), they trace the shadow of the block in the 'morning' and 'evening'.

Mastery criterion
Students draw long shadows on opposite sides of the block for morning and evening.
Materials
Small blocks, Paper, Pencils, Flashlights
Safety
Strictly enforce that students must not look at the real Sun. This activity uses flashlights only.
Access and differentiation
Guide the flashlight for students who struggle to create the arc motion smoothly.
Time rationale
10 minutes for setup and safety reminder, 20 minutes for shadow tracing, 10 minutes for discussion.

act-rot-sunpath-prac2 · 30 min · practice

Students are given a simple map with East and West labeled. They must draw a Sun on the side where it would appear in the morning and write a one-sentence reason based on Earth's rotation.

Mastery criterion
The Sun is drawn on the East side, and the sentence mentions Earth spinning West to East.
Materials
Worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters for the reasoning portion.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instruction, 15 minutes for drawing and writing, 5 minutes for review.

act-rot-sunpath-prac3 · 40 min · practice

Students stand in a circle around a central lamp (Sun). They slowly rotate their bodies to the left (West to East) and note which shoulder (East) sees the light first.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify that their left side (representing East) enters the light before their face.
Materials
Central lamp (no shade)
Safety
Ensure the lamp cord is taped down to prevent tripping. Lamp bulb should not be too hot.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to sit in swivel chairs if standing and rotating is difficult.
Time rationale
10 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for the physical simulation, 10 minutes for debriefing.

act-rot-sunpath-assess · 30 min · assessment

Based on the fact that Earth rotates from West to East, predict where you will see the Sun in the morning and explain why using your globe model.

Mastery criterion
Prediction is East, justified by demonstrating that the eastern side of a location rotates into the light first on the globe.
Materials
Globe, Flashlight
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use the block and shadow model to explain if they prefer it over the globe.
Time rationale
5 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for individual assessments, 5 minutes for wrap-up.

act-rot-timezones-teach · 45 min · teach

Introduce the concept of time zones. Place a sticker on El Salvador and one on Spain on a globe. Shine a light and rotate the globe, showing that Spain enters the light before El Salvador, meaning their day starts earlier.

Mastery criterion
Students can state that different places have different times because the Sun hits them at different moments.
Materials
Globe, Flashlight, Stickers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use highly contrasting stickers (e.g., neon colors) for visibility.
Time rationale
15 minutes for introduction, 20 minutes for the globe demonstration, 10 minutes for questions.

act-rot-timezones-prac1 · 40 min · practice

Students work in pairs with a globe. One points to El Salvador, the other to a country far to the East (like Japan). They rotate the globe into a light source and determine who eats breakfast first.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify that the country to the East experiences morning (and breakfast) first.
Materials
Globes, Flashlights
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Pre-mark the two countries on the globes for students who struggle with geography.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for pair work, 10 minutes for class discussion.

act-rot-timezones-prac2 · 40 min · practice

Students look at a simplified, color-coded time zone map. They answer questions like: 'If it is noon in the red zone, is it morning or afternoon in the blue zone to the East?'

Mastery criterion
Students correctly deduce that zones to the East are later in the day.
Materials
Simplified time zone maps, Worksheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use maps with only 3 or 4 distinct zones to reduce visual clutter.
Time rationale
10 minutes to explain the map, 20 minutes for worksheet completion, 10 minutes for review.

act-rot-timezones-prac3 · 40 min · practice

Students are given a scenario where they must call a relative in Europe. They must decide if they should call during their own morning or evening to ensure the relative is awake, justifying their choice based on rotation.

Mastery criterion
Students choose morning, reasoning that Europe is ahead in time and evening there would be too late.
Materials
Scenario cards, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual timeline showing El Salvador time vs Europe time side-by-side.
Time rationale
10 minutes for scenario reading, 20 minutes for writing the decision and justification, 10 minutes for sharing.

act-rot-timezones-assess · 40 min · assessment

Look at a simplified time zone map. If it is 12:00 PM (noon) in El Salvador, determine if it is earlier or later in a country located far to the East, like Spain.

Mastery criterion
Student states it is later in Spain because it is to the East and rotated into the sunlight before El Salvador.
Materials
Simplified time zone map
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the assessment prompt aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
10 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for independent assessment, 10 minutes for collection and transition.

act-rev-orbit-teach · 40 min · teach

Explain Earth's revolution around the Sun. Place a large yellow ball (Sun) in the center of the room. Walk a smaller globe around the Sun in a large circle, explaining this path is the orbit and takes 365 days (1 year).

Mastery criterion
Students can define revolution as Earth's path around the Sun and state it takes one year or 365 days.
Materials
Large yellow ball, Globe
Safety
Ensure the walking path is clear of tripping hazards.
Access and differentiation
Have students count out loud or clap to represent the passing of days as the globe moves to emphasize the length of time.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explanation, 15 minutes for the physical demonstration, 10 minutes for questions.

act-rev-orbit-prac1 · 40 min · practice

Students create a floor model of the orbit. One student stands in the center as the Sun. Another student holds a globe and walks the orbital path, ensuring they also spin the globe (rotation) while walking (revolution).

Mastery criterion
Students successfully demonstrate both rotation and revolution simultaneously without confusing the two.
Materials
Globes
Safety
Ensure students walk slowly to avoid dizziness or collisions.
Access and differentiation
If doing both motions is too complex, have the student just focus on walking the orbital path first.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for group practice, 10 minutes for debriefing.

act-rev-orbit-prac2 · 30 min · practice

Students use clay to make a small Sun and a small Earth. They place them on a piece of paper and draw the orbital path with a marker, labeling it '365 days'.

Mastery criterion
The model shows the Earth on a drawn circular/elliptical path around the central Sun, correctly labeled.
Materials
Clay, Paper, Markers
Safety
Ensure clay is not ingested.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn orbital paths for students who need spatial guidance.
Time rationale
10 minutes for material distribution, 15 minutes for modeling and drawing, 5 minutes for cleanup.

act-rev-orbit-assess · 30 min · assessment

Draw a diagram showing the Earth and the Sun. Draw an arrow to show the movement of revolution and label how long one complete movement takes.

Mastery criterion
Drawing shows Earth circling the Sun, with an arrow indicating the path, labeled '365 days' or '1 year'.
Materials
Paper, Pencils, Crayons
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to verbally state the time if they struggle with writing numbers.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for drawing, 5 minutes for collection.

act-rev-orbit-ret1 · 20 min · retrieval

Quick whiteboard activity: Teacher says 'Show me the path of revolution'. Students quickly draw the Sun, Earth, and the orbital path on their mini whiteboards and hold them up.

Mastery criterion
Students draw a circle or ellipse around a central point representing the Sun.
Materials
Mini whiteboards, Dry erase markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide whiteboards with a dot in the center to help anchor the drawing.
Time rationale
5 minutes for distribution, 10 minutes for drawing and holding up, 5 minutes for feedback.

act-rev-orbit-ret2 · 20 min · retrieval

True or False game. Teacher reads statements like 'Earth's orbit takes 1 day' or 'Revolution is when Earth goes around the Sun'. Students stand up for True and sit down for False.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify true statements about revolution and its 365-day duration.
Materials
Safety
Ensure chairs are pushed in to avoid tripping when standing up and sitting down.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use thumbs up/thumbs down instead of standing/sitting.
Time rationale
5 minutes for rules, 10 minutes for the game, 5 minutes for summary.

act-rev-leapyear-teach · 40 min · teach

Explain that Earth's orbit actually takes 365 days and about 6 hours. Use 4 blocks, each representing 6 hours. Show that over 4 years, these blocks add up to 24 hours, creating one extra day (leap year).

Mastery criterion
Students can state that the extra 6 hours each year add up to a full 24-hour day every four years.
Materials
Blocks or linking cubes
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use a clock face to visually add the 6 hours (quarter of a day) four times to make a full circle.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explanation, 15 minutes for the block demonstration, 10 minutes for questions.

act-rev-leapyear-prac1 · 40 min · practice

Students work in groups with linking cubes. They build four towers of 365 cubes (represented by a large block) and add one small cube (6 hours) to each. They then combine the 4 small cubes to make a 'new day' block.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully group the four 6-hour cubes to demonstrate the creation of the extra day.
Materials
Linking cubes, Large blocks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Pre-count the cubes for students to save time and focus on the concept.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for group modeling, 10 minutes for discussion.

act-rev-leapyear-prac2 · 30 min · practice

Students look at calendars for February over a 5-year period. They must identify the leap year and write a sentence explaining why that specific year has 29 days based on Earth's orbit.

Mastery criterion
Students identify the year with 29 days and write that it happens because the extra hours from the orbit added up.
Materials
Printed calendars, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the 28th and 29th days on the calendars to draw attention to the change.
Time rationale
10 minutes for calendar observation, 15 minutes for writing, 5 minutes for review.

act-rev-leapyear-prac3 · 40 min · practice

Students are given a hypothetical scenario: 'What if Earth's orbit took exactly 365 days with no extra hours?' They must write or draw what would happen to our calendar (no leap years).

Students sort a series of image cards (umbrellas, dry cracked earth, green lush trees, dusty roads) into two columns: Dry Season and Rainy Season.

Standard classroom safety.

act-rev-localseasons-prac2 · 30 min · practice

Using the local crops context, students analyze when farmers might plant maize versus when they harvest coffee, linking these activities to the need for water (rainy season) or dry conditions.

Mastery criterion

Materials
Information sheets on maize and coffee
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation

Time rationale
10 minutes for reading, 15 minutes for analysis and matching, 5 minutes for sharing.

act-rev-localseasons-prac3 · 40 min · practice

Students create a two-panel drawing. On one side, they draw their school during the dry season; on the other, during the rainy season, including appropriate clothing for themselves in the drawing.

Mastery criterion
Drawings accurately reflect the environmental conditions and appropriate clothing for both local seasons.
Materials
Paper, Crayons or colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation

10 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for drawing, 10 minutes for sharing with a partner.

act-rev-localseasons-assess · 20 min · assessment

Name the two main seasons that are most noticeable in El Salvador and write one characteristic of each.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly names the dry and rainy seasons and provides a valid characteristic (e.g., lots of rain, dry dusty ground).

Assessment worksheet
Safety
Standard classroom safety.

Allow verbal responses for students who struggle with writing.

5 minutes for instructions, 10 minutes for writing, 5 minutes for collection.

act-rev-hazards-teach · 40 min · teach

Discuss how intense rain during the rainy season can cause natural hazards like floods and landslides. Show a simple physical model: pour water over a mound of loose soil in a tray to demonstrate a landslide.

Mastery criterion
Students can explain that too much water makes the soil loose, leading to landslides during the rainy season.
Materials
Tray, Loose soil, Watering can
Safety
Ensure water and soil are kept in the tray to prevent slipping hazards on the floor.
Access and differentiation
Use a sponge to show how the ground absorbs water until it is full, making the concept more concrete.
Time rationale
15 minutes for discussion, 15 minutes for the physical demonstration, 10 minutes for questions.

act-rev-hazards-prac1 · 40 min · practice

Students are given pictures of different landscapes (a steep hill with no trees, a flat paved area, a riverbank). They must decide which area is most vulnerable to a landslide during the rainy season and justify why.

Mastery criterion
Students select the steep hill and justify it by stating the rain will wash the loose soil down the slope.
Materials
Landscape pictures, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence frames: 'I think the [landscape] is vulnerable because...'

10 minutes for picture observation, 20 minutes for reasoning and writing, 10 minutes for class discussion.

act-rev-hazards-prac2 · 40 min · practice

Using the water and sanitation context, students read a short scenario about a town's drinking water pipes breaking due to a river overflowing. They must infer which season this occurred in and explain their reasoning.

Mastery criterion

Materials
Scenario worksheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.

10 minutes for reading, 20 minutes for writing the inference and justification, 10 minutes for review.

act-rev-hazards-assess · 30 min · assessment

Read a short description of a landslide blocking a road. Decide during which season (dry or rainy) this is most likely to happen and justify your answer.

Mastery criterion

Assessment worksheet

Standard classroom safety.

5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for independent work, 5 minutes for collection.

Limitations: The physical models of Earth and Sun are vastly out of scale regarding both size and distance, which must be explicitly communicated to avoid spatial misconceptions.; The explanation of seasons is simplified; the role of Earth's axial tilt in causing the four global seasons is introduced but may be highly abstract for second graders, hence the focus on local dry/rainy seasons.; Safety protocols strictly prohibit looking directly at the Sun to track its apparent movement; all solar tracking must be done via shadows or models.; The distinction between weather and climate is simplified for this grade level.

Living organisms

Students enter Grade 2 with basic recognition of common plants and animals. In this unit, they formalize their understanding by following a logical sequence: first exploring plant structures, needs, and uses, then transitioning to animal traits, diets, habitats, and conservation. Finally, they study fungi as a distinct group, comparing their biology and uses to plants and animals. In Grade 3, students should revisit these classifications to explore complex food webs and specific ecosystem interactions.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 6 planning weeks.

Plant and Fungi Characteristics and Uses

Understanding the basic biology of plants and fungi, including their nutritional needs and uses, builds a foundation for ecological awareness and recognizing the importance of these organisms in daily human life.

identify basic plant parts (roots, stem, leaves)
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Label a simple diagram of a plant with roots, stem, and leaves.
Expected response
Roots at the bottom, stem in the middle, leaves on the sides.
Scoring rule
Passes if all three parts are correctly labeled.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly points to and names the roots, stem, and leaves of a plant.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants are just leaves and flowers.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Students can identify and point out the parts of a plant. · Source page 17 · paragraph p17-paragraph-11
identify plant roots and stems as structures for water and mineral transport
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a diagram of a plant, label the parts responsible for absorbing and transporting water.
Expected response
The student labels the roots for absorption and the stem for transport.
Scoring rule
Passes if both roots and stem are correctly identified with their respective transport functions.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the root as the part that absorbs water and the stem as the part that transports it.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants drink water through their leaves.; Roots only serve to hold the plant in the ground.
Local prerequisites
plant-part-identification
Scientific support
  • Plants absorb water and minerals through their roots. · Source page 21 · paragraph p21-paragraph-14
describe the basic outputs of photosynthesis as food and oxygen
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Explain what a plant produces when it makes its own food using sunlight.
Expected response
The plant produces its own food and releases oxygen into the air.
Scoring rule
Passes if the response includes both food production and oxygen release.
Mastery evidence
Student states that plants make their own food and release oxygen.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants get their food from the soil.; Plants breathe in oxygen just like humans do all the time.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Plants produce oxygen when making their own food. · Source page 26 · paragraph p26-paragraph-9
categorize plants based on their utility to humans such as medicinal, food, or raw materials
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Sort a list of plants (e.g., corn, mint, cotton) into categories: food, medicine, and raw materials.
Expected response
Corn is food, mint is medicine, cotton is raw material.
Scoring rule
Passes if all provided plants are placed in a plausible utility category.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly sorts given plants into categories of human use.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All plants are used for food.; Medicines only come from chemicals in a lab, not plants.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Plants are used to satisfy human needs. · Source page 27 · paragraph p27-paragraph-10
distinguish fungi from plants based on their heterotrophic nutrition through absorption
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Decide whether a mushroom is a plant or not, and justify your answer using evidence about how it gets its food.
Expected response
A mushroom is not a plant because it cannot make its own food; it absorbs food from decomposing matter.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student states fungi are not plants and cites their heterotrophic/absorptive feeding method.
Mastery evidence
Student justifies why a mushroom is not a plant by referencing its heterotrophic nature and absorptive feeding method.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Fungi are a type of plant.; Fungi make their own food using sunlight.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Fungi are heterotrophs that obtain food by absorption, often by decomposing matter. · Source page 57 · paragraph p57-paragraph-14
describe the utility and potential harm of fungi to humans
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
List one way fungi can be helpful to humans and one way they can be harmful.
Expected response
Helpful: food/medicine. Harmful: can cause diseases/poisonous.
Scoring rule
Passes if one valid utility and one valid harm are listed.
Mastery evidence
Student can name at least one useful application of fungi and one potential harm.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All fungi are poisonous.; Fungi have no use for humans.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Fungi have utility for humanity but can also cause diseases. · Source page 60 · paragraph p60-paragraph-8

Animal Characteristics, Classification, and Conservation

Classifying animals by physical traits, diet, and relationship to humans helps students organize biological diversity and fosters a sense of responsibility towards wildlife conservation.

match animal physical traits to their method of locomotion in specific habitats
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given pictures of unfamiliar animals (e.g., an axolotl, an ostrich, a centipede), infer their primary movement method and circle the body part that allows it.
Expected response
Axolotl matches swim (circles tail/gills/fins), ostrich matches walk/run (circles legs), centipede matches walk (circles legs).
Scoring rule
Passes if all animals are matched correctly with the corresponding body part identified.
Mastery evidence
Student pairs animals with their primary mode of movement based on observable body parts.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All animals with legs can walk on land.; Animals choose how to move regardless of their body parts.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Some animal body parts are adapted to allow them to move. · Source page 39 · paragraph p39-paragraph-8
classify animals into dietary groups based on their food sources
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Read the descriptions of what a cow, a lion, and a bear eat. Classify each as a herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore.
Expected response
Cow is a herbivore, lion is a carnivore, bear is an omnivore.
Scoring rule
Passes if all three animals are correctly classified according to their described diets.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly categorizes animals as herbivores, carnivores, or omnivores based on a description of their diet.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All animals eat meat.; Animals that eat plants are called omnivores.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Animals are grouped into herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores based on their diet. · Source page 67 · paragraph p67-paragraph-10
differentiate domestic animals from wild animals based on human care and habitat
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Decide whether a monkey found in the forest should be taken home as a pet. Justify your answer using evidence about wild animals.
Expected response
No, the monkey is a wild animal and should not be a pet because it needs to live freely in nature and could get sick or depressed.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student decides against keeping the wild animal and provides a justification based on its natural habitat or well-being.
Mastery evidence
Student justifies why a specific animal is wild and should not be kept as a pet.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Any animal can be a pet if you catch it.; Wild animals rely on humans for food.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Wild animals should not be kept as pets. · Source page 48 · paragraph p48-paragraph-9
propose actions to protect wild animals from human threats
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Read a scenario where a visitor wants to feed a wild animal. Write a verbal response explaining why they shouldn't and what they should do instead.
Expected response
You shouldn't feed them because human food can make them sick and they need to find their own food. You should just observe them quietly.
Scoring rule
Passes if the proposed rule directly mitigates a human threat to wild animals.
Mastery evidence
Student suggests a realistic action to protect local wildlife.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Protecting animals only means putting them in cages.; Human actions do not affect wild animals.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • It is important for humanity to protect animals. · Source page 50 · paragraph p50-paragraph-8

Pre-prepared celery in colored water, Diagrams of plants

10 minutes for introduction, 15 minutes for observing the celery, 15 minutes for explaining the diagram.

Limitations: The curriculum simplifies fungal nutrition and plant capillary action for Grade 2 comprehension.; The distinction between wild and feral animals is introduced but may require careful teacher mediation to avoid confusion.; Safety constraints limit direct observation of certain wild animals and fungi, relying on secondary sources and controlled experiments.

Technical objects and care of organisms

Students enter with basic observational skills of their environment. In this unit, they progress to actively manipulating materials to build functional objects (measuring tools, bridges, energy devices) and structures that support living organisms. The next grade will revisit these concepts with more formal standard units of measurement, complex forces, and deeper ecological interdependence.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 2. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Designing and testing physical systems

Students explore physical properties, forces, and energy by building and testing their own measuring instruments, rigid structures, and energy-transforming devices.

measure the circumference of spherical objects using string and a ruler
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide students with a spherical fruit, a piece of string, and a ruler. Ask them to determine the distance around the thickest part of the fruit and record the measurement in centimeters.
Expected response
The student wraps the string around the fruit, marks or cuts it at the exact meeting point, lays it flat against the ruler, and records the correct length in cm.
Scoring rule
Pass if the recorded measurement is within 1 cm of the actual circumference and the string method was used correctly; fail if the string is not aligned with the ruler or the measurement is off by more than 1 cm.
Mastery evidence
Students can accurately wrap a string around a spherical object, mark the intersection, and measure the resulting string segment with a ruler.
Diagnostic hypotheses
String must be stretched extremely tight to get an accurate measurement, which distorts the actual circumference.; The length of the string is unrelated to the size of the object once removed from it.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Indirect measurement of circumference can be done using string and a ruler. · Source page 78 · paragraph p78-paragraph-23
construct a two-pan balance to compare the mass of small objects using a non-standard unit
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Ask students to build a balance using a clothes hanger, string, and two cups, and then determine how many marbles equal the mass of a small eraser.
Expected response
The student builds a balanced hanger, places the eraser in one cup, and adds marbles one by one to the other cup until the hanger is level again, recording the number of marbles.
Scoring rule
Pass if the balance is constructed symmetrically and the student correctly identifies the equilibrium point; fail if the cups are tied at unequal lengths or the student stops adding marbles before equilibrium.
Mastery evidence
Students can assemble a functional balance using a hanger and cups, and use it to find how many non-standard units (e.g., marbles) equal the mass of a given object.
Diagnostic hypotheses
A balance measures weight in standard units only, not relative mass using arbitrary objects.; If the pans are at different heights initially, the balance will still work correctly without calibration.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • A balance compares an unknown mass with known masses until equilibrium is reached. · Source page 79 · paragraph p79-paragraph-5
evaluate the load capacity of flat versus folded paper bridges using coins
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Have students place coins one by one on the center of a flat paper bridge until it collapses, then repeat the process with a fan-folded paper bridge, and state which design is stronger and why based on their data.
Expected response
The student records that the folded bridge holds significantly more coins and justifies that the folds make the paper stiffer and better able to support the load.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly records the data for both bridges and justifies the strength of the folded bridge using the coin count evidence; fail if the conclusion contradicts the data or lacks justification.
Mastery evidence
Students can test and compare the strength of different paper bridge designs, concluding that folding the paper increases its structural resistance.
Diagnostic hypotheses
A flat piece of paper is always weaker than a folded one, regardless of how it is supported.; Adding weight to the edges of the bridge is the same as adding it to the center.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Folding paper into a fan shape changes its structural resistance. · Source page 89 · paragraph p89-paragraph-16
identify the transformation of electrical energy to thermal energy in a simple closed circuit
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Show students a safe, teacher-led demonstration of a battery connected to a pencil lead with a small piece of wax on it. Ask them to observe the wax melting and name the type of energy transformation occurring.
Expected response
The student states that electrical energy from the battery is changing into thermal energy (heat) in the pencil lead, evidenced by the melting wax.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly identifies both electrical and thermal energy in the transformation; fail if they identify the wrong types of energy (e.g., mechanical or light).
Mastery evidence
Students can observe a simple circuit and state that the electrical energy from the battery is transforming into thermal energy (heat) in the conductor.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Batteries only produce electricity for light or movement, not heat.; The wire gets hot because it is absorbing heat from the surrounding air.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Electrical current flowing through a conductor can increase its temperature. · Source page 93 · paragraph p93-paragraph-11
construct a mechanical device that uses twisted rubber bands to generate motion
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Instruct students to build a rolling device using CDs, a cardboard tube, and rubber bands, twist the rubber band mechanism, and release it on the floor to demonstrate motion.
Expected response
The student successfully builds the device, twists the rubber band to store energy, and releases it, causing the device to roll across the floor.
Scoring rule
Pass if the device is assembled correctly and demonstrates motion upon release; fail if the rubber band is not secured properly to store energy or the device cannot roll.
Mastery evidence
Students can assemble a device using rubber bands and a tube, twist the bands to store elastic potential energy, and release it to observe mechanical motion.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Rubber bands create energy out of nothing when they spin.; The more you twist a rubber band, the less energy it has because it gets smaller.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Elastic potential energy is stored when an elastic body is deformed by force. · Source page 119 · paragraph p119-paragraph-3

Designing structures for the care of living organisms

Students differentiate between domestic and wild organisms and apply their understanding of basic needs to build supportive structures like insect hotels and terrariums.

classify animals as domestic or wild based on their reliance on human care
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide a list of animals (e.g., dog, chicken, iguana, bee). Ask the student to sort them into 'domestic' and 'wild' categories and provide one reason for their sorting.
Expected response
The student correctly sorts the animals (dog/chicken as domestic, iguana/bee as wild) and states that domestic animals live with and depend on humans, while wild animals live in nature independently.
Scoring rule
Pass if all animals are correctly categorized and the reasoning references human dependence vs. independent survival; fail if categories are mixed up or the reasoning is based solely on animal size or danger.
Mastery evidence
Students can categorize a list of animals into domestic or wild, explaining that domestic animals rely on humans while wild animals survive on their own instincts.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All animals that live outside are wild, even farm animals.; Wild animals are always dangerous and aggressive towards humans.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Domestic animals are those accustomed to living with humans. · Source page 120 · paragraph p120-paragraph-11
construct a shelter for wild insects using recycled cylindrical containers and hollow tubes
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Ask students to create an insect shelter by cutting paper straws or bamboo sticks to the length of a recycled can and packing them tightly inside.
Expected response
The student cuts the tubes to the correct length and packs them securely into the container so they do not fall out, creating multiple small hollow spaces.
Scoring rule
Pass if the tubes are cut to size and packed tightly enough to stay in place; fail if the tubes are loose, stick out too far, or do not provide hollow spaces.
Mastery evidence
Students can assemble an insect hotel by cutting and packing hollow tubes tightly into a recycled cylindrical container to provide shelter for wild insects.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Insects do not need shelter because they live in the dirt.; Any box can be an insect hotel, regardless of what is inside it.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Hollow tubes placed inside a container can serve as a shelter structure for insects. · Source page 103 · paragraph p103-paragraph-9
justify the placement of an insect hotel in a low-traffic area to avoid disturbing the animals
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Ask students to choose a location in the schoolyard or at home to place their insect hotel and write one sentence explaining why that location is best for the insects.
Expected response
The student selects a quiet, low-traffic area (like a garden corner or under a tree) and explains that insects need a place where they won't be bothered by people walking by.
Scoring rule
Pass if the chosen location is low-traffic and the justification explicitly mentions avoiding disturbance to the insects; fail if the location is high-traffic or the justification is based on human convenience rather than animal needs.
Mastery evidence
Students can select an appropriate location for their constructed insect hotel and defend their choice based on the behavioral needs of the insects (e.g., avoiding human disturbance).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Insect hotels should be placed where humans can touch and play with them constantly.; Insects prefer loud, busy areas because there is more food there.
Local prerequisites
build-insect-hotel
Scientific support
  • Insect shelters should be placed in quiet areas because insects are disturbed by human traffic. · Source page 105 · paragraph p105-paragraph-17
construct a miniature garden (terrarium) providing soil and space for a small plant
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide students with a clear plastic container, small rocks, soil, and a small plant. Ask them to assemble a terrarium that supports the plant's growth.
Expected response
The student places a layer of rocks at the bottom for drainage, adds soil, carefully plants the specimen, and adds decorative elements if desired.
Scoring rule
Pass if the terrarium has distinct layers (rocks then soil) and the plant is securely placed in the soil; fail if the layers are missing or the plant's roots are exposed.
Mastery evidence
Students can layer rocks and soil in a clear container to plant a small specimen, creating a functional miniature garden.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants in a terrarium do not need water or light because they are inside a container.; A terrarium is just a pot; the arrangement of rocks and soil does not matter.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • A terrarium is a miniature garden that can house plants and decorative elements. · Source page 113 · paragraph p113-paragraph-6
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

ms1-teach · 30 min · teach

Demonstrate how to wrap a string around a spherical fruit, mark the meeting point, and measure the string segment with a ruler. Have students replicate the process with an orange.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully wrap the string, mark it accurately, and read the measurement on the ruler within 1 cm of accuracy.
Materials
Oranges, String, Rulers, Markers
Safety
Ensure students do not wrap string around fingers or necks.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-marked string for students who struggle with holding the string and marking simultaneously.
Time rationale
10 minutes for demonstration, 15 minutes for guided student practice, 5 minutes for recording results.

ms1-prac1 · 60 min · practice

Students work in pairs to measure the circumference of various classroom objects (globes, balls, thick markers) using string and rulers, recording their data in a table.

Mastery criterion

Materials
String, Rulers, Assorted spherical and cylindrical objects, Data tables
Safety
Clear floor space to prevent tripping while gathering objects.
Access and differentiation
Offer objects of vastly different sizes to challenge advanced students to manage longer string segments.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup, 40 minutes of active measuring and recording, 10 minutes sharing results.

ms1-prac2 · 60 min · practice

Students measure the circumference of different local crops (like small pumpkins or large maize cobs) using string and rulers to determine which crop has the largest girth.

Mastery criterion

Materials
String, Rulers, Maize cobs, Small pumpkins or gourds
Safety
Ensure crops are clean and free of sharp edges or pests.
Access and differentiation
Provide magnifying glasses for students who need help reading the small millimeter lines on the ruler.
Time rationale
15 minutes introduction and material distribution, 35 minutes measuring, 10 minutes conclusion.

ms1-assess · 30 min · assessment

Provide students with a spherical fruit, a piece of string, and a ruler. Ask them to determine the distance around the thickest part of the fruit and record the measurement in centimeters.

Mastery criterion
The recorded measurement is within 1 cm of the actual circumference and the string method is used correctly.
Materials
Spherical fruits, String, Rulers, Recording sheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety; no eating the fruits.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal reporting of the measurement for students with writing difficulties.

5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes individual assessment, 5 minutes collection.

ms2-teach · 45 min · teach

Guide students step-by-step to build a balance using a clothes hanger, string, and two cups. Demonstrate how to find equilibrium using identical marbles.

Clothes hangers, String, Paper cups, Marbles

15 minutes demonstration, 20 minutes guided construction, 10 minutes testing equilibrium.

ms2-prac1 · 60 min · practice

Students use their constructed balances to compare the mass of various classroom items (erasers, pencils, glue sticks) against a standard non-standard unit (marbles), recording the equivalents.

10 minutes setup, 40 minutes weighing and recording, 10 minutes cleanup.

Students use their balances to determine the mass of hypothetical household items purchased with a hypothetical dollar budget, using coins as the non-standard mass unit.

Pair students so one can stabilize the hanger while the other adds coins.

ms2-assess · 45 min · assessment

Ask students to build a balance using a clothes hanger, string, and two cups, and then determine how many marbles equal the mass of a small eraser.

Mastery criterion
The balance is constructed symmetrically and the student correctly identifies the equilibrium point with the correct number of marbles.

5 minutes setup, 20 minutes measuring, 5 minutes cleanup.

Have students place coins one by one on the center of a flat paper bridge until it collapses, then repeat with a fan-folded bridge, and state which design is stronger and why based on data.

Mastery criterion
The student records that the folded bridge holds significantly more coins and justifies that the folds make the paper stiffer.

Perform a teacher-led demonstration connecting a battery to a pencil lead with a small piece of wax on it. Have students observe the wax melting as a visual indicator of heat and identify the energy change.

Battery-operated fan, Flashlight, Graphite circuit setup, Worksheets

Safety
No physical appliances used, only paper diagrams.

ms4-assess · 30 min · assessment

Show students a safe, teacher-led demonstration of a battery connected to a pencil lead with a small piece of wax on it. Ask them to observe the wax melting and name the type of energy transformation occurring.

Mastery criterion
The student states that electrical energy from the battery is changing into thermal energy (heat) in the pencil lead, using the melting wax as evidence.

Battery, Wires, Pencil lead, Small piece of wax, Assessment slips
Safety
