Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use highly familiar local animals for examples.
Time rationale
10 minutes explanation, 10 minutes guided group sorting.

ms6-prac1 · 45 min · practice

Students work in small groups to sort a deck of 20 animal cards into 'domestic' and 'wild' piles, discussing their reasoning for each.

Mastery criterion
Groups correctly sort at least 18 out of 20 cards based on human reliance.
Materials
Decks of animal cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide cards with both pictures and words for early readers.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 30 minutes group sorting, 10 minutes class review.

ms6-prac2 · 45 min · practice

Students draw one domestic animal and one wild animal found in El Salvador (e.g., iguanas, tacuacines, or various birds), writing one sentence for each explaining how it gets its food.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the food source (human provided vs. independently found).
Materials
Drawing paper, Crayons or markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters: 'The [animal] gets food from...'
Time rationale
10 minutes context discussion, 25 minutes drawing and writing, 10 minutes sharing.

ms6-assess · 20 min · assessment

Provide a list of animals (e.g., dog, chicken, iguana, bee). Ask the student to sort them into 'domestic' and 'wild' categories and provide one reason for their sorting.

Mastery criterion
All animals are correctly categorized and the reasoning references human dependence vs. independent survival.
Materials
Assessment worksheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the list of animals aloud for students who need reading support.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 15 minutes independent work.

ms6-ret1 · 20 min · retrieval

Play a quick game where the teacher calls out an animal name and students move to the left side of the room for 'domestic' and the right side for 'wild'.

Mastery criterion
Students consistently move to the correct side of the room based on the animal's classification.
Materials
List of animals
Safety
Ensure clear pathways to prevent tripping while moving.
Access and differentiation
Allow students with mobility issues to point left or right instead of walking.
Time rationale
5 minutes rules explanation, 15 minutes active gameplay.

ms6-ret2 · 20 min · retrieval

Students complete a quick matching worksheet connecting pictures of animals to either a 'house/farm' icon (domestic) or a 'forest/jungle' icon (wild).

Mastery criterion
Students correctly draw lines matching the animals to their appropriate habitat icons.
Materials
Matching worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use high-contrast images for visually impaired students.
Time rationale
5 minutes distribution, 10 minutes completion, 5 minutes self-correction.

ms7-teach · 40 min · teach

Demonstrate how to measure and cut paper straws to the length of a recycled can, and pack them tightly inside to create hollow spaces for insects.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully cut straws to the correct length and pack them so they do not fall out when the can is inverted.
Materials
Recycled clean cans, Paper straws or bamboo sticks, Scissors
Safety
Ensure cans have no sharp edges. Monitor scissor use.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-cut straws for students with severe fine motor limitations.
Time rationale
10 minutes demonstration, 25 minutes guided construction, 5 minutes inversion test.

ms7-prac1 · 60 min · practice

Students build a second insect hotel using a different container shape (e.g., a square milk carton) and natural materials like hollow twigs, ensuring tight packing.

Mastery criterion
Students adapt their packing technique to the new shape, ensuring materials are secure and provide hollow spaces.
Materials
Clean milk cartons (tops cut off), Hollow twigs, Scissors or small pruning shears
Safety
Teacher handles pruning shears if twigs are thick. Ensure cartons are washed.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to work in pairs to hold the carton while packing.
Time rationale
15 minutes material selection, 35 minutes construction, 10 minutes cleanup.

ms7-prac2 · 60 min · practice

Students decorate the outside of their insect hotels using natural materials (leaves, bark) glued to the exterior to help it blend into a natural environment.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully attach natural camouflage to the exterior without blocking the hollow tube entrances.
Materials
Constructed insect hotels, Leaves, bark, small stones, Non-toxic glue
Safety
Ensure glue is non-toxic and students wash hands after handling natural materials.
Access and differentiation
Provide double-sided tape as an alternative to liquid glue for less mess.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 40 minutes decorating, 10 minutes drying and cleanup.

ms7-assess · 40 min · assessment

Ask students to create an insect shelter by cutting paper straws to the length of a recycled can and packing them tightly inside.

Mastery criterion
The tubes are cut to size and packed tightly enough to stay in place when the can is tilted.
Materials
Recycled cans, Paper straws, Scissors
Safety
Check cans for sharp edges before assessment.
Access and differentiation
Mark a line on the straws for students who struggle with measuring the length.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 30 minutes independent construction, 5 minutes teacher checking.

ms8-teach · 20 min · teach

Discuss why insects need quiet places. Show pictures of a busy playground and a quiet garden corner, asking students to infer which is better for an insect hotel and why.

Mastery criterion
Students verbally identify the quiet garden and reason that insects avoid human disturbance.
Materials
Pictures of high-traffic and low-traffic areas
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use clear, contrasting images to make the difference in traffic obvious.
Time rationale
10 minutes discussion of insect needs, 10 minutes scenario analysis.

ms8-prac1 · 45 min · practice

Take students on a walk around the schoolyard. Have them select a specific spot for their insect hotel and draw a map marking the location, noting why it is low-traffic.

Mastery criterion
Students select a viable low-traffic spot and note its quiet nature on their map.
Materials
Clipboards, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Keep students within designated safe boundaries of the schoolyard.
Access and differentiation
Pair students to collaborate on one map if drawing is challenging.
Time rationale
25 minutes schoolyard walk and selection, 15 minutes mapping, 5 minutes return.

ms8-prac2 · 45 min · practice

Students review a map of a hypothetical park and mark an 'X' where they would place an insect hotel, writing a justification based on avoiding human paths.

Mastery criterion
Students place the 'X' away from paths and playgrounds, justifying it with the need to avoid disturbance.
Materials
Printed park maps, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the human paths in a bright color to help visual processing.
Time rationale
10 minutes map reading instruction, 25 minutes independent work, 10 minutes sharing.

ms8-assess · 20 min · assessment

Ask students to choose a location in the schoolyard or at home to place their insect hotel and write one sentence explaining why that location is best for the insects.

Mastery criterion
The chosen location is low-traffic and the justification explicitly mentions avoiding disturbance to the insects.
Materials
Assessment sheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal justification for students who cannot write a full sentence.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 15 minutes writing.

ms9-teach · 45 min · teach

Demonstrate how to layer small rocks for drainage, add soil, and carefully plant a small specimen in a clear plastic container to create a terrarium.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully replicate the layers (rocks, then soil) and plant their specimen securely.
Materials
Clear plastic containers, Small rocks, Potting soil, Small plants, Spoons (for digging)
Safety
Ensure students wash hands thoroughly after handling soil. Do not use soil with chemical fertilizers.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-measured cups of rocks and soil to simplify the layering process.
Time rationale
15 minutes demonstration, 25 minutes guided construction, 5 minutes cleanup.

ms9-prac1 · 60 min · practice

Students add decorative elements (small plastic animals, colored stones) to their terrariums and lightly water the soil, observing how the water drains into the rock layer.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully water the plant without flooding it, observing the drainage layer's function.
Materials
Constructed terrariums, Decorative stones/toys, Small watering cans or spray bottles
Safety
Wipe up any spilled water immediately to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Use spray bottles instead of watering cans to prevent accidental overwatering by students with poor motor control.
Time rationale
15 minutes decoration, 20 minutes watering and observation, 25 minutes drawing their terrarium.

ms9-prac2 · 60 min · practice

Students build a second, smaller terrarium using a plastic cup, focusing on planting a seed (like maize) instead of a live plant, ensuring the soil depth is appropriate.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly layer rocks and soil, and plant the seed at the correct depth.
Materials
Clear plastic cups, Small rocks, Soil, Maize seeds
Safety
Ensure seeds are not treated with toxic fungicides (use food-grade or untreated seeds). Wash hands after.
Access and differentiation
Mark a line on the cup to show how much soil is needed.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 40 minutes construction and planting, 10 minutes cleanup.

ms9-assess · 45 min · assessment

Provide students with a clear plastic container, small rocks, soil, and a small plant. Ask them to assemble a terrarium that supports the plant's growth.

Mastery criterion
The terrarium has distinct layers (rocks then soil) and the plant is securely placed in the soil with roots covered.
Materials
Clear plastic containers, Small rocks, Soil, Small plants
Safety
Wash hands after handling soil.
Access and differentiation
Provide verbal prompts for the order of layers if a student freezes.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 30 minutes independent construction, 10 minutes cleanup and teacher evaluation.

Limitations: The Joule effect experiment with pencil lead poses a minor burn risk and requires strict adult supervision; alternative thermal indicators could be used.; The distinction between domestic and wild animals is simplified for 2nd grade and does not cover feral or captive-bred wild animals.; Testing paper bridges with coins assumes uniform coin weight, which may vary slightly in practice.

Environment and health

Students enter second grade with basic recognition of their body parts and immediate surroundings. This unit builds on that foundation by introducing the relationship between human actions, environmental hazards, and personal health. The prerequisites within the unit ensure students first identify risks before formulating emergency plans, and recognize poor hygiene before justifying specific preventative measures. In future grades, students will revisit these concepts to explore complex ecosystems, the biological mechanisms of diseases, and global climate change.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Environmental Hazards and Human Impact

Students learn to identify risks in their environment, distinguish between natural hazards and human-made disasters, and understand how human actions like deforestation and waste generation impact the earth.

identify common accident risks in daily environments
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide an image of a messy classroom and ask the student to circle three things that could cause an accident.
Expected response
The student circles a spilled liquid, a toy on the floor, and an open cabinet door.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correctly identified risk, up to 3 points.
Mastery evidence
Student can point out at least three potential accident risks in a given illustration of a home or school.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Accidents only happen outside the home.; Accidents are always caused by natural events.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Accidents can happen anywhere and at any time. · Source page 133 · paragraph p133-paragraph-5
differentiate the probability of harm from a hazard
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Ask the student to select the correct definition of 'risk' from a multiple-choice list.
Expected response
Risk is the probability of suffering harmful consequences from a hazard.
Scoring rule
Pass/Fail based on selecting the correct definition.
Mastery evidence
Student can match the definition of risk to the probability of suffering harmful consequences.
Diagnostic hypotheses
A hazard and a risk are exactly the same thing.; Risks cannot be reduced by human action.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Risk is defined as the probability of suffering harmful consequences. · Source page 170 · paragraph p170-paragraph-4
formulate safe actions to take during an emergency
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Present a novel scenario (e.g., a flood warning while at home) and ask the student to describe or draw the safe action to take in that specific context.
Expected response
The student describes moving to higher ground or following their family's emergency plan.
Scoring rule
Pass if the action is a recognized safety measure for the given scenario.
Mastery evidence
Student can state one safe action to take during a specific emergency like an earthquake or flood.
Diagnostic hypotheses
During an earthquake, you should run outside as fast as possible.; Emergency plans are only for adults to know.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • It is crucial for students to know what to do in an emergency. · Source page 142 · paragraph p142-paragraph-13
analyze the effect of plant cover on soil erosion using a physical model
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Show the student a picture of a steep, bare dirt hill and a picture of a hill covered in grass and trees. Ask them to predict which hill will lose more soil during a heavy rainstorm and explain why.
Expected response
The bare dirt hill will lose more soil because it lacks plant roots to hold the soil in place.
Scoring rule
1 point for selecting the correct hill, 1 point for a logical justification involving plants holding the soil.
Mastery evidence
Student can predict which environment will lose more soil based on the presence or absence of vegetation.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants make soil dirtier.; Water washes away the same amount of soil regardless of what is on top of it.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Water running through soil with plant cover comes out clear. · Source page 147 · paragraph p147-paragraph-12
classify household waste into biodegradable and non-biodegradable
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide a list of items (apple core, plastic bottle, glass jar, banana peel) and ask the student to sort them into two bins: biodegradable and non-biodegradable.
Expected response
Apple core and banana peel in biodegradable; plastic bottle and glass jar in non-biodegradable.
Scoring rule
Pass if all items are sorted correctly.
Mastery evidence
Student can sort a list of common waste items into biodegradable and non-biodegradable categories.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All trash disappears into the ground quickly.; Plastic is made by nature and decomposes easily.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Non-biodegradable waste usually comes from human-made products. · Source page 151 · paragraph p151-paragraph-7

Personal Health and Food Safety

Students explore how personal hygiene, food safety, and medical prevention (vaccines) work together to protect the human body from diseases.

identify actions that represent poor personal hygiene
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Read a list of actions and ask the student to mark the ones that can cause illness due to poor hygiene.
Expected response
The student marks 'Not washing hands after going to the bathroom'.
Scoring rule
Pass if the correct poor hygiene practices are identified.
Mastery evidence
Student can identify actions that fail to maintain personal hygiene.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Washing hands is only necessary when they look visibly dirty.; Hygiene only involves taking a shower.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Not washing hands after using the bathroom is a cause of illness. · Source page 154 · paragraph p154-paragraph-10
describe the role of vaccines in creating body defenses
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Ask the student to explain in one sentence what a vaccine does inside the body.
Expected response
A vaccine helps the body make defenses to fight off sickness.
Scoring rule
Pass if the response mentions creating defenses or protecting against future illness.
Mastery evidence
Student can state that vaccines help the body create defenses against diseases.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Vaccines are medicine that cures you when you are already sick.; Vaccines are only for babies.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Vaccines create defenses in the body. · Source page 160 · paragraph p160-paragraph-7
recognize the need to prepare or cook certain foods before consumption
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Show images of raw chicken, an apple, and raw beans. Ask the student which ones must be cooked before eating.
Expected response
Raw chicken and raw beans.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly identifies the foods that require cooking.
Mastery evidence
Student can identify foods that require preparation or cooking before eating.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All foods can be eaten exactly as they are found in nature.; Cooking is only for making food taste better, not for safety.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Some foods require preparation and cannot be eaten raw. · Source page 165 · paragraph p165-paragraph-4
justify the necessity of handwashing to remove invisible disease-causing organisms
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Show the student two petri dishes from a handwashing experiment (one with bacterial growth from unwashed hands, one clean from washed hands). Ask them to infer which dish was touched by unwashed hands and justify their answer.
Expected response
The dish with growth was touched by unwashed hands because invisible organisms were transferred to it.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student mentions invisible organisms, germs, or things we cannot see that cause illness.
Mastery evidence
Student can explain why we must wash hands even if they do not look dirty.
Diagnostic hypotheses
If hands look clean, they have no germs.; Water alone is enough to remove all disease-causing organisms.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Handwashing removes invisible organisms that cause diseases. · Source page 160 · paragraph p160-paragraph-7
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-accident-risks · 40 min · teach

Display a large poster of a messy classroom. Guide students to point out objects that could cause someone to trip, fall, or get hurt. Discuss why each identified object is a risk.

Mastery criterion
Student points to and names at least three objects that pose a risk in the poster.
Materials
Large poster of a messy classroom, Pointer stick
Safety
Ensure the actual classroom floor is clear of tripping hazards during the activity.
Access and differentiation
Provide a smaller, high-contrast version of the poster for students with visual impairments.
Time rationale
10 minutes for introduction, 20 minutes for guided identification and discussion, 10 minutes for summarizing.

practice-accident-risks-1 · 40 min · practice

Students sort illustrated cards into two piles: safe situations and unsafe situations (risks).

Mastery criterion
Student correctly sorts all unsafe situation cards into the risk pile.
Materials
Sets of illustrated scenario cards
Safety
Use laminated cards with rounded corners to prevent paper cuts.
Access and differentiation
Pair students to discuss the cards before sorting.
Time rationale
10 minutes explaining the sorting rules, 20 minutes of sorting, 10 minutes reviewing answers as a class.

practice-accident-risks-2 · 40 min · practice

Students view photographs of different rooms in a house and circle the accident risks using a dry-erase marker.

Mastery criterion
Student circles at least three distinct risks across the provided photographs.
Materials
Laminated photographs of house rooms, Dry-erase markers, Erasers
Safety
Ensure dry-erase markers are non-toxic and used in a ventilated area.
Access and differentiation
Provide photographs with fewer objects for students who get easily overwhelmed by visual clutter.
Time rationale
10 minutes distributing materials and explaining, 20 minutes of independent work, 10 minutes of peer review.

practice-accident-risks-3 · 40 min · practice

Students draw a picture of a playground and intentionally include three accident risks, then trade with a partner to find them.

Mastery criterion
Student successfully draws three recognizable risks and identifies the risks in their partner's drawing.
Materials
Blank paper, Crayons or colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety with drawing materials.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to verbally describe the risks they want to draw if fine motor skills are developing.
Time rationale
20 minutes for drawing, 10 minutes for trading and finding, 10 minutes for class sharing.

assess-accident-risks · 30 min · assessment

Provide a worksheet with an image of a messy kitchen. Students must independently circle three things that could cause an accident.

Mastery criterion
Student circles a spilled liquid, an open cabinet door, and a tripping hazard.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read instructions aloud and allow pointing instead of circling for students needing motor support.
Time rationale
5 minutes setup, 20 minutes for independent completion, 5 minutes collection.

teach-hazard-risk · 40 min · teach

Bridge the concept of physical risks (like tripping, learned previously) to natural events. Use wooden blocks to build a tall, unstable tower representing a local hazard (like the San Salvador volcano or a local fault line). Place a toy figure far away, then close to it. Explain that the hazard is the event itself, but the risk (probability of harm) changes based on where the figure stands.

Mastery criterion
Student can verbally state that the tower is the hazard and standing close is the risk.
Materials
Wooden blocks, Small toy figure
Safety
Ensure the block tower is small enough not to cause injury when it falls.
Access and differentiation
Use larger, brightly colored blocks for better visibility.
Time rationale
15 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes guided discussion, 10 minutes checking for understanding.

practice-hazard-risk-1 · 40 min · practice

Students match cards showing a natural event (hazard) with cards showing the probability of harm (risk) based on human location.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly pairs the hazard cards with their corresponding risk definition cards.
Materials
Matching card sets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide fewer pairs to match for students who need a modified workload.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 20 minutes matching activity, 10 minutes review.

practice-hazard-risk-2 · 40 min · practice

Read scenarios about local Salvadoran hazards (e.g., earthquakes on the San Salvador fault, heavy rains in vulnerable areas). Students hold up a red card if the scenario describes a hazard, and a yellow card if it describes a risk.

Mastery criterion
Student holds up the correct card for at least 4 out of 5 scenarios.
Materials
Red and yellow construction paper cards, Scenario script
Safety
Ensure students remain seated while holding up cards to avoid collisions.
Access and differentiation
Provide visual cues on the cards (e.g., a warning sign on red, a person on yellow).
Time rationale
10 minutes explaining the rules, 20 minutes reading scenarios and voting, 10 minutes discussing the answers.

assess-hazard-risk · 30 min · assessment

Students complete a multiple-choice question selecting the correct definition of 'risk' from three options.

Mastery criterion
Student selects the option defining risk as the probability of suffering harmful consequences.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the options aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup and reading instructions, 15 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.

retrieve-hazard-risk-1 · 20 min · retrieval

Quick recall game: The teacher says a word (either a hazard like 'rain' or a risk like 'flooded house'). Students stand up for hazard, sit down for risk.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies the difference through physical movement.
Materials
Safety
Ensure chairs are pushed in to prevent tripping when standing and sitting.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use hand signals instead of standing/sitting if mobility is an issue.
Time rationale
5 minutes explaining rules, 15 minutes playing the game.

retrieve-hazard-risk-2 · 20 min · retrieval

Exit ticket: Students write or dictate one sentence explaining what a risk is before leaving for recess.

Mastery criterion
Student's sentence includes the concept of probability of harm or getting hurt.
Materials
Small slips of paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal dictation to the teacher for students who struggle with writing.
Time rationale
5 minutes distributing paper, 10 minutes writing, 5 minutes collecting at the door.

teach-emergency-action · 45 min · teach

Demonstrate the 'Drop, Cover, and Hold on' technique for earthquakes. Explain each step clearly. Have students practice the motion step-by-step under their desks.

Mastery criterion
Student successfully demonstrates dropping, covering their head/neck, and holding onto a sturdy object.
Materials
Sturdy desks
Safety
Ensure desks are stable and floors are clear of sharp objects before students drop.
Access and differentiation
Provide alternative protective postures for students using wheelchairs.
Time rationale
15 minutes explanation and demonstration, 20 minutes guided practice, 10 minutes debrief.

practice-emergency-action-1 · 45 min · practice

Role-play activity: The teacher calls out 'Earthquake!' at random times during a 30-minute period. Students must immediately execute the safe action.

Mastery criterion
Student reacts promptly and correctly assumes the safe position without prompting.
Materials
Safety
Remind students not to run or push others when moving to take cover.
Access and differentiation
Give a visual warning (like flashing lights) slightly before the verbal cue for students with auditory processing delays.
Time rationale
10 minutes setting expectations, 30 minutes of embedded practice during another light activity, 5 minutes review.

practice-emergency-action-2 · 45 min · practice

Students create a simple three-panel comic strip showing a character feeling an earthquake, taking cover, and waiting safely.

Mastery criterion
Student's comic accurately depicts a recognized safety measure in the middle panel.
Materials
Comic strip templates, Pencils, Crayons
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn characters that students can cut and paste into the panels.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes drawing, 10 minutes sharing comics.

practice-emergency-action-3 · 45 min · practice

Students sequence a set of mixed-up picture cards showing the steps of an emergency evacuation plan for various hazards, including earthquakes, floods, and landslides.

Mastery criterion
Student places the evacuation steps in a logical, safe order for the given hazard.
Materials
Sets of sequence cards covering multiple hazards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Number the backs of the cards so students can self-check their sequence.
Time rationale
10 minutes explanation, 20 minutes sequencing, 15 minutes discussing why the order matters.

assess-emergency-action · 30 min · assessment

Present a novel scenario: a heavy rainstorm causes a flood warning near their home. Students draw or write one safe action they should take in this specific context.

Mastery criterion
Student draws or writes about a recognized safety measure for floods, such as moving to higher ground.
Materials
Blank paper, Pencils, Crayons
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal responses for students who cannot draw or write clearly.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.

teach-erosion-model · 60 min · teach

Relate the activity to local issues like landslides in Nejapa or sedimentation of the Lempa River. Set up three plastic bottle halves: one with bare soil, one with dead leaves, one with live plants. Pour equal amounts of water through each. Ask students to observe the runoff water color and infer why the plant bottle has clear water, protecting the 'hillside'.

Mastery criterion
Student states that the roots hold the soil, preventing it from washing away.
Materials
3 plastic bottle halves, Soil, Dead leaves, Small live plants with roots, Water, Clear collection cups
Safety
Ensure any cut plastic edges are taped to prevent scratches. Clean up water spills immediately to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Provide magnifying glasses for students to closely examine the roots holding the soil.
Time rationale
15 minutes setup and hypothesis, 20 minutes conducting the pour, 25 minutes discussion and reasoning.

practice-erosion-model-1 · 60 min · practice

Students repeat the erosion model experiment, but this time they tilt the bottles at a steeper angle to simulate a steep hill. They observe and discuss how the angle affects the amount of soil washed away.

Mastery criterion
Student infers that a steeper angle causes more soil to wash away, but plants still offer the best protection.
Materials
Erosion model bottles, Water, Clear cups, Blocks to prop up bottles
Safety
Wipe up any spilled water immediately.
Access and differentiation
Assign specific roles (pourer, observer, recorder) to ensure all students participate according to their strengths.
Time rationale
15 minutes setup, 25 minutes experimenting, 20 minutes comparing results with the flat model.

practice-erosion-model-2 · 60 min · practice

Students test the erosion model by pouring water very slowly (light rain) versus very quickly (heavy storm) into the bare soil bottle, comparing the runoff.

Mastery criterion
Student reasons that faster water flow carries more soil away.
Materials
Erosion model bottles (bare soil), Water, Clear cups, Watering can with a sprinkle spout, Cup for fast pouring
Safety
Conduct the activity outdoors or over a large plastic tarp to manage mud.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn observation charts for students to color in the darkness of the water.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 30 minutes conducting the two pours, 20 minutes reasoning discussion.

practice-erosion-model-3 · 60 min · practice

Students compare the erosion of regular garden soil versus sandy soil in the bare-soil model, observing which washes away faster.

Mastery criterion
Student observes and states which soil type resulted in dirtier runoff water.
Materials
Erosion model bottles, Garden soil, Sandy soil, Water, Clear cups
Safety
Ensure students wash hands thoroughly after handling soil.
Access and differentiation
Use highly contrasting soil colors (e.g., dark potting soil vs light sand) for clear visual results.
Time rationale
15 minutes preparing the new soils, 25 minutes testing, 20 minutes discussing findings.

assess-erosion-model · 40 min · assessment

Show the student a picture of a steep, bare dirt hill and a picture of a hill covered in grass and trees. Ask them to predict which hill will lose more soil during a heavy rainstorm and explain why using their knowledge of roots.

Mastery criterion
Student selects the bare dirt hill and provides a logical justification involving the lack of roots to hold the soil.
Materials
Pictures of a bare hill and a forested hill
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use gestures (like interlacing fingers) to explain how roots hold soil if they lack the vocabulary.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup, 25 minutes conducting individual verbal assessments, 5 minutes wrap-up.

teach-waste-types · 40 min · teach

Introduce the concepts of biodegradable (nature breaks it down) and non-biodegradable (nature cannot easily break it down). Show clean examples of each and sort them into two labeled bins as a class.

Mastery criterion
Student can correctly identify the bin for an apple core and a plastic bottle during the demonstration.
Materials
Clean apple core (or picture), Clean plastic bottle, Two labeled bins
Safety
Ensure all physical waste items are clean, sanitized, and free of sharp edges.
Access and differentiation
Use bins with distinct colors (e.g., green for biodegradable, black for non-biodegradable) and picture labels.
Time rationale
15 minutes explanation, 15 minutes guided sorting, 10 minutes review.

practice-waste-types-1 · 40 min · practice

Relay race: Students pick a picture card of a waste item from a pile and run to drop it in the correct biodegradable or non-biodegradable hoop.

Mastery criterion
Student places their assigned cards in the correct hoops.
Materials
Picture cards of waste items, Two hula hoops
Safety
Ensure the running path is clear of obstacles to prevent tripping.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to walk instead of run, or have the hoops brought to their desks.
Time rationale
10 minutes explaining rules, 20 minutes playing the relay, 10 minutes checking the hoops together.

practice-waste-types-2 · 40 min · practice

Students cut out pictures of various items from old magazines and paste them onto a T-chart labeled Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable.

Mastery criterion

Limitations: The curriculum simplifies the distinction between natural hazards and disasters, which may require teacher clarification to avoid confusion.; The biological mechanism of vaccines is highly abstracted for second graders and does not cover immune system specifics.; The soil erosion model uses plastic bottles and may not perfectly replicate large-scale geological processes, requiring human review to ensure students do not form misconceptions about scale.

Grade 3

Measurements and forces

The unit begins by establishing the necessity of standardized measurements and the correct selection of instruments based on the physical properties of objects. Once students can reliably measure and quantify physical properties, the focus shifts to how objects interact through forces. Students first identify basic pushes and pulls, then explore specific forces like friction, magnetism, and gravity. The unit culminates in understanding that forces can act simultaneously to either cause motion or maintain equilibrium, requiring students to synthesize their knowledge of individual forces into complex systems.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Measurement of physical properties using standard units and instruments

Students must transition from arbitrary comparisons to standardized measurements, understanding that the choice of instrument and unit depends on the magnitude and nature of the property being measured.

match standard units (cm, kg, L) to corresponding physical quantities of household items
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a list of 5 items (e.g., milk, cereal, pencil), match each to the correct unit of measurement (L, g, cm).
Expected response
Milk - L, Cereal - g, Pencil - cm.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct match. Pass requires 4 points.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly matches at least 4 out of 5 items to their appropriate measurement unit.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All numbers on packaging represent weight.; Liquids and solids are measured using the same units.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Everyday products have specific units for volume and mass. · Source page 10 · paragraph p10-paragraph-6
measure the length of small objects using a ruler in centimeters
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Use a ruler to measure the length of a sticky note and a pencil in centimeters.
Expected response
Sticky note is approximately 7 cm; pencil is approximately 15 cm (depending on actual objects provided).
Scoring rule
Measurement must be within +/- 0.5 cm of the actual length.
Mastery evidence
Student measures 2 objects accurately to the nearest centimeter.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Starting measurement from the edge of the ruler instead of the zero mark.; Mixing inches and centimeters.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Centimeters are the standard unit for length measurements in these activities. · Source page 11 · paragraph p11-paragraph-5
justify the selection of a measuring instrument based on the object's size or mass
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Choose whether to use a bathroom scale or a kitchen scale to measure a spoonful of salt, and explain why.
Expected response
Kitchen scale, because a spoonful of salt is too light to move the indicator on a bathroom scale.
Scoring rule
Must select kitchen scale AND state that the bathroom scale is not sensitive enough for small masses.
Mastery evidence
Student selects the correct instrument and provides a valid reason based on scale or precision.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Any scale can measure any mass accurately.; A ruler is always the best tool for measuring length, regardless of how small the object is.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Large scales cannot accurately measure very small masses like a spoonful of salt. · Source page 18 · paragraph p18-paragraph-7
evaluate the reliability of a measuring instrument based on its physical condition
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Look at a picture of a ruler with a broken end (missing the zero mark). Decide if it is reliable for measuring and explain why.
Expected response
It is not reliable because the starting point is missing, which will make the measurements incorrect.
Scoring rule
Must state it is unreliable AND link the physical damage to inaccurate readings.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies a damaged instrument as unreliable and explains why.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All instruments give correct readings regardless of damage.; Calibration is permanent.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • A reliable instrument is one that functions correctly and can be trusted for accurate measurements. · Source page 19 · paragraph p19-paragraph-6
identify thermometers as instruments for measuring temperature
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Identify which instrument is used to measure body temperature from a set of images.
Expected response
The clinical thermometer.
Scoring rule
Must select the thermometer and state it measures temperature.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies a thermometer and its purpose.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Thermometers measure heat, not temperature.; All thermometers look the same.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Thermometers are used to measure temperature in medical and everyday contexts. · Source page 15 · paragraph p15-paragraph-12

Analysis of forces, motion, and equilibrium in physical systems

Students need to recognize that forces are interactions that cause changes in motion or maintain equilibrium, moving beyond the intuitive idea that force is only a property of living things or heavy objects.

classify actions as pushes or pulls that initiate or stop motion
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a list of actions (e.g., kicking a ball, stopping a rolling ball, pressing a doorbell), classify each as a push or a pull.
Expected response
Kicking - push, stopping a rolling ball - push, pressing doorbell - push.
Scoring rule
Correct classification of the primary force direction for at least 4 actions.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly classifies 4 out of 5 actions as push or pull.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Forces are only needed to start motion, not to stop it.; Only humans can apply forces.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Forces are required not only to start movement but also to stop it. · Source page 21 · paragraph p21-paragraph-7
predict friction as a force that opposes motion in everyday scenarios
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Predict which surface (a smooth tile or a rough carpet) will stop a sliding toy car faster and explain why using the concept of friction.
Expected response
The rough carpet will stop the car faster because it applies more friction against the car's movement.
Scoring rule
Must correctly predict the rougher surface and explicitly name friction as the opposing force.
Mastery evidence
Student identifies friction as the opposing force in a given scenario.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Friction only happens on rough surfaces.; Friction helps things move faster.
Local prerequisites
identify-push-pull
Scientific support
  • Friction is a force that opposes motion. · Source page 23 · paragraph p23-paragraph-7
predict the relative amount of force required to move objects of different masses
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
If you have an empty box and a box full of books, predict which one requires more force to push across the floor and explain why.
Expected response
The box full of books requires more force because it has more mass.
Scoring rule
Must select the heavier box AND explicitly link the required force to the object's mass.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly predicts which object requires more force and justifies it using mass.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Larger objects always require more force, regardless of mass (confusing volume with mass).; The same force moves all objects equally.
Local prerequisites
identify-push-pull
Scientific support
  • The amount of force required to move an object is proportional to its mass. · Source page 24 · paragraph p24-paragraph-5
draw the pattern of a magnetic field using iron filings
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
After placing a paper over a magnet and sprinkling iron filings, draw the pattern you observe.
Expected response
A drawing showing lines of filings connecting the two ends (poles) of the magnet, with the highest concentration at the poles.
Scoring rule
Drawing must show distinct poles where filings cluster.
Mastery evidence
Student draws a pattern showing concentration of filings at the poles.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Magnets attract all metals.; The magnetic force is only at the very ends of the magnet.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Iron filings can be sprinkled over a magnet to observe its effects. · Source page 26 · paragraph p26-paragraph-6
describe gravity as a constant downward pull exerted by the Earth
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
What force causes a dropped pencil to fall to the ground instead of floating?
Expected response
Gravity pulls the pencil down toward the Earth.
Scoring rule
Must identify gravity and state its direction (downward/towards Earth).
Mastery evidence
Student describes gravity as the force pulling objects toward the Earth.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Gravity only affects heavy objects.; Gravity stops working when things are falling.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The text introduces gravity as the intuitive downward pull from our planet. · Source page 27 · paragraph p27-paragraph-4
balance a physical system to demonstrate forces in equilibrium
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Balance a ruler on a fulcrum. Explain how the forces create rotational equilibrium (torque).
Expected response
The forces on both sides create equal and opposite torque, resulting in rotational equilibrium.
Scoring rule
Must state that forces are acting AND that they cancel each other out (or are equal/balanced).
Mastery evidence
Student successfully balances an object and identifies that forces are still present.
Diagnostic hypotheses
If an object is not moving, there are no forces acting on it.; Equilibrium only happens when objects are perfectly symmetrical.
Local prerequisites
explain-gravity
Scientific support
  • Equilibrium can involve rotational forces known as torque. · Source page 33 · paragraph p33-paragraph-6
describe projectile motion as a combination of forward and vertical movement
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Launch a small object with a catapult and draw its path, describing the directions it moves.
Expected response
A drawing of a curved path, noting it moves forward and up/down.
Scoring rule
Must show a curved trajectory and mention both forward and vertical motion.
Mastery evidence
Student describes the curved path of a launched object.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Objects only move in straight lines.; Forward motion and falling are completely separate.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Projectile motion involves moving both up/down and forward/backward. · Source page 34 · paragraph p34-paragraph-3
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-units · 45 min · teach

Introduce standard units (g, L, cm) by displaying common household items and explicitly teaching which unit corresponds to mass, volume, and length.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly states the unit used for mass, volume, and length when prompted.
Materials
Empty milk carton, Cereal box, Pencil, Whiteboard
Safety
Ensure all containers are empty and clean to prevent spills or allergic reactions.
Access and differentiation
Provide physical labels with unit symbols for students to hold and place next to objects, supporting visual and tactile learners without changing the cognitive task.
Time rationale
10 mins introduction, 20 mins direct instruction with examples, 15 mins guided group identification.

practice-units · 45 min · practice

Students sort a variety of everyday items into stations based on whether they are measured in grams, pounds (libras), liters, or centimeters, discussing local market contexts.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly sorts at least 8 out of 10 items into the correct measurement station.
Materials
Various clean household items (bottles, boxes, string, bags of beans or rice), Sorting bins labeled g, libras, L, cm
Safety
Use plastic containers instead of glass to prevent breakage.
Access and differentiation
Include items with highly distinct properties (e.g., very long string vs. heavy bag of sand) for students needing clearer physical cues.
Time rationale
10 mins setup and instructions, 25 mins active sorting, 10 mins class review and correction.

assess-units · 45 min · assessment

Students complete a matching task where they draw lines connecting 5 drawn items (milk, cereal, pencil, water bottle, rope) to their correct unit (L, g, cm).

Mastery criterion
Student correctly matches at least 4 out of 5 items to their appropriate measurement unit.
Materials
Printed assessment sheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety; ensure adequate lighting and seating.
Access and differentiation
Read the names of the items aloud for students with reading difficulties, maintaining the requirement to match the unit independently.
Time rationale
10 mins instruction, 25 mins independent work, 10 mins collection and transition.

teach-measure-cm · 45 min · teach

Demonstrate how to align the zero mark of a ruler with the edge of an object and read the measurement in centimeters.

Mastery criterion
Student can verbally explain the importance of starting at the zero mark.
Materials
Large demonstration ruler, Giant sticky note, Standard rulers for students
Safety
Ensure rulers have rounded edges to prevent poking injuries.
Access and differentiation
Use rulers with high-contrast markings for students with visual impairments.

15 mins demonstration, 20 mins guided practice measuring a single object together, 10 mins Q&A.

practice-measure-cm · 60 min · practice

Students work in pairs to measure and record the length of 5 specific classroom objects (e.g., desk edge, book, pencil) in centimeters.

Mastery criterion
Student records measurements that are within +/- 0.5 cm of the actual length.
Materials
Rulers, Recording sheets, Classroom objects
Safety
Clear aisles so students can move safely around the classroom while measuring.
Access and differentiation
Provide objects with flat, rigid edges to make alignment easier for students developing fine motor skills.

10 mins instruction, 40 mins active measuring in pairs, 10 mins sharing results.

assess-measure-cm · 45 min · assessment

Students independently measure the length of a provided sticky note and a pencil using a ruler, recording their answers in centimeters.

Mastery criterion
Student measures both objects accurately to the nearest centimeter (+/- 0.5 cm).
Materials
Sticky notes, Pencils, Rulers, Assessment sheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.

Provide a ruler with a physical stop at the zero mark for students with severe motor tremors, maintaining the cognitive task of reading the number.

Students are given cards with pictures of various items (e.g., a single coffee bean, a sack of basic grains like beans or rice) and must sort them by which scale is appropriate, justifying their choice.

assess-select-instrument · 60 min · assessment

Students write a short paragraph choosing whether to use a bathroom scale or a kitchen scale to measure a spoonful of salt, explaining their reasoning.

Assessment sheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.

Students look at a picture of a ruler missing the zero mark and write whether it is reliable for measuring, explaining why.

Standard classroom safety.

retrieve-reliability-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Quick recall: Show an image of a kitchen scale with a missing weighing pan. Ask students to write down if it is reliable and why.

Projector or printed image, Paper, Pencils

Standard classroom safety.

practice-friction · 60 min · practice

assess-friction · 60 min · assessment

Limitations: The concept of mass versus weight is simplified for Grade 3; gravity is treated as a downward pull without distinguishing between mass and weight mathematically.; Friction is introduced conceptually without calculating coefficients.; Magnetic fields are observed in 2D using iron filings, which may limit the understanding of 3D field lines.; Equilibrium is explored through simple balancing tasks, avoiding formal vector addition.

Earth interactions

Students enter Grade 3 with a basic understanding of observable material properties (states of matter) and general landscape features from Grades 1 and 2. In this unit, they transition to understanding dynamic changes (physical/chemical, reversible/irreversible) and the concept of mixtures. This physical science foundation is then applied to Earth systems, where students learn that rocks undergo continuous transformation (rock cycle) and that Earth's structure (volcanoes, interior layers, atmosphere) is driven by the physical properties and interactions of these materials. This prepares them for Grade 4, where they will explore more complex chemical reactions, tectonic plate movements, and detailed atmospheric phenomena.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 6 planning weeks.

Changes in Matter and Mixtures

Students build on their understanding of basic material properties to explore how matter interacts, changes, and combines. This foundational physical science skill transitions students from observing static properties to analyzing dynamic processes, preparing them for more complex chemical concepts in later grades.

classify observable changes in everyday materials as physical or chemical based on the formation of new substances
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide students with descriptions of three events: baking bread, tearing paper, and rusting metal. Ask them to classify each as a physical or chemical change.
Expected response
Tearing paper is a physical change. Baking bread and rusting metal are chemical changes.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correct classification. Full mastery requires 3/3 correct classifications.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly identify whether a given scenario represents a physical or chemical change based on whether a new substance is formed.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe that any change in appearance (like dissolving or tearing) is a chemical change.; Students might think chemical changes only happen in laboratories, not in everyday life.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Matter undergoes modifications that are classified into physical and chemical changes. · Source page 42 · paragraph p42-paragraph-4
categorize material transformations as reversible or irreversible
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Show images of a broken cup, melted ice, and burned paper. Ask students to categorize each change as reversible or irreversible.
Expected response
Melted ice is reversible. The broken cup and burned paper are irreversible.
Scoring rule
Pass/Fail: Must correctly categorize all three items based on the possibility of returning to the initial state.
Mastery evidence
Students can determine if a material can return to its original state after a specific change.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may assume all physical changes are reversible and all chemical changes are irreversible.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Irreversible changes occur when matter cannot return to its initial state. · Source page 43 · paragraph p43-paragraph-20
distinguish substances as simple or compound based on particle composition
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Ask students to define simple and compound substances and provide a theoretical example based on particle types.
Expected response
Simple substances are made of the same kind of particles (e.g., a substance made only of blue particles), while compound substances are made of combinations of different particles (e.g., a substance made of blue and red particles joined together).
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly defining simple substances; 1 point for compound substances; 1 point for providing a valid theoretical example for each.
Mastery evidence
Students can state the difference between simple and compound substances using the concept of particle types.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students might confuse simple substances with single objects, regardless of their chemical makeup.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Substances are simple if made of one type of particle, and compound if made of different particles. · Source page 45 · paragraph p45-paragraph-6
classify combinations of substances as homogeneous or heterogeneous mixtures
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Present a mixture of water with food coloring and a mixture of water with sand. Ask students to classify each as homogeneous or heterogeneous.
Expected response
Water with food coloring is homogeneous. Water with sand is heterogeneous.
Scoring rule
Must correctly classify both mixtures to demonstrate mastery.
Mastery evidence
Students can visually and conceptually distinguish between mixtures where components are visible (heterogeneous) and where they are not (homogeneous).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think that if a mixture is a liquid, it must be homogeneous.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Mixtures can be classified into homogeneous and heterogeneous categories. · Source page 47 · paragraph p47-paragraph-10
select mechanical or physical separation methods based on mixture component properties
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Given a novel mixture of dry beans and salt, ask students to select a separation method and justify their choice based on the properties of the materials.
Expected response
Use a sieve to separate the salt from the beans, because the salt particles are much smaller than the beans.
Scoring rule
1 point for selecting the correct method; 1 point for justifying based on the specific property.
Mastery evidence
Students can decide on the most appropriate separation method for a specific mixture and justify their choice using the physical properties of the components.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe that any separation tool (like a filter) works for any type of mixture.
Local prerequisites
classify-mixtures
Scientific support
  • Separation methods are chosen based on the specific properties of the mixture's components. · Source page 47 · paragraph p47-paragraph-14

Earth Materials and Systems

This skill connects the observable surface of the Earth (rocks, volcanoes) to the unobservable interior and atmosphere. It develops spatial and systemic thinking, allowing students to understand that Earth is dynamic and composed of interacting layers and processes.

classify rocks as igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic based on observable features
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide descriptions of three rocks: one with visible shell fragments, one formed from cooled lava, and one deformed by deep heat and pressure. Ask students to classify each.
Expected response
The rock with shells is sedimentary, the one from lava is igneous, and the deformed one is metamorphic.
Scoring rule
Must correctly classify all three rocks based on their described formation characteristics.
Mastery evidence
Students can use descriptions of rock characteristics (e.g., containing fossils, formed from cooling magma) to classify them into the three main groups.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think all rocks are formed in the same way or that rocks never change.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Rocks are divided into three large groups according to their origin: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. · Source page 58 · paragraph p58-paragraph-5
sequence the external and internal processes that form and transform rocks
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide cards with the terms: weathering, erosion, deformation, and melting. Ask students to sequence them to show the order of processes that transform a surface rock into magma.
Expected response
Weathering -> Erosion -> Deformation -> Melting.
Scoring rule
Pass/Fail: The sequence must logically follow the breakdown of surface rock to its eventual melting.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly order the processes (weathering, erosion, deformation, melting) that transform one type of rock into another.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students might view the rock cycle as a single, one-way path rather than a continuous, multi-directional process.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • External and internal processes form and transform rocks, constituting the rock cycle. · Source page 55 · paragraph p55-paragraph-18
predict the resulting volcanic structure based on magma composition and eruption type
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Provide data showing a volcano has historically erupted with thick, slow-moving lava and large ash clouds. Ask students to predict its shape (shield or stratovolcano) and justify their prediction.
Expected response
It will be a stratovolcano because the thick lava and ash pile up steeply around the vent rather than spreading out.
Scoring rule
1 point for predicting stratovolcano; 1 point for justifying based on the accumulation of thick lava and ash.
Mastery evidence
Students can deduce the shape of a volcano by analyzing evidence about its eruption style (effusive vs. explosive) and the materials it ejects.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students often believe all volcanoes are tall, cone-shaped mountains that explode violently.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The shape of a volcano is determined by the composition of the magma. · Source page 59 · paragraph p59-paragraph-8
describe Earth's interior layers and their relative densities
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Ask students to name the three main compositional layers of the Earth and state why they do not mix together.
Expected response
Crust, mantle, and core. They do not mix because they have different densities.
Scoring rule
1 point for naming the layers; 1 point for identifying density/physical properties as the reason they separate.
Mastery evidence
Students can identify the main layers of the Earth (crust, mantle, core) and state that they separate based on different physical properties like density.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think the Earth is completely solid all the way through or hollow inside.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The Earth's interior is divided into compositional layers including the mantle and the core. · Source page 61 · paragraph p61-paragraph-3
justify the necessity of atmospheric oxygen for combustion and living organisms
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Present a scenario where a town is located in a valley with poor air circulation, leading to a buildup of exhaust gases. Ask students to justify why this is dangerous for the residents, using their knowledge of atmospheric gases.
Expected response
The buildup of exhaust gases displaces the oxygen in the air, which humans need to breathe and survive.
Scoring rule
1 point for linking the dangerous scenario to a lack of oxygen; 1 point for connecting atmospheric oxygen to human survival.
Mastery evidence
Students can use evidence from observations (like a candle going out when covered) to argue that oxygen is a necessary component of the air for specific processes.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students might think the atmosphere is just empty space or that air is a single uniform gas rather than a mixture.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The air contains oxygen, which is essential for maintaining life on the planet. · Source page 66 · paragraph p66-paragraph-8
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

act-1-teach · 45 min · teach

Observe teacher tear paper and mix baking soda with vinegar. Discuss and classify each change as physical or chemical based on whether a new substance is formed.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify tearing as physical and mixing as chemical, citing the formation of bubbles as evidence of a new substance.
Materials
paper, baking soda, vinegar, clear cups, tray
Safety
Teacher handles vinegar and baking soda. Students observe from a safe distance. Goggles worn by teacher.
Access and differentiation
Provide visual cue cards showing 'new stuff made' for chemical and 'same stuff' for physical.

15 mins introduction, 15 mins demonstration, 15 mins guided discussion and classification.

act-1-p1 · 75 min · practice

Rotate through stations observing safe changes: melting ice, dissolving sugar in water, and observing pre-rusted steel wool. Classify each change on a recording sheet.

Mastery criterion

Materials
ice cubes, sugar, water, cups, pre-rusted steel wool in sealed jars, recording sheets
Safety
Steel wool is sealed in jars to prevent handling of sharp or rusty edges. Spills wiped immediately.
Access and differentiation
Pair students for collaborative reading of station instructions.
Time rationale
15 mins setup and instructions, 45 mins station rotation (15 mins each), 15 mins wrap-up.

act-1-p2 · 75 min · practice

Sort picture cards of everyday scenarios (e.g., baking bread, cutting wood, rotting fruit, molding clay) into physical and chemical change categories.

Mastery criterion
Students accurately sort at least 8 out of 10 cards into the correct categories.
Materials
sets of picture cards, sorting mats
Safety
Standard classroom safety. No hazardous materials used.
Access and differentiation
Provide a reference sheet with definitions and one example of each change type.
Time rationale
15 mins review, 45 mins sorting activity and peer checking, 15 mins whole-class review.

act-1-assess · 45 min · assessment

Read descriptions of three events: baking bread, tearing paper, and rusting metal. Write down whether each is a physical or chemical change.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly classify all three events (tearing = physical, baking/rusting = chemical).
Materials
assessment worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the descriptions aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 25 mins independent work, 10 mins collection and transition.

act-2-teach · 30 min · teach

Observe the teacher melt an ice cube and then show a pre-frozen ice cube. Then observe the teacher cut an apple. Discuss which change can be undone.

Mastery criterion
Students state that melting is reversible because water can be frozen again, while cutting an apple is irreversible.
Materials

Limitations: The rock cycle is simplified to basic observable steps, omitting complex intermediate metamorphic and igneous processes.; Using liquid density columns to model Earth's interior may inadvertently reinforce the misconception that the mantle is entirely liquid, requiring careful teacher framing.; Chemical changes are introduced conceptually through observable phenomena; molecular-level explanations are deferred to later grades.; Safety constraints prevent the use of actual combustion or hazardous chemical mixing by students; these must be demonstrated by adults or simulated.

Water

Students begin by identifying macroscopic water bodies and their distribution on Earth, moving to dynamic processes like surface flow and infiltration. They then transition to microscopic properties, exploring solubility and concentration. Finally, they apply these physical properties to separate mixtures, culminating in the design of multi-step physical separation methods to address water contamination.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 2. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Analyzing the components and dynamics of the Earth's hydrosphere

Students build a foundational understanding of where water is located on Earth and how it moves through surface and subsurface systems, connecting these processes to the needs of living organisms.

classify images of water bodies into rivers, lakes, oceans, glaciers, and aquifers
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a set of 5 photographs showing different water bodies, write the correct name (river, lake, ocean, glacier, aquifer) under each.
Expected response
The student labels the ocean as saltwater, the glacier as solid ice, and correctly identifies the river, lake, and aquifer.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct label. Minimum 4 points for mastery.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies at least 4 out of 5 water body types from visual representations.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All bodies of water contain fresh water.; Aquifers are underground rivers rather than water stored in porous rock or soil.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The hydrosphere includes various bodies of water such as lakes, rivers, and seas. · Source page 77 · paragraph p77-paragraph-4
represent the proportion of salt water to fresh water on Earth using a 100-part grid
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using a 10x10 grid representing all the water on Earth, color the squares to show how much is salt water (blue) and how much is fresh water (green).
Expected response
97 squares colored blue and 3 squares colored green.
Scoring rule
Pass if exactly 97 and 3 squares are colored and correctly labeled.
Mastery evidence
Student colors exactly 97 parts for salt water and 3 parts for fresh water.
Diagnostic hypotheses
There is more fresh water than salt water on Earth because we drink it every day.
Local prerequisites
identify-hydrosphere-components
Scientific support
  • 97% of Earth's water is salt water and 3% is fresh water. · Source page 74 · paragraph p74-paragraph-6
construct a physical model demonstrating how rainfall increases river flow towards a lake
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using clay and a tray, build a model of a river flowing into a lake. Pour water to simulate rain and describe what happens to the river's water level.
Expected response
The model shows a continuous path from high to low ground. The written description states that adding 'rain' makes the river carry more water.
Scoring rule
Pass if the model has a clear slope and the description correctly links simulated rain to increased river volume.
Mastery evidence
Student builds a sloped channel leading to a basin and demonstrates increased flow when water is poured.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Rivers flow backwards when it rains.; Rain does not affect the amount of water in a river.
Local prerequisites
identify-hydrosphere-components
Scientific support
  • Increased rainfall results in rivers carrying more water. · Source page 76 · paragraph p76-paragraph-10
describe the process of water infiltration through soil layers to recharge an aquifer
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Draw a diagram showing what happens to rain after it falls on the ground, labeling the movement of water through the soil.
Expected response
Diagram shows rain falling, arrows pointing downwards through soil/sand layers, and water collecting at the bottom (aquifer).
Scoring rule
Pass if arrows correctly show downward movement through soil layers to an underground collection area.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately sequences the movement of water from the surface through porous materials.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Water stays on the surface forever.; Soil is solid and water cannot pass through it.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Infiltration is the process of water penetrating soil layers to reach an aquifer. · Source page 83 · paragraph p83-paragraph-8
predict the physical effects of drought on local plants and animals using evidence of water needs
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Read the scenario about a region with no rain for 6 months. Predict what will happen to the local trees and birds, and justify your answer.
Expected response
Trees will dry up or lose leaves, and birds will have to migrate or might die because all living things need water to survive.
Scoring rule
Pass if the prediction includes a negative impact on both plants and animals, justified by their biological need for water.
Mastery evidence
Student justifies the negative impact of water scarcity on specific living organisms.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants can survive indefinitely without water by just using sunlight.; Drought only affects humans, not wild animals.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Droughts negatively affect living beings and ecosystems. · Source page 99 · paragraph p99-paragraph-7
sequence the stages of human water use from environmental extraction to wastewater return
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Arrange the provided cards (Extraction from river/well, Human consumption/use, Wastewater discharge) in the correct order and draw arrows between them.
Expected response
Extraction -> Human consumption/use -> Wastewater discharge.
Scoring rule
Pass if the three stages are in the exact correct chronological order.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly orders the stages of extraction, use, and return.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Tap water comes directly from the clouds into the pipes.; Wastewater disappears and never returns to the environment.

Investigating water as a solvent and methods for separating mixtures

Students explore the physical properties of water by creating and separating mixtures, developing early chemistry concepts such as solubility, concentration, and physical separation techniques.

classify common household solids as soluble or insoluble in water based on mixing tests
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Mix salt, sand, sugar, and soil into separate cups of water. Stir well. Write down which substances are soluble and which are insoluble.
Expected response
Soluble: salt, sugar. Insoluble: sand, soil.
Scoring rule
Pass if salt/sugar are marked soluble and sand/soil are marked insoluble.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly categorizes at least 3 out of 4 tested substances.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All powders dissolve in water.; If a substance disappears in water, it ceases to exist.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Substances that dissolve in water are soluble, and those that do not are insoluble. · Source page 86 · paragraph p86-paragraph-2
order colored solutions by intensity to determine relative concentration
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Look at the three cups of drink mix. Order them from least concentrated to most concentrated. Explain how you know.
Expected response
Lightest color -> medium color -> darkest color. The darker the color, the more powder is dissolved in the water.
Scoring rule
Pass if the order is correct and the explanation links color intensity to the amount of dissolved substance.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly sequences solutions from least to most concentrated and justifies the order.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Darker color means the water is dirty, not more concentrated.; Amount of powder does not change the color of the water.
Local prerequisites
classify-solubility
Scientific support
  • A more intense color in a solution indicates a higher concentration of the dissolved substance. · Source page 90 · paragraph p90-paragraph-7
distinguish solutions, colloids, and suspensions using visual clarity and settling behavior
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the terms (Solution, Colloid, Suspension) to their descriptions: 1. Particles settle at the bottom. 2. Particles are invisible and don't settle. 3. Particles don't settle but scatter light.
Expected response
1. Suspension, 2. Solution, 3. Colloid.
Scoring rule
Pass if all three terms are correctly matched to their descriptions.
Mastery evidence
Student matches the type of dispersion to its observable characteristics.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All mixtures with water are solutions.; Colloids and solutions are exactly the same because both can look clear.
Local prerequisites
classify-solubility
Scientific support
  • Solutions have invisible dissolved particles, while colloids have larger particles visible against the light. · Source page 93 · paragraph p93-paragraph-10
separate a liquid from a settled solid by carefully pouring off the liquid
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a cup of water with settled sand, carefully pour the water into an empty cup without transferring the sand.
Expected response
The student pours the liquid slowly, leaving the solid sediment in the original cup.
Scoring rule
Pass if the new cup contains mostly clear water and the original cup retains the sand.
Mastery evidence
Student successfully pours water leaving the majority of the sediment behind.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Decantation removes all impurities, even dissolved ones.; You must shake the mixture before pouring.
Local prerequisites
differentiate-dispersions
Scientific support
  • Decantation involves pouring the supernatant liquid into another container without disturbing the sediment. · Source page 96 · paragraph p96-paragraph-2
separate suspended solids from water using a porous barrier (cotton or filter paper)
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Set up a funnel with cotton. Pour a mixture of water and dirt through it. Observe and record what stays in the cotton and what passes through.
Expected response
The dirt/solids stay in the cotton filter, and clearer water passes through into the container below.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly sets up the filter and accurately records the separation of solid and liquid.
Mastery evidence
Student sets up a filter and successfully passes a mixture through it, trapping solids.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Filters can remove dissolved sugar or salt from water.; Water cannot pass through cotton.
Local prerequisites
differentiate-dispersions
Scientific support
  • Filtration can be performed by placing cotton over a strainer to cover all spaces. · Source page 96 · paragraph p96-paragraph-4
propose a multi-step method combining decantation and filtration to clean a sample of dirty water
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
You have a bucket of muddy water with leaves and rocks. Write a step-by-step plan using decantation and filtration to make the water look clear.
Expected response
1. Let the water sit so rocks and heavy mud settle. 2. Decant (pour) the top water into a new container. 3. Filter the decanted water through cotton/sand to remove small floating dirt.
Scoring rule
Pass if the plan includes both settling/decantation first, followed by filtration.
Mastery evidence
Student designs a logical sequence using both settling and filtering to improve water clarity.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Filtered water is immediately safe to drink without chemical or biological treatment.; One single step is always enough to clean highly contaminated water.
Local prerequisites
perform-decantation, perform-filtration
Scientific support
  • Water cleaning can involve sequential steps like filtration through rocks and sand. · Source page 101 · paragraph p101-paragraph-8
