Limitations: Models of aquifers and rivers simplify complex geological processes and scale.; Visual concentration tests are qualitative and do not measure exact molarity.; Classroom filtration and decantation do not produce potable water; biological and chemical contaminants remain.; The distinction between colloids and suspensions can be ambiguous with everyday materials without specialized equipment.

Plants

Students enter Grade 3 with basic recognition of plant parts (roots, stems, leaves, flowers) from early childhood education. In this unit, they formalize this into systems (shoot/root) and connect specific functions (transport, photosynthesis, reproduction) to these organs. They also expand their definition of plants to include non-flowering varieties. Furthermore, they shift from viewing plants as static objects to dynamic organisms that respond to stimuli (tropisms and nasties). In subsequent grades, students will revisit these concepts to explore the cellular mechanisms behind these functions (e.g., xylem/phloem, chloroplasts) and the hormonal control of tropisms (e.g., auxins), which are too abstract for Grade 3.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Plant Structures and Reproduction

Students build foundational knowledge of plant anatomy by categorizing organs into systems and understanding their specific roles in survival and reproduction, moving from observable vegetative parts to reproductive structures.

classify plant organs into shoot and root systems
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a diagram of a complete plant, label the shoot system and root system, and list the organs belonging to each.
Expected response
The root system includes the roots below ground; the shoot system includes the stem, leaves, flowers, and fruits above ground.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly identifying the root system; 1 point for the shoot system; 1 point for correctly listing the organs in each.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly assign roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits to either the shoot or root system.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All plant parts above ground are stems and all below are roots.; Leaves are not considered organs.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Plants are divided into the shoot system above ground and the root system below ground. · Source page 105 · paragraph p105-paragraph-12
explain the transport and support functions of stems and roots
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Write a short explanation of what would happen to a plant if its stem could no longer transport water, and how the roots normally help prevent this.
Expected response
If the stem cannot transport water, the leaves and flowers will wilt and die. Roots normally absorb this water from the soil and anchor the plant.
Scoring rule
1 point for mentioning roots absorb water; 1 point for stems transporting it; 1 point for mentioning the support/anchoring function.
Mastery evidence
Students can describe how roots absorb and stems transport water and nutrients, while both provide structural support.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Roots only anchor the plant and do not absorb anything.; Stems only hold leaves and do not transport water.
Local prerequisites
classify-plant-systems
Scientific support
  • Stems and roots function to transport water and food, and to support the plant. · Source page 108 · paragraph p108-paragraph-7
distinguish between transpiration and photosynthesis based on their primary outcomes
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the processes of transpiration and photosynthesis to their correct descriptions regarding water loss and food production.
Expected response
Transpiration matches with losing water and cooling; photosynthesis matches with producing food.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly defining transpiration; 1 point for correctly defining photosynthesis.
Mastery evidence
Students can state that transpiration is the loss of water to cool the plant, while photosynthesis is the production of food.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants eat soil to get their food.; Transpiration is how plants breathe oxygen.
Local prerequisites
classify-plant-systems
Scientific support
  • Transpiration is the process by which plants lose water and cool themselves. · Source page 106 · paragraph p106-paragraph-8
identify the components of flowers and their role in fruit and seed formation
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Order the stages of plant reproduction from flower to seed dispersal and state the function of the fruit.
Expected response
Flower blooms -> pollination -> fruit forms -> fruit protects and transports seeds.
Scoring rule
1 point for correct sequence; 1 point for stating the fruit houses/transports seeds.
Mastery evidence
Students can identify that flowers produce fruits after pollination, and fruits contain seeds for reproduction.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Fruits are just food for humans and have no purpose for the plant.; Flowers turn into leaves after blooming.
Local prerequisites
classify-plant-systems
Scientific support
  • After pollination, the fruit forms to house and transport seeds. · Source page 113 · paragraph p113-paragraph-7
contrast the reproductive structures of seedless plants and conifers with flowering plants
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given images of a fern with sorus, a pine tree with cones, and a tomato plant, identify how each reproduces (spores, naked seeds, or seeds in fruit).
Expected response
Fern reproduces by spores; pine tree by naked seeds in cones; tomato by seeds inside a fruit.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly identifying the reproductive method of each of the three plant types.
Mastery evidence
Students can categorize a plant as seedless (using spores), a conifer (using cones/naked seeds), or a flowering plant based on its reproductive structures.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All plants have flowers and seeds.; Ferns produce microscopic seeds instead of spores.
Local prerequisites
identify-flower-fruit-roles
Scientific support
  • Plants are divided into seedless plants (like ferns and mosses) and seed plants. · Source page 129 · paragraph p129-paragraph-4

Plant Behavioral Responses

Students explore how plants interact with their environment, distinguishing between slow growth movements (tropisms) and rapid movements (nasties), fostering observational and reasoning skills.

define tropisms as slow, directional growth responses to environmental stimuli
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Describe what a tropism is and provide one reason why it is difficult to observe a tropism happening in real time.
Expected response
A tropism is a slow growth response toward or away from a stimulus. It is hard to observe because it happens very slowly over days.
Scoring rule
1 point for defining tropism as a slow/directional response; 1 point for explaining it takes days to observe.
Mastery evidence
Students can explain that tropisms are slow movements where the plant grows toward or away from a specific stimulus.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants cannot move at all.; Plants grow towards the sun instantly.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Tropisms are slow responses plants use to move toward or away from a stimulus. · Source page 123 · paragraph p123-paragraph-4
classify plant growth movements as gravitropism, hydrotropism, phototropism, or thigmotropism
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Read four scenarios of plant growth (e.g., roots growing toward a leaky pipe, a stem bending toward a window) and label each with the correct tropism name.
Expected response
Roots to pipe = hydrotropism; stem to window = phototropism; roots down = gravitropism; vine wrapping = thigmotropism.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correctly identified tropism (4 points total).
Mastery evidence
Students can identify the specific type of tropism occurring when given a scenario of a plant responding to light, gravity, water, or touch.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Roots grow down only because they are heavy.; Plants only respond to light, not water or gravity.
Local prerequisites
define-tropisms
Scientific support
  • Gravitropism is the plant's response to the stimulus of gravity. · Source page 123 · paragraph p123-paragraph-6
define nasties as rapid, non-directional movements in response to stimuli
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Explain what a nastia is and give an example of how it differs in speed from a tropism.
Expected response
A nastia is a fast plant movement that doesn't follow the direction of the stimulus, unlike a tropism which is slow.
Scoring rule
1 point for mentioning it is fast; 1 point for mentioning it is non-directional.
Mastery evidence
Students can state that nasties are fast responses that do not depend on the direction of the stimulus.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All plant movements are called tropisms.; Plants that close their leaves are trying to eat insects.
Local prerequisites
define-tropisms
Scientific support
  • Seismonasty is a plant's response to relatively strong tactile stimuli. · Source page 128 · paragraph p128-paragraph-10
differentiate between tropisms and nasties using observable evidence of speed and direction
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
A student touches a Mimosa plant and its leaves fold instantly. Another student places a plant on its side and its stem grows upward over a week. Identify which is a tropism and which is a nastia, and justify your answer using speed and direction.
Expected response
The Mimosa folding is a nastia because it is fast and non-directional. The stem growing upward is a tropism because it is slow and directional (against gravity).
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly identifying both; 1 point for justifying based on speed; 1 point for justifying based on direction.
Mastery evidence
Students can analyze a described plant movement, determine if it is a tropism or nastia, and justify their choice using evidence of speed and directionality.
Diagnostic hypotheses
If a plant moves, it must be a nastia.; Tropisms and nasties are just different words for the same thing.
Local prerequisites
classify-specific-tropisms, define-nasties
Scientific support
  • Tropisms are slow responses in the direction of the stimulus. · Source page 129 · paragraph p129-paragraph-24

Limitations: The distinction between transpiration and photosynthesis is simplified to their primary observable outcomes (water loss vs. food production); chemical equations are omitted.; Cellular mechanisms of water transport (capillary action, xylem) are not introduced.; The hormonal basis of tropisms (auxins) is excluded to maintain developmental appropriateness.; Observation of tropisms in inquiry activities relies on consolidated time estimates, as the actual biological process takes days.; Context tasks assume access to printed images if actual local plants are unavailable.

Animals

Students enter Grade 3 with basic knowledge of animal habitats and simple needs. In this unit, they progress to analyzing specific anatomical structures (symmetry, feeding, respiration) and life cycles (metamorphosis). They then apply this anatomical understanding to classify animals into major invertebrate and vertebrate groups, culminating in the use of dichotomous keys. The next grade should revisit dichotomous keys with more complex traits and explore internal anatomy in greater depth, moving beyond external morphological features.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 6 planning weeks.

Analyzing Animal Anatomy and Physiology

Students build foundational knowledge of animal biology by examining how physical structures and developmental stages relate to survival, movement, and environmental adaptation.

identify the type of body symmetry in animal images
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Look at images of a butterfly, a sea star, a sea sponge, a dog, and a jellyfish. State the type of symmetry for each.
Expected response
Butterfly: bilateral; Sea star: radial; Sponge: asymmetrical; Dog: bilateral; Jellyfish: radial.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct identification based on the presence of a central axis, midline, or lack thereof.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the symmetry type of at least 4 out of 5 given animals.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Assuming all animals have bilateral symmetry; Confusing radial symmetry with circular shapes that lack a central axis
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The textbook states that some animals have radial symmetry around a central axis. · Source page 135 · paragraph p135-paragraph-4
sequence the developmental stages of an animal undergoing metamorphosis
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Arrange the cards showing egg, larva, pupa, and adult mosquito in the correct chronological order.
Expected response
Egg, Larva, Pupa, Adult.
Scoring rule
Pass if all four stages are placed in the exact correct sequence.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly orders the four stages of mosquito development.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Believing all animals look like miniature adults when born; Thinking the pupa is a dead or inactive stage with no internal changes
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Mosquitoes develop through distinct stages, starting with eggs turning into larvae. · Source page 137 · paragraph p137-paragraph-15
classify animal movements as positive or negative taxisms in response to stimuli
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Read 4 scenarios: a moth flying toward light, an earthworm moving away from light, a plant leaning toward the sun, and a cockroach hiding in the dark. Classify each movement as a positive or negative taxism.
Expected response
Moth: positive; Earthworm: negative; Plant: positive; Cockroach: negative.
Scoring rule
Correct if movement toward a stimulus is labeled positive and movement away is labeled negative.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly classifies 3 out of 4 scenarios as positive or negative taxisms.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Thinking animals move randomly without external triggers; Confusing positive taxism with 'good' and negative with 'bad'
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Taxisms are directional movements either toward (positive) or away from (negative) a stimulus. · Source page 145 · paragraph p145-paragraph-3
relate anatomical structures to specific feeding methods
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match 4 animal structures (strong beak, long tongue, tentacles, sharp claws) to their feeding functions (cracking seeds, sucking nectar, catching prey, tearing meat).
Expected response
Strong beak: cracking seeds; Long tongue: sucking nectar; Tentacles: catching prey; Sharp claws: tearing meat.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct match between structure and function.
Mastery evidence
Student matches 4 different structures to their correct feeding function.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Assuming all animals chew food with teeth; Thinking tentacles are only used for movement
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Animals have specific anatomical structures adapted for their unique feeding methods. · Source page 143 · paragraph p143-paragraph-11
compare respiratory structures based on the animal's aquatic or terrestrial habitat
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Analyze a description of a newly discovered animal with moist skin and gills, and deduce its habitat, justifying the choice with evidence about respiratory structures.
Expected response
The animal lives in water because gills are adapted to extract dissolved oxygen from water, not air.
Scoring rule
Pass if the response correctly links gills to extracting oxygen from water and lungs to extracting oxygen from air.
Mastery evidence
Student justifies why a specific respiratory structure is suited for water or air.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Believing all animals breathe through lungs; Thinking aquatic animals do not need oxygen
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The textbook states that the concentration of dissolved oxygen is higher in air than in water. · Source page 144 · paragraph p144-paragraph-4

Classifying Animals using Morphological Traits

Students apply their understanding of animal anatomy to categorize biodiversity, moving from broad distinctions (vertebrate vs. invertebrate) to specific groups, culminating in the use of scientific tools like dichotomous keys.

distinguish between vertebrates and invertebrates based on the presence of a backbone
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Sort the following 10 animals into vertebrates and invertebrates: dog, spider, snail, fish, frog, earthworm, butterfly, snake, crab, and bird.
Expected response
Vertebrates: dog, fish, frog, snake, bird. Invertebrates: spider, snail, earthworm, butterfly, crab.
Scoring rule
Pass if sorted correctly based on the presence or absence of an internal skeleton/backbone.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly sorts 8 out of 10 animals into vertebrate or invertebrate categories.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Thinking all hard-shelled animals are vertebrates; Believing snakes are invertebrates because they bend easily
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Vertebrates are characterized by having an internal skeleton with a backbone. · Source page 157 · paragraph p157-paragraph-13
categorize invertebrates into major groups using morphological traits
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Observe 5 different unknown animal specimens or detailed pictures and categorize them into their invertebrate groups based on their visible morphological traits.
Expected response
Correctly categorizes the 5 specimens into mollusks, arthropods, worms, sponges, or cnidarians based on traits like shells, jointed legs, or soft bodies.
Scoring rule
Pass if the correct group is named based on the key morphological trait provided.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the invertebrate group for 4 out of 5 descriptions.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Confusing mollusks with arthropods if both have shells; Thinking all worms belong to the exact same species
Local prerequisites
distinguish-skeletons
Scientific support
  • Mollusks are characterized by soft bodies and sometimes protective shells. · Source page 156 · paragraph p156-paragraph-4
  • Sponges are simple animals full of holes for water circulation. · Source page 149 · paragraph p149-paragraph-9
  • Cnidarians have a hollow sac shape with surrounding tentacles. · Source page 150 · paragraph p150-paragraph-4
  • Annelid worms have elongated bodies with segments or rings. · Source page 151 · paragraph p151-paragraph-8
  • Arthropods possess a hard outer covering. · Source page 155 · paragraph p155-paragraph-4
categorize vertebrates into classes based on skin covering and reproduction
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Observe pictures of 5 different local animals (e.g., a local bat, a sea turtle, a tilapia, a frog, a parrot) and categorize them into their vertebrate class based on their visible skin covering and described reproductive method.
Expected response
Correctly categorizes the 5 animals into mammals, reptiles, fish, amphibians, or birds.
Scoring rule
Pass if categorized correctly based on traits like hair, scales, feathers, and live birth vs. eggs.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 animals based on their skin covering.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Thinking all animals that live in water are fish; Believing bats are birds because they fly
Local prerequisites
distinguish-skeletons
Scientific support
  • Vertebrate groups can be distinguished by their skin coverings, such as scales for reptiles and hair for mammals. · Source page 160 · paragraph p160-paragraph-19
use a simple dichotomous key to identify an animal
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Use the provided dichotomous key to identify the vertebrate class of 3 different animals shown in pictures (e.g., a frog, a snake, a dog).
Expected response
Follows the correct path for each animal to reach its class.
Scoring rule
Pass if the final identification matches the path dictated by the key for at least 3 animals.
Mastery evidence
Student successfully identifies 3 animals using a provided 3-step dichotomous key.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Reading all options at once instead of following the step-by-step path; Guessing the animal without using the key
Local prerequisites
categorize-vertebrates, categorize-invertebrates
Scientific support
  • A dichotomous key involves choosing between two options at each step to identify an organism. · Source page 158 · paragraph p158-paragraph-4
justify the classification of an animal into a specific group using anatomical evidence
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
A whale lives in the ocean, but it has hair, breathes air with lungs, and gives birth to live young. Justify why it is classified as a mammal and not a fish.
Expected response
It is a mammal because it has hair, breathes with lungs, and gives birth to live young, whereas fish have gills and scales.
Scoring rule
Pass if the justification relies on anatomical traits rather than habitat.
Mastery evidence
Student provides at least two anatomical reasons for classifying an animal into a specific group.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Classifying based on habitat rather than anatomy
Local prerequisites
use-dichotomous-key
Scientific support
  • The textbook states that not all tetrapods, such as sea turtles, whales, and seals, currently live on land. · Source page 161 · paragraph p161-paragraph-4

Limitations: The classification of invertebrates is highly simplified for Grade 3, grouping diverse phyla into broad categories (e.g., 'vermiforms' instead of distinguishing annelids, nematodes, and platyhelminthes).; The concept of respiration is simplified to basic structures without detailing cellular respiration.; The dichotomous key practice is limited to highly distinct, observable traits, avoiding ambiguous or microscopic features.

Microorganisms

Students enter Grade 3 with basic knowledge of living vs. non-living things and visible animal/plant traits. This unit introduces the microscopic world, requiring them to abstractly conceptualize organisms they cannot see. They progress from identifying basic cellular structures (prokaryotic/eukaryotic) to understanding how these structures interact with their environment (e.g., soap breaking down lipid layers). The second half of the unit applies this biological understanding to everyday phenomena: decomposition and food preservation. In future grades, students will explore cellular biology and ecosystems in greater depth.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Characterizing Microscopic Life and Pathogens

Students must first understand the structural and functional differences between various microscopic entities (cells, bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa) before they can understand how they interact with the environment and human health.

classify visual models of cells as prokaryotic or eukaryotic based on the presence of a nucleus
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide students with two diagrams of cells, one with a distinct nucleus and one without. Ask them to label each as prokaryotic or eukaryotic and circle the feature that helped them decide.
Expected response
The student labels the cell with a nucleus as eukaryotic and circles the nucleus. The student labels the cell without a nucleus as prokaryotic.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly labeling both cells; 1 point for circling the nucleus in the eukaryotic cell.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies whether a given cell model is prokaryotic or eukaryotic by checking for a nucleus.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Cells are classified as prokaryotic if they lack a nucleus and eukaryotic if they have one. · Source page 169 · paragraph p169-paragraph-7
identify characteristics of living organisms such as metabolism and independent reproduction
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a list of characteristics, select the ones that define a living organism.
Expected response
Student selects metabolism and independent reproduction.
Scoring rule
1 point for selecting metabolism; 1 point for selecting independent reproduction.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies metabolism and reproduction as key traits of living organisms.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Viruses are not considered living because they lack cells, metabolism, and the ability to reproduce independently, which are traits associated with living things. · Source page 171 · paragraph p171-paragraph-3
identify characteristics of viruses that distinguish them from living organisms
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Give students a checklist of traits (has cells, needs a host to reproduce, has a metabolism, causes infections). Ask them to check only the traits that apply to viruses.
Expected response
The student checks 'needs a host to reproduce' and 'causes infections', leaving 'has cells' and 'has a metabolism' unchecked.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly identifying that viruses need a host and cause infections; 1 point for correctly omitting cells and metabolism.
Mastery evidence
Student selects the traits that make viruses non-living, specifically their lack of cells and inability to reproduce without a host.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
micro-cell-types, micro-living-traits
Scientific support
  • Viruses lack cells, lack metabolism, and can only reproduce using other living beings. · Source page 171 · paragraph p171-paragraph-3
describe protective covers of pathogens
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Describe the outer layer of some pathogens that protects them.
Expected response
Some pathogens have protective covers, like a cell wall, capsule, or oily layers.
Scoring rule
1 point for mentioning a protective cover.
Mastery evidence
Student states that pathogens have protective covers.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Pathogens can have protective covers, such as cell walls and capsules. · Source page 171 · paragraph p171-paragraph-10
model the breakdown of pathogen lipid layers using oil, water, and detergent
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Ask students to draw a three-step comic strip showing what happens to an 'oily pathogen' when washed with only water versus when washed with water and soap.
Expected response
The drawing shows water sliding off the oily pathogen in step 1, soap attaching to the oil in step 2, and the pathogen's layer breaking apart in step 3.
Scoring rule
1 point for showing water failing to break the oil; 1 point for showing soap successfully breaking the oily layer.
Mastery evidence
Student demonstrates and explains that detergent is required to mix oil and water, representing how soap breaks apart the oily protective layer of pathogens.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
micro-pathogen-structure
Scientific support
  • Detergents can disassemble the protective covers of pathogens, eliminating both bacteria and viruses. · Source page 172 · paragraph p172-paragraph-8
evaluate experimental data on household substances to purify water
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Ask the student to name one common household substance used to purify water and describe how they could test if it works on stagnant water.
Expected response
Bleach (lejía). We can test it by adding it to stagnant water and observing if the microorganisms stop moving or disappear.
Scoring rule
1 point for naming a substance like bleach; 1 point for describing an observational test.
Mastery evidence
Student identifies a purification substance and proposes a basic observational test.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Common household substances can be identified and tested for their efficacy in purifying water against microorganisms. · Source page 179 · paragraph p179-paragraph-6
describe characteristics of fungi and protozoa
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the organism (Fungi, Protozoa) to its characteristic (grows from spores on food, hunts in stagnant water).
Expected response
Fungi matches with growing from spores on food; Protozoa matches with hunting in stagnant water.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correct match.
Mastery evidence
Student can describe at least one distinct characteristic of fungi (spores/food) and protozoa (water/hunting).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Fungi and protozoa are the same as bacteria.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Fungi develop from spores when food is available. · Source page 182 · paragraph p182-paragraph-5
  • Protozoa can live in stagnant water and hunt other microorganisms. · Source page 170 · paragraph p170-paragraph-4

Analyzing Microbial Decomposition and Preservation

Once students understand what microorganisms are, they apply this knowledge to observable macroscopic phenomena: how microbes break down food and how humans manipulate environments to prevent this.

identify moisture, temperature, and oxygen as optimal conditions for microbial growth
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Give students a list of environments (dry and cold, wet and warm, dry and hot). Ask them to circle the environment where a piece of bread will grow mold the fastest.
Expected response
The student circles 'wet and warm'.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly identifying the wet and warm environment as optimal for microbial growth.
Mastery evidence
Student lists the environmental factors that accelerate the reproduction of decomposing microorganisms.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Microorganisms require optimal conditions like moisture and adequate temperatures to survive. · Source page 184 · paragraph p184-paragraph-13
predict the preservation outcome of removing water from food using salt
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Show a picture of fresh fish and a picture of fish covered in thick salt. Ask the student to predict which will last longer without rotting and explain why using the word 'water' or 'moisture'.
Expected response
The student predicts the salted fish will last longer because the salt removes the water, and microorganisms need water to survive and rot the food.
Scoring rule
1 point for choosing the salted fish; 1 point for explaining that salt removes moisture needed by microbes.
Mastery evidence
Student predicts that salted food will not decompose quickly because the lack of water prevents microorganism survival.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
micro-decomposition-conditions
Scientific support
  • Dehydration involves removing water from food, which can be done by adding salt. · Source page 187 · paragraph p187-paragraph-3
justify the use of refrigeration to slow down microbial proliferation in food
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Ask the student: 'Why do we put milk in the refrigerator instead of leaving it on the table? Explain what happens to the microorganisms in the cold.'
Expected response
We put milk in the fridge to stop it from spoiling quickly. The cold temperature slows down the growth and reproduction of microorganisms.
Scoring rule
1 point for stating it prevents spoiling; 1 point for clarifying that cold slows down microbial proliferation.
Mastery evidence
Student explains that low temperatures do not necessarily kill microbes but slow down their reproduction.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
micro-decomposition-conditions
Scientific support
  • Refrigeration and freezing lower the temperature of food to prevent the proliferation of microorganisms. · Source page 188 · paragraph p188-paragraph-3
describe the role of beneficial microorganisms in creating environments toxic to pathogens during fermentation
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide a short text about cheese making. Ask the student to write one sentence explaining how the 'good' bacteria in cheese protect it from 'bad' bacteria.
Expected response
The good bacteria produce substances like acid that create a toxic environment for the bad bacteria, keeping the food safe.
Scoring rule
1 point for mentioning that good bacteria produce substances (acid/alcohol); 1 point for stating this stops bad bacteria (pathogens).
Mastery evidence
Student describes how some microbes produce acid or alcohol that keeps harmful pathogens away.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Local prerequisites
micro-decomposition-conditions
Scientific support
  • Microorganisms in fermented food control pathogens by creating a toxic environment for themselves and other microorganisms. · Source page 189 · paragraph p189-paragraph-4
identify local Salvadoran food preservation methods like encurtido and drying fish
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Name two local methods used to preserve food for a long time without a refrigerator, as discussed in class.
Expected response
Encurtido (pickling) and drying (like dried fish).
Scoring rule
1 point for each correct method named.
Mastery evidence
Student identifies encurtido and drying as methods to preserve food.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Encurtido and drying are just for flavor, not preservation.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Encurtido is a technique where foods are submerged in salt or vinegar to preserve them. · Source page 190 · paragraph p190-paragraph-12
  • Drying fish is a method observed locally that prevents decomposition. · Source page 186 · paragraph p186-paragraph-11

act-soap-prac-1 · 45 min · practice

Limitations: The unit simplifies the complexity of viral reproduction and the diversity of the protist kingdom to suit Grade 3 comprehension.; Models of cells and pathogens are highly abstracted.; Safety constraints prevent the actual culturing of unknown environmental bacteria, relying instead on controlled decomposition of common foods or visual simulations.

Grade 4

Machines and energy

Students enter Grade 4 with a basic understanding of pushes, pulls, and the general concept that living things and machines need energy to function. This unit progresses by formalizing the mechanical advantage of simple machines, specifically focusing on levers and their components (fulcrum, effort, load). Once students understand how individual simple machines manipulate force, they learn to deconstruct complex machines. The progression then shifts from mechanical force to electrical energy, teaching students to track energy transformations and quantify consumption. Calculating consumption (Watts x hours) is a strict prerequisite for calculating monetary cost. This quantitative approach to energy prepares students for Grade 5, where they will explore more abstract forms of energy, work, and environmental impacts of energy generation.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 0. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Analyze simple and complex machines

Students transition from recognizing basic tools to analyzing the mechanical advantage and components of simple and complex machines, laying the groundwork for understanding forces and work.

classify everyday tools into the six groups of simple machines
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide students with images of a knife, a ramp, a doorknob, a seesaw, and a screw. Ask them to write the name of the simple machine group each belongs to.
Expected response
Knife: wedge; Ramp: inclined plane; Doorknob: wheel and axle; Seesaw: lever; Screw: screw.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct classification. Mastery is 4/5 points.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly categorizes at least 4 out of 5 provided everyday tools into their corresponding simple machine type.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think only modern, motorized devices are machines.; Students may confuse a wedge with an inclined plane.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Simple machines are classified into six specific groups. · Source page 11 · paragraph p11-paragraph-5
categorize levers into first, second, and third class based on component positions
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Show a diagram of a wheelbarrow. Ask the student to label the fulcrum, effort, and load, and state which class of lever it is.
Expected response
Fulcrum at the wheel, load in the middle, effort at the handles. It is a second-class lever.
Scoring rule
Correctly labeling the three components (1 point) and correctly identifying it as a second-class lever (1 point).
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the class of a lever by locating the fulcrum, effort (power), and load (resistance).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe the fulcrum is always in the middle of a lever.
Local prerequisites
identify-simple-machines
Scientific support
  • Second-class levers have the resistance located between the fulcrum and the power (effort). · Source page 18 · paragraph p18-paragraph-7
locate lever components (fulcrum, effort, load) in human body movements
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Ask the student to stand on their tiptoes and then draw a simple diagram of their foot, labeling the fulcrum, effort, and load.
Expected response
Diagram showing the toes as the fulcrum, the ankle/body weight as the load, and the calf muscle pulling up as the effort.
Scoring rule
Correctly identifying the toes as the fulcrum and the general positions of load and effort.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately maps the parts of a lever to a specific human joint movement.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think bones move on their own without acting as mechanical levers.
Local prerequisites
classify-levers
Scientific support
  • The human body uses joints as fulcrums, such as the tips of the toes when moving ankles. · Source page 15 · paragraph p15-paragraph-39
predict the change in required effort when the distance to the fulcrum is altered
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Present a scenario where a heavy box needs to be lifted with a plank. Ask the student to decide where to place the rock (fulcrum) to make it easiest to lift, and justify their choice using the law of the lever.
Expected response
Place the rock as close to the box as possible. This increases the distance between the effort and the fulcrum, requiring less power to lift the heavy resistance.
Scoring rule
Decision to place fulcrum near the load (1 point) and justification mentioning the distance between fulcrum and effort (1 point).
Mastery evidence
Student justifies how moving the fulcrum closer to the load decreases the effort required.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think that the length of the lever does not affect the force needed, only the weight of the object does.
Local prerequisites
classify-levers
Scientific support
  • To apply less effort, the distance between the fulcrum and the effort must be increased. · Source page 19 · paragraph p19-paragraph-4
differentiate the individual simple machines that make up a complex machine
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Show a picture of a bicycle. Ask the student to name two simple machines found in it and point out where they are.
Expected response
Wheel and axle (the wheels/pedals), levers (the brakes), screws (holding parts together).
Scoring rule
1 point for each correctly identified and located simple machine (max 2 points).
Mastery evidence
Student identifies at least two different simple machines within a given complex machine.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may view a complex machine as a single indivisible unit rather than a combination of simple machines.
Local prerequisites
identify-simple-machines
Scientific support
  • Complex machines are composed of two or more simple machines connected together. · Source page 20 · paragraph p20-paragraph-5

Evaluate energy transformations and consumption in technological systems

Understanding how technology uses and transforms energy allows students to make informed, quantitative decisions about energy consumption and conservation in their daily lives.

sort technological examples into hard, soft, and flexible categories
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a list (a smartphone, a business plan, a wooden chair, a software algorithm), sort them into 'Hard Technology' and 'Soft Technology'.
Expected response
Hard: smartphone, wooden chair. Soft: business plan, software algorithm.
Scoring rule
All 4 items must be sorted correctly for mastery.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly sorts tangible products and intangible knowledge/processes into hard and soft technology.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think technology only refers to electronic devices like smartphones or computers.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Hard technology consists of tangible products that can be seen and touched. · Source page 29 · paragraph p29-paragraph-5
describe the input and output energy forms in common household appliances
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Describe the energy transformation that occurs when you turn on an electric fan.
Expected response
Electrical energy is transformed into mechanical (kinetic) energy.
Scoring rule
Must state both the correct input (electrical) and output (mechanical/kinetic) energy.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately identifies the initial energy source and the resulting energy form for a given device.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe appliances 'use up' energy completely rather than transforming it into other forms like heat or motion.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Energy undergoes transformations when used by household appliances. · Source page 9 · paragraph p9-paragraph-8
calculate total energy consumption using power rating and time
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
A television uses 100 W of power. If it is turned on for 4 hours, what is the total energy consumption in Watt-hours?
Expected response
400 Watt-hours (or 400 Wh).
Scoring rule
Correct numerical answer (400) and unit (Wh) required for mastery.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly multiplies watts by hours to find total watt-hours consumed.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students might add power and time instead of multiplying them to find consumption.
Local prerequisites
identify-energy-transformations
Scientific support
  • Energy consumption is calculated by multiplying the appliance's power by the hours it is used. · Source page 34 · paragraph p34-paragraph-12
calculate the monetary cost of energy consumption using a given rate
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
If a household consumes 50 kWh in a month and the cost is $0.20 per kWh, what is the total cost of the energy consumed?
Expected response
$10.00
Scoring rule
Correct mathematical calculation resulting in $10.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly multiplies the calculated energy consumption by the unit cost to find the total expense.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may confuse power (Watts) with the monetary cost directly without factoring in time.
Local prerequisites
calculate-energy-consumption
Scientific support
  • The total cost is obtained by multiplying the energy consumption by the local price per kWh. · Source page 34 · paragraph p34-paragraph-12
justify actions to reduce energy consumption based on appliance usage patterns
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Read a scenario where a family leaves their microwave and TV plugged in all day while at work. Propose one action they should take to lower their energy bill and explain why it works.
Expected response
They should unplug the appliances when not in use because electronic devices still consume energy even when turned off (phantom load).
Scoring rule
Must propose unplugging/turning off at the source (1 point) and justify it by mentioning energy consumed while off (1 point).
Mastery evidence
Student proposes a valid action to save energy and justifies it using the concept of phantom load or unnecessary usage time.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think that appliances plugged in but turned off do not consume any energy at all.
Local prerequisites
calculate-energy-cost
Scientific support
  • Electronic devices consume energy even when turned off, so they should be disconnected to save energy. · Source page 34 · paragraph p34-paragraph-15
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-identify-simple-machines · 30 min · teach

Introduce the six simple machines by displaying physical examples (a ruler for a lever, a spool for a wheel and axle, a doorstop for a wedge, a ramp for an inclined plane, a screw, and a basic pulley). Explain the defining characteristic of each group.

Mastery criterion
Student can verbally state the defining feature of at least three simple machines when prompted.
Materials
ruler, spool, doorstop, small ramp, screw, toy pulley
Safety
Ensure the screw and wedge do not have dangerously sharp points.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual anchor chart with icons representing each of the six simple machines.
Time rationale
10 minutes for direct instruction, 15 minutes for guided observation of the physical items, 5 minutes for closing summary.

practice-1-identify-simple-machines · 30 min · practice

Students work in pairs to sort 24 picture cards of everyday objects (e.g., knife, doorknob, seesaw, slide) into six labeled piles corresponding to the simple machine groups.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly sorts at least 20 out of 24 cards into the proper simple machine categories.
Materials
sets of 24 picture cards, category labels
Safety
Standard classroom safety; ensure clear pathways during group work.
Access and differentiation
Include the name of the object on the picture card to assist with vocabulary recognition.
Time rationale
5 minutes setup, 20 minutes sorting activity, 5 minutes peer review.

practice-2-identify-simple-machines · 30 min · practice

Conduct a classroom scavenger hunt where students must find and list at least one real-world example of each of the six simple machines within the room (e.g., door hinges, pencil sharpener).

Mastery criterion
Student lists at least four valid examples of simple machines found in the classroom.
Materials
clipboards, scavenger hunt worksheets
Safety
Instruct students not to climb on furniture or touch electrical outlets during the search.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist with hints (e.g., 'Look near the door for a wheel and axle').
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes active searching, 5 minutes sharing findings.

practice-3-identify-simple-machines · 30 min · practice

Students create a 'Simple Machines Mini-Book' by folding paper and drawing one example of each of the six simple machines, labeling them correctly.

Mastery criterion
Student produces a mini-book with six distinct, correctly labeled simple machine drawings.

Limitations: The textbook simplifies the law of the lever, focusing on qualitative relationships (distance vs. effort) rather than strict mathematical torque equations, which is appropriate for Grade 4 but limits precise physics calculations.; Energy consumption calculations ignore efficiency losses (heat, friction) and assume constant power draw, which is a simplification of real-world electrical behavior.; The text suggests an experiment holding a spiral over a lit candle. For safety, this must be adapted to a teacher demonstration or use a safe heat source (like a radiator or hot water) to prevent burn and fire risks.; The distinction between hard and soft technology can be philosophically complex; the unit simplifies this to tangible vs. intangible, which may require teacher mediation for edge cases like software.

Nutrition

Students enter Grade 4 with basic knowledge of food groups and plant parts from early primary. In this unit, they transition to quantitative nutrition (kcal, BMI) and trace food origins through supply chains. In Grade 5, they will revisit human body systems, exploring how nutrients are absorbed and transported at a cellular level, building on this macro-level understanding.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 6 planning weeks.

Nutritional Analysis and Human Health

Students move from qualitative descriptions of food to quantitative analysis of energy and body metrics, establishing a foundation for understanding human metabolism and health.

classify common foods into macronutrients, micronutrients, and their origin
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a list of foods (e.g., rice, chicken, orange), sort them into a table with columns for macronutrients/micronutrients and animal/vegetal origin.
Expected response
Rice is a macronutrient (vegetal), chicken is a macronutrient (animal), orange provides micronutrients (vegetal).
Scoring rule
1 point per correct classification of both nutrient type and origin.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly categorize a list of 10 common foods by their primary nutrient type and origin.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All foods provide the same type of energy.; Vitamins provide caloric energy.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Foods are composed of different materials called nutrients. · Source page 42 · paragraph p42-paragraph-6
calculate total kilocalories from a given set of food items using nutritional data

applying
Assessment task

Expected response
The student provides the correct sum of kilocalories based on the specific values in the table.
Scoring rule
Correct mathematical sum matching the table values.
Mastery evidence
Students accurately sum the kilocalories of a provided meal using a nutritional reference table.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Larger portions of food always have more kilocalories than smaller portions of high-fat foods.
Local prerequisites
classify-nutrients
Scientific support
  • Foods provide specific amounts of kilocalories that can be recorded and calculated. · Source page 47 · paragraph p47-paragraph-8
predict the required duration of physical activity to expend a specific caloric intake
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
If you consume a 470 kcal snack, predict how long you must play basketball to expend that energy, using the activity chart. Justify your answer.
Expected response
I must play basketball for about 1 hour because the chart indicates that 1 hour of basketball burns approximately 470 kcal.
Scoring rule
Prediction matches the chart data and includes a justification based on energy balance.
Mastery evidence
Students justify the choice and duration of an activity needed to balance a specific caloric intake.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All physical activities burn calories at the same rate.
Local prerequisites
calculate-energy
Scientific support
  • Higher caloric intake requires more physical activity to expend the energy. · Source page 49 · paragraph p49-paragraph-23
measure human height in centimeters and mass in kilograms using standard tools
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Demonstrate the correct posture and procedure to measure a classmate's height using a stadiometer and mass using a scale, recording the data with units.
Expected response
Student removes shoes, stands straight against the wall for height, and stands still in the center of the scale for mass, recording values in cm and kg.
Scoring rule
Observation of correct procedure (shoes off, straight posture) and accurate recording of units.
Mastery evidence
Students follow standard procedures to measure height and mass accurately.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Mass and weight are the exact same concept in all contexts.; Shoes and accessories do not affect anthropometric measurements.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Accurate anthropometric measurement requires removing items that interfere with height or mass. · Source page 55 · paragraph p55-paragraph-5
calculate Body Mass Index (BMI) using the formula mass/height squared
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Calculate the BMI for a student with a mass of 30 kg and a height of 1.2 meters. Show your work.
Expected response
BMI = 30 / (1.2 * 1.2) = 30 / 1.44 = 20.83.
Scoring rule
Correct substitution into the formula and accurate final calculation.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly apply the BMI formula given mass in kg and height in meters.
Diagnostic hypotheses
BMI directly measures body fat percentage.
Local prerequisites
measure-anthropometry
Scientific support
  • BMI is calculated by dividing mass in kg by height in meters squared. · Source page 56 · paragraph p56-paragraph-12

Food Production and Supply Chains

Connecting nutritional needs to agricultural sources helps students understand the environmental and logistical effort required to sustain human diets.

identify the basic steps of plant cultivation including soil preparation, sowing, and care
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
List three essential steps a farmer or urban gardener must take to cultivate a plant successfully.
Expected response
Preparation of the soil, sowing seeds or transplanting, and providing care like watering and pest control.
Scoring rule
Includes at least three distinct, accurate steps of cultivation.
Mastery evidence
Students list and describe the main activities involved in cultivating plants.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants only need water and sunlight, not specific soil preparation or pest control.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Cultivating plants involves specific sequential activities like soil preparation, sowing, and care. · Source page 70 · paragraph p70-paragraph-4
sequence the stages of a food supply chain from production to consumption
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Draw a flowchart showing the steps a tomato takes from being grown on a farm to being eaten at home.
Expected response
Flowchart includes growing/harvesting, transportation, selling at a market/store, and purchasing/preparing at home.
Scoring rule
Logical sequence of at least four distinct supply chain stages.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly order the steps a food item takes from a farm to a local market.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Food in supermarkets is produced in the back of the store.
Local prerequisites
identify-agriculture
Scientific support
  • A supply chain involves multiple activities and distribution methods to bring a product to the consumer. · Source page 65 · paragraph p65-paragraph-7
contrast the resource requirements and transportation steps of local versus imported foods
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain why an apple imported from another country might cost more and take longer to arrive than a mango grown in your town, using the concept of supply chain links.
Expected response
The imported apple has more links in its supply chain, requiring more transportation, fuel, and time to cross borders, whereas the local mango travels a shorter distance.
Scoring rule
Explanation explicitly references the number of links or distance in the supply chain as the cause for increased resources/time.
Mastery evidence
Students justify why imported foods require more resources and time than local foods.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Imported foods are always fresher than local foods.
Local prerequisites
sequence-supply-chain
Scientific support
  • Products from further away have more steps in their supply chain. · Source page 65 · paragraph p65-paragraph-7
construct a bar chart representing survey data on food consumption or origin
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using the data table showing how many students ate local vs. imported fruits, draw a bar chart with labeled axes and a title.
Expected response
A bar chart with 'Type of Fruit' on the x-axis, 'Number of Students' on the y-axis, correctly scaled bars, and a descriptive title.
Scoring rule
Chart includes title, labeled axes, correct scale, and accurate bar heights.
Mastery evidence
Students create an accurate bar chart from a given data table.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The height of a bar does not need to align with a specific numerical scale.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Graphical representation helps visualize study results easily. · Source page 69 · paragraph p69-paragraph-18
justify the separation of raw and cooked foods to maintain food safety
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Why is it important to use a different knife for cutting raw chicken and slicing cooked bread? Justify your answer.
Expected response
Using the same knife can transfer germs from the raw chicken to the bread, which can make you sick since the bread won't be cooked to kill the germs.
Scoring rule
Identifies the transfer of germs/contamination from raw to cooked food as the reason.
Mastery evidence
Students explain the health risks of cross-contamination between raw and cooked foods.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Washing hands once a day is enough to keep all food safe.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Raw foods must be separated from cooked foods. · Source page 53 · paragraph p53-paragraph-9

teach-classify-nutrients · 60 min · teach

Safety

Time rationale
15 minutes for introduction, 25 minutes for modeling the sorting process, and 20 minutes for guided group sorting.

practice-classify-nutrients · 75 min · practice

Reduce the number of food cards to 10 for students needing more time.

10 minutes setup, 45 minutes for sorting and gluing, 20 minutes for peer review.

assess-classify-nutrients · 60 min · assessment

Students complete a written table where they must classify a provided list of 10 foods (e.g., rice, chicken, orange) by their primary nutrient type and origin.

Limitations: BMI calculations do not account for muscle mass variations or specific developmental stages of individual children.; Caloric expenditure estimates are simplified averages and do not reflect individual metabolic rates.; Supply chain models omit complex economic factors like tariffs, subsidies, and global market fluctuations.

Nature and interactions

Students enter 4th grade with basic knowledge of plants, animals, and weather. This unit introduces formal ecological organization (biotic/abiotic, food chains, interactions) and connects it to Earth systems (weather measurement, geological hazards, risk mapping). The next grade will deepen into specific biome characteristics, complex biogeochemical cycles, and quantitative climate data analysis.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 2. Unit allocation: 6 planning weeks.

Ecological Interactions and Ecosystem Dynamics

Students build a foundational understanding of ecosystems by categorizing components, mapping energy flow, and analyzing interactions, which prepares them to predict ecological consequences.

classify components of a local environment into biotic and abiotic categories
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a list of 10 items found in a local park, classify each as biotic or abiotic.
Expected response
Biotic: trees, insects, fallen leaves, fungi. Abiotic: rocks, sunlight, soil, water.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct classification. Mastery requires 8/10.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 environmental items into biotic and abiotic categories.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All non-moving things in nature are abiotic.; Dead plants are considered abiotic.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Ecosystems contain biotic and abiotic components. · Source page 74 · paragraph p74-paragraph-16
construct a food chain model using producers, consumers, and decomposers
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using provided cards of local organisms, arrange them into a food chain and draw arrows showing energy flow.
Expected response
Grass (producer) -> Grasshopper (primary consumer) -> Frog (secondary consumer) -> Fungi (decomposer).
Scoring rule
Pass/Fail based on correct sequence and arrow direction indicating energy flow.
Mastery evidence
Students build a valid food chain with at least three trophic levels and correct directional arrows.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Energy flows from consumers to producers.; Decomposers are not part of the food chain.
Local prerequisites
g4-u3-eco-components
Scientific support
  • Energy enters the ecosystem through producers. · Source page 85 · paragraph p85-paragraph-10
distinguish the habitat location from the ecological niche function of a specific animal
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Read a description of an otter and underline its habitat in blue and its niche in red.
Expected response
Blue underline: riverbanks with abundant vegetation. Red underline: semi-aquatic predator that controls fish populations.
Scoring rule
1 point for correct habitat identification, 1 point for correct niche identification.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly identify the habitat and the niche from a descriptive paragraph of an animal.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Habitat and niche mean the exact same thing.; An animal's niche is only what it eats.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • A habitat is defined as the physical place where an organism lives. · Source page 104 · paragraph p104-paragraph-4
categorize ecological interactions as predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, or parasitism
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Read 5 short scenarios of animal interactions and label each with the correct ecological term.
Expected response
Scenario 1 (tick on dog): Parasitism. Scenario 2 (bees and flowers): Mutualism.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct label. Mastery is 4/5.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly label 4 out of 5 interaction scenarios.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All interactions result in one organism being harmed.; Competition only happens between different species.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Ecological interactions include predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism. · Source page 88 · paragraph p88-paragraph-10
predict the ecological consequences of removing a specific population from a food chain
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain what would happen to the frog and grass populations if all grasshoppers were removed from the food chain.
Expected response
The frog population would decrease due to lack of food, and the grass population would increase because fewer insects are eating it.
Scoring rule
1 point for predicting predator decrease, 1 point for predicting prey increase, 1 point for logical justification.
Mastery evidence
Students provide a logical prediction supported by evidence of energy flow disruption.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Removing one species only affects its direct predator or prey.; Ecosystems immediately replace missing species with new ones.
Local prerequisites
g4-u3-eco-foodchain, g4-u3-eco-interactions
Scientific support
  • The absence of an organism in a food chain prompts analysis of systemic consequences. · Source page 85 · paragraph p85-paragraph-4

Earth Systems, Hazards, and Risk Mitigation

Students transition from biological ecosystems to the physical Earth systems that impact them, learning to measure weather, model geological events, and evaluate community risks.

measure simulated rainfall volume using a graduated scale in millimeters
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Read the water level in three different simulated pluviometers and record the measurements in millimeters.
Expected response
26 mm, 15 mm, 42 mm.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct reading within +/- 2mm.
Mastery evidence
Students accurately read the water level on a millimeter scale within a 2mm margin of error.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Rainfall is measured by the weight of the water.; A wider container collects 'more' rain in terms of measurement depth.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Rainfall amount is determined by reading the water mark on a scale. · Source page 91 · paragraph p91-paragraph-15
classify geological events as internal or external phenomena
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Sort a list of events (earthquake, landslide, volcanic eruption, tsunami, rockfall) into internal and external phenomena.
Expected response
Internal: earthquake, volcanic eruption, tsunami. External: landslide, rockfall.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct classification. Mastery is 4/5.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly classify 4 out of 5 geological events.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All natural disasters come from inside the Earth.; Landslides are caused by tectonic plates directly.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support

demonstrate the release of gas in a simulated volcanic eruption using a chemical reaction
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Perform the volcano simulation and draw a diagram labeling the liquid mixture and the escaping gas.

Diagram showing the volcano structure, the liquid mixture inside, and bubbles labeled as carbon dioxide gas escaping the crater.
Scoring rule
Pass/Fail based on the presence of the labeled gas component in the diagram.

evaluate the vulnerability of specific locations using a community risk map

reasoning
Assessment task

Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

act-eco-comp-teach · 30 min · teach

Introduce the concepts of biotic and abiotic components. Show a tray of mixed items (rocks, soil, water, leaves, twigs, plastic insects) and model how to classify them into two distinct groups on the board.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally state the difference between biotic and abiotic components.
Materials
tray, rocks, soil, water in a sealed jar, leaves, twigs, plastic insects
Safety
Ensure soil is clean potting soil to avoid pathogens. Wash hands after handling.
Access and differentiation
Provide visual cue cards with symbols (a plant for biotic, a rock for abiotic) for students who need visual support.
Time rationale
10 minutes for introduction and definition, 15 minutes for modeling the sorting process, 5 minutes for closing questions.

act-eco-comp-prac1 · 60 min · practice

Students go on a guided walk around the schoolyard to observe the environment. They carry a clipboard and draw or write 5 biotic and 5 abiotic items they find, then return to class to share.

Mastery criterion

Materials
clipboards, paper, pencils
Safety
Establish clear boundaries for the schoolyard walk. Do not touch unknown plants or animals.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw items instead of writing words.
Time rationale
10 minutes prep and instructions, 30 minutes observation walk, 20 minutes sharing and categorizing in class.

act-eco-comp-prac2 · 60 min · practice

Provide students with nature magazines. They must cut out 10 pictures of environmental items and glue them onto a T-chart labeled Biotic and Abiotic.

Materials
nature magazines, scissors, glue, T-chart worksheets
Safety
Use blunt-tip scissors.
Access and differentiation
Pre-cut images for students with fine motor difficulties.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 35 minutes cutting and sorting, 15 minutes peer review.

act-eco-comp-assess · 30 min · assessment

Students are given a written list of 10 items found in a local park and must classify each as biotic or abiotic by checking the correct box.

Mastery criterion

Materials
assessment worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
