Limitations: Risk maps created in class are simplified educational models and do not replace professional geological surveys for actual emergency planning.; The volcano simulation demonstrates gas release and pressure but does not accurately represent magma thermodynamics or tectonic friction.; Ecological interaction scenarios are simplified; in reality, species often engage in multiple types of interactions simultaneously.

Solar System

Students enter with basic recognition of the Sun, Earth, and Moon from early grades. This unit formalizes the mechanics of their interactions (orbits, phases, eclipses) and expands the scope to the entire Solar System and historical models. In future grades, students should revisit these concepts to understand gravitational forces mathematically and explore stellar life cycles.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Earth, Moon, and Sun System Dynamics

Understanding the local celestial neighborhood is foundational before expanding to the broader solar system. This skill builds from the physical properties of the Sun and Moon to the dynamic interactions that cause observable phenomena like day/night, seasons, moon phases, and eclipses.

identify the internal and external layers of the Sun using a diagram
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Label a cross-section diagram of the Sun with its five main layers and write a one-sentence description of the core.
Expected response
Labels: Core, Radiative Zone, Convective Zone, Photosphere, Chromosphere. Core description: It is where the Sun's energy is produced.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correctly placed label and 1 point for an accurate description of the core's function.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly labels the core, radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere, and chromosphere on a blank diagram.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The Sun is a solid burning ball of fire.; The Sun has a solid surface like Earth.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The Sun's energy is generated in its core. · Source page 112 · paragraph p112-paragraph-4
explain the phenomena of day, night, and seasons as consequences of Earth's rotation and translation
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Write a paragraph explaining why it is night in El Salvador when it is day in Japan, and how Earth's translation combined with its axial tilt causes the wet and dry seasons in El Salvador.
Expected response
Day and night happen because Earth rotates on its axis. Seasons happen because Earth translates around the Sun while its axis is tilted.
Scoring rule
1 point for connecting Earth's rotation to the specific day/night difference between El Salvador and Japan, and 1 point for connecting translation and tilt to El Salvador's wet/dry seasons.
Mastery evidence
Student articulates that rotation causes day/night, and explicitly explains that the constant orientation of Earth's axial tilt during translation causes seasons, including local wet/dry seasons.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Seasons are caused by the Earth getting closer to or farther from the Sun.; The Sun moves around the Earth to create day and night.
Local prerequisites
earth-axial-tilt
Scientific support
  • Earth's rotation causes the day and night cycle. · Source page 120 · paragraph p120-paragraph-3
explain the 23-degree inclination of Earth's axis and its constant orientation
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Draw the Earth orbiting the Sun at four different points, ensuring the axis is drawn with a consistent 23-degree tilt pointing in the same direction.
Expected response
Drawings show the axis tilted and parallel to itself at all four positions.
Scoring rule
1 point for showing tilt, 1 point for consistent orientation.
Mastery evidence
Student describes the Earth's axis as tilted at 23 degrees and maintains this tilt as it orbits the Sun.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The Earth's axis points straight up and down.; The axis wiggles back and forth every year to cause seasons.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Earth's axis of rotation is tilted at 23 degrees. · Source page 119 · paragraph p119-paragraph-12
describe the precession and nutation movements of the Earth's axis
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the terms 'precession' and 'nutation' to their correct definitions regarding Earth's axis.
Expected response
Precession: change in orientation of the rotation axis. Nutation: periodic oscillation or wobble of the axis.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly defining precession and 1 point for nutation.
Mastery evidence
Student defines precession as the slow change in axis orientation and nutation as the periodic oscillation or wobble.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Earth only has two movements: rotation and translation.; The Earth's axis is perfectly stable and never changes its orientation.
Local prerequisites
earth-primary-movements
Scientific support
  • Nutation is the periodic oscillation of Earth's axis of rotation. · Source page 122 · paragraph p122-paragraph-5
summarize the physical characteristics of the Moon and the giant impact hypothesis of its formation
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Write two sentences describing the surface of the Moon and one sentence explaining the most accepted hypothesis of how it formed.
Expected response
The Moon has a rocky surface with craters and no atmosphere. It likely formed when a Mars-sized body collided with the early Earth.
Scoring rule
Mentions rocky surface/no atmosphere (1 pt) and the giant impact hypothesis (1 pt).
Mastery evidence
Student describes the Moon as a rocky body with no atmosphere and explains that it likely formed from debris after a massive collision with Earth.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The Moon is made of cheese or emits its own light.; The Moon was captured by Earth's gravity fully formed.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The most accepted hypothesis for the Moon's formation is a giant impact. · Source page 114 · paragraph p114-paragraph-7
predict the visible phase of the Moon based on its relative position to the Earth and Sun
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Given a diagram showing the Sun, Earth, and Moon in a 90-degree alignment, predict the moon phase visible from Earth and justify the answer.
Expected response
First or third quarter moon. We see half of the illuminated side because the Moon is at a 90-degree angle relative to the Earth and Sun.
Scoring rule
Correctly identifies the quarter phase (1 pt) and justifies it based on the viewing angle of the illuminated half (1 pt).
Mastery evidence
Student accurately determines the moon phase given a top-down diagram of the Sun, Earth, and Moon.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Moon phases are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.; The Moon changes its actual shape throughout the month.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Moon phases depend on the Moon's orbital position relative to Earth. · Source page 117 · paragraph p117-paragraph-5
differentiate the alignment conditions required to produce solar and lunar eclipses using a shadow model
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Given a scenario of a planet with two moons at different distances, predict which moon creates a larger shadow cone (umbra) on the planet and justify how this affects the duration of a solar eclipse.
Expected response
The closer moon creates a larger umbra on the planet, resulting in a longer solar eclipse.
Scoring rule
Correctly identifies the closer moon creates a larger umbra (1 pt) and links it to a longer eclipse duration (1 pt).
Mastery evidence
Student predicts the effects of moon distance on shadow cone size and eclipse duration, moving beyond simple alignment recall.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Eclipses happen every month.; A solar eclipse is when the Earth blocks the Sun.
Local prerequisites
moon-phases-modeling
Scientific support
  • A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. · Source page 124 · paragraph p124-paragraph-4

Solar System Composition and Models

After understanding the local Earth-Moon-Sun system, students expand their perspective to the entire solar system. This skill covers historical models of the universe, the classification of planets, minor celestial bodies, and human efforts to explore space.

compare the arrangement of celestial bodies in the geocentric and heliocentric models
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Create a Venn diagram comparing the geocentric and heliocentric models, noting what is at the center of each.
Expected response
Geocentric: Earth at center. Heliocentric: Sun at center. Both: Include planets and the Moon.
Scoring rule
Correctly identifies the center for both models (1 pt) and notes a similarity (1 pt).
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the center of the universe/solar system in both models and the relative motion of the planets.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The heliocentric model was always accepted by scientists.; The geocentric model placed the Sun at the center.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The heliocentric model places the Sun at the center. · Source page 110 · paragraph p110-paragraph-8
interpret scale models representing the relative distances of planets from the Sun
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using a scale where 1 step equals 0.4 Astronomical Units, calculate how many steps are needed to represent a planet that is 1.2 AU away from the Sun.
Expected response
3 steps.
Scoring rule
Correctly calculates the number of steps based on the provided scale (1 pt).
Mastery evidence
Student uses a scale to determine relative distances and recognizes that outer planets are much farther apart than inner planets.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Planets are evenly spaced out in the solar system.; Planets are very close to each other as seen in textbook illustrations.
Local prerequisites
historical-solar-models
Scientific support
  • Scale models can be used to represent astronomical distances. · Source page 111 · paragraph p111-paragraph-3
classify the planets of the solar system into rocky and gas giants based on their physical properties
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a data table of four unknown planets with their densities (e.g., 5.4 g/cm3 vs 1.3 g/cm3) and surface types, classify each as a rocky planet or gas giant and justify the classification.
Expected response
Planets with high density (>3 g/cm3) and solid surfaces are rocky; planets with low density (<2 g/cm3) and gaseous envelopes are gas giants.
Scoring rule
Correctly sorts the unknown planets (1 pt) and justifies using the density data (1 pt).
Mastery evidence
Student categorizes unknown planets into telluric (rocky) and gas giants by applying the criteria of density and composition.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All planets have a solid surface you can walk on.; Gas giants are made of air and have no mass.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The solar system contains rocky planets and gas giants. · Source page 125 · paragraph p125-paragraph-10
distinguish between asteroids, comets, meteoroids, meteors, and meteorites based on their composition and location
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the terms (asteroid, comet, meteoroid, meteor, meteorite) to their descriptions, including their location (space, atmosphere, ground).
Expected response
Comet: icy. Asteroid: rocky. Meteoroid: space rock. Meteor: burning in atmosphere. Meteorite: landed on Earth.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correct match.
Mastery evidence
Student defines asteroids and comets, and distinguishes between meteoroids (in space), meteors (in atmosphere), and meteorites (on ground).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Asteroids and comets are the exact same thing.; Shooting stars are actual stars falling from the sky.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Asteroids are rocky bodies smaller than planets but larger than meteoroids. · Source page 129 · paragraph p129-paragraph-6
  • Meteorites are meteoroids that reach the Earth's surface. · Source page 132 · paragraph p132-paragraph-6
differentiate between natural satellites and artificial satellites
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Explain the difference between a natural satellite and an artificial satellite, giving one example of each.
Expected response
Natural satellites are space bodies that orbit planets, like the Moon. Artificial satellites are machines made by humans put into orbit, like the Hubble telescope.
Scoring rule
Correctly defines both types (1 pt) and provides valid examples for both (1 pt).
Mastery evidence
Student explains that natural satellites are celestial bodies orbiting planets, while artificial satellites are human-made objects placed in orbit.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All satellites are machines built by humans.; The Moon is the only satellite in the universe.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Artificial satellites are distinct from natural satellites like the Moon. · Source page 130 · paragraph p130-paragraph-7
identify the main objectives of historical space missions such as Apollo and Voyager
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task

Expected response
Apollo 11 brought the first humans to the Moon. Voyager probes explored the outer planets and are leaving the solar system.
Scoring rule
Correctly identifies Apollo's lunar landing (1 pt) and Voyager's deep space/outer planet exploration (1 pt).
