Limitations: Scale models of the solar system in classrooms severely distort the relative sizes of planets and their distances.; The giant impact hypothesis is presented as the primary model for lunar formation, omitting alternative historical hypotheses for simplicity.; Orbital mechanics are simplified to circular or basic elliptical paths without addressing Kepler's laws mathematically.

Human body: matter and energy

Students enter Grade 4 with basic knowledge of external body parts and basic needs like eating and breathing. In this unit, they transition to understanding internal organ systems and their specific functions in processing matter and energy. They learn to view the body as an integrated set of systems rather than isolated parts. In future grades, they will revisit these systems to explore cellular respiration, hormonal regulation, and complex diseases.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 1. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Functions and structures of human body systems

Students must first understand the individual structures and specific functions of the digestive, respiratory, circulatory, and excretory systems before they can comprehend how these systems interact to sustain life.

sequence the organs of the digestive tract and their role in food transit
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a set of cards with digestive organ names, arrange them in the correct order of food transit and match each with a simple function description.
Expected response
Mouth (chewing), pharynx/esophagus (transit), stomach (mixing/acid), intestines (absorption).
Scoring rule
Passes if the sequence is anatomically correct and at least three organs are matched with their correct function.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly orders the digestive organs and states one basic function for each.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Food goes directly into the stomach without passing through the esophagus; The stomach is the only organ involved in digestion
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The mouth is the initial organ of the digestive system where mechanical digestion begins. · Source page 140 · paragraph p140-paragraph-5
distinguish mechanical and chemical digestion using macroscopic models
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Observe a demonstration of crushed food versus food mixed with a chemical solvent, and classify which represents mechanical digestion and which represents chemical digestion, providing a reason.
Expected response
Crushing represents mechanical digestion because the pieces get smaller but stay the same material. The solvent represents chemical digestion because the substance changes.
Scoring rule
Passes if both types are correctly identified and the justification mentions size reduction versus substance change.
Mastery evidence
Student differentiates between physical breakdown (mechanical) and substance transformation (chemical).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Chewing is the only form of digestion; Saliva only moistens food but does not change it chemically
Local prerequisites
digestive-sequence
Scientific support
  • Mechanical digestion by teeth reduces food size to facilitate chemical digestion by saliva. · Source page 140 · paragraph p140-paragraph-5
identify the primary gases exchanged during human respiration
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Complete a diagram showing a human face with arrows pointing in and out of the nose, labeling the primary gas needed for life and the primary waste gas expelled.
Expected response
Inward arrow labeled Oxygen; outward arrow labeled Carbon Dioxide.
Scoring rule
Passes if oxygen is identified as entering and carbon dioxide as exiting.
Mastery evidence
Student names oxygen as the required gas and carbon dioxide as the expelled waste gas.
Diagnostic hypotheses
We breathe in pure oxygen and breathe out pure carbon dioxide; Air is a single uniform gas
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Respiration involves taking in oxygen and eliminating carbon dioxide. · Source page 141 · paragraph p141-paragraph-5
model the movements of inspiration and expiration using a balloon mechanism
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using a bottle-and-balloon model, pull and push the bottom membrane and describe what happens to the inner balloons and which respiratory movement each action represents.
Expected response
Pulling the membrane inflates the inner balloons (inspiration). Pushing the membrane deflates them (expiration).
Scoring rule
Passes if the physical action is correctly paired with the terms inspiration and expiration.
Mastery evidence
Student manipulates a model to demonstrate how volume changes cause air to enter or leave the simulated lungs.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Lungs move on their own like muscles; Air forces the lungs to expand, rather than lung expansion drawing air in
Local prerequisites
respiratory-gases
Scientific support
  • Lungs expand and contract to move air, which can be modeled using balloons. · Source page 145 · paragraph p145-paragraph-18
classify blood vessels based on the direction of blood flow relative to the heart
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Read three short descriptions of blood vessels and classify each as an artery or a vein based on the direction of blood flow described.
Expected response
Vessels carrying blood from the heart to organs are arteries; vessels carrying blood from organs to the heart are veins.
Scoring rule
Passes if all descriptions are correctly classified based on flow direction.
Mastery evidence
Student distinguishes arteries from veins based on whether they carry blood away from or toward the heart.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All blood vessels do the same thing; Arteries only exist in the arms and veins only in the legs
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Arteries transport blood from the heart to the body's organs. · Source page 155 · paragraph p155-paragraph-8
describe the role of kidneys in filtering waste from the blood to produce urine
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Write a short paragraph explaining what happens to blood when it passes through the kidneys and what liquid is formed as a result.
Expected response
The kidneys filter waste out of the blood. This waste mixes with water to form urine, which is then eliminated.
Scoring rule
Passes if the response mentions filtering/cleaning blood and the production of urine.
Mastery evidence
Student explains that kidneys act as filters to remove waste substances from the blood.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Urine comes directly from the stomach; Kidneys digest food
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Kidneys are responsible for removing waste products from the blood. · Source page 160 · paragraph p160-paragraph-6

System integration and physiological responses

After understanding individual systems, students must reason about how these systems interact dynamically to meet the body's changing demands, such as during exercise or waste accumulation.

predict changes in vital capacity and breathing rate in response to physical activity
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Compare a person sitting down with a person running. Predict which person will displace more water in a spirometer model and justify the prediction using the body's need for oxygen.
Expected response
The running person will displace more water because exercise increases the body's demand for oxygen, causing deeper and faster breathing.
Scoring rule
Passes if the prediction is correct and the justification explicitly links physical activity to an increased need for oxygen.
Mastery evidence
Student justifies why breathing rate and air volume exchange increase after physical exertion.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Breathing rate is always constant; Exercise only affects the muscles, not the lungs
Local prerequisites
respiratory-mechanics
Scientific support
  • Physical exercise increases vital capacity because the body demands more oxygen. · Source page 145 · paragraph p145-paragraph-18
correlate heart rate variations with different levels of physical activity
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Measure resting pulse, then measure pulse after one minute of jumping. Explain why the number of beats per minute changed.
Expected response
The pulse increased after jumping because the heart has to pump blood faster to deliver oxygen and nutrients to the working muscles.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student records a higher active pulse and justifies it by the need to transport substances (blood/oxygen/nutrients) faster.
Mastery evidence
Student connects increased physical activity to an increased heart rate to supply nutrients and oxygen.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The heart beats at the same speed all day; Heart rate increases only when you are scared
Local prerequisites
circulatory-vessels
Scientific support
  • The heart pumps blood to all body organs, a process that adapts to physical demands. · Source page 151 · paragraph p151-paragraph-5
justify the circulatory system as the transport network connecting digestion, respiration, and excretion
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Draw a simple diagram showing the heart, lungs, intestines, and kidneys. Draw arrows showing what the blood picks up and drops off at each organ, and write a sentence justifying why the circulatory system is like a delivery truck.
Expected response
Blood picks up oxygen at lungs and nutrients at intestines, drops off waste at kidneys. It is like a truck because it transports necessary items to cells and takes away garbage.
Scoring rule
Passes if the transport of at least two specific substances (oxygen, nutrients, or waste) is correctly linked to their respective source/destination organs.
Mastery evidence
Student explains how blood acts as the vehicle moving nutrients from intestines, oxygen from lungs, and waste to kidneys.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Food and air travel through the same tubes; Systems work completely independently of each other
Local prerequisites
digestive-sequence, respiratory-gases, circulatory-vessels, excretory-filtration
Scientific support
  • The circulatory system transports nutrients, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and waste throughout the body. · Source page 161 · paragraph p161-paragraph-6
relate water consumption to the volume and characteristics of urine produced
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Analyze a scenario where Person A drinks 3 liters of water a day and Person B drinks 1 liter. Predict whose urine will be darker and explain why based on the concentration of waste.
Expected response
Person B will have darker urine because there is less water to mix with the body's waste, making it more concentrated.
Scoring rule
Passes if the prediction is correct and the reasoning mentions the ratio of water to waste substances.
Mastery evidence
Student infers that higher water intake dilutes waste, affecting urine color and volume.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Drinking water does not affect urine; Urine is just the water we drink that bypassed the stomach
Local prerequisites
excretory-filtration
Scientific support
  • Urine characteristics are determined by the waste substances produced by the body's use of nutrients. · Source page 159 · paragraph p159-paragraph-9
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

ds-teach-1 · 50 min · teach

Introduce the digestive system organs using a large wall diagram. Spend 15 minutes tracing the path of food from the mouth, through the esophagus, to the stomach and intestines. Spend 20 minutes having students create their own labeled diagrams in their notebooks. Spend 15 minutes discussing the basic function of each organ (mouth for chewing, esophagus for transit, stomach for mixing, intestines for absorption).

Mastery criterion
Student correctly labels the mouth, esophagus, stomach, and intestines in order.
Materials
Large wall diagram of digestive system, Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
Ensure students remain seated while drawing to avoid tripping over chairs.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn outlines for students who struggle with drawing.
Time rationale
15 mins for direct instruction, 20 mins for drawing, 15 mins for discussion ensures thorough initial exposure.

ds-practice-1 · 50 min · practice

Students work in pairs with a set of 10 cards (5 organ names, 5 functions). Spend 10 minutes reviewing the organs. Spend 25 minutes playing a matching game where they must pair the organ with its function and place them in the correct transit order. Spend 15 minutes reviewing the correct sequence as a class.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly pairs at least 4 out of 5 organs with their functions and places them in order.
Materials
Sets of organ and function cards
Safety
Ensure card edges are rounded to prevent paper cuts.
Access and differentiation
Include visual icons on the cards for emerging readers.
Time rationale
10 mins review, 25 mins active matching, 15 mins class review allows for repeated exposure and correction.

ds-practice-2 · 50 min · practice

Students create a 3D paper model of the digestive tract. Spend 10 minutes cutting out organ shapes. Spend 25 minutes gluing them in the correct sequence onto a body outline. Spend 15 minutes writing one sentence next to each organ describing its function.

Mastery criterion
Student's 3D model shows the correct anatomical sequence and includes accurate function descriptions.
Materials
Paper organ cutouts, Glue, Body outline sheets, Scissors
Safety
Use blunt-tip scissors for cutting.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-cut shapes for students with fine motor difficulties.
Time rationale
10 mins cutting, 25 mins assembly, 15 mins writing provides a tactile learning experience with adequate time for each step.

ds-assess-1 · 30 min · assessment

Administer a written assessment where students are given a list of digestive organs and must draw arrows to show the path of food, then write one basic function for each organ.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly orders the digestive organs and states one basic function for each.
Materials
Printed assessment sheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow oral responses for students with writing difficulties.
Time rationale
30 minutes is sufficient for a focused, independent written task.

dt-teach-1 · 60 min · teach

Demonstrate mechanical vs. chemical digestion. Spend 15 minutes crushing a cracker (mechanical). Spend 15 minutes placing a cracker in water and another in vinegar to observe changes (chemical model). Spend 30 minutes discussing how crushing changes size but not substance, while the liquid changes the substance's properties.

Mastery criterion
Student can verbally distinguish between physical breakdown and substance transformation.
Materials
Crackers, Water, Vinegar, Clear cups, Pestle or heavy spoon
Safety
Ensure students do not eat the crackers used in the demonstration. Use safety goggles when handling vinegar.
Access and differentiation
Use larger, more visible food items if needed for visual clarity.
Time rationale
15 mins for mechanical demo, 15 mins for chemical demo setup and observation, 30 mins for deep discussion and conceptualization.

dt-practice-1 · 60 min · practice

Students perform their own digestion modeling. Spend 20 minutes crushing chalk (mechanical). Spend 20 minutes placing chalk in vinegar (chemical). Spend 20 minutes writing a comparison of the two processes in their notebooks, identifying which represents mechanical and which represents chemical digestion.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies crushing as mechanical and dissolving as chemical digestion in their written comparison.
Materials
Chalk pieces, Vinegar, Small cups, Popsicle sticks for crushing
Safety
Ensure good ventilation when using vinegar. Do not ingest chalk or vinegar.
Access and differentiation
Provide a graphic organizer for the written comparison.
Time rationale
20 mins per activity phase ensures students have time to observe, process, and document their findings.

dt-assess-1 · 40 min · assessment

Students observe a video or live demonstration of paper being torn (mechanical) and paper being burned (chemical - modeled via video only for safety). They must write a paragraph classifying each and relating it to human digestion.

Mastery criterion
Student differentiates between physical breakdown (mechanical) and substance transformation (chemical) with correct justification.
Materials
Video of paper tearing and burning, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Do not perform burning in the classroom; use video only.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters for the justification paragraph.
Time rationale
10 mins observation, 30 mins for writing and refining the justification.

dt-retrieval-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Quick recall activity: Spend 10 minutes reviewing previous notes. Spend 20 minutes sorting 10 scenario cards (e.g., 'chewing an apple', 'saliva breaking down starch') into 'Mechanical' or 'Chemical' digestion piles.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly sorts at least 8 out of 10 scenario cards.
Materials
Scenario cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read cards aloud for students who need reading support.
Time rationale
10 mins review and 20 mins sorting provides a focused retrieval practice session.

dt-retrieval-2 · 30 min · retrieval

Think-pair-share retrieval: Spend 10 minutes individually writing down the definitions of mechanical and chemical digestion from memory. Spend 10 minutes discussing with a partner. Spend 10 minutes sharing with the class.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately recalls and communicates the difference between the two types of digestion.
Materials
Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw their definitions instead of writing.
Time rationale
10 mins per phase ensures structured recall and peer validation.

rg-teach-1 · 40 min · teach

Introduce respiratory gases. Spend 15 minutes explaining that humans breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Spend 15 minutes drawing a large face on the board with arrows indicating gas exchange. Spend 10 minutes having students copy the diagram and label the gases.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly labels oxygen entering and carbon dioxide exiting the nose/mouth.
Materials
Whiteboard, Markers, Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-drawn face for students to label.
Time rationale
15 mins instruction, 15 mins modeling, 10 mins student practice is a solid introductory block.

rg-practice-1 · 60 min · practice

Create a 'gas exchange' comic strip. Spend 15 minutes brainstorming the journey of an oxygen molecule entering the body and a carbon dioxide molecule leaving. Spend 45 minutes drawing and coloring a 4-panel comic strip illustrating this process.

Mastery criterion
Comic strip accurately depicts oxygen going in and carbon dioxide coming out.
Materials
Comic strip templates, Colored pencils, Markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to work in pairs to complete the comic.
Time rationale
15 mins brainstorming and 45 mins drawing allows for creative expression of the concept.

rg-assess-1 · 30 min · assessment

Students are given a diagram of a human face with two blank arrows (one pointing in, one pointing out). They must label the arrows with the correct gases.

Mastery criterion
Student names oxygen as the required gas and carbon dioxide as the expelled waste gas.
Materials
Assessment diagrams, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank (Oxygen, Carbon Dioxide, Nitrogen) for spelling support.
Time rationale
30 minutes is ample time for a simple labeling assessment.

rm-teach-1 · 60 min · teach

Demonstrate lung mechanics using a pre-made bottle-and-balloon model. Spend 20 minutes showing how pulling the bottom membrane inflates the inner balloons (inspiration) and pushing deflates them (expiration). Spend 40 minutes letting students take turns manipulating the model and describing what they feel and see.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies pulling as inspiration and pushing as expiration.
Materials
Bottle-and-balloon lung model
Safety
Ensure the cut edges of the plastic bottle are covered with tape to prevent scratches.
Access and differentiation
Verbally guide students who need help connecting the model parts to human anatomy.
Time rationale
20 mins demonstration and 40 mins hands-on exploration ensures all students interact with the model.

rm-practice-1 · 60 min · practice

Students build their own simple lung models. Spend 30 minutes assembling a model using a plastic cup, a straw, and two balloons. Spend 30 minutes testing the models and writing down how the volume changes affect the air inside.

Mastery criterion
Student successfully builds a working model and writes that expanding the space pulls air in.
Materials
Plastic cups, Straws, Balloons, Tape, Rubber bands
Safety
Supervise the use of rubber bands to prevent snapping.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-assembled models for students with severe fine motor limitations.
Time rationale
30 mins assembly and 30 mins testing/writing provides a full hands-on engineering and observation cycle.

rm-practice-2 · 60 min · practice

Role-play respiratory mechanics. Spend 20 minutes assigning roles (diaphragm, lungs, air). Spend 40 minutes practicing and performing a physical representation where the 'diaphragm' moves down, the 'lungs' expand, and 'air' rushes in, then reversing the process.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately performs their role in the sequence of inspiration and expiration.
Materials
Space to move around
Safety
Ensure the area is clear of obstacles to prevent tripping during the role-play.
Access and differentiation
Assign less physically demanding roles (like 'air') to students with mobility issues.
Time rationale
20 mins setup and 40 mins active role-play solidifies the mechanical sequence kinesthetically.

rm-assess-1 · 40 min · assessment

Students are given a bottle-and-balloon model one by one. They must demonstrate inspiration and expiration, and verbally explain which action represents which respiratory movement.

Mastery criterion
Student manipulates a model to demonstrate how volume changes cause air to enter or leave the simulated lungs.
Materials
Bottle-and-balloon lung model
Safety
Ensure the model is sturdy and safe to handle.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to point to diagrams if they are non-verbal.
Time rationale
40 minutes allows time to assess each student individually or in small groups.

cv-teach-1 · 45 min · teach

Introduce arteries and veins. Spend 20 minutes explaining that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood to the heart. Spend 25 minutes drawing a simplified circulatory loop on the board, using red for arteries and blue for veins (noting this is a pedagogical convention).

Mastery criterion
Student can state the direction of blood flow for arteries and veins.
Materials
Whiteboard, Red and blue markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use clear directional arrows for visual learners.
Time rationale
20 mins explanation and 25 mins diagramming provides a clear, paced introduction.

cv-practice-1 · 65 min · practice

Vessel mapping activity. Spend 15 minutes reviewing the concepts. Spend 35 minutes having students trace a body outline on large paper and draw the heart, adding red yarn for arteries (away) and blue yarn for veins (toward). Spend 15 minutes labeling the yarn.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly places and labels arteries (away from heart) and veins (toward heart).
Materials
Large paper, Red and blue yarn, Glue, Markers
Safety
Ensure students do not wrap yarn around fingers or necks.
Access and differentiation
Provide smaller, desk-sized templates for students who cannot work on the floor.
Time rationale
15 mins review, 35 mins active mapping, 15 mins labeling allows for a comprehensive mapping exercise.

cv-assess-1 · 30 min · assessment

Students read three short descriptions of blood vessels (e.g., 'This vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs') and classify each as an artery or a vein.

Mastery criterion
Student distinguishes arteries from veins based on whether they carry blood away from or toward the heart.
Materials
Printed assessment sheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the descriptions aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
30 minutes is sufficient for reading and classifying three descriptions.

ef-teach-1 · 50 min · teach

Introduce the kidneys as filters. Spend 20 minutes explaining how blood passes through the kidneys, which remove waste to form urine. Spend 30 minutes demonstrating filtration by pouring a mixture of water and sand through a coffee filter, comparing the filter to a kidney.

Mastery criterion
Student can explain that kidneys filter waste from the blood.
Materials
Coffee filters, Funnels, Water, Sand, Clear cups
Safety
Ensure students do not drink the water/sand mixture.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual diagram of the kidney alongside the physical filter model.
Time rationale
20 mins explanation and 30 mins demonstration provides a strong analogy for the concept.

ef-practice-1 · 60 min · practice

Students perform their own filtration experiment. Spend 20 minutes setting up funnels with different materials (paper towel, cotton). Spend 20 minutes pouring 'dirty' water (water with soil) through them. Spend 20 minutes writing how this models the kidney cleaning the blood.

Mastery criterion
Student writes that the filter catches waste while letting clean liquid pass, just like a kidney.
Materials
Funnels, Paper towels, Cotton balls, Water, Soil, Cups
Safety
Wash hands after handling soil. Do not ingest the materials.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to dictate their written response.
Time rationale
20 mins setup, 20 mins experiment, 20 mins reflection ensures a complete inquiry cycle.

ef-assess-1 · 30 min · assessment

Students write a short paragraph explaining what happens to blood when it passes through the kidneys and what liquid is formed as a result.

Mastery criterion
Student explains that kidneys act as filters to remove waste substances from the blood to produce urine.
Materials
Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank (Blood, Filter, Waste, Urine, Kidney).
Time rationale
30 minutes is adequate for drafting and reviewing a short paragraph.

er-teach-1 · 50 min · teach

Introduce the link between exercise and respiration. Spend 15 minutes discussing why the body needs oxygen. Spend 20 minutes having students count their breaths for one minute while sitting. Spend 15 minutes discussing what they expect to happen if they run.

Mastery criterion
Student predicts that breathing rate will increase with exercise due to oxygen demand.
Materials
Stopwatch
Safety
Ensure students are seated calmly during the resting measurement.
Access and differentiation
Help students who struggle with counting by tapping the desk for each breath.
Time rationale
15 mins discussion, 20 mins baseline measurement, 15 mins prediction sets up the reasoning task.

er-practice-1 · 60 min · practice

Test the exercise-respiration link. Spend 20 minutes having students jog in place for two minutes, then immediately count their breaths for one minute. Spend 40 minutes graphing the resting vs. active breath counts and writing a justification for the difference based on oxygen need.

Mastery criterion
Student graphs the data and justifies the increase by stating the body needs more oxygen during exercise.
Materials
Stopwatch, Graph paper, Pencils
Safety
Ensure students have enough space to jog in place without hitting others. Do not force students with asthma to overexert.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-labeled graph axes.
Time rationale
20 mins active testing and 40 mins graphing/writing allows for careful data processing.

er-assess-1 · 40 min · assessment

Students are given a scenario comparing a person sitting and a person running. They must predict which person will displace more water in a spirometer model and justify the prediction using the body's need for oxygen.

Mastery criterion
Student justifies why breathing rate and air volume exchange increase after physical exertion.
Materials
Printed scenarios, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow oral justification for students who struggle with writing.
Time rationale
40 minutes provides time to read the scenario, think, and write a reasoned response.

ec-teach-1 · 50 min · teach

Introduce the link between exercise and circulation. Spend 20 minutes teaching students how to find their pulse on their wrist or neck. Spend 30 minutes having them measure their resting pulse for one minute and recording it, discussing what the pulse represents.

Mastery criterion
Student can locate their pulse and record their resting heart rate.
Materials
Stopwatch
Safety
Instruct students not to press too hard on their necks.
Access and differentiation
Use a digital pulse oximeter for students who cannot find their pulse manually.
Time rationale
20 mins instruction on finding pulse and 30 mins measurement/discussion ensures accuracy.

ec-practice-1 · 60 min · practice

Test the exercise-circulation link. Spend 20 minutes having students do jumping jacks for one minute, then immediately measure their pulse. Spend 40 minutes comparing this to their resting pulse and writing an explanation of why the heart beats faster (to deliver oxygen/nutrients).

Mastery criterion
Student records a higher active pulse and justifies it by the need to transport substances faster.
Materials
Stopwatch, Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
Ensure safe spacing for jumping jacks. Monitor students for overexertion.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to do arm circles instead of jumping jacks if mobility is limited.
Time rationale
20 mins activity/measurement and 40 mins analysis/writing provides a complete reasoning cycle.

ec-assess-1 · 40 min · assessment

Students are given a data table showing a person's heart rate at rest and after running. They must write a paragraph explaining why the number of beats per minute changed, referencing oxygen and nutrients.

Mastery criterion
Student connects increased physical activity to an increased heart rate to supply nutrients and oxygen.
Materials
Printed data tables, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a cloze paragraph (fill-in-the-blanks) for students needing support.
Time rationale
40 minutes allows for careful analysis of the data and drafting a reasoned explanation.

sti-teach-1 · 60 min · teach

Introduce the circulatory system as a transport network. Spend 20 minutes reviewing the functions of the lungs, intestines, and kidneys. Spend 40 minutes drawing a large map on the board showing blood picking up oxygen (lungs) and nutrients (intestines), and dropping off waste (kidneys).

Mastery criterion
Student can verbally explain that blood connects the other systems by transporting materials.
Materials
Whiteboard, Colored markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use physical props (e.g., a toy truck) to model the blood moving between stations.
Time rationale
20 mins review and 40 mins mapping integrates prior knowledge into a new conceptual framework.

sti-practice-1 · 60 min · practice

Create an integration poster. Spend 15 minutes planning a diagram showing the heart, lungs, intestines, and kidneys. Spend 45 minutes drawing the organs and adding arrows with labels showing what blood picks up and drops off at each location.

Mastery criterion
Poster accurately shows oxygen/nutrients being picked up and waste being dropped off.
Materials
Poster board, Markers, Rulers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-printed organ images for students to glue and connect with arrows.
Time rationale
15 mins planning and 45 mins drawing allows for a detailed, accurate synthesis project.

sti-practice-2 · 60 min · practice

Role-play the transport system. Spend 20 minutes setting up stations (Lungs, Intestines, Kidneys, Cells) and assigning roles (Blood cells carrying tokens). Spend 40 minutes running the simulation where 'blood' picks up 'oxygen' (blue tokens) and 'nutrients' (green tokens), delivers them to 'cells', and takes 'waste' (red tokens) to 'kidneys'.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly navigates the stations, picking up and dropping off the correct tokens.
Materials
Colored tokens (blue, green, red), Signs for stations
Safety
Ensure clear walking paths between stations to prevent collisions.
Access and differentiation
Pair students up to navigate the stations together.
Time rationale
20 mins setup and 40 mins active simulation solidifies the dynamic nature of the integration.

sti-assess-1 · 45 min · assessment

Students draw a simple diagram showing the heart, lungs, intestines, and kidneys, draw arrows showing what blood picks up and drops off, and write a sentence justifying why the circulatory system is like a delivery truck.

Mastery criterion
Student explains how blood acts as the vehicle moving nutrients, oxygen, and waste to their correct locations.
Materials
Blank paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a template with the organs already drawn, requiring only the arrows and sentence.
Time rationale
45 minutes provides ample time for drawing, labeling, and writing the justification.

sti-retrieval-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Quick mapping recall. Spend 10 minutes reviewing the transport concept. Spend 20 minutes having students quickly sketch the four main organs (heart, lungs, intestines, kidneys) on a whiteboard and draw the transport arrows from memory.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly draws the transport arrows between the organs from memory.
Materials
Small whiteboards, Dry erase markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use their notes for the first 5 minutes of the sketching phase.
Time rationale
10 mins review and 20 mins sketching is a fast-paced retrieval exercise.

sti-retrieval-2 · 30 min · retrieval

Verbal explanation recall. Spend 15 minutes having students write a short 'elevator pitch' explaining how the body systems work together. Spend 15 minutes having them present their pitch to a partner without looking at their notes.

Mastery criterion
Student verbally explains the integration of the systems accurately without notes.
Materials
Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a list of key words (oxygen, nutrients, waste, blood) to include in the pitch.
Time rationale
15 mins writing and 15 mins speaking provides structured verbal retrieval practice.

wwr-teach-1 · 45 min · teach

Introduce water regulation. Spend 15 minutes explaining that urine is a mix of water and waste. Spend 30 minutes demonstrating concentration by mixing a set amount of yellow food coloring (representing waste) into a small amount of water (dark) and a large amount of water (light).

Mastery criterion
Student can explain that more water makes the waste less concentrated (lighter color).
Materials
Clear cups, Water, Yellow food coloring
Safety
Ensure students do not drink the colored water.
Access and differentiation
Use a very stark contrast in water volumes to make the color difference obvious.
Time rationale
15 mins explanation and 30 mins demonstration clearly models the concept of concentration.

wwr-practice-1 · 65 min · practice

Students model water regulation. Spend 20 minutes having students mix 1 drop of coloring into 50ml of water and 1 drop into 200ml of water. Spend 45 minutes writing a scenario about two people drinking different amounts of water and explaining why their urine would look like the two cups.

Mastery criterion
Student writes that the person drinking less water has more concentrated, darker urine.
Materials
Clear cups, Water, Food coloring, Droppers, Notebooks
Safety
Do not ingest the colored water. Clean up spills promptly to avoid slipping.
Access and differentiation
Provide a structured scenario template for the writing portion.
Time rationale
20 mins modeling and 45 mins writing allows for deep reasoning and application to a real-world scenario.

wwr-assess-1 · 30 min · assessment

Students analyze a written scenario where Person A drinks 3 liters of water a day and Person B drinks 1 liter. They must predict whose urine will be darker and explain why based on the concentration of waste.

Mastery criterion
Student infers that higher water intake dilutes waste, affecting urine color and volume.
Materials
Printed scenarios, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw the cups of water and urine to support their written explanation.
Time rationale
30 minutes is sufficient for reading, predicting, and justifying the response.

Limitations: The models used for digestion (vinegar/gummies) and respiration (balloons) are macroscopic simplifications that do not capture cellular-level chemical exchanges.; Heart rate and breathing rate measurements are subject to student error and should not be used for medical diagnosis.; The distinction between oxygenated and deoxygenated blood using red and blue colors is a pedagogical convention, not an anatomical reality.; Activities involving bodily fluids (like observing urine) are strictly observational at home; no bodily fluids are handled in the classroom.

Human body: motion and interactions

Students enter Grade 4 with basic knowledge of external body parts and the five senses. In this unit, they advance to understanding internal systems: the musculoskeletal system for support and protection of vital organs, and the nervous system for processing sensory input and coordinating responses. The prerequisite logic dictates that students first identify anatomical structures before modeling their mechanical interactions, and finally predicting coordinated responses to stimuli. Similarly, for the reproductive system, identifying distinct male and female organs precedes classifying them, understanding fertilization and menstruation, and relating hormonal changes to puberty. In Grade 5, students will revisit these systems to explore cellular-level functions and more complex metabolic processes.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Integration of the locomotor and nervous systems in the human body

Students must understand how the skeletal and muscular systems provide structure, movement, and protection, and how the nervous system coordinates these actions based on sensory input.

identify major bones, joints, and the vital organs they protect
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a blank diagram of the human skeleton, label the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, circle three joints, and draw/label the brain, heart, and lungs in their protected locations.
Expected response
Labels placed correctly on the bones. Circles on joints. Brain drawn in skull, heart and lungs drawn within the ribs.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct bone/joint label, 1 point per correctly placed vital organ. Minimum 8 out of 11 to pass.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly points out major bones and joints, and identifies where the brain, heart, and lungs are protected.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Bones are solid and dead structures; The skeleton only provides shape and has no protective function
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The skeleton is a set of bones providing a firm structure and protection. · Source page 166 · paragraph p166-paragraph-7
  • The skeleton protects vital organs like the brain, heart, and lungs. · Source page 168 · paragraph p168-paragraph-9
classify types of joints based on their mobility
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the type of joint (immobile, semi-mobile, mobile) to its description and provide one example of where a mobile joint is found.
Expected response
Immobile: no movement. Semi-mobile: little movement. Mobile: moves in many directions (e.g., knee, elbow).
Scoring rule
Passes if all three types are correctly matched to their movement description.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly classifies joints as immobile, semi-mobile, or mobile.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All joints move in the same way; Immobile joints are not actually joints
Local prerequisites
identify-skeletal-structures
Scientific support
  • Joints are classified by their range of motion into immobile, semi-mobile, and mobile. · Source page 170 · paragraph p170-paragraph-4
demonstrate how muscles pull on bones to create movement using a mechanical model
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using a cardboard and string model of an arm, pull the string and describe what happens to the cardboard pieces.
Expected response
When the string is pulled, it acts like a muscle pulling on the bone, causing the arm to bend at the joint.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student explicitly states that the muscle pulls the bone to create movement.
Mastery evidence
Student manipulates a model to show that muscle contraction pulls the bone, causing the joint to bend.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Muscles push bones to move them; Bones move on their own without muscles
Local prerequisites
identify-joint-types
Scientific support
  • Muscles attach to bones and pull them to allow movement. · Source page 171 · paragraph p171-paragraph-8
identify the five senses and their corresponding organs
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
List the five senses and write the organ responsible for each.
Expected response
Sight (eyes), Hearing (ears), Smell (nose), Taste (tongue), Touch (skin).
Scoring rule
Passes if all 5 senses and organs are correctly paired.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly pairs each of the five senses with its corresponding organ.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Senses work independently of the body's nervous system
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The five senses correspond to the ears, nose, eyes, tongue, and skin. · Source page 180 · paragraph p180-paragraph-4
locate the brain, spinal cord, and nerves on a human body outline
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Draw the central and peripheral nervous system on a blank human silhouette, using different colors for the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
Expected response
Drawing shows the brain in the head, connected to a spinal cord running down the center, with nerves branching out to the arms and legs.
Scoring rule
Passes if all three components are drawn in their correct relative anatomical positions.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately places the brain in the head, the spinal cord down the back, and nerves branching out to the limbs.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The brain is the only part of the nervous system; Nerves are the same as blood vessels
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The nervous system relates functions and stimuli of different body parts. · Source page 182 · paragraph p182-paragraph-4
identify the lobes of the brain and the cerebellum
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a diagram of the brain, label the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, occipital lobe, temporal lobe, and cerebellum.
Expected response
Labels placed correctly on the corresponding sections of the brain diagram.
Scoring rule
Passes if at least 4 out of 5 structures are correctly labeled.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly labels the frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, as well as the cerebellum.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The brain is a single, uniform mass without distinct sections
Local prerequisites
map-nervous-system
Scientific support
  • The brain includes the frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, and the cerebellum. · Source page 182 · paragraph p182-paragraph-3
sequence the path of a sensory stimulus from a sense organ to the brain
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Order the provided cards to show what happens when you touch a hot surface, from the moment of touch to the brain registering pain.
Expected response
1. Skin touches hot surface. 2. Nerves in skin detect heat. 3. Signal travels up nerves to spinal cord and brain. 4. Brain registers pain.
Scoring rule
Passes if the sequence strictly follows the receptor to nerve to brain pathway.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly orders the steps from stimulus detection to brain processing.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Sense organs process information themselves without the brain; Reaction happens before the brain receives the signal
Local prerequisites
identify-senses, map-nervous-system
Scientific support
  • Neurons capture information from sense organs and send it to the brain. · Source page 185 · paragraph p185-paragraph-5
predict the coordinated musculoskeletal response to a specific environmental stimulus
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Read the scenario: You see a ball flying towards your face. Write a short paragraph predicting how your nervous, muscular, and skeletal systems will work together to catch or dodge it.
Expected response
The eyes see the ball and send a signal to the brain. The brain decides to catch it and sends signals through nerves to the arm muscles. The muscles pull on the arm bones to move the hands and catch the ball.
Scoring rule
Passes if the response includes sensory input, brain processing, and muscle-bone interaction for movement.
Mastery evidence
Student logically describes how the nervous system receives a stimulus and commands the musculoskeletal system to react.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Movement happens independently of the nervous system; Only one system works at a time
Local prerequisites
model-muscle-bone-interaction, trace-sensory-pathway
Scientific support
  • We respond to stimuli through the joint action of the nervous and musculoskeletal systems. · Source page 177 · paragraph p177-paragraph-5

Structure of the human reproductive system and changes during puberty

Students need to identify the basic anatomical structures of the male and female reproductive systems, understand fertilization and menstruation, and relate biological changes to hormones during puberty.

identify the main organs of the female reproductive system on a diagram
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a diagram of the female reproductive system, label the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina.
Expected response
Labels correctly placed: ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, vagina.
Scoring rule
Passes if at least 3 out of 4 organs are correctly labeled.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly labels the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina on a diagram.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The reproductive system is the same in all humans; The stomach is where a baby grows
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The female reproductive system consists of the vagina, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. · Source page 188 · paragraph p188-paragraph-7
identify the main organs of the male reproductive system on a diagram
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a diagram of the male reproductive system, label the testes, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, urethra, and penis.
Expected response
Labels correctly placed for all 7 organs.
Scoring rule
Passes if at least 5 out of 7 organs are correctly labeled.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly labels the testes, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, urethra, and penis on a diagram.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Male and female internal organs are identical
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The male reproductive system includes testes, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, urethra, and penis. · Source page 188 · paragraph p188-paragraph-7
classify organs as belonging to the male or female reproductive system
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Sort the following organs into a two-column table for Male and Female: Uterus, Testes, Ovaries, Prostate, Vagina, Vas Deferens.
Expected response
Male: Testes, Prostate, Vas Deferens. Female: Uterus, Ovaries, Vagina.
Scoring rule
Passes if all 6 organs are placed in the correct column.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately sorts a list of reproductive organs into male and female categories.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Both sexes have a uterus; Ovaries and testes perform completely unrelated functions
Local prerequisites
identify-female-reproductive-organs, identify-male-reproductive-organs
Scientific support
  • Male and female reproductive systems have distinct organs. · Source page 188 · paragraph p188-paragraph-7
explain the basic processes of fertilization and menstruation
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Write a brief definition for fertilization and menstruation, mentioning the specific organ where each occurs.
Expected response
Fertilization is the meeting of the ovocyte and male gamete in the oviducts. Menstruation is the shedding of the endometrium from the uterus when there is no fertilization.
Scoring rule
Passes if both processes are defined and linked to the correct organ.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the oviducts as the site of fertilization and the uterus as the site of menstruation.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Menstruation is an illness; Fertilization happens in the uterus
Local prerequisites
identify-female-reproductive-organs
Scientific support
  • Fertilization occurs in the oviducts. · Source page 189 · paragraph p189-paragraph-22
  • Menstruation is the shedding of the endometrium from the uterus. · Source page 189 · paragraph p189-paragraph-24
relate the role of sex hormones to physical changes during puberty
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Match the hormone to the biological sex it primarily affects during puberty, and list one reason why these hormones are important.
Expected response
Testosterone matches Male. Estrogen and Progesterone match Female. They are important because they cause the bodily changes during puberty.
Scoring rule
Passes if hormones are correctly matched to the sexes and the role in causing puberty changes is stated.
Mastery evidence
Student links specific hormones to the onset of puberty changes.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Puberty happens at the exact same age for everyone; Changes during puberty are only external
Local prerequisites
compare-reproductive-systems
Scientific support
  • Puberty consists of bodily changes produced mainly by sex hormones. · Source page 190 · paragraph p190-paragraph-5
list care practices for the reproductive system
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Write a list of three care practices for maintaining a healthy reproductive system.
Expected response
Daily bathing, wearing clean underwear, regular medical checkups.
Scoring rule
Passes if three valid care practices are listed.
Mastery evidence
Student lists at least three appropriate care or hygiene practices for the reproductive system.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The reproductive system does not require special care
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • It is important to list and practice care for the reproductive system. · Source page 190 · paragraph p190-paragraph-9
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-skeletal-structures · 45 min · teach

Introduce the human skeleton using a large anatomical poster. Point out and name the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and major joints (elbows, knees, shoulders). Have students repeat the names and locate the general area on their own bodies over their clothes.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally repeat the names of the 5 major bones and 3 joints when pointed to on the poster.
Materials
Large anatomical poster of the human skeleton, Pointer stick
Safety
Ensure students do not poke or hit themselves or others when locating bones on their bodies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a smaller, desk-sized version of the poster for students with visual impairments.
Time rationale
15 minutes for introduction, 20 minutes for guided identification, and 10 minutes for verbal repetition and checking.

prac-clay-bones · 45 min · practice

Students use modeling clay to form the shapes of the skull, ribs, spine, femur, and humerus, placing them on a cardboard body outline. They must place small clay balls to represent the joints.

Mastery criterion
Clay bones are placed in the correct anatomical positions on the cardboard outline.
Materials
Modeling clay, Cardboard body outlines, Reference diagrams
Safety
Wash hands after using clay. Do not ingest clay.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-rolled clay cylinders for students with fine motor difficulties.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup and instruction, 25 minutes modeling and placing, 10 minutes cleanup and review.

prac-skeleton-puzzle · 45 min · practice

Students work in pairs to assemble a life-size paper skeleton puzzle on the floor, labeling the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and circling the joints with a marker.

Mastery criterion
Puzzle is assembled correctly and all required bones and joints are accurately labeled.
Materials
Pre-cut paper skeleton pieces, Markers, Tape
Safety
Ensure clear floor space to prevent tripping.
Access and differentiation
Provide a reference image of the completed puzzle for guidance.
Time rationale
15 minutes assembling, 20 minutes labeling, 10 minutes peer review.

assess-skeletal-structures · 30 min · assessment

Given a blank diagram of the human skeleton, label the skull, ribs, spine, femur, humerus, and circle three joints.

Mastery criterion
Labels placed correctly on the skull, ribs, spine, femur, and humerus. Circles placed on elbows, knees, or shoulders.
Materials
Printed blank skeleton diagrams, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank for students who struggle with spelling.
Time rationale
5 minutes instruction, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.

teach-muscle-bone-model · 60 min · teach

Guide students step-by-step to build a mechanical model of an arm using two pieces of cardboard joined by a brass fastener (joint) and a string attached to one piece (muscle). Demonstrate how pulling the string moves the cardboard.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully assemble the model and can make the cardboard bend by pulling the string.
Materials
Cardboard strips, Brass fasteners, String, Tape, Hole punches
Safety
Use caution with hole punches and brass fasteners to avoid pinching fingers.
Access and differentiation
Pre-punch holes in the cardboard for students who lack hand strength.
Time rationale
15 minutes explanation, 30 minutes guided construction, 15 minutes demonstration.

prac-leg-model · 60 min · practice

Students design and build a model of a leg (knee joint) using craft sticks and rubber bands, exploring how the rubber band must be positioned to pull the lower stick upward.

Mastery criterion
Model demonstrates that the rubber band (muscle) must cross the joint to pull the lower stick (bone).
Materials
Craft sticks, Rubber bands, Tape, Small hinges or brass fasteners
Safety
Ensure rubber bands are not overstretched to prevent snapping.
Access and differentiation
Provide a partially assembled model for students to complete.
Time rationale
10 minutes design planning, 35 minutes building, 15 minutes testing and adjusting.

prac-hand-model · 60 min · practice

Students create a mechanical hand model by taping cut straws (bones) onto a paper hand outline and threading string (tendons/muscles) through them. Pulling the strings bends the paper fingers.

Mastery criterion
Students explain that pulling the string simulates muscle contraction pulling on bones to bend the fingers.
Materials
Paper, Plastic straws, String, Tape, Scissors
Safety
Use blunt-tipped scissors. Ensure strings are not wrapped tightly around real fingers.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-cut straw pieces.
Time rationale
15 minutes cutting and taping straws, 25 minutes threading string, 20 minutes testing and explaining.

assess-muscle-bone-interaction · 30 min · assessment

Using the previously built cardboard and string model of an arm, pull the string and write a short description of what happens to the cardboard pieces and how this relates to real muscles and bones.

Mastery criterion
Student explicitly states that the muscle (string) pulls the bone (cardboard) to create movement at the joint.
Materials
Student-built cardboard models, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow oral explanations for students with writing difficulties.
Time rationale
10 minutes manipulating the model, 20 minutes writing the explanation.

teach-map-nervous · 45 min · teach

Project a diagram of the nervous system. Explain the central (brain, spinal cord) and peripheral (nerves) parts. Have students trace a human silhouette on large paper and draw the brain, spinal cord, and nerves in different colors.

Mastery criterion
Silhouette includes the brain in the head, spinal cord down the back, and nerves branching to limbs, color-coded correctly.
Materials
Projector, Large butcher paper, Markers in three colors
Safety
Ensure students use non-toxic markers.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn silhouettes for groups that need more time.
Time rationale
15 minutes explanation, 20 minutes drawing, 10 minutes review.

prac-yarn-nervous-system · 45 min · practice

Students use different colored yarn and glue to map the brain, spinal cord, and nerves onto a cardboard body outline.

Mastery criterion
Yarn is glued in the correct anatomical positions representing the three main components.
Materials
Cardboard outlines, Three colors of yarn, Liquid glue, Scissors
Safety
Use blunt-tipped scissors. Avoid getting glue in eyes.
Access and differentiation
Pre-cut yarn lengths for students with fine motor challenges.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes gluing yarn, 10 minutes drying and sharing.

prac-color-code-nervous · 45 min · practice

Students receive a detailed printed diagram of the human body and must color-code the brain red, the spinal cord blue, and the nerves yellow, then add a legend.

Mastery criterion
Diagram is accurately color-coded with a matching legend.
Materials
Printed diagrams, Colored pencils or crayons
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use high-contrast diagrams for visually impaired students.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes coloring, 10 minutes peer check.

assess-map-nervous · 30 min · assessment

Draw the central and peripheral nervous system on a blank human silhouette, using different colors for the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.

Mastery criterion
Drawing shows the brain in the head, connected to a spinal cord running down the center, with nerves branching out to the arms and legs.
Materials
Blank human silhouettes on paper, Colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist of the three parts to ensure none are forgotten.
Time rationale
5 minutes instruction, 20 minutes drawing, 5 minutes collection.

teach-sensory-pathway · 50 min · teach

Explain the sensory pathway. Conduct a whole-class role-play where students act as the skin, nerves, spinal cord, and brain, passing a message (a ball) from the 'skin' to the 'brain' when a stimulus is introduced.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally explain the sequence of the message passing from skin to brain.
Materials
A soft ball or beanbag
Safety
Ensure the ball is passed gently, not thrown.
Access and differentiation
Assign roles based on mobility and comfort levels.
Time rationale
20 minutes explanation, 20 minutes role-play, 10 minutes debrief.

prac-storyboard-sensory · 50 min · practice

Students draw a 4-panel storyboard illustrating the sequence of events when a person touches a cold ice cube, showing the stimulus, nerve transmission, spinal cord routing, and brain processing.

Mastery criterion
Storyboard panels are in the correct chronological order showing the pathway to the brain.
Materials
Storyboard templates, Pencils, Colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn panels that students only need to sequence and caption.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 30 minutes drawing, 10 minutes sharing.

prac-card-sort-pathway · 50 min · practice

Students work in small groups to sort sets of cards representing different sensory scenarios (e.g., smelling a flower, hearing a bell) into the correct pathway order.

Mastery criterion
All card sets are ordered correctly from stimulus to brain.
Materials
Sets of pathway cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use images on the cards alongside text for emerging readers.
Time rationale
10 minutes instruction, 30 minutes sorting multiple sets, 10 minutes review.

assess-sensory-pathway · 30 min · assessment

Order the provided cards to show what happens when you touch a hot surface, from the moment of touch to the brain registering pain.

Mastery criterion
Sequence strictly follows: Skin touches hot surface -> Nerves detect heat -> Signal travels to spinal cord and brain -> Brain registers pain.
Materials
Assessment card sets, Glue, Paper
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the cards aloud for students who need reading support.
Time rationale
5 minutes instruction, 20 minutes sorting and gluing, 5 minutes collection.

teach-motor-response · 60 min · teach

Present a scenario: catching a falling object. Discuss as a class how the eyes, brain, nerves, muscles, and bones work together. Model how to write a logical prediction of this coordinated response.

Mastery criterion
Students contribute to a class chart detailing the step-by-step integration of the three systems.
Materials
Whiteboard, Markers, A soft object to drop
Safety
Ensure the dropped object is soft and lightweight.
Access and differentiation
Provide a graphic organizer for students to take notes during the discussion.
Time rationale
20 minutes demonstration and discussion, 25 minutes collaborative writing, 15 minutes review.

prac-sharp-stone-response · 60 min · practice

Students write a paragraph predicting the coordinated response of the nervous, muscular, and skeletal systems when a person steps on a sharp stone barefoot.

Mastery criterion
Paragraph includes sensory input from the foot, brain processing, and muscle-bone interaction to lift the foot.
Materials
Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety. Do not use real sharp stones.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters (e.g., 'First, the nerves in the foot...').
Time rationale
15 minutes scenario analysis, 30 minutes writing, 15 minutes peer review.

assess-motor-response · 30 min · assessment

Read the scenario: You see a ball flying towards your face. Write a short paragraph predicting how your nervous, muscular, and skeletal systems will work together to catch or dodge it.

Mastery criterion
Response includes sensory input (eyes), brain processing, and muscle-bone interaction for movement.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a graphic organizer with three boxes (Sensory, Brain, Movement) to structure the response.
Time rationale
5 minutes reading scenario, 25 minutes writing.

retrieval-hot-plate · 20 min · retrieval

Quick write: Explain the system coordination that happens when you accidentally touch a hot plate and pull your hand away.

Mastery criterion
Briefly mentions nerves detecting heat, brain processing, and muscles pulling arm bones away.
Materials
Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow bullet points instead of full sentences.
Time rationale
5 minutes prompt, 10 minutes writing, 5 minutes review.

retrieval-loud-noise · 20 min · retrieval

Draw a quick flowchart showing the system coordination when you hear a loud noise and turn your head to look.

Mastery criterion
Flowchart shows ears -> nerves -> brain -> nerves -> neck muscles -> neck bones.
Materials
Whiteboards, Dry-erase markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a template with empty boxes and arrows.
Time rationale
5 minutes prompt, 10 minutes drawing, 5 minutes holding up whiteboards for check.

teach-female-organs · 45 min · teach

Use an anatomical diagram to introduce the female reproductive system. Point out and explain the location of the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina.

Mastery criterion
Students can point to the correct organs on the diagram when named.
Materials
Anatomical diagrams (projected or large poster)
Safety
Maintain a respectful and scientific environment. Do not ask students to relate this to their own bodies.
Access and differentiation
Provide individual copies of the diagram for closer viewing.
Time rationale
20 minutes instruction, 15 minutes guided identification, 10 minutes review.

prac-model-female-organs · 45 min · practice

Students use playdough to create a 2D model of the female reproductive system on a paper plate, labeling the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina with toothpick flags.

Mastery criterion
Playdough shapes roughly match the anatomical structure and are labeled correctly.
Materials
Playdough, Paper plates, Toothpicks, Sticky labels
Safety
Wash hands after using playdough. Do not ingest.
Access and differentiation
Provide a stencil for the basic shape.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup, 25 minutes modeling and labeling, 10 minutes cleanup.

prac-match-female-organs · 45 min · practice

Students play a matching game where they match the name of the female reproductive organ to a card showing its specific shape isolated from the rest of the system.

Mastery criterion
All organ names are correctly matched to their corresponding shapes.

Sets of matching cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Include a brief description of the shape on the name card (e.g., 'almond-shaped' for ovaries).

10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes playing the game, 10 minutes review.

Given a diagram of the female reproductive system, label the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina.

Mastery criterion

Students work in pairs with a deck of cards containing names of reproductive organs. They must sort them into two physical boxes labeled 'Male' and 'Female'.

prac-comparative-poster · 40 min · practice

Students create a comparative poster with two columns, drawing one key organ for each system and listing the other organs below it.

assess-compare-systems · 30 min · assessment

prac-puberty-brochure · 45 min · practice

assess-hormones-puberty · 30 min · assessment

teach-joint-types · 45 min · teach

Introduce the three types of joints (immobile, semi-mobile, mobile) using a presentation and physical demonstrations. Have students move their own bodies to feel the difference between mobile joints (knees, elbows) and semi-mobile joints (spine), and point to immobile joints (skull).

Mastery criterion

teach-five-senses · 45 min · teach

Introduce the five senses (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch) and their corresponding organs (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin) using a large chart. Discuss how each organ helps us perceive the environment.

Mastery criterion

Materials
Large chart of the five senses, Flashcards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation

20 minutes instruction, 15 minutes guided practice with flashcards, 10 minutes review.

teach-brain-lobes · 45 min · teach

Project a diagram of the brain and introduce the frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, as well as the cerebellum. Explain their locations and have students point to the approximate areas on their own heads.

Projector, Brain diagrams

teach-fertilization-menstruation · 45 min · teach

Explain the basic processes of fertilization (meeting of ovocyte and male gamete in the oviducts) and menstruation (shedding of the endometrium from the uterus if no fertilization occurs) using simple, age-appropriate diagrams.

teach-reproductive-care · 40 min · teach

Discuss the importance of hygiene and care for the reproductive system. Brainstorm a list of care practices (e.g., daily bathing, clean underwear) and write them on the board.
