Limitations: The mechanical models of muscles and bones simplify the complex biomechanics of real joints.; The representation of the nervous system focuses on macroscopic pathways, omitting neurotransmitters and cellular action potentials.; Discussions of puberty are limited to basic biological changes and hygiene, requiring careful pedagogical handling to avoid stigmatization.; The assessment of reasoning relies on written or verbal predictions, which may be constrained by students expressive language skills.

Grade 5

Physical quantities

The unit begins by establishing the fundamental language of measurement: identifying SI units and applying their writing rules. Once the language is set, students move to practical application by taking direct measurements. These direct measurements serve as the prerequisite for calculating derived quantities (like volume and density) and converting units. In the second half of the unit, the focus shifts to data quality. Students learn to process raw data through rounding and scientific notation. They then develop reasoning skills by evaluating the precision and accuracy of their data and classifying the sources of error. Finally, they synthesize these concepts by calculating how errors propagate when direct measurements are used to find derived quantities.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Measurement and SI Conventions

Establishes the foundational understanding of the International System of Units, enabling students to correctly identify, format, measure, calculate, and convert physical quantities.

classify physical quantities as fundamental or derived SI units
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide students with a list of 10 physical quantities (e.g., length, speed, mass, volume). Ask them to sort them into two columns: Fundamental SI Units and Derived SI Units.
Expected response
Length and mass are placed in the Fundamental column; speed and volume are placed in the Derived column.
Scoring rule
1 point per correctly classified quantity. Mastery is 8/10 correct.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly categorize a given list of physical quantities into fundamental and derived SI units.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think volume is a fundamental unit because it is commonly used.; Students might confuse the instrument used to measure with the unit itself.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The SI system defines seven fundamental measurable properties of nature. · Source page 11 · paragraph p11-paragraph-9
format measurement values and symbols according to SI writing rules
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Give students a text with 5 incorrectly formatted measurements (e.g., 10Kgs, 5m, 20 SECS). Ask them to rewrite the text applying SI rules.
Expected response
10 kg, 5 m, 20 s.
Scoring rule
1 point per correctly formatted measurement. Mastery is 4/5 correct.
Mastery evidence
Students can rewrite incorrectly formatted measurements following SI rules.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may pluralize symbols (e.g., writing 'kgs' instead of 'kg').; Students might write the number and symbol without a space (e.g., '5m').
Local prerequisites
g5u1-identify-si-units
Scientific support
  • SI symbols are written in lowercase letters unless derived from a proper name. · Source page 21 · paragraph p21-paragraph-4
record direct measurements of length, mass, and time using standard instruments
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide a wooden block. Ask students to measure and record its length in cm, its mass in g, and the time it takes to slide down a ramp in s.
Expected response
Length: 15.2 cm, Mass: 45 g, Time: 1.5 s (values within instrument tolerance).
Scoring rule
1 point per measurement within the acceptable tolerance range of the instrument. Mastery is 3/3 correct.
Mastery evidence
Students can use a ruler, balance, and stopwatch to obtain and record accurate measurements of given objects.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may start measuring from the edge of the ruler instead of the zero mark.; Students might read the scale from an angle, causing parallax error.
Local prerequisites
g5u1-apply-si-rules
Scientific support
  • Direct measurements are taken for various physical quantities using specific instruments. · Source page 12 · paragraph p12-paragraph-5
calculate derived quantities such as volume, speed, and density from direct measurements
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide the mass (50 g) and volume (25 cm3) of an object. Ask students to calculate its density and state the derived unit.
Expected response
Density = 50 / 25 = 2 g/cm3.
Scoring rule
1 point for correct numerical calculation, 1 point for correct derived unit. Mastery is 2/2.
Mastery evidence
Students can apply mathematical formulas to direct measurements to find derived quantities.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may add instead of multiply when calculating volume or area.; Students might invert the formula for speed, dividing time by distance.
Local prerequisites
g5u1-measure-direct
Scientific support
  • Derived magnitudes are created by combining two or more fundamental magnitudes. · Source page 13 · paragraph p13-paragraph-4
convert measurement values between different units using conversion factors
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given that 1 inch = 2.54 cm, ask students to convert a measurement of 10 inches into centimeters.
Expected response
10 inches * 2.54 cm/inch = 25.4 cm.
Scoring rule
1 point for correct setup, 1 point for correct final answer. Mastery is 2/2.
Mastery evidence
Students can use given conversion factors to translate a measurement from one unit to another.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may multiply instead of divide when converting from a smaller to a larger unit.; Students might think conversion changes the actual physical size of the object.
Local prerequisites
g5u1-calculate-derived
Scientific support
  • Conversions are necessary when dealing with measurements in different units. · Source page 25 · paragraph p25-paragraph-6

Data Processing and Error Analysis

Develops critical thinking regarding the reliability of measurements, teaching students to process data accurately through rounding and scientific notation, and to evaluate errors.

round decimal measurement values to a specified number of significant figures
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide the number 45.367. Ask students to round it to two decimal places.
Expected response
45.37
Scoring rule
1 point for correct rounding based on the digit 7. Mastery is 1/1.
Mastery evidence
Students can apply standard rounding rules to truncate decimal values correctly.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may always round up regardless of the next digit.; Students might round sequentially from right to left instead of looking only at the first discarded digit.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • If the first discarded digit is greater than 5, the preceding digit is increased by one. · Source page 23 · paragraph p23-paragraph-5
translate standard numerical values into scientific notation using base 10
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Ask students to write the number 0.0008 in scientific notation.
Expected response
8 x 10^-4
Scoring rule
1 point for correct coefficient (8), 1 point for correct exponent (-4). Mastery is 2/2.
Mastery evidence
Students can convert large and small standard numbers into proper scientific notation.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may use a coefficient greater than 10.; Students might confuse positive and negative exponents for large and small numbers.
Local prerequisites
g5u1-apply-rounding
Scientific support
  • Scientific notation uses base 10 powers to express very large or very small quantities. · Source page 24 · paragraph p24-paragraph-3
evaluate measurement sets to determine their precision and accuracy
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Given a true value of 10.0 g, and a student's measurements of 8.1 g, 8.2 g, and 8.1 g, ask students to decide if the measurements are accurate and/or precise, and justify their choice.
Expected response
The measurements are precise because they are close to each other, but not accurate because they are far from the true value of 10.0 g.
Scoring rule
1 point for identifying high precision, 1 point for identifying low accuracy, 1 point for valid justification. Mastery is 3/3.
Mastery evidence
Students can analyze a set of measurements compared to a known true value and justify whether they are precise, accurate, both, or neither.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think precision and accuracy mean the exact same thing.; Students might assume a highly precise instrument is automatically accurate even if uncalibrated.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Precision and accuracy are two distinct and important characteristics of measuring instruments. · Source page 34 · paragraph p34-paragraph-5
categorize measurement discrepancies as personal, instrumental, or environmental errors
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Provide a scenario: 'A metal ruler expands on a very hot day, causing length measurements to be slightly off.' Ask students to classify this error and justify their choice.
Expected response
Environmental error, because the temperature of the surroundings caused the instrument to change.
Scoring rule
1 point for correct classification, 1 point for logical justification based on the environment. Mastery is 2/2.
Mastery evidence
Students can read scenarios describing measurement issues and correctly classify the type of error involved.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe all errors are due to human mistakes.; Students might think electronic instruments cannot have errors.
Local prerequisites
g5u1-differentiate-precision-accuracy
Scientific support
  • Measurement errors are classified into personal, instrumental, and environmental categories. · Source page 34 · paragraph p34-paragraph-6
compute the propagated error in area calculations from direct measurements
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a length of 10 cm (error 0.1 cm) and width of 5 cm (error 0.1 cm), ask students to calculate the area and its propagated error using the provided formula.
Expected response
Area = 50 cm2. Error calculation follows the specific formula taught (e.g., relative error addition).
Scoring rule
1 point for correct area, 1 point for correct error propagation calculation. Mastery is 2/2.
Mastery evidence
Students can calculate the area of a rectangle and apply basic error propagation rules to find the uncertainty of the area.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may simply add the absolute errors when multiplying measurements.; Students might ignore the error entirely when calculating the final area.
Local prerequisites
g5u1-classify-errors
Scientific support
  • Calculating the area involves multiplying measurements, which also requires calculating the propagation of their errors. · Source page 33 · paragraph p33-paragraph-7
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

g5u1-act-teach-1-1 · 60 min · teach

Students review a set of everyday objects and their labels (e.g., a 1 L bottle, a 500 g bag of beans). They create a two-column chart in their notebooks, classifying the units found on the labels into fundamental SI units and derived SI units based on a reference table provided by the teacher.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly classify at least 8 out of 10 provided units into the correct columns.
Materials
Everyday product packaging with measurement labels, Reference table of SI units, Notebooks
Safety
Ensure product packaging is clean and free of allergens or hazardous residues.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual sorting mat with icons representing fundamental vs derived concepts for students who need visual aids.
Time rationale
15 mins introduction and label observation, 30 mins chart creation and classification, 15 mins class review and correction.

g5u1-act-teach-1-2 · 60 min · teach

Students receive a 'badly written' science report containing multiple SI formatting errors (e.g., 5Kgs, 10 M, 20secs). They must act as editors, crossing out the errors and writing the correct SI format above them, then write a short rule justification for each correction.

Mastery criterion
Students identify and correct at least 4 out of 5 formatting errors using proper SI rules.
Materials
Printed 'badly written' science reports, Red pens for editing
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist of the 4 main SI rules (lowercase, no plural, space, no period) for quick reference.
Time rationale
10 mins rule explanation, 30 mins editing task, 20 mins peer review and discussion.

g5u1-act-teach-1-3 · 90 min · teach

Students rotate through three measurement stations: Length (measuring a desk with a meter stick), Mass (measuring a rock with a balance), and Time (timing a pendulum swing with a stopwatch). They record their direct measurements in a structured data table.

Mastery criterion
Students record measurements with the correct numerical value and unit, within the tolerance of the instruments used.
Materials
Meter sticks, Balances, Rocks, String and weights for pendulums, Stopwatches
Safety
Ensure pendulums are swung in clear areas to avoid hitting anyone. Heavy rocks should be handled carefully to avoid dropping on toes.
Access and differentiation
Use digital balances or stopwatches with large displays for students with visual impairments.
Time rationale
15 mins station instructions, 60 mins rotating through stations (20 mins each), 15 mins data comparison.

g5u1-act-teach-1-4 · 90 min · teach

Students measure the three dimensions of a rectangular block to calculate its volume. Then, they measure its mass and use the calculated volume to determine its density. They record all steps and final derived quantities in their notebooks.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly apply the volume and density formulas, arriving at accurate derived quantities with proper units.
Materials
Rectangular wooden or plastic blocks, Rulers, Balances, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide formula cards with step-by-step calculation templates (fill-in-the-blank style) for students who struggle with multi-step math.
Time rationale
20 mins direct measurement, 40 mins calculations, 30 mins sharing and verifying results.

g5u1-act-teach-1-5 · 90 min · teach

Students are given a recipe or a building plan with measurements in non-SI units (e.g., inches, pounds). They use provided conversion factors to translate all measurements into SI units, showing their multiplication or division steps clearly.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully convert at least 3 out of 4 measurements, showing correct mathematical steps.
Materials
Worksheets with non-SI measurements, Conversion factor tables, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow the use of calculators and provide a worked example at the top of the worksheet.
Time rationale
20 mins explanation of conversion factors, 50 mins conversion practice, 20 mins review.

g5u1-act-teach-2-1 · 60 min · teach

Students receive a set of raw calculator outputs from division problems (e.g., 10/3 = 3.333333). They practice applying the three rounding rules to round these numbers to one and two decimal places, explaining which rule they used for each.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly round 4 out of 5 numbers to the specified decimal places.
Materials
Worksheets with raw decimal numbers, Rounding rules reference sheet
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use number lines to visually show which rounded number the raw decimal is closer to.
Time rationale
15 mins rule review, 30 mins rounding practice, 15 mins peer checking.

g5u1-act-teach-2-2 · 60 min · teach

Students play a matching game where they pair cards showing standard large/small numbers (e.g., distance to the sun, size of a cell) with their corresponding scientific notation cards. They then write three of their own examples.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly match all cards and write at least two valid original examples of scientific notation.
Materials
Sets of matching cards (standard vs scientific notation), Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Color-code the exponent sign (positive for large, negative for small) on introductory cards.
Time rationale
15 mins explanation, 30 mins matching game, 15 mins independent writing.

g5u1-act-teach-2-3 · 60 min · teach

Students throw wet paper balls at a drawn target on the board. They analyze the grouping of the hits to determine if the throws were precise (grouped together), accurate (near the center), both, or neither, and write a short justification.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the precision and accuracy of the target hits and provide a logical justification based on the definitions.
Materials
Paper balls, Water (to slightly wet the paper), Target drawn on the board or poster
Safety
Ensure paper balls are only thrown at the designated target. Clean up any water spills immediately to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters for the justification (e.g., 'The throws were precise because...').
Time rationale
20 mins throwing activity, 20 mins group analysis, 20 mins writing justifications.

g5u1-act-teach-2-4 · 60 min · teach

Students read a series of short case studies describing failed scientific experiments or measurements. They must highlight the source of the error, categorize it as personal, instrumental, or environmental, and propose a way to prevent it.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly categorize the error in 3 out of 4 case studies and provide a plausible prevention method.
Materials
Printed case studies, Highlighters
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the case studies aloud for students with reading difficulties and discuss the errors orally before writing.
Time rationale
15 mins introduction to error types, 30 mins case study analysis, 15 mins class discussion.

g5u1-act-teach-2-5 · 90 min · teach

Students measure the dimensions of their textbook using a ruler, noting the instrument's minimum division as the error. They calculate the area of the book cover and apply the taught formula to find the propagated error of the area.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly calculate the area and apply the error propagation formula to find the final uncertainty.
Materials
Textbooks, Rulers, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a step-by-step calculation template that breaks the error propagation formula into smaller, manageable math operations.
Time rationale
20 mins measuring and identifying instrument error, 40 mins area and error calculations, 30 mins reviewing steps.

g5u1-act-practice-1 · 60 min · practice

Students create a 'Measurement Passport' where they list 5 fundamental and 5 derived quantities, writing their correct SI symbols and formatting a hypothetical measurement for each.

Mastery criterion
All 10 quantities are correctly classified and formatted according to SI rules.
Materials
Blank 'passport' booklets (folded paper), Markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use their reference charts from previous lessons.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 40 mins creating passports, 10 mins sharing.

g5u1-act-practice-2 · 90 min · practice

Students build a small ramp and roll a toy car down it. They measure the distance of the ramp and the time it takes the car to reach the bottom, then calculate the derived quantity of speed.

Mastery criterion
Students accurately record distance and time, and correctly calculate speed using the v=d/t formula.
Materials
Toy cars, Cardboard for ramps, Meter sticks, Stopwatches
Safety
Ensure cars are rolled in designated areas so no one trips on them.
Access and differentiation
Pair students so one can focus on timing while the other focuses on releasing the car.
Time rationale
20 mins setup, 40 mins data collection, 30 mins calculations.

g5u1-act-practice-3 · 60 min · practice

Students solve a 'conversion maze' worksheet where the correct converted answer leads them to the next problem, eventually guiding them to the finish line.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully navigate the maze by correctly solving at least 80% of the conversion problems.
Materials
Conversion maze worksheets, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide the conversion factors directly next to each problem in the maze.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 40 mins maze solving, 10 mins checking the path.

g5u1-act-practice-4 · 60 min · practice

Students are given a list of highly precise astronomical and microscopic data (e.g., 0.000004567 m). They must first round the numbers to three significant figures, then convert the rounded numbers into scientific notation.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly round and convert at least 4 out of 5 complex numbers.
Materials
Worksheets with astronomical/microscopic data
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual guide showing how to count decimal places for the exponent.
Time rationale
15 mins review, 35 mins independent practice, 10 mins review.

g5u1-act-practice-5 · 60 min · practice

Students analyze a mock lab report that contains flawed data. They must write a short paragraph evaluating the precision and accuracy of the data and identifying whether the likely cause was a personal, instrumental, or environmental error.

Mastery criterion
Students write a coherent paragraph correctly identifying the accuracy/precision state and logically categorizing the error source.
Materials
Mock lab reports
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a paragraph template with fill-in-the-blanks for key terms.
Time rationale
15 mins reading the report, 30 mins writing the analysis, 15 mins sharing.

g5u1-act-practice-6 · 90 min · practice

Students calculate the volume of a large box in cubic centimeters, then use conversion factors to convert their final derived answer into cubic meters.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly calculate the initial volume and successfully apply the cubic conversion factor.
Materials
Large cardboard boxes, Rulers or measuring tapes, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide the specific cubic conversion factor (1 m3 = 1,000,000 cm3) explicitly.
Time rationale
30 mins measuring and initial calculation, 40 mins conversion, 20 mins review.

g5u1-act-practice-7 · 60 min · practice

Students practice error propagation by calculating the area of the classroom floor using measurements provided by the teacher, including the instrumental error of the measuring tape used.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly apply the error propagation formula to the classroom area calculation.
Materials
Worksheets with provided measurements and errors, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to work in pairs to verify each other's math steps.
Time rationale
10 mins setup, 40 mins calculations, 10 mins review.

g5u1-act-inquiry-1 · 120 min · practice

Students design an experiment to find the density of an irregularly shaped object (like a stone) using water displacement. They must record direct measurements, calculate the derived density, and identify any potential errors in their procedure.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully determine the density and logically identify at least one source of error in their method.
Materials
Graduated cylinders, Water, Small stones, Balances
Safety
Wipe up any spilled water immediately to prevent slipping. Handle glass cylinders with care.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual diagram of the water displacement method.
Time rationale
30 mins experimental design, 40 mins execution and measurement, 30 mins calculations, 20 mins error analysis.

g5u1-act-inquiry-2 · 120 min · practice

Students compare two different measuring instruments (e.g., a standard ruler vs a tailor's tape) by measuring the same object multiple times. They analyze the precision and accuracy of both, calculate the area and propagated error using data from both, and conclude which instrument is better for the task.

Mastery criterion
Students justify their choice of instrument based on calculated error propagation and concepts of precision/accuracy.
Materials
Standard rulers, Tailor's measuring tapes, Rectangular objects (e.g., desks)
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a structured comparison table to help organize the data from both instruments.
Time rationale
40 mins data collection with both instruments, 50 mins calculations, 30 mins writing conclusions.

g5u1-act-assessment-1 · 60 min · assessment

Students complete a comprehensive written and practical test where they classify units, correct formatting, take a direct measurement of a provided object, calculate its volume, and convert the result to a different unit.

Mastery criterion
Students score at least 80% on the combined tasks according to the specific scoring rules of each micro-skill.
Materials
Printed assessments, Small objects for measuring, Rulers, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow extra time and provide a quiet environment for students who need it.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 50 mins assessment completion.

g5u1-act-assessment-2 · 60 min · assessment

Students complete a written test involving rounding data, converting to scientific notation, analyzing a data set for precision/accuracy, classifying described errors, and performing one error propagation calculation.

Mastery criterion
Students score at least 80% on the combined tasks according to the specific scoring rules of each micro-skill.
Materials
Printed assessments, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow extra time and provide a quiet environment for students who need it.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 50 mins assessment completion.

g5u1-act-retrieval-1a · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given a quick 'flash' challenge on the board with mass and volume data for three mystery materials. They race to calculate the density of each.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly calculate the density for all three materials.
Materials
Whiteboard and markers, Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow the use of calculators.
Time rationale
5 mins setup, 15 mins calculation race, 10 mins review.

g5u1-act-retrieval-1b · 30 min · retrieval

Students review a previous lab's data table that has missing derived values (speed and volume). They must recalculate the missing values from the provided direct measurements.

Mastery criterion
Students accurately fill in the missing derived values using the correct formulas.
Materials
Worksheets with incomplete data tables
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide the formulas at the top of the page.
Time rationale
5 mins instructions, 20 mins calculations, 5 mins review.

g5u1-act-retrieval-2a · 30 min · retrieval

Students play a quick game of 'Rounding Bingo' where the teacher calls out raw decimals and a rounding rule (e.g., 'round to one decimal place'), and students mark the correct rounded number on their cards.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify and mark the rounded numbers, achieving a 'Bingo'.
Materials
Bingo cards with rounded numbers, Markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Pair students up to play on a single card.
Time rationale
5 mins rules, 20 mins gameplay, 5 mins verification.

g5u1-act-retrieval-2b · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given a grocery receipt with prices having three decimal places (hypothetical scenario). They must round all prices to two decimal places (standard currency format) and calculate the new total.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly round all prices and find the accurate total.
Materials
Mock grocery receipts
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow the use of calculators for the final addition.
Time rationale
5 mins instructions, 20 mins rounding and adding, 5 mins review.

g5u1-act-bridge-1 · 60 min · bridge

Students revisit their density calculations from a previous lesson. The teacher introduces the concept that the mass and volume measurements had errors. Students now apply the error propagation formula to their previously calculated derived density.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully integrate the error propagation formula with their prior density calculations.
Materials
Previous lesson notebooks, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Walk through the first calculation together as a class on the board.
Time rationale
15 mins concept bridge explanation, 30 mins calculations, 15 mins review.

Limitations: The calculation of error propagation is simplified for primary level; complex calculus-based propagation is avoided in favor of basic arithmetic rules provided in the text.; Scientific notation is limited to basic base-10 translations suitable for 5th grade, avoiding complex operations with exponents.; The distinction between precision and accuracy is taught conceptually and visually, without introducing standard deviation or advanced statistical variance.; Context tasks are limited to hypothetical scenarios to avoid requiring actual financial or sensitive local data.

Mechanics

The unit begins by establishing fundamental kinematic concepts (distance vs. displacement, coordinate systems) to describe motion accurately. It then moves to classifying specific types of motion (MRU, MCU). With motion described, the progression shifts to dynamics, using Newton's First Law to predict motion states based on forces, and exploring rotational forces (torque). Finally, the unit introduces mechanical energy as an alternative framework for analyzing physical systems, covering elastic, gravitational, and kinetic energy, culminating in the reasoning of energy transformations. Prerequisites are strictly internal: understanding distance/displacement is required before classifying MRU, and understanding MRU is required before predicting equilibrium states. Energy transformations require prior understanding of both potential and kinetic energy.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 2. Unit allocation: 6 planning weeks.

Kinematics and Dynamics

Students transition from qualitative descriptions of motion to quantitative and vector-based analysis, establishing the foundation for understanding how forces affect translational and rotational motion.

differentiate distance traveled and displacement on a 2D Cartesian grid
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a grid with a starting point, a path with three turns, and an endpoint, calculate the total distance traveled and draw the displacement vector.
Expected response
The student sums the lengths of the path segments for distance and draws a straight arrow from start to finish for displacement.
Scoring rule
Passes if distance is the sum of segments and displacement is a single straight vector; fails if the two are confused.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies distance as a scalar path length and displacement as a vector from origin to final position.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe that distance and displacement are always the same value.; Students may think displacement depends on the path taken rather than just initial and final positions.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Distance is a scalar quantity. · Source page 44 · paragraph p44-paragraph-3
locate a specific point on a map using latitude and longitude coordinates
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a map with a coordinate grid, mark the location corresponding to 13 degrees North and 89 degrees West.
Expected response
The student places a mark at the intersection of the specified latitude and longitude lines.
Scoring rule
Passes if the mark is at the correct intersection; fails if axes are swapped.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately finds a location on a map given its latitude and longitude.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may confuse latitude (horizontal lines) with longitude (vertical lines).; Students may reverse the order of coordinates when reading a map.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Locations on a map can be found using geographic coordinates. · Source page 43 · paragraph p43-paragraph-6
classify motion as Uniform Rectilinear Motion (MRU) based on trajectory and constant speed
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Review a data table showing an object's position every second. Determine if the motion is MRU and justify the choice.
Expected response
The student states it is MRU because the position changes by the same amount each second along a straight line.
Scoring rule
Passes if both straight trajectory and constant speed are cited; fails if only one is mentioned.
Mastery evidence
Student identifies MRU by verifying both a straight trajectory and equal distances covered in equal time intervals.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think any straight-line motion is MRU, ignoring the constant speed requirement.
Local prerequisites
differentiate-distance-displacement
Scientific support
  • MRU is characterized by covering equal distances in equal times. · Source page 48 · paragraph p48-paragraph-7
classify motion as Uniform Circular Motion (MCU) based on circular trajectory and constant angular speed
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Observe a spinning wheel with a mark. If the mark completes one full rotation every 2 seconds steadily, classify the motion.
Expected response
The student classifies it as MCU because the trajectory is circular and the time per rotation is constant.
Scoring rule
Passes if classified as MCU with reference to circular path and constant rotation rate; fails otherwise.
Mastery evidence
Student identifies MCU by verifying a circular path and equal angles covered in equal times.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe that because speed is constant, velocity is also constant in MCU, ignoring the change in direction.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • MCU requires a circular trajectory. · Source page 49 · paragraph p49-paragraph-6
predict the state of rest or constant velocity of an object when the net force is zero
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
A block is sliding on a frictionless surface at a constant speed. Predict what will happen to its motion if no additional forces are applied, and justify using forces.
Expected response
The block will continue moving at the same constant speed in a straight line because the net force is zero.
Scoring rule
Passes if prediction is constant velocity due to zero net force; fails if student predicts it will eventually stop without a force.
Mastery evidence
Student uses Newton's First Law to predict that zero net force results in either rest or constant velocity.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think that if an object is moving, there must be a net forward force acting on it.
Local prerequisites
classify-mru
Scientific support
  • An object remains in its state of motion if the net force is zero. · Source page 54 · paragraph p54-paragraph-21
justify the change in rotational effectiveness based on the distance from the fulcrum
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain why it is easier to open a heavy door by pushing near the handle rather than near the hinges.
Expected response
Pushing near the handle increases the lever arm distance, which creates a greater torque for the same amount of force.
Scoring rule
Passes if the relationship between distance from hinges (lever arm) and rotational effect (torque) is clearly stated; fails if only force is mentioned.
Mastery evidence
Student explains that applying force further from the axis of rotation increases the torque.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe that the same force always produces the same rotation regardless of where it is applied.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Torque measures the effectiveness of a force in causing rotation. · Source page 59 · paragraph p59-paragraph-5

Mechanical Energy and Transformations

Students learn to analyze physical systems through the lens of energy, understanding that energy can be stored, transferred, and transformed, which provides an alternative to force-based analysis.

identify elastic potential energy in stretched or compressed springs and rubber bands
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Look at a picture of a stretched slingshot and a relaxed slingshot. Identify which one has elastic potential energy and state why.
Expected response
The stretched slingshot has elastic potential energy because it is deformed and stores energy to snap back.
Scoring rule
Passes if the stretched state is linked to stored elastic energy; fails if energy is attributed to the relaxed state.
Mastery evidence
Student recognizes that deformed elastic objects store energy that can be released as motion.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think energy is only present when an object is actively moving.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Elastic potential energy is associated with the force of a spring. · Source page 68 · paragraph p68-paragraph-4
compare the gravitational potential energy of objects at different heights
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Two identical books are placed on shelves. Book A is 1 meter high, Book B is 2 meters high. Compare their gravitational potential energy.
Expected response
Book B has more gravitational potential energy because it is at a greater height.
Scoring rule
Passes if the higher object is correctly identified as having more potential energy; fails if height is ignored.
Mastery evidence
Student determines that higher elevation results in greater gravitational potential energy for a given mass.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe that heavier objects always have more potential energy regardless of height.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Gravitational potential energy depends on the object's height before descending. · Source page 67 · paragraph p67-paragraph-20
compare the kinetic energy of objects moving at different speeds
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Two identical toy cars are rolling. Car X rolls at 2 m/s and Car Y rolls at 4 m/s. Which has more kinetic energy?
Expected response
Car Y has more kinetic energy because it is moving faster.
Scoring rule
Passes if the faster car is chosen due to its higher speed; fails if the slower car is chosen or speed is deemed irrelevant.
Mastery evidence
Student relates kinetic energy to the motion of an object, recognizing that faster objects of the same mass have more kinetic energy.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may confuse kinetic energy with speed, not realizing mass also plays a role.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Kinetic energy is associated with the motion of an object before impact. · Source page 67 · paragraph p67-paragraph-20
justify the transformation between potential and kinetic energy in a closed mechanical system
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
A pendulum swings from its highest point to its lowest point. Justify what happens to its potential and kinetic energy during this swing.
Expected response
As it falls, its height decreases so potential energy decreases, but its speed increases so kinetic energy increases. The potential energy transforms into kinetic energy.
Scoring rule
Passes if the inverse relationship and transformation between the two energy types are explicitly stated; fails if energy is described as being lost or created.
Mastery evidence
Student explains how potential energy converts to kinetic energy (and vice versa) while total mechanical energy is conserved.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think energy disappears when a moving object stops at the top of a hill.
Local prerequisites
compare-gravitational-potential, compare-kinetic-energy
Scientific support
  • Mechanical energy is conserved in a closed system during transformations. · Source page 69 · paragraph p69-paragraph-21
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-distance-displacement · 60 min · teach

Students walk a specific path marked on the classroom floor (e.g., 3 steps forward, 4 steps right). They measure the total path length with a measuring tape (distance) and then measure the straight line from start to finish (displacement). They record both values and write a definition for each based on their physical experience.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly record a larger value for distance than displacement and define distance as the path taken and displacement as the straight-line change in position.
Materials
Measuring tapes, Masking tape for floor marks
Safety
Ensure the walking path is clear of tripping hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a scaled drawing of the path on paper for students with mobility issues to measure with a ruler instead.
Time rationale
15 mins setup and instruction, 30 mins physical activity and measurement, 15 mins recording and discussion.

teach-geographic-coordinates · 60 min · teach

Students receive a map with a latitude and longitude grid. The teacher models finding a specific coordinate. Students then practice finding 3 specific coordinates provided by the teacher, marking them with a dot, and writing the name of the feature located there.

Mastery criterion
Students accurately place dots at the correct intersections of latitude and longitude for all 3 given coordinates.
Materials
Printed maps with coordinate grids, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use maps with larger, color-coded grid lines (e.g., red for latitude, blue for longitude) for visual support.
Time rationale
20 mins modeling and explanation, 30 mins guided practice, 10 mins review.

teach-classify-mru · 60 min · teach

Students analyze a video or simulation of a car moving along a straight track. They record the car's position every 2 seconds in a data table. They calculate the distance covered in each interval, observe that it is constant, and write a statement classifying the motion as MRU based on the straight path and constant speed.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly calculate equal distances for equal time intervals and explicitly state both MRU conditions (straight line, constant speed).
Materials
Video or simulation of constant speed motion, Stopwatches, Data recording sheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-filled time intervals on the data sheet so students only need to focus on recording position.
Time rationale
15 mins introduction, 30 mins data collection and calculation, 15 mins conclusion writing.

teach-classify-mcu · 60 min · teach

Students observe a marked spinning object (like a bicycle wheel or a top). They use a stopwatch to time how long it takes for the mark to complete 5 full rotations, then calculate the time per rotation. They write a paragraph classifying the motion as MCU, citing the circular path and constant time per rotation.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly calculate the period of rotation and justify the MCU classification using the circular trajectory and constant rotation rate.
Materials
Spinning objects (tops, wheels), Stopwatches
Safety
Ensure spinning objects are stable and students keep fingers away from moving spokes.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual checklist of MCU characteristics for students to check off as they observe.
Time rationale
15 mins setup, 30 mins observation and timing, 15 mins writing classification.

teach-predict-equilibrium · 60 min · teach

Students analyze scenarios presented on cards (e.g., a book resting on a table, a hockey puck gliding on frictionless ice). For each, they draw force arrows (gravity, normal force, applied force, friction). If forces cancel out (net force zero), they predict the resulting motion (rest or constant velocity) and justify their reasoning in writing.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly draw canceling force arrows and predict either rest or constant velocity, citing zero net force.
Materials
Scenario cards, Whiteboards and markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn force arrows that students must label and balance, reducing the drawing burden.
Time rationale
20 mins direct instruction on Newton's First Law, 30 mins scenario analysis, 10 mins sharing predictions.

teach-torque-lever-arm · 60 min · teach

Students push a classroom door closed using one finger at three different points: near the hinge, in the middle, and near the handle. They rank the points by how much effort was required. They then draw a diagram of the door, labeling the axis of rotation and the lever arm distances, and write a justification for why the handle position is most effective.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the handle position as requiring the least force and justify this by referencing the longer lever arm distance from the axis of rotation.
Materials
Classroom doors, Diagram worksheets
Safety
Ensure fingers are not pinched in the door hinges.
Access and differentiation
Provide a fill-in-the-blank template for the justification paragraph.
Time rationale
20 mins physical experience with doors, 20 mins diagramming, 20 mins writing justifications.

teach-elastic-potential · 60 min · teach

Students examine various objects: a relaxed rubber band, a stretched rubber band, an uncompressed spring, and a compressed spring. They categorize which objects currently store elastic potential energy and draw diagrams showing the deformation that causes the stored energy.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify only the stretched/compressed objects as having elastic potential energy and illustrate the deformation.
Materials
Rubber bands, Springs (safe, low tension)
Safety
Require safety goggles when manipulating stretched rubber bands or springs to prevent eye injury.
Access and differentiation
Use highly visual, color-coded springs where compression is obvious.
Time rationale
15 mins introduction, 30 mins hands-on categorization and drawing, 15 mins review.

teach-gravitational-potential · 60 min · teach

Students drop a small ball into a container of sand from three different heights (0.5m, 1m, 1.5m). They measure the depth of the crater formed each time as an indicator of energy. They record the data and write a conclusion comparing the gravitational potential energy at the different heights.

Mastery criterion
Students record deeper craters for greater heights and conclude that higher elevation means greater gravitational potential energy.
Materials
Small balls (e.g., golf balls), Containers of sand, Rulers, Meter sticks
Safety
Ensure sand is not thrown; sweep up any spills immediately to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Provide a structured data table with pre-labeled height columns.
Time rationale
15 mins setup, 30 mins dropping and measuring, 15 mins writing conclusions.

teach-kinetic-energy · 60 min · teach

Students roll a toy car down a ramp into a lightweight block. They do this from a low release point (slow speed at bottom) and a high release point (fast speed at bottom). They measure how far the block is pushed each time. They write a statement comparing the kinetic energy of the car at the two different speeds.

Mastery criterion
Students measure a greater push distance for the faster car and conclude that higher speed results in greater kinetic energy.
Materials
Toy cars, Ramps (cardboard or wood), Lightweight blocks (e.g., empty small boxes), Rulers
Safety
Keep rolling objects on the floor or tables; do not launch them in the air.
Access and differentiation
Use a digital speedometer app (if teacher-operated) to make the speed difference concrete.
Time rationale
15 mins setup, 30 mins rolling and measuring, 15 mins writing comparisons.

teach-energy-transformation · 60 min · teach

Students build a simple pendulum with string and a washer. They release it and observe the swing. They draw the pendulum at three positions: highest point, lowest point, and opposite highest point. They label where potential energy is max/min and where kinetic energy is max/min, and write a paragraph justifying how energy transforms between the two forms during the swing.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly label max potential at the top, max kinetic at the bottom, and justify the continuous transformation between height and speed.
Materials
String, Washers or small weights, Tape, Paper and pencils
Safety
Ensure weights are securely tied so they do not fly off during swinging.
Access and differentiation
Provide a diagram template of the pendulum swing for students to label.
Time rationale
15 mins building, 20 mins observation and diagramming, 25 mins writing justification.

inquiry-grid-mapping · 90 min · practice

Students design an obstacle course on a grid drawn on the playground. They map a path through the obstacles, measure the total distance of the path, and then measure the direct displacement from start to finish. They present their map and measurements to the class.

Mastery criterion
Accurate measurement of both path distance and straight-line displacement, clearly distinguishing the two in their presentation.
Materials
Chalk, Measuring tapes, Playground space
Safety
Ensure the playground surface is safe and obstacles are not tripping hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use smaller tabletop grids and toy figures if outdoor mobility is an issue.
Time rationale
30 mins designing and drawing grid, 30 mins measuring, 30 mins presentations.

practice-map-reading · 60 min · practice

Students receive a list of 5 geographic coordinates. They must locate each on a provided map, identify the geographical feature or city at that location, and record it in a table.

Mastery criterion
Correct identification of at least 4 out of 5 locations based on the coordinates.
Materials
Maps with lat/long grids, Coordinate lists
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a magnifying glass for students who have difficulty reading small map print.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 40 mins independent practice, 10 mins peer review.

inquiry-mru-drops · 90 min · practice

Students set up a tall clear bottle filled with oil. They drop a small bead into the oil and use a stopwatch to time its descent past evenly spaced marks on the bottle. They graph position vs. time and use the straight-line graph to justify classifying the motion as MRU.

Mastery criterion
Students produce a linear graph and correctly argue that the constant slope indicates constant speed, fulfilling MRU criteria.
Materials
Clear plastic bottles, Vegetable oil, Small beads, Stopwatches, Markers, Graph paper
Safety
Clean up any oil spills immediately to prevent slipping. Do not ingest the oil.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn axes on the graph paper.
Time rationale
30 mins setup and data collection, 30 mins graphing, 30 mins analysis and writing.

inquiry-mcu-spinning · 90 min · practice

Students build a simple centrifuge using a salad spinner. They place a small marked object inside, spin it at a steady rate, and attempt to count rotations per 10 seconds. They analyze the difficulty of maintaining constant angular speed and write a report on whether their manual spinning truly achieved MCU.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly apply the definition of MCU to evaluate their own experimental setup, noting variations in rotation speed.
Materials
Salad spinners, Small objects (e.g., erasers), Stopwatches
Safety
Ensure the salad spinner lid is securely fastened before spinning.
Access and differentiation
Have students work in pairs: one spins and one times/counts.
Time rationale
20 mins setup, 40 mins experimentation and data collection, 30 mins report writing.

practice-forces-equilibrium · 60 min · practice

Students are given a worksheet with 5 diagrams of objects with various force vectors applied. They must calculate the net force for each. If the net force is zero, they predict the object's motion state (rest or constant velocity) and justify it.

Mastery criterion
Accurate calculation of net force and correct prediction of motion state based on Newton's First Law.
Materials
Worksheets with force diagrams
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use only horizontal or vertical forces (no angles) to simplify net force calculation.
Time rationale
15 mins review of vector addition, 35 mins independent practice, 10 mins review.

inquiry-torque-doors · 90 min · practice

Students use a spring scale to pull open a heavy door from three different measured distances from the hinge. They record the force required at each distance. They graph Force vs. Distance from Hinge and write a conclusion justifying the inverse relationship based on torque requirements.

Mastery criterion
Students collect accurate force data showing less force is needed further from the hinge, and justify this using the concept of lever arm and torque.
Materials
Spring scales, Measuring tapes, Classroom doors
Safety
Ensure students do not pull the spring scales beyond their maximum limit to prevent snapping.
Access and differentiation
Provide a structured data table and graph axes.
Time rationale
30 mins data collection, 30 mins graphing, 30 mins analysis and conclusion.

inquiry-rubber-bands · 90 min · practice

Students build a simple rubber band launcher using cardboard tubes. They measure how far a paper ball is launched when the rubber band is pulled back 2 cm, 4 cm, and 6 cm. They record the data and write a summary identifying how the stretch distance relates to the stored elastic potential energy.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify that greater stretch (deformation) stores more elastic potential energy, evidenced by the longer launch distance.
Materials
Cardboard tubes, Rubber bands, Paper balls, Rulers, Measuring tapes
Safety
Students must wear safety goggles. Never aim launchers at people.
Access and differentiation
Pre-cut the cardboard tubes for students who struggle with scissors.
Time rationale
40 mins building launchers, 30 mins testing and measuring, 20 mins writing summary.

inquiry-ramps-marbles · 90 min · practice

Students roll marbles of different masses down a ramp from different heights into a plastic cup. They measure how far the cup slides. They conduct trials varying only height (to test gravitational potential) and then varying only mass (to test kinetic energy impact). They write a report comparing the effects.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly isolate variables, showing that greater height (more potential energy) and greater mass (more kinetic energy) both result in the cup sliding further.
Materials
Marbles of different masses, Ramps, Plastic cups, Rulers
Safety
Keep marbles on the floor to prevent slipping hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a step-by-step experimental procedure checklist.
Time rationale
20 mins setup, 40 mins conducting trials, 30 mins report writing.

practice-energy-transformation · 90 min · practice

Students analyze a diagram of a roller coaster track with 4 labeled points. They must write a paragraph for each point, justifying the relative amounts of potential and kinetic energy based on the height and expected speed, and explaining the transformations between points.

Mastery criterion
Accurate justification of energy states at all 4 points, clearly describing the continuous transformation between potential and kinetic energy.
Materials
Roller coaster diagrams, Writing materials
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank (e.g., increases, decreases, transforms, maximum, minimum).
Time rationale
20 mins review of concepts, 50 mins independent analysis and writing, 20 mins peer review.

assessment-kinematics · 60 min · assessment

Students complete a written assessment featuring scenario-based questions requiring them to calculate displacement, read map coordinates, classify motion types from data tables, predict motion from force diagrams, and justify torque applications.

Mastery criterion
Students score 80% or higher on the rubric, demonstrating accurate application and reasoning across all kinematics and dynamics micros.
Materials
Printed assessments
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow extra time or oral explanation of reasoning for students with writing difficulties.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 50 mins assessment completion.

assessment-energy · 60 min · assessment

Students complete a written assessment analyzing diagrams of mechanical systems (springs, ramps, pendulums), comparing energy states, and justifying energy transformations.

Mastery criterion
Students score 80% or higher on the rubric, demonstrating accurate identification, comparison, and reasoning regarding mechanical energy.
Materials
Printed assessments
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide larger diagrams and clear, bold text.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 50 mins assessment completion.

retrieval-distance-disp-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given a blank grid and a starting point. The teacher reads a sequence of movements. Students draw the path, calculate total distance, and draw/measure the displacement vector. They compare answers with a partner.

Mastery criterion
Accurate drawing of the path and correct calculation of both distance and displacement.

Grid paper, Rulers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation

5 mins instructions, 15 mins drawing and calculating, 10 mins partner comparison.

retrieval-distance-disp-2 · 30 min · retrieval

Students analyze three pre-drawn paths on a grid. They must identify which path has the longest distance, which has the longest displacement, and write a sentence explaining why the two answers are different.

Mastery criterion
Correct identification of the longest distance and displacement, with a clear explanation distinguishing path length from straight-line change.
Materials
Worksheets with pre-drawn paths
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation

5 mins instructions, 20 mins independent work, 5 mins review.

retrieval-energy-trans-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Students watch a short video of a skateboarder in a half-pipe. They sketch the half-pipe, mark three positions, and write a brief justification of how potential and kinetic energy transform as the skater moves back and forth.

Mastery criterion
Accurate justification of energy transformation, noting max potential at the edges and max kinetic at the bottom.
Materials
Video clip of a skateboarder, Paper and pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation

10 mins video observation, 20 mins sketching and writing.

retrieval-energy-trans-2 · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given a set of cards showing different stages of a bouncing ball. They must sequence the cards and write a sentence for each transition explaining the energy transformation occurring (e.g., falling: potential to kinetic; hitting ground: kinetic to elastic potential).

Mastery criterion
Correct sequencing of cards and accurate description of energy transformations at each stage.
Materials
Sets of sequencing cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a template with sentence starters for the explanations.

5 mins instructions, 20 mins sequencing and writing, 5 mins review.

bridge-math-physics · 60 min · bridge

Students review Cartesian coordinate graphing from math class. They plot a series of points to form a shape, then calculate the distance of the perimeter and the displacement from the first point to the last point (which should be zero if closed).

Graph paper, Rulers

Standard classroom safety.

Students work in groups to map out a multi-leg journey across the school courtyard. They use measuring tapes to record the distance of each leg and sum them up for the total distance. Finally, they measure the straight-line displacement from the start to the end point and compare the two values.

Students accurately measure and sum the path segments for distance and correctly measure the straight-line displacement, explaining the difference.

Measuring tapes, Chalk, Clipboards and paper

retrieval-mru-mcu · 30 min · retrieval

Students are shown 4 short video clips of different motions (a car on a straight highway, a spinning fan, a bouncing ball, a pendulum). They must quickly classify each as MRU, MCU, or neither, and write one sentence justifying their choice.

Mastery criterion
Correct classification of MRU and MCU with accurate reference to trajectory and constant speed/rotation.

Video clips, Whiteboards and markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Pause videos to allow extra processing time.

10 mins video viewing, 15 mins writing, 5 mins review.

retrieval-forces · 30 min · retrieval

Students receive a quick quiz with 3 force diagrams. They must calculate the net force for each and predict if the object will remain at rest/constant velocity or accelerate.

Accurate net force calculation and correct prediction of the motion state.

Printed quizzes

Standard classroom safety.

Limitations: The distinction between speed and velocity is simplified for 5th grade, focusing primarily on straight-line vs. circular paths rather than full vector algebra.; Friction and air resistance are largely ignored in energy transformation tasks to allow for clear conservation reasoning.; The MCU activity relies on manual spinning, which will not produce perfect constant angular velocity; this limitation is used as a teaching point in the inquiry task.; Teacher review is required for all written justifications to assess the quality of reasoning, as automated or simple rubric scoring may miss nuances in student explanations.

Atomic structure

The unit begins with the historical development of atomic models, establishing the particulate nature of matter. It then focuses on identifying and calculating subatomic particles. This knowledge is applied to understand isotopes and relative atomic mass. Next, students explore how the transfer of electrons creates ions and drives electrostatic interactions. Finally, the progression introduces a simplified quantum mechanical model, focusing on energy levels and basic electron arrangements.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Atomic Structure, Isotopes, and Interactions

Students build a foundational understanding of matter by exploring historical models, subatomic particles, isotopes, and how electron transfer leads to electrostatic interactions.

describe the historical evolution of atomic models
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the scientist to their proposed atomic model.
Expected response
Thomson is matched with the plum pudding model, Rutherford with the nucleus, etc.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correct match.
Mastery evidence
Students can describe key features of historical atomic models.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The current atomic model was discovered all at once.; Old models are completely useless.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Many scientists throughout history have investigated the composition of matter, leading to different atomic models. · Source page 76 · paragraph p76-paragraph-9
label a visual model of an atom distinguishing the nucleus and electron cloud
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Provide a blank diagram of an atom. Ask the student to label the nucleus, protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Expected response
The student labels the central dense area as the nucleus containing protons and neutrons, and the outer area as containing electrons.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly labeling the nucleus; 1 point for correctly placing protons/neutrons inside and electrons outside.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly identify the nucleus (containing protons and neutrons) and the electron cloud in a given atomic model.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Atoms are solid spheres with no internal structure.; Electrons are located inside the nucleus along with protons.
Local prerequisites
describe-historical-models
Scientific support
  • The atom has a central, dense nucleus. · Source page 75 · paragraph p75-paragraph-6
calculate the number of neutrons in an atom given its mass number and atomic number
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given an atom of Calcium with a mass number of 40 and an atomic number of 20, calculate the number of neutrons.
Expected response
40 - 20 = 20 neutrons.
Scoring rule
1 point for setting up the correct subtraction; 1 point for the correct final answer.
Mastery evidence
Students can subtract the atomic number from the mass number to find the number of neutrons.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The atomic number represents the total number of particles in the atom.; Neutrons and protons always exist in equal numbers in every atom.
Local prerequisites
label-subatomic-particles
Scientific support
  • Neutrons are calculated by subtracting protons from the mass number. · Source page 78 · paragraph p78-paragraph-11
differentiate isotopes of the same element from atoms of different elements based on proton and neutron counts
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Atom X has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Atom Y has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Are they the same element? Justify your answer.
Expected response
Yes, they are isotopes of the same element because they have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
Scoring rule
1 point for identifying them as the same element/isotopes; 1 point for justifying based on equal protons and unequal neutrons.
Mastery evidence
Students can analyze particle counts to determine if two atoms are isotopes of the same element or different elements.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Isotopes are completely different elements.; Changing the number of neutrons changes the chemical identity of the atom.

calculate the relative atomic mass using isotopic mass and natural abundance percentages
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element with two isotopes: Isotope A (mass 10, abundance 20%) and Isotope B (mass 11, abundance 80%).
Expected response
(10 * 0.20) + (11 * 0.80) = 2 + 8.8 = 10.8
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly setting up the weighted average; 1 point for the correct final calculation.
Mastery evidence
Students can multiply isotopic masses by their abundance percentages and sum them to find relative atomic mass.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Atomic mass is just a simple average of the mass numbers of all isotopes.; All isotopes of an element exist in equal amounts in nature.

classify atoms as cations or anions based on the loss or gain of electrons

applying

applying
Assessment task

Quantum Numbers and Electron Configuration

After understanding basic atomic structure, students transition to a more abstract model of the atom, learning how electrons are organized in energy levels, sublevels, and orbitals, which dictates chemical behavior.

match quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) to their corresponding physical meaning in the atom
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match the principal quantum number (n) to its correct description from a list of options.
Expected response
The principal quantum number (n) determines the energy level of the electron.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly matching 'n' to 'energy level'.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly associate each of the four quantum numbers with its description (energy level, sublevel, orbital orientation, spin).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Quantum numbers represent exact physical coordinates like GPS.; All electrons in an atom can have the exact same quantum numbers.
Local prerequisites
label-subatomic-particles
Scientific support
  • The principal quantum number determines the energy level. · Source page 91 · paragraph p91-paragraph-7
write the electron configuration of an element up to Z=20 using the Moeller diagram
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Write the electron configuration for Sulfur (Z=16).
Expected response
1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4
Scoring rule
1 point for correct order of orbitals; 1 point for correct superscript numbers adding up to 16.
Mastery evidence
Students can use the diagonal rule to write the correct electron configuration for a given atomic number.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Electrons fill energy levels sequentially without overlapping (e.g., all of level 3 fills before level 4).; The 'p' sublevel can hold up to 10 electrons.
Local prerequisites
match-quantum-numbers
Scientific support
  • Electrons fill lower energy orbitals first according to the Aufbau principle. · Source page 96 · paragraph p96-paragraph-6
draw orbital diagrams applying Hund's rule and Pauli exclusion principle
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Draw the orbital diagram for the 2p sublevel containing 3 electrons.
Expected response
Three separate boxes/lines, each containing one upward-pointing arrow.
Scoring rule
1 point for placing one electron in each orbital; 1 point for all arrows pointing in the same direction.
Mastery evidence
Students can represent electrons as arrows in boxes/lines, ensuring single occupancy before pairing and opposite spins for paired electrons.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Electrons pair up in orbitals before filling empty orbitals in the same sublevel.; Two electrons in the same orbital can have the same spin direction.
Local prerequisites
write-electron-configuration
Scientific support
  • Electrons are placed one by one in each orbital with upward spin first. · Source page 96 · paragraph p96-paragraph-6
relate electron configuration to the ability to form compounds
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task

1 point for mentioning outer electrons; 1 point for mentioning giving/taking electrons.

Limitations: The quantum mechanical model is highly simplified for 5th-grade comprehension; concepts like wave-particle duality and probability density functions are omitted.; Atomic models are presented as representations to aid understanding, not as direct physical observations of atoms.; Calculations of relative atomic mass use simplified, whole-number isotopic masses and clean percentages, which may not reflect the exact precision of real-world mass spectrometry data.; Safety constraints prevent the use of actual radioactive isotopes; all isotope discussions are theoretical or rely on secondary data.

Periodic table

Students enter Grade 5 with basic notions of matter. This unit introduces the systematic organization of elements, starting from historical attempts to the modern periodic table based on atomic number and electron configuration. The progression moves from macroscopic uses of elements to atomic structure (groups, periods, electron configuration), then to periodic trends (atomic radius, ionization energy), and finally to how elements combine (ions, oxidation numbers, chemical formulas). In future grades, students will revisit these concepts to explore complex chemical bonding and stoichiometry.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 4 planning weeks.

Analyzing the organization and properties of elements in the periodic table

Understanding how elements are organized based on their atomic structure and properties is fundamental for predicting chemical behavior.

identify historical models of element classification such as Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' octaves
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task

Expected response

Scoring rule
1 point for each correctly matched historical model and explanation.
Mastery evidence

Diagnostic hypotheses

Local prerequisites

Scientific support
  • Döbereiner's triads were an early attempt to systematize chemical elements. · Source page 108 · paragraph p108-paragraph-10
identify protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task

Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may confuse the location of protons and electrons.; Students might think all atoms have the same number of neutrons as protons.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The textbook asks students to determine the number of protons, electrons, and neutrons for an atom given its atomic number. · Source page 116 · paragraph p116-paragraph-2
locate elements in the periodic table using their group and period numbers
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a blank periodic table grid, write the symbol for Sodium (Na) in Group 1, Period 3.
Expected response
Writes 'Na' in the intersection of the first column and the third row.
Scoring rule
Pass if the symbol is placed in the exact correct cell.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately finds the symbol of an element given its group and period coordinates.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may confuse groups (columns) with periods (rows).; Students might start counting periods from the second row, ignoring hydrogen and helium.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Columns in the periodic table are called groups. · Source page 111 · paragraph p111-paragraph-6
classify elements into specific families like alkali metals, halogens, and noble gases based on their group
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Color Group 1 (excluding hydrogen) and label it as 'alkali metals'.
Expected response
Colors Group 1 (excluding hydrogen) and labels it 'metales alcalinos' (alkali metals).
Scoring rule
Pass if the correct group is colored and labeled accurately.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the family name for a given group of elements.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think hydrogen is an alkali metal because it is in Group 1.; Students might group transition metals with representative elements.
Local prerequisites
locate-elements-group-period
Scientific support
  • Group 1 elements, excluding hydrogen, are classified as alkali metals. · Source page 111 · paragraph p111-paragraph-6
justify the position of an element in the periodic table using its outermost electron configuration
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Explain why Lithium (Li) and Sodium (Na) are in the same group based on their electron configuration.
Expected response
Both elements have one electron in their outermost energy level (orbital s), which places them in Group 1.
Scoring rule
Pass if the response explicitly connects the single outer electron to the group placement.
Mastery evidence
Student explains that elements in the same group share similar outer electron configurations, which dictates their position.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think the total number of electrons determines the group number directly.; Students might not realize that elements in the same group have similar outer electron configurations.
Local prerequisites
locate-elements-group-period, identify-atomic-structure
Scientific support
  • An element's electron configuration determines its location on the periodic table. · Source page 113 · paragraph p113-paragraph-4
predict the relative atomic radius of elements based on their position in a group or period
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Given Potassium (K) and Bromine (Br) in the same period, and Lithium (Li) and Potassium (K) in the same group, predict which has a larger atomic radius and state why.
Expected response
Potassium has a larger radius than Bromine because increased nuclear charge pulls electrons closer across a period. Potassium is larger than Lithium because it has more electron shells down a group.
Scoring rule
Pass if Potassium is selected in both cases and the justification mentions the trends across a period and down a group.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly predicts which of two elements has a larger atomic radius based on periodic trends across a period and down a group.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may assume that atomic radius always increases as atomic number increases across a period.; Students might think adding more electrons in the same period makes the atom larger.
Local prerequisites
locate-elements-group-period
Scientific support
  • The textbook asks students to identify how atomic radius increases in a group and period. · Source page 115 · paragraph p115-paragraph-8

Interpreting chemical formulas and ion formation

Transitioning from individual elements to compounds requires understanding how atoms gain or lose electrons to form ions and how these are represented in chemical formulas.

identify the types of elements and the number of atoms of each in a simple chemical formula
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
List the elements and the number of atoms for each in the formula H2O.
Expected response
Hydrogen: 2 atoms, Oxygen: 1 atom.
Scoring rule
Pass if both elements and their exact atom counts are correct.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly lists the elements and their respective atom counts from a given formula.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may ignore subscripts and assume one atom of each element is present.; Students might confuse a subscript with a coefficient.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • A chemical formula indicates the composition of a substance. · Source page 124 · paragraph p124-paragraph-5
determine whether an atom becomes a cation or an anion based on the loss or gain of electrons
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
If a Chlorine atom gains one electron, determine if it becomes a cation or an anion.
Expected response
It becomes an anion.
Scoring rule
Pass if 'anion' is stated.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the resulting ion type when an atom gains or loses electrons.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think gaining electrons results in a positive charge.; Students might confuse protons and electrons when determining charge.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • An atom that loses electrons is a cation, and one that gains electrons is an anion. · Source page 115 · paragraph p115-paragraph-11
predict the size of an ionic radius compared to its neutral atom
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Predict whether a sodium cation (Na+) is larger or smaller than a neutral sodium atom (Na), and justify your answer.
Expected response
Smaller, because it has lost its outermost electron, reducing the electron cloud size.
Scoring rule
Pass if 'smaller' is selected and the loss of an electron is mentioned.
Mastery evidence
Student predicts and justifies the size difference between an ion and its neutral counterpart.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think a cation is larger than its neutral atom because it is 'positive'.; Students might assume ions and neutral atoms of the same element have the same size.

Scientific support

+2

Pass if +2 is provided.
