Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-historical-models · 40 min · teach

Present the historical progression of element classification using visual diagrams of Dobereiner triads, Chancourtois telluric helix, and Newlands octaves. Students observe the diagrams and trace the patterns described by each scientist using colored markers on printed handouts.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly matches the name of the historical model with its visual representation.
Materials
Printed diagrams of historical models, Colored markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-highlighted patterns for students needing visual support.
Time rationale
15 minutes for direct instruction on the three models, 15 minutes for guided tracing of patterns, 10 minutes for summarizing.

teach-locate-elements · 40 min · teach

Introduce the modern periodic table layout, defining groups as vertical columns and periods as horizontal rows. Demonstrate how to find an element using its group and period coordinates, similar to a map grid. Students practice finding three guided examples.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately finds the symbol of an element given its group and period coordinates.
Materials
Large periodic table poster, Individual periodic table handouts
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use a ruler or L-shaped cardboard tool to help students track rows and columns visually.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explanation of groups and periods, 15 minutes for guided examples, 10 minutes for independent check.

practice-locate-elements · 50 min · practice

Students play a coordinate mapping game in pairs. One student calls out a group and period number, and the other must identify the element symbol at that intersection on their blank periodic table grid, writing it in the correct cell.

Student correctly writes the element symbol in the exact cell corresponding to the given group and period.
Materials
Blank periodic table grids, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a partially filled grid with key anchor elements for reference.

10 minutes for game setup and rules, 30 minutes of gameplay, 10 minutes for role reversal and wrap-up.

assess-locate-elements · 40 min · assessment

Limitations: The historical models (triads, octaves) are highly simplified for primary level.; Electron configuration is introduced conceptually without full quantum mechanical depth.; Oxidation numbers are presented as fixed for representative groups, ignoring variable oxidation states of transition metals.

Space science

The unit begins with the macro-scale of the universe, exploring its expansion and the evidence for it (redshift). It then narrows down to the formation of our solar system via accretion and the life cycle of stars. Once the cosmic context is established, the progression shifts to Earth, examining its internal layers, crust formation, and protective magnetosphere. Finally, the unit covers human efforts to explore this space environment through various spacecraft and satellite designs. Prerequisites ensure students understand expansion before analyzing redshift, star stages before predicting stellar death, and Earth's layers before explaining crust formation or the magnetosphere.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Cosmic Evolution and Solar System Formation

Students build a foundational understanding of the universe's scale and history, moving from the abstract expansion of the universe to the concrete formation of our solar system and the life cycle of stars.

construct a physical model demonstrating the increasing distance between galaxies
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using a balloon with marked dots, inflate it and measure the distances between dots before and after inflation to show expansion.
Expected response
The distances between all dots increase proportionally as the balloon inflates, modeling how galaxies move apart.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student correctly records the initial and final distances and states that all points moved away from each other.
Mastery evidence
Student successfully creates a model showing proportional expansion between points.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Galaxies themselves expand in size; The universe has a specific center point from which everything expands
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The expansion of the universe is evidence of the Big Bang theory. · Source page 131 · paragraph p131-paragraph-29
interpret redshift data to determine if a celestial body is moving away
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Given a scenario where a galaxy's light spectrum shifts toward red, determine the direction of its movement relative to Earth and justify the answer.
Expected response
The galaxy is moving away from Earth because its light waves are stretching, which is called redshift.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student links the red shift to the stretching of wavelengths and the object moving away.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies that a shift toward longer wavelengths indicates an object is moving away.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Redshift means the star is physically turning red in color
Local prerequisites
model-universe-expansion
Scientific support
  • Redshift is a phenomenon involving the change in wavelength. · Source page 131 · paragraph p131-paragraph-30
sequence the stages of planetary formation through accretion
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Arrange a set of cards describing dust, chondrules, meteoroids, asteroids, planetesimals, and planets in the correct order of formation.
Expected response
Dust particle, chondrule, meteoroid, asteroid, planetesimal, planet.
Scoring rule
Passes if all stages are placed in the correct sequential order of increasing size.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly orders the stages from dust particles to a full planet.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Planets were formed fully intact from the beginning
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Planets formed through the accretion of matter. · Source page 136 · paragraph p136-paragraph-2
categorize stellar bodies into their corresponding life cycle stages
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Match descriptions of stellar characteristics to the correct stage name (e.g., nebula, red giant).
Expected response
Matches 'interstellar cloud of gas and dust' to nebula, and 'small, hot, cooling star' to white dwarf.
Scoring rule
Passes if at least 3 out of 4 stages are correctly matched to their descriptions.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies nebulae, main sequence stars, red giants, and white dwarfs.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All stars end up as black holes
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • A nebula is an interstellar cloud of dust and gas where stars are born. · Source page 139 · paragraph p139-paragraph-6
predict the final evolutionary stage of a star based on its mass
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Given two stars, one with low mass and one with extremely high mass, predict their final evolutionary stages and explain why.
Expected response
The low-mass star will become a white dwarf, and the high-mass star will become a supernova and then a black hole or neutron star, because mass determines a star's evolutionary path.
Scoring rule
Passes if the prediction correctly aligns mass with the final stage and references mass as the determining factor.
Mastery evidence
Student deduces that high-mass stars become supernovae/black holes while low-mass stars become white dwarfs.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Massive stars live longer because they have more fuel
Local prerequisites
classify-star-stages
Scientific support
  • A star's evolutionary phases depend on its mass. · Source page 141 · paragraph p141-paragraph-4

Earth's Structure and Space Exploration

Connects the broader cosmic context to our own planet's formation and structure, and explores how humanity investigates these phenomena through space technology.

label the internal layers of the Earth on a diagram
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Label a cross-section diagram of the Earth with its four main layers.
Expected response
Crust on the outside, then mantle, outer core, and inner core at the center.
Scoring rule
Passes if all four layers are labeled in the correct order from exterior to interior.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The Earth is completely solid all the way through
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The outer core is composed of liquid iron and nickel. · Source page 148 · paragraph p148-paragraph-11
summarize the terrestrial model of Earth's crust formation
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Write a brief summary explaining how the Earth's crust formed according to the terrestrial model.
Expected response
The Earth's crust formed when the early Earth's magma ocean cooled down over time, creating a solid outer layer.
Scoring rule
Passes if the summary mentions the cooling of magma or internal processes forming the solid layer.
Mastery evidence
Student explains that the crust formed from the cooling of a magma ocean.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The crust was formed by asteroids crashing into Earth
Local prerequisites
identify-earth-layers
Scientific support
  • The terrestrial model explains the formation of the Earth's crust. · Source page 152 · paragraph p152-paragraph-6
justify the importance of the magnetosphere for planetary habitability
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain what would happen to Earth's habitability if the magnetosphere suddenly disappeared, using evidence about solar wind.
Expected response
If the magnetosphere disappeared, solar wind and energy would hit Earth directly, making it uninhabitable because the shield that absorbs and deflects this energy would be gone.
Scoring rule
Passes if the student connects the absence of the magnetosphere to the destructive impact of solar wind on habitability.
Mastery evidence
Student argues that without the magnetosphere, solar wind would make Earth uninhabitable.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The magnetosphere blocks all sunlight from reaching Earth
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Earth's magnetosphere absorbs energy from the solar wind. · Source page 151 · paragraph p151-paragraph-3
distinguish between space stations, satellites, and rovers based on their functions
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given descriptions of a space station, a satellite, and a rover, identify which vehicle matches each description.
Expected response
Matches 'orbiting habitat for humans' to space station, 'orbiting communication device' to satellite, and 'surface exploration vehicle' to rover.
Scoring rule
Passes if all three vehicles are correctly matched to their functional descriptions.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies the purpose of different space exploration vehicles.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All spacecraft carry human astronauts
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • A space station is an artificial construction designed for activities in outer space. · Source page 144 · paragraph p144-paragraph-4
design a diagram of a satellite including power, communication, and scientific instruments
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Draw a diagram of a satellite and label its container, power source, scientific instruments, and communication system.
Expected response
A drawing showing a central body (container), solar panels (power), cameras/sensors (instruments), and an antenna (communication), all labeled.
Scoring rule
Passes if the diagram includes and correctly labels at least three of the four required components.
Mastery evidence
Student creates a functional diagram with all required satellite components labeled.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Satellites do not need a power source once in space
Local prerequisites
differentiate-spacecraft
Scientific support
  • Satellites require a container to hold and protect their instruments. · Source page 145 · paragraph p145-paragraph-7
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-universe-expansion · 60 min · teach

Students work in pairs to draw dots on a deflated balloon, measure the distances between them with a flexible tape, inflate the balloon halfway, measure again, and then inflate fully and measure a final time. They record the data in a table and write a conclusion about how the distance between all points increases simultaneously.

Mastery criterion
Student successfully creates a model showing proportional expansion between points and records accurate measurements.
Materials
round balloons, permanent markers, flexible measuring tapes, data recording sheets
Safety
Ensure students do not over-inflate balloons to prevent popping near faces. Students with latex allergies should use alternative silicone balloons or observe.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn tables for data collection. For advanced students, ask them to calculate the ratio of expansion between different pairs of dots.
Time rationale
10 minutes for introduction and safety, 20 minutes for the three stages of inflation and measurement, 15 minutes for data analysis, and 15 minutes for group discussion and conclusion writing.

practice-universe-expansion · 60 min · practice

Students use a large elastic band with evenly spaced marks to model expansion along a single line of sight between galaxies. One student holds the end while another stretches it along a meter stick. They record the positions of the marks at rest, at 50cm stretch, and at 100cm stretch, graphing the movement of each mark relative to the starting point.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately graphs the positions showing that marks further away move a greater distance than marks closer to the origin.
Materials
thick elastic bands with permanent marker dots, meter sticks, graph paper, pencils
Safety
Students must wear safety goggles to protect eyes in case the elastic band snaps or slips.
Access and differentiation
Provide graph paper with pre-labeled axes. Challenge fast finishers to predict the position of a hypothetical mark beyond the elastic band's current length.
Time rationale
15 minutes for setup and safety briefing, 25 minutes for stretching and recording data, 20 minutes for graphing and peer review.

assess-universe-expansion · 45 min · assessment

Students are given a worksheet with a diagram of a grid representing space with galaxies at specific coordinates. They must draw a second grid showing the universe expanded by a factor of two, placing the galaxies at their new coordinates and writing a short explanation of the model.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly plots the new coordinates (doubling the distance from the origin) and states that all points moved away from each other.
Materials
assessment worksheets with grids, rulers, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies. Ensure clear walkways during the assessment.
Access and differentiation
Allow the use of a calculator for coordinate multiplication. Provide a partially started grid for students needing visual support.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 25 minutes for independent grid drawing and calculation, 10 minutes for writing the explanation.

teach-explain-redshift · 60 min · teach

Students use a coiled spring toy (slinky) to model light waves. They stretch the spring while moving one end away from a stationary observer to simulate how wavelengths lengthen (redshift). They then review three hypothetical star spectrum charts and justify which stars are moving away based on the shift of absorption lines toward the red end.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies that a shift toward longer wavelengths indicates an object is moving away and justifies this using the wave model.
Materials
coiled spring toys, printed spectrum charts showing normal and shifted absorption lines, colored pencils
Safety
Ensure students do not release the stretched spring toy abruptly to avoid pinching fingers or hitting others.
Access and differentiation
Provide a reference chart showing the visible light spectrum with wavelengths labeled. Ask advanced students to explain what a blueshift would mean.
Time rationale
15 minutes for the physical spring model, 20 minutes for analyzing the spectrum charts, 25 minutes for writing the justification and class sharing.

practice-explain-redshift · 60 min · practice

Students are given a set of cards with data from different galaxies, including their observed spectral lines compared to laboratory standards. They must sort the galaxies into 'moving away', 'moving closer', or 'stationary', and write a paragraph justifying their sorting based on the stretching or compressing of the light waves.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately sorts the galaxies and links the red shift to the stretching of wavelengths and the object moving away.
Materials
galaxy data cards, sorting mats, notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the specific absorption lines on the cards for easier comparison. Require advanced students to order the 'moving away' galaxies by speed based on the degree of shift.
Time rationale
10 minutes for card distribution and instructions, 30 minutes for sorting and group discussion, 20 minutes for independent writing.

assess-explain-redshift · 45 min · assessment

Students read a scenario about a newly discovered galaxy whose light spectrum is heavily shifted toward the red end. They must write a formal scientific response determining the direction of its movement relative to Earth and justifying their answer using the concept of wavelength stretching.

Mastery criterion
Student links the red shift to the stretching of wavelengths and the object moving away in a clear written response.
Materials
assessment prompt sheets, pens
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a sentence starter for the justification section. Do not reduce the requirement to explain the wavelength stretching.
Time rationale
10 minutes for reading the scenario, 25 minutes for drafting the response, 10 minutes for review and editing.

retrieval-1-explain-redshift · 30 min · retrieval

Students participate in a quick-write activity where they are shown a single image of a stretched wave and a compressed wave. They must identify which represents redshift and explain why this means a galaxy is moving away from Earth.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies the stretched wave as redshift and explains it indicates movement away from the observer.
Materials
projector or printed images of waves, index cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal responses for students with writing difficulties, recorded by the teacher.
Time rationale
5 minutes to display the image and explain the prompt, 15 minutes for writing, 10 minutes for peer exchange and discussion.

retrieval-2-explain-redshift · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given a true/false quiz with statements about light waves and galaxy movement. For every false statement, they must rewrite it to make it true, specifically focusing on the relationship between redshift and expansion.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies false statements and rewrites them to accurately reflect that redshift means wavelengths are stretching as objects move away.
Materials
true/false worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a glossary of terms (wavelength, spectrum, redshift) for reference.
Time rationale
15 minutes to complete the quiz, 15 minutes to review answers as a class and correct misconceptions.

teach-sequence-accretion · 60 min · teach

Students use different sizes of modeling clay to represent the stages of accretion. They start with tiny specks (dust), combine them into small balls (chondrules), then larger lumps (meteoroids/asteroids), and finally a large sphere (planet). They label each stage on a large piece of paper.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly orders and models the stages from dust particles to a full planet.
Materials
modeling clay in various colors, large construction paper, markers
Safety
Ensure students wash hands after using clay. Do not allow tasting or throwing of clay.
Access and differentiation
Provide printed labels with definitions for students to match to their clay models. Challenge advanced students to write the relative size of each stage.
Time rationale
10 minutes for introduction, 30 minutes for building the clay models sequentially, 20 minutes for labeling and gallery walk.

practice-sequence-accretion · 60 min · practice

Students work in small groups with a set of 20 cards containing images and descriptions of accretion stages. They must race to arrange them in the correct chronological order of formation, then create a timeline poster gluing the cards in sequence.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly orders the stages from dust particles to a full planet on their timeline.
Materials
sets of accretion stage cards, glue sticks, poster board
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Number the backs of the cards for self-checking for students who struggle. Require advanced students to add transitional arrows explaining the physical process (gravity/collisions).
Time rationale
15 minutes for the sorting activity, 30 minutes for creating the timeline poster, 15 minutes for presenting posters to the class.

assess-sequence-accretion · 45 min · assessment

Students complete a matching and sequencing worksheet where they must draw lines connecting the terms (dust, chondrules, meteoroids, asteroids, planetesimals, planets) to their definitions, and then write them in a numbered list from smallest/earliest to largest/latest.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly orders the stages from dust particles to a full planet and matches them to their descriptions.
Materials
assessment worksheets, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank with the terms. Do not provide the order.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 25 minutes for independent completion, 10 minutes for collection and quiet reading.

teach-classify-star-stages · 60 min · teach

Students are given a set of 'stellar profile' folders containing characteristics (temperature, size, composition) of different star stages. They work in groups to categorize the profiles into nebula, main sequence, red giant, and white dwarf, using a reference text to verify their classifications.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies nebulae, main sequence stars, red giants, and white dwarfs based on their characteristics.
Materials
stellar profile folders, reference texts on star life cycles, categorization graphic organizers
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Highlight key characteristics in the profiles for easier reading. Ask advanced students to identify which stage our Sun is currently in.
Time rationale
15 minutes for reading the reference text, 30 minutes for analyzing and categorizing the profiles, 15 minutes for class review and correction.

practice-classify-star-stages · 60 min · practice

Students play a matching game where they must pair a card with a visual representation of a star stage to a card with its text description. Once all pairs are found, they glue them into their notebooks and write one additional fact for each stage.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly matches at least 3 out of 4 stages to their descriptions and visuals.
Materials
matching card sets, notebooks, glue, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide fewer cards per round for students who get overwhelmed. Require advanced students to write two facts per stage.
Time rationale
20 minutes for the matching game, 25 minutes for gluing and writing facts, 15 minutes for peer review.

assess-classify-star-stages · 45 min · assessment

Students complete a written quiz where they are given four descriptions of stellar characteristics and must write the correct stage name next to each description without a word bank.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies nebulae, main sequence stars, red giants, and white dwarfs from descriptions.
Materials
quiz papers, pens
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank for students with IEPs requiring memory support. The cognitive demand of matching remains.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 30 minutes for quiz completion, 10 minutes for collection.

teach-predict-star-death · 60 min · teach

Students analyze a flowchart showing the life cycles of stars based on initial mass. They are given two case studies: Star A (0.8 solar masses) and Star B (25 solar masses). They must trace the path of each star on the flowchart and write a justification for their final evolutionary stages based on the mass data.

Mastery criterion
Student deduces that high-mass stars become supernovae/black holes while low-mass stars become white dwarfs, referencing mass as the determining factor.
Materials
star life cycle flowcharts, case study sheets, highlighters
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a simplified flowchart with fewer intermediate steps. Ask advanced students to explain why mass dictates the core temperature and fusion rate.
Time rationale
15 minutes for flowchart analysis, 25 minutes for tracing the case studies, 20 minutes for writing the justification.

practice-predict-star-death · 60 min · practice

Students are given a list of ten hypothetical stars with their masses listed in solar masses. They must create a T-chart predicting whether each star will end as a white dwarf or undergo a supernova, and write a summary paragraph explaining the rule they used to make their predictions.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly categorizes the stars based on mass and articulates that high mass leads to supernovae and low mass to white dwarfs.
Materials
list of hypothetical stars, notebooks, rulers
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide the specific mass threshold (e.g., 8 solar masses) explicitly on the worksheet. Challenge advanced students to research and include neutron stars in their predictions.
Time rationale
10 minutes for setup, 30 minutes for categorizing the ten stars, 20 minutes for writing the summary paragraph.

assess-predict-star-death · 45 min · assessment

Students are presented with a short text describing two newly observed stars nearing the end of their lives, one very massive and one similar to our Sun. They must write a short essay predicting their final stages and explaining why their paths diverge.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly aligns mass with the final stage and references mass as the determining factor in their essay.
Materials
assessment prompts, lined paper, pens
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw a diagram to accompany and support their written explanation.
Time rationale
10 minutes for reading the prompt, 35 minutes for writing the essay.

teach-identify-earth-layers · 60 min · teach

Students build a cross-section model of the Earth using four different colors of modeling dough. They cut the sphere in half to reveal the layers and use toothpicks with paper flags to label the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies and labels the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core in the correct order.
Materials
four colors of modeling dough, plastic knives or dental floss for cutting, toothpicks, sticky labels
Safety
Ensure students use safe cutting tools (floss or dull plastic knives). Wash hands after handling dough.
Access and differentiation
Provide a reference diagram for students to check their work. Ask advanced students to write the state of matter (solid/liquid) on each flag.
Time rationale
10 minutes for material distribution, 30 minutes for building and cutting the model, 20 minutes for labeling and peer checking.

practice-identify-earth-layers · 60 min · practice

Students are given a large blank diagram of the Earth's cross-section. They must color each layer, draw a line to a text box, and write the name of the layer along with one key fact (e.g., composition or state of matter) sourced from their textbook.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly labels all four layers in the correct order from exterior to interior.
Materials
blank Earth diagrams, colored pencils, textbooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-filled text boxes with missing words for students who need writing support.
Time rationale
15 minutes for coloring, 30 minutes for researching facts and labeling, 15 minutes for class review.

assess-identify-earth-layers · 45 min · assessment

Students complete a diagram labeling quiz where they must write the names of the four main layers of the Earth in the correct boxes pointing to a cross-section image.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core in the correct order.
Materials
quiz diagrams, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank. The task of spatial identification remains the same.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 30 minutes for independent completion, 10 minutes for collection.

teach-describe-crust-formation · 60 min · teach

Students mix cornstarch and water to create a thick paste representing magma. They spread it in a shallow dish and observe as it dries and forms a solid crust on top, drawing a storyboard with three panels showing the wet mixture, the drying process, and the final solid crust, writing a descriptive caption for each.

Mastery criterion
Student explains that the crust formed from the cooling and solidifying of a magma ocean in their storyboard.
Materials
cornstarch, water, shallow dishes, storyboard templates, colored pencils
Safety
Do not ingest the mixture. Wash hands after the activity.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters for the captions. Ask advanced students to include the role of volcanic outgassing in their storyboards.
Time rationale
20 minutes for the mixture preparation and observation, 30 minutes for drawing and writing the storyboard, 10 minutes for sharing.

practice-describe-crust-formation · 60 min · practice

Students read a short text about the terrestrial model of crust formation. They must highlight key terms (magma, cooling, solid, crust) and then write a 5-sentence summary explaining the process in their own words, imagining they are explaining it to a younger sibling.

Mastery criterion
Student's summary mentions the cooling of magma or internal processes forming the solid layer.
Materials
reading passages, highlighters, notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a graphic organizer to help structure the summary. Challenge advanced students to compare this process to the formation of ice on a lake.
Time rationale
20 minutes for reading and highlighting, 30 minutes for drafting the summary, 10 minutes for peer reading.

assess-describe-crust-formation · 45 min · assessment

Students are given a prompt asking them to explain how the Earth's crust formed according to the terrestrial model. They must write a brief summary without using their notes.

Mastery criterion
Student explains that the crust formed from the cooling of a magma ocean.
Materials
assessment paper, pens
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw a diagram to supplement their written summary if they struggle with writing.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for writing, 5 minutes for collection.

teach-explain-magnetosphere · 60 min · teach

Students place a bar magnet inside a plastic bag and sprinkle iron filings on top to visualize a magnetic field. The teacher uses a fan (solar wind) to blow lightweight particles (confetti) at the bag, showing how a physical barrier deflects them. Students then write an argument explaining why Earth's magnetic field is necessary for life, using the demonstration as an analogy.

Mastery criterion
Student argues that without the magnetosphere, solar wind would make Earth uninhabitable, connecting the shield concept to habitability.
Materials
bar magnets, ziploc bags, iron filings, small fan, paper confetti, notebooks
Safety
Iron filings must remain sealed in plastic bags or clear containers to prevent inhalation or eye irritation. Keep fan away from water.
Access and differentiation
Provide a vocabulary list (deflect, solar wind, magnetic field). Ask advanced students to research and mention auroras as evidence of this deflection.
Time rationale
25 minutes for the hands-on demonstration and observation, 25 minutes for writing the argument, 10 minutes for class discussion.

practice-explain-magnetosphere · 60 min · practice

Students analyze a case study of Mars, which lost its magnetosphere. They read data about Mars' current atmosphere and surface radiation levels. They must write a comparative paragraph justifying what would happen to Earth's habitability if its magnetosphere disappeared, using the Mars data as evidence.

Mastery criterion
Student connects the absence of the magnetosphere to the destructive impact of solar wind on habitability, using evidence.
Materials
Mars case study sheets, notebooks, pens
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the key data points on the Mars sheet. Require advanced students to explain the role of Earth's liquid outer core in generating the field.
Time rationale
20 minutes for reading the case study, 30 minutes for writing the comparative paragraph, 10 minutes for peer review.

assess-explain-magnetosphere · 45 min · assessment

Students answer a constructed-response question: 'Explain what would happen to Earth's habitability if the magnetosphere suddenly disappeared. Use evidence about solar wind in your answer.'

Mastery criterion
Student connects the absence of the magnetosphere to the destructive impact of solar wind on habitability.
Materials
assessment prompts, pens
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a graphic organizer for planning the response before writing.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for writing the response, 5 minutes for collection.

retrieval-1-explain-magnetosphere · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given a 'What If?' scenario card stating the Earth's core has completely solidified, stopping the magnetic field. They have 15 minutes to sketch a before-and-after picture of Earth's surface and write a brief caption explaining the change in habitability.

Mastery criterion
Student illustrates and explains that the loss of the magnetic field allows solar wind to reach the surface, destroying habitability.
Materials
scenario cards, drawing paper, colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to focus only on the written explanation if drawing is a barrier.
Time rationale
5 minutes to read the scenario, 20 minutes to draw and write, 5 minutes to share with a partner.

retrieval-2-explain-magnetosphere · 30 min · retrieval

Students participate in a 'Think-Pair-Share' where they must verbally justify to a partner why astronauts traveling to Mars face higher radiation risks than those on the International Space Station (which is within Earth's magnetosphere). They then write down their partner's best point.

Mastery criterion
Student articulates that the magnetosphere blocks solar wind/radiation, and leaving it removes that protection.
Materials
notebooks, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a map showing the ISS orbit relative to the magnetosphere for visual context.
Time rationale
10 minutes for individual thinking and notes, 10 minutes for paired discussion, 10 minutes for writing down the final point.

teach-differentiate-spacecraft · 60 min · teach

Students examine large posters of a space station, a satellite, and a rover. They work in groups to list the visible features of each (e.g., wheels, solar panels, living quarters). They then match functional descriptions provided by the teacher to the correct vehicle based on their feature lists.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies the purpose of different space exploration vehicles and matches them to their descriptions.
Materials
large posters of spacecraft, feature list worksheets, functional description cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide descriptions with bolded keywords (e.g., 'human habitat', 'surface'). Ask advanced students to identify the specific names of real-world examples (e.g., ISS, Curiosity).
Time rationale
20 minutes for examining posters and listing features, 25 minutes for matching descriptions, 15 minutes for class review.

practice-differentiate-spacecraft · 60 min · practice

Students create a foldable brochure with three sections: Space Station, Satellite, and Rover. In each section, they must draw a simple icon, write its primary function, and list whether it carries humans, orbits a body, or lands on a surface.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies the functions and characteristics of space stations, satellites, and rovers in their brochure.
Materials
blank paper for folding, colored pencils, reference notes
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-folded brochures with section titles already written. Challenge advanced students to add a fourth section for 'Probes'.
Time rationale
10 minutes for folding and setup, 40 minutes for creating the content of the brochure, 10 minutes for a gallery walk.

assess-differentiate-spacecraft · 45 min · assessment

Students complete a multiple-choice and short-answer quiz where they are given descriptions of missions (e.g., 'We need to monitor weather patterns from orbit without a crew') and must identify which vehicle (space station, satellite, or rover) is required.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly matches all three vehicles to their functional descriptions in the mission scenarios.
Materials
quiz papers, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Read the scenarios aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 30 minutes for quiz completion, 10 minutes for collection.

teach-design-satellite · 60 min · teach

Students act as aerospace engineers. They are given a list of required satellite components (container, power source, scientific instruments, communication system). They use craft materials to build a 3D prototype of a satellite, ensuring all four components are present and identifiable, then present their model to the class.

Mastery criterion
Student creates a functional model with all required satellite components included and identifiable.
Materials
cardboard boxes, aluminum foil, pipe cleaners, bottle caps, glue, tape
Safety
Ensure safe use of scissors. Avoid sharp edges on cans or plastics if used.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist of the four components for students to check off as they build. Ask advanced students to explain how their specific instrument gathers data.
Time rationale
10 minutes for design briefing, 35 minutes for building the prototype, 15 minutes for presentations.

practice-design-satellite · 60 min · practice

Students read a brief informational text about El Salvador's volcanic chain (e.g., the Apaneca-Ilamatepec range). They then draw a detailed blueprint of a satellite designed to monitor this volcanic activity. They must label the container, solar panels (power), infrared cameras (instruments), and antenna (communication), and write a sentence for each explaining its specific role in this mission.

Mastery criterion
Student creates a diagram with all required satellite components labeled and explained in the context of the mission.
Materials
informational text on Salvadoran volcanoes, blueprint paper, rulers, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a template with the basic shape of the container already drawn. Challenge advanced students to include a propulsion system for orbit correction.
Time rationale
15 minutes for mission briefing and planning, 30 minutes for drawing and labeling, 15 minutes for writing the explanations.

assess-design-satellite · 45 min · assessment

Students are given a specific mission context (e.g., monitoring weather patterns over the ocean). They must design a satellite for this mission, drawing a diagram and justifying their choice of scientific instruments, power source, container, and communication system based on the mission's novel context.

Mastery criterion
Student diagram includes and correctly labels all four required components, with a valid justification for their specific design choices.
Materials
blank paper, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank of the four components for students who need memory support. The application of drawing and labeling remains.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for drawing, labeling, and justifying, 5 minutes for collection.

practice-2-model-universe-expansion · 60 min · practice

Students use a large rubber band with evenly spaced dots to model expansion. They stretch the band along a ruler, record the new positions of the dots, and calculate the proportional increase in distance to reinforce the concept of universal expansion.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately records the distances and explains that points further away move a greater distance, modeling expansion.
Materials
large rubber bands, rulers, markers, data tables
Safety
Students must wear safety goggles to protect their eyes in case the rubber band snaps.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn data tables. Challenge advanced students to graph the relationship between initial distance and distance moved.
Time rationale
15 minutes for setup and safety, 25 minutes for data collection, 20 minutes for analysis and discussion.

practice-2-sequence-accretion · 60 min · practice

Students create a six-panel comic strip illustrating the accretion process. They must draw and label each stage (dust, chondrules, meteoroids, asteroids, planetesimals, planets) in the correct chronological order.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly sequences all six stages of accretion and provides accurate visual representations for each.
Materials
comic strip templates, colored pencils, reference notes
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide templates with the terms already written in order for students who need support. Ask advanced students to include captions explaining the role of gravity.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 40 minutes for drawing and labeling, 10 minutes for sharing.

practice-2-identify-earth-layers · 60 min · practice

Students construct a 2D foldable model of the Earth using concentric paper circles of decreasing sizes. They must label each layer (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core) and write its state of matter (solid or liquid) underneath the flap.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly orders the four layers from exterior to interior and accurately identifies their states of matter.
Materials
colored paper circles, scissors, glue or brass fasteners, markers
Safety
Ensure safe use of scissors.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-cut circles for students with fine motor difficulties.
Time rationale
15 minutes for cutting and assembly, 30 minutes for labeling and writing facts, 15 minutes for peer review.

practice-2-design-satellite · 60 min · practice

Students are given a 'flawed' blueprint of a satellite that is missing key components or has them incorrectly labeled. They must identify the errors, redraw the blueprint correctly, and ensure the container, power source, scientific instruments, and communication system are all present and properly labeled.

Mastery criterion
Student successfully identifies the missing/incorrect components and produces a corrected diagram with all four required parts labeled.
Materials
flawed blueprint worksheets, blank paper, rulers, pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the areas on the flawed blueprint where errors are located. Challenge advanced students to add a propulsion system to their corrected design.
Time rationale
15 minutes for analyzing the flawed blueprint, 35 minutes for redrawing and labeling, 10 minutes for class discussion.

Limitations: The physical models for universe expansion (balloon) and accretion (clay) are highly simplified and do not account for gravity or three-dimensional space accurately.; The distinction between different types of galaxies and complex stellar nucleosynthesis is reduced to basic categories suitable for primary education.; The assessment of reasoning tasks requires human review to evaluate the quality of the student's justification.; Safety constraints mean that actual chemical reactions or high-energy physics cannot be demonstrated; simulations and analogies are used instead.

Earth science

Students begin by understanding deep time and Earth's dynamic history through relative dating, fossils, and plate tectonics. This macro-level understanding logically leads to the study of earthquakes and volcanoes as surface manifestations of these internal dynamics. The focus then shifts to the Earth's surface, exploring how geological processes and weathering create soil. Students analyze soil properties, texture, and erosion, culminating in the practical application of land use capacity. This sequence connects deep geological history to observable surface phenomena and environmental conservation.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 7 planning weeks.

Earth's History and Tectonic Dynamics

Understanding Earth's history and internal dynamics is fundamental to grasping how the planet's surface has evolved over time. This skill connects deep time concepts with observable phenomena like earthquakes and volcanoes.

sequence geological events using relative dating principles
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a diagram of sedimentary rock layers with embedded fossils, sequence the layers from oldest to youngest.
Expected response
The bottom layer is the oldest, and the top layer is the youngest, following the principle of superposition.
Scoring rule
Correctly sequences all layers in the provided diagram.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly order a series of geological events from oldest to youngest based on their relative positions.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe that relative dating provides an exact age in years.; Students might think all rock layers were formed at the exact same time.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Relative dating determines the sequential order of events without providing an exact age. · Source page 156 · paragraph p156-paragraph-11
order the stages of the fossilization process
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Arrange four descriptions of an organism dying, being buried, compacting into rock, and being exposed in the correct chronological order.
Expected response
1. Death of organism, 2. Burial by sediments, 3. Compaction into sedimentary rock, 4. Exposure through erosion or excavation.
Scoring rule
All four stages must be placed in the exact chronological sequence.
Mastery evidence
Students can arrange the steps of fossilization in chronological order.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students often think fossils are actual bones rather than rocks shaped like bones.; Students may believe fossilization happens quickly after an organism dies.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Fossilization involves the death of an organism, followed by burial in sedimentary materials which compact to form rocks that preserve the fossil. · Source page 161 · paragraph p161-paragraph-13
identify mass extinctions and biodiversity explosions in the geological time scale
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Identify the periods of mass extinctions and the Cambrian explosion on a provided geological time scale.
Expected response
Correctly points out the extinction events and the Cambrian explosion.
Scoring rule
Accurately identifies the events on the timeline.
Mastery evidence
Students can identify mass extinctions and biodiversity explosions on a geological time scale.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think extinctions only happen to dinosaurs.; Students might believe biodiversity explosions happen overnight.
Local prerequisites
relative-dating
Scientific support
  • An extinction is defined as the total or partial disappearance of species in a specific period. · Source page 164 · paragraph p164-paragraph-2
classify tectonic plate boundaries as convergent, divergent, or transform
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given three diagrams showing arrows of plate movement (moving apart, colliding, sliding past), classify each as convergent, divergent, or transform.
Expected response
Colliding arrows indicate convergent, separating arrows indicate divergent, and sliding arrows indicate transform boundaries.
Scoring rule
Correctly classifies all three boundary types based on the directional arrows.
Mastery evidence
Students can identify the type of plate boundary based on the direction of plate movement.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think continents float on the ocean rather than being part of tectonic plates.; Students might believe plate boundaries only exist on land.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Convergent boundaries occur when tectonic plates collide and one is introduced or subducts beneath the other. · Source page 169 · paragraph p169-paragraph-14
distinguish earthquake magnitude from intensity based on energy and surface effects
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Read two reports: one detailing the energy released at the epicenter and another describing the structural damage in a city. Identify which report describes magnitude and which describes intensity, justifying the choice.
Expected response
The report on energy released describes magnitude, while the report on structural damage describes intensity, because intensity measures surface effects.
Scoring rule
Correctly identifies both terms and provides a justification based on energy versus surface effects.
Mastery evidence
Students can differentiate between magnitude and intensity by analyzing descriptions of earthquake events.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students often use magnitude and intensity interchangeably.; Students may think a high magnitude earthquake always causes high intensity damage everywhere.
Local prerequisites
plate-boundaries
Scientific support
  • Intensity refers to surface effects, while magnitude refers to the amount of energy released. · Source page 172 · paragraph p172-paragraph-3
identify physical and chemical parameters used to monitor volcanic activity
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Select the correct volcanic monitoring parameters from a mixed list that includes seismic activity, wind speed, gas emissions, and lunar phases.
Expected response
Seismic activity and gas emissions.
Scoring rule
Selects only the correct volcanic parameters without including unrelated environmental factors.
Mastery evidence
Students can select valid volcanic monitoring parameters from a list of environmental indicators.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think volcanoes erupt without any prior warning signs.; Students might confuse weather changes with volcanic monitoring parameters.
Local prerequisites
plate-boundaries
Scientific support
  • Seismic activity is a key parameter monitored to detect changes in volcanoes. · Source page 175 · paragraph p175-paragraph-7

Soil Formation, Properties, and Conservation

Transitioning from deep Earth processes, this skill focuses on the surface, teaching students how geological and biological factors create soil, determine its properties, and dictate its sustainable use.

label soil horizons in a cross-sectional profile
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Label a diagram of a soil profile with the correct horizons based on provided descriptions of color, organic matter, and rock content.
Expected response
Labels the top layer as organic/surface horizon, middle as subsoil, and bottom as parent material/bedrock based on the descriptions.
Scoring rule
Correctly matches all provided descriptions to the corresponding layers in the diagram.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly identify and label the different horizons in a soil profile based on physical characteristics.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think soil is a uniform mixture all the way down to the Earth's core.; Students might believe topsoil is the only layer that matters for ecosystems.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Soil is divided into distinct layers called horizons, each with specific physical and chemical characteristics. · Source page 179 · paragraph p179-paragraph-4
calculate the percentage of sand, silt, and clay in a soil sample
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given the total volume of a settled soil sample in a jar and the volume of its sand layer, calculate the percentage of sand in the sample.
Expected response
Divides the volume of the sand layer by the total volume and multiplies by 100 to find the percentage.
Scoring rule
Provides the correct mathematical calculation and final percentage.
Mastery evidence
Students can determine the textural composition of a soil sample using volume measurements.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may confuse soil texture with soil fertility.; Students might think all soil particles are the same size.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Soil texture is a critical physical property that determines functions like the percentage of voids. · Source page 179 · paragraph p179-paragraph-6
predict the effect of vegetation cover on soil erosion rates
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Predict which of two inclined soil trays (one bare, one covered with grass) will lose more soil when equal amounts of water are poured over them, and justify the choice using evidence of root stabilization.
Expected response
The bare soil tray will lose more soil because the grass tray has roots that act as a stabilizer, protecting the soil from being washed away.
Scoring rule
Correctly predicts the bare soil will erode more and justifies it by referencing the stabilizing effect of vegetation.
Mastery evidence
Students can predict and justify how the presence of vegetation reduces soil erosion compared to bare soil.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe that water always causes the same amount of erosion regardless of the surface.; Students might think plants only extract nutrients and do not provide structural support to soil.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Vegetation protects soil from erosion by acting as a stabilizing reinforcement. · Source page 182 · paragraph p182-paragraph-4
categorize land use types based on soil capacity and natural aptitude
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Match descriptions of land plots (e.g., flat fertile plains vs. steep rocky hillsides) to their ideal potential use categories (e.g., intensive agriculture vs. forest conservation).
Expected response
Matches flat fertile plains to intensive agriculture and steep rocky hillsides to forest conservation.
Scoring rule
Correctly categorizes all provided land descriptions to their appropriate use capacity.
Mastery evidence
Students can match descriptions of land characteristics to their ideal potential use.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think any type of land can be used for intensive agriculture if enough fertilizer is added.; Students might confuse current land use with potential land use capacity.
Local prerequisites
soil-horizons
Scientific support
  • Land use capacity is classified based on the soil's natural aptitude for specific types of production. · Source page 188 · paragraph p188-paragraph-3
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-relative-dating · 60 min · teach

Introduce the principle of superposition by stacking different colored sand and gravel in clear plastic cups. Explain that the bottom layer was deposited first and is the oldest. Students observe the model and practice identifying the oldest and youngest layers.

Mastery criterion
Students can correctly state that the bottom layer is the oldest and the top layer is the youngest in a physical model.
Materials
Clear plastic cups, Colored sand, Small gravel, Spoons
Safety
Ensure students do not ingest sand or gravel. Sweep up any spills immediately to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-stacked cups with highly contrasting colors for students who need clearer visual distinctions.
Time rationale
15 minutes for introduction and safety briefing, 25 minutes for building the physical models, 20 minutes for guided observation and discussion.

prac1-relative-dating · 75 min · practice

Students analyze paper diagrams of sedimentary rock layers containing different shapes representing fossils. They must sequence the layers from oldest to youngest and write a short paragraph explaining their reasoning based on the principle of superposition.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly sequence the layers and explicitly mention that lower layers were deposited before upper layers.
Materials
Printed diagrams of rock layers, Pencils, Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety. Ensure proper lighting for reading diagrams.
Access and differentiation
Offer diagrams with fewer layers (e.g., 3 instead of 5) to focus on the core concept before increasing complexity.
Time rationale
15 minutes to review the task, 40 minutes for independent analysis and writing, 20 minutes for peer review and correction.

prac2-relative-dating · 75 min · practice

Students create a 2D paper collage representing a geological cross-section. They cut out different textured papers to represent rock layers, glue them in a specific sequence, and label the relative age of each layer from oldest to youngest.

Mastery criterion
The collage is correctly labeled with the bottom-most layer identified as the oldest and the top-most as the youngest.
Materials
Textured paper, Scissors, Glue sticks, Markers, Cardboard base
Safety
Instruct on safe scissor handling. Ensure adequate spacing between students while cutting.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-cut paper strips for students with fine motor skill difficulties.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 45 minutes for cutting and assembling the collage, 20 minutes for labeling and presenting to the teacher.

assess-relative-dating · 45 min · assessment

Given a diagram of sedimentary rock layers with embedded fossils, sequence the layers from oldest to youngest on the provided assessment sheet.

Mastery criterion
Correctly sequences all layers in the provided diagram from bottom (oldest) to top (youngest).
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal explanation of the sequence for students who struggle with written assessments.
Time rationale
10 minutes for distributing materials and reading instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion of the assessment.

teach-fossilization-stages · 60 min · teach

Present a storyboard detailing the four stages of fossilization: death, burial by sediments, compaction into rock, and exposure. Discuss each stage using visual aids and emphasize the chronological order.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally repeat the four stages of fossilization in the correct order.
Materials
Storyboard posters, Whiteboard, Markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a printed mini-storyboard for students to keep at their desks for closer reference.
Time rationale
20 minutes for the storyboard presentation, 20 minutes for guided group discussion, 20 minutes for a whole-class verbal sequencing exercise.

prac1-fossilization-stages · 75 min · practice

Students receive a set of mixed description cards detailing the fossilization process. They must sort the cards into the correct chronological timeline and glue them onto a timeline poster.

Mastery criterion
All description cards are glued in the exact chronological sequence: death, burial, compaction, exposure.
Materials
Sets of description cards, Poster paper, Glue sticks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Include simple icons on the text cards (e.g., a skull for death, a shovel for burial) to support reading comprehension.
Time rationale
15 minutes for sorting practice, 40 minutes for finalizing the sequence and gluing, 20 minutes for gallery walk to review peers' timelines.

prac2-fossilization-stages · 75 min · practice

Students create a four-panel comic strip illustrating the stages of fossilization for a fictional organism. They must include captions for each panel describing the specific stage.

Mastery criterion
The comic strip accurately depicts and describes death, burial, compaction, and exposure in order.
Materials
Blank comic strip templates, Colored pencils, Rulers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide templates with pre-drawn backgrounds where students only need to draw the organism and write the captions.
Time rationale
15 minutes for brainstorming the organism, 40 minutes for drawing and writing captions, 20 minutes for sharing with a partner.

assess-fossilization-stages · 45 min · assessment

Arrange four descriptions of an organism dying, being buried, compacting into rock, and being exposed in the correct chronological order on the assessment sheet.

Mastery criterion
All four stages must be placed in the exact chronological sequence.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use larger font sizes and increased line spacing on the assessment sheet.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.

teach-plate-boundaries · 60 min · teach

Demonstrate plate movements using foam blocks on a table. Show blocks colliding (convergent), moving apart (divergent), and sliding past each other (transform). Draw corresponding arrows on the board.

Mastery criterion
Students can match the physical movement of the foam blocks to the terms convergent, divergent, and transform.
Materials
Foam blocks, Whiteboard, Markers
Safety
Ensure foam blocks are clean and free of small tearable pieces to prevent choking hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to physically manipulate the foam blocks themselves to feel the directional movements.
Time rationale
20 minutes for teacher demonstration, 25 minutes for students to practice with blocks in small groups, 15 minutes for summarizing on the board.

prac1-plate-boundaries · 75 min · practice

Students analyze abstract maps showing tectonic plates with directional arrows. They must color-code the boundaries (e.g., red for convergent, blue for divergent, green for transform) based on the arrows.

Mastery criterion
All boundaries on the map are correctly color-coded according to the directional arrows.
Materials
Printed maps with arrows, Colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a reference key on the desk showing the arrow patterns next to the boundary names.
Time rationale
15 minutes for reviewing the color code, 45 minutes for map analysis and coloring, 15 minutes for teacher verification.

prac2-plate-boundaries · 75 min · practice

Students complete a matching puzzle activity where they connect three pieces: the boundary name, a diagram of the arrows, and a simple drawing of the resulting geological feature (e.g., trench, ridge).

Mastery criterion
Students successfully assemble all three-piece puzzles correctly matching name, arrows, and feature.
Materials
Cardboard puzzle pieces
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use self-correcting puzzle cuts so only the correct pieces physically fit together.
Time rationale
10 minutes for explaining the puzzle mechanics, 45 minutes for group puzzle solving, 20 minutes for recording the matches in notebooks.

assess-plate-boundaries · 45 min · assessment

Given three diagrams showing arrows of plate movement (moving apart, colliding, sliding past), classify each as convergent, divergent, or transform.

Mastery criterion
Correctly classifies all three boundary types based on the directional arrows.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide the three vocabulary words in a word bank at the top of the page.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.

ret1-plate-boundaries · 45 min · retrieval

Students participate in a rapid flashcard game in pairs. One student shows a card with arrows, and the other must quickly name the boundary type. They tally correct answers.

Mastery criterion
Students can instantly recall and state the correct boundary type for the given arrow diagram.
Materials
Flashcards with arrow diagrams
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use hand gestures (colliding hands, sliding hands) before saying the word to reinforce memory.
Time rationale
10 minutes for pairing and distributing cards, 25 minutes for the flashcard game, 10 minutes for class debrief.

ret2-plate-boundaries · 45 min · retrieval

Students are given a mixed stack of 15 small diagrams showing various plate movements. They must sort them into three labeled bins (Convergent, Divergent, Transform) as quickly and accurately as possible.

Mastery criterion
All 15 diagrams are placed in the correct bins based on their arrows.
Materials
Small printed diagrams, Three labeled bins per group
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Reduce the number of diagrams to 9 for students who need a more focused task.
Time rationale
10 minutes for setup, 25 minutes for the sorting activity, 10 minutes for checking the bins as a class.

teach-earthquake-measurement · 60 min · teach

Explain the difference between magnitude (energy released) and intensity (surface damage). Demonstrate by dropping a heavy book and a light book onto a tray of sand from the same height (magnitude difference), then dropping the heavy book onto sand vs a hard desk (intensity/surface effect difference).

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally distinguish that magnitude is about the energy of the event, while intensity is about the observable effects on the surface.
Materials
Heavy book, Light book, Tray of sand, Hard desk surface
Safety
Ensure students stand back during the drop demonstration to avoid sand splashing into eyes.
Access and differentiation
Provide a simple T-chart on the board listing 'Energy' under Magnitude and 'Damage/Effects' under Intensity.
Time rationale
20 minutes for the drop demonstrations, 25 minutes for explicit instruction and defining terms, 15 minutes for Q&A.

prac1-earthquake-measurement · 75 min · practice

Students read excerpts from historical hazard reports. They use a yellow highlighter for sentences describing energy released (magnitude) and a pink highlighter for sentences describing structural damage (intensity). They write a sentence justifying one of their choices.

Mastery criterion
Correctly highlights energy descriptions in yellow and damage descriptions in pink, with a logical written justification.
Materials
Printed report excerpts, Yellow and pink highlighters, Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Pre-underline the key sentences in the text so the student only has to decide which color to use.
Time rationale
15 minutes for reading the text, 40 minutes for highlighting and writing justifications, 20 minutes for class discussion.

prac2-earthquake-measurement · 75 min · practice

Students write two short fictional news reports about the same earthquake. Report A must focus strictly on the magnitude (seismograph readings, energy). Report B must focus strictly on the intensity (how people felt it, damage to buildings).

Mastery criterion
Report A contains only energy-related facts; Report B contains only surface-effect descriptions.
Materials
Writing paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters (e.g., 'The seismograph recorded an energy release of...' and 'Citizens reported seeing...')
Time rationale
15 minutes for brainstorming, 45 minutes for drafting the two reports, 15 minutes for sharing with a partner.

assess-earthquake-measurement · 45 min · assessment

Read two short reports: one detailing the energy released at the epicenter and another describing the structural damage in a city. Identify which report describes magnitude and which describes intensity, justifying the choice.

Mastery criterion
Correctly identifies both terms and provides a justification based on energy versus surface effects.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to circle key words in the reports that helped them make their decision.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent reading and writing.

teach-volcano-monitoring · 60 min · teach

Introduce the physical and chemical parameters used to monitor volcanoes (seismic activity, gas emissions). Contrast these with unrelated environmental factors (wind speed, lunar phases) using a sorting activity on the board.

Mastery criterion
Students can correctly identify seismic activity and gas emissions as valid monitoring parameters.
Materials
Whiteboard, Magnetic word cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use images alongside the words on the magnetic cards (e.g., a seismograph line for seismic activity).
Time rationale
20 minutes for direct instruction, 25 minutes for the interactive board sorting, 15 minutes for summarizing.

prac1-volcano-monitoring · 75 min · practice

Students review a mock data log from an observatory. The log contains mixed data (seismic tremors, gas levels, rainfall, wind direction). Students must cross out the irrelevant data and circle the parameters that indicate volcanic activity.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully filter the log, circling only seismic and gas data while crossing out weather data.
Materials
Mock data logs, Pencils, Red markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the data categories in different colors to help students distinguish between the types of information before filtering.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explaining the data log format, 40 minutes for independent filtering, 20 minutes for reviewing the correct answers.

prac2-volcano-monitoring · 75 min · practice

Students design a paper layout for a volcanic monitoring station. They are given a budget of hypothetical points and a catalog of sensors (seismometers, gas sniffers, anemometers, telescopes). They must select only the valid volcanic sensors to 'purchase' and place on their map.

Mastery criterion
The final station design includes only seismometers and gas sensors, rejecting unrelated equipment.
Materials
Station layout templates, Sensor catalogs, Pencils, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-calculated budget sheet so the focus remains on selecting the correct sensors rather than the math.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explaining the catalog and budget, 45 minutes for selecting sensors and drawing the layout, 15 minutes for sharing designs.

assess-volcano-monitoring · 45 min · assessment

Select the correct volcanic monitoring parameters from a mixed multiple-choice list that includes seismic activity, wind speed, gas emissions, and lunar phases.

Mastery criterion
Selects only seismic activity and gas emissions without including unrelated environmental factors.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read the list of options aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.

teach-soil-horizons · 60 min · teach

Build a physical soil profile model in a large clear jar using whole cookies (bedrock), crushed cookies (subsoil), and chocolate cereal (organic topsoil). Discuss the physical characteristics of each horizon as it is added.

Mastery criterion
Students can identify the three main layers in the jar model and state one physical characteristic of each.
Materials
Large clear jar, Whole cookies, Crushed cookies, Chocolate cereal, Labels
Safety
Ensure students do not eat the materials to maintain hygiene. Check for food allergies if handling is involved.
Access and differentiation
Provide a printed diagram of the jar model with fill-in-the-blank labels for students to complete during the demonstration.
Time rationale
20 minutes for building the model, 25 minutes for discussing characteristics, 15 minutes for labeling the jar as a class.

prac1-soil-horizons · 75 min · practice

Students receive a blank cross-sectional diagram of soil and a text describing the color, organic matter, and rock content of three horizons. They must color the diagram accordingly and label each horizon.

Mastery criterion
The diagram is colored to match the descriptions (e.g., dark top, rocky bottom) and correctly labeled with horizon names.
Materials
Blank diagrams, Text descriptions, Colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the color words in the text description to guide the coloring process.
Time rationale
15 minutes for reading the descriptions, 45 minutes for coloring and labeling, 15 minutes for peer comparison.

prac2-soil-horizons · 75 min · practice

Students examine sealed transparent bags containing different safe soil materials (e.g., dark potting soil, sandy subsoil, gravel). They must match each bag to its likely horizon based on visual characteristics and justify their choice in writing.

Mastery criterion
Correctly matches the dark soil to the surface horizon, sandy to subsoil, and gravel to parent material, with valid justifications.
Materials
Sealed bags of soil/gravel, Observation sheets, Pencils
Safety
Ensure bags are securely sealed to prevent inhalation of dust or soil spills.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist of characteristics (dark, light, rocky, soft) for students to tick off as they observe the bags.
Time rationale
15 minutes for observation, 40 minutes for matching and writing justifications, 20 minutes for class discussion.

assess-soil-horizons · 45 min · assessment

Label a diagram of a soil profile with the correct horizons based on provided descriptions of color, organic matter, and rock content.

Mastery criterion
Correctly matches all provided descriptions to the corresponding layers in the diagram.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank of horizon names.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.

teach-soil-texture · 60 min · teach

Demonstrate soil texture by showing a pre-settled jar of soil and water. Point out the distinct layers of sand, silt, and clay. Measure the total height of the soil and the height of the sand layer with a ruler, and calculate the percentage of sand on the board.

Mastery criterion
Students can follow the calculation steps and understand that the sand layer's volume relative to the total volume determines its percentage.
Materials
Pre-settled jar of soil and water, Ruler, Whiteboard, Markers
Safety
Ensure the glass jar is handled carefully to prevent breakage.
Access and differentiation
Use a jar with very distinct, contrasting layers to make visual identification easier.
Time rationale
20 minutes for observing the jar, 25 minutes for step-by-step calculation on the board, 15 minutes for guided practice with hypothetical numbers.

prac1-soil-texture · 75 min · practice

Students work in groups with pre-settled plastic jars of different soil samples. They use rulers to measure the total soil height and the sand layer height, then calculate the percentage of sand for their specific jar.

Mastery criterion
Accurately measures the layers in millimeters and correctly calculates the sand percentage using the formula.
Materials
Pre-settled plastic jars of soil, Rulers, Calculators, Worksheets
Safety
Use plastic jars instead of glass to prevent breakage. Ensure lids are taped shut.
Access and differentiation
Provide a step-by-step calculation template where students only need to plug in their measurements.
Time rationale
15 minutes for measuring, 40 minutes for calculations and verifying with group members, 20 minutes for reporting results to the class.

prac2-soil-texture · 75 min · practice

Given a worksheet with hypothetical volume data for five different soil samples, students calculate the sand percentage for each and create a bar graph comparing the sand content of the samples.

Mastery criterion
All five percentages are calculated correctly and accurately represented on the bar graph.
Materials
Data worksheets, Graph paper, Calculators, Rulers, Colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-labeled axes on the graph paper.
Time rationale
10 minutes for reviewing the data, 35 minutes for calculations, 30 minutes for graphing.

assess-soil-texture · 45 min · assessment

Given the total volume of a settled soil sample in a jar and the volume of its sand layer, calculate the percentage of sand in the sample.

Mastery criterion
Provides the correct mathematical calculation and final percentage.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Calculators, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Include the formula (Sand Volume / Total Volume x 100) at the top of the page.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent calculation.

teach-erosion-vegetation · 60 min · teach

Demonstrate erosion by pouring equal amounts of water over two inclined trays: one with bare soil and one covered with a patch of grass. Collect the runoff in clear cups to show the difference in soil loss. Discuss how roots stabilize the soil.

Mastery criterion
Students can observe and state that the grass tray lost less soil because the roots held the soil in place.
Materials
Two plastic trays, Soil, Grass patch, Watering can, Clear cups
Safety
Wipe up any spilled water immediately to prevent slipping hazards.
Access and differentiation
