Allow students to closely inspect the root structure of an extra grass patch to make the abstract concept of 'stabilization' concrete.
Time rationale
20 minutes for setup and demonstration, 25 minutes for observation and discussion of the runoff, 15 minutes for summarizing the role of roots.

prac1-erosion-vegetation · 75 min · practice

Students design an experiment on paper to test different types of ground cover (e.g., leaves, twigs, planted seeds) against erosion. They must write a hypothesis predicting which cover will be most effective and justify it based on the concept of soil stabilization.

Mastery criterion
The experimental design includes a control (bare soil) and variables, with a logical hypothesis referencing root or cover stabilization.
Materials
Experiment design templates, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a list of possible ground covers for students to choose from rather than generating them from scratch.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explaining the components of an experimental design, 45 minutes for drafting the design and hypothesis, 15 minutes for peer review.

prac2-erosion-vegetation · 75 min · practice

Students analyze photographs of different hillsides (some forested, some deforested). They must predict which areas are at highest risk for erosion during a heavy rainstorm and write a paragraph justifying their predictions using evidence of vegetation cover.

Mastery criterion
Correctly identifies deforested areas as high risk and justifies the prediction by explaining the lack of root stabilization.
Materials
Printed photographs of hillsides, Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence frames for the justification paragraph (e.g., 'I predict this hillside will erode more because...').
Time rationale
15 minutes for analyzing the photos, 40 minutes for writing predictions and justifications, 20 minutes for class discussion.

assess-erosion-vegetation · 45 min · assessment

Predict which of two inclined soil trays (one bare, one covered with grass) will lose more soil when equal amounts of water are poured over them, and justify the choice using evidence of root stabilization.

Mastery criterion
Correctly predicts the bare soil will erode more and justifies it by referencing the stabilizing effect of vegetation.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw a diagram alongside their written justification to help express their reasoning.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.

ret1-erosion-vegetation · 45 min · retrieval

Students complete a quick-write activity comparing the structural role of plant roots in soil to the role of steel rebar in concrete, explaining how both provide internal stabilization.

Mastery criterion
The writing clearly draws a parallel between roots holding soil together and rebar holding concrete together.
Materials
Writing paper, Pencils, Picture of rebar in concrete (for reference)
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Discuss the rebar analogy as a class for 5 minutes before beginning the writing task.
Time rationale
10 minutes for introducing the analogy, 25 minutes for writing, 10 minutes for sharing.

ret2-erosion-vegetation · 45 min · retrieval

Students create a concept map connecting the terms: Vegetation, Roots, Soil Stability, Water Runoff, and Erosion. They must write linking verbs on the arrows between the terms.

Mastery criterion
The concept map logically connects the terms, showing that vegetation/roots increase stability and decrease erosion/runoff.
Materials
Blank paper, Pencils, Rulers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a partially completed map where students only need to fill in the linking verbs.
Time rationale
10 minutes for reviewing the terms, 25 minutes for creating the map, 10 minutes for comparing maps with a partner.

teach-land-use-capacity · 60 min · teach

Introduce the concept of land use capacity by showing pictures of flat, fertile plains and steep, rocky hillsides. Discuss why the flat land is suited for intensive agriculture and the steep land for forest conservation based on soil aptitude.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally match the flat land to agriculture and the steep land to conservation.
Materials
Large photographs of different landscapes, Whiteboard, Markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use highly contrasting images (e.g., a lush cornfield vs a jagged cliff) to make the initial concept obvious.
Time rationale
20 minutes for image analysis, 25 minutes for direct instruction on capacity categories, 15 minutes for Q&A.

prac1-land-use-capacity · 75 min · practice

Students sort profile cards of different land plots (describing slope, soil depth, and rockiness) into ideal use categories (intensive agriculture, pasture, forest conservation).

Mastery criterion
All profile cards are sorted into the correct use category based on their physical descriptions.
Materials
Sets of land profile cards, Category sorting mats
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Include small visual icons on the profile cards (e.g., a steep angle icon for high slope) to aid reading comprehension.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explaining the categories, 40 minutes for sorting the cards in groups, 20 minutes for reviewing the correct placements.

prac2-land-use-capacity · 75 min · practice

Students create a land-use map for a fictional town. They are given a base map with topographical lines and soil descriptions. They must color-code areas for agriculture, forestry, and urban development based on the land's capacity.

Mastery criterion
The map correctly assigns agriculture to flat/fertile areas and forestry to steep/rocky areas.
Materials
Base maps with topography, Soil description keys, Colored pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a simplified map with only three distinct zones to color-code.
Time rationale
15 minutes for reading the map key, 45 minutes for analyzing the zones and coloring, 15 minutes for displaying the maps.

assess-land-use-capacity · 45 min · assessment

Match descriptions of land plots (e.g., flat fertile plains vs. steep rocky hillsides) to their ideal potential use categories (e.g., intensive agriculture vs. forest conservation).

Mastery criterion
Correctly categorizes all provided land descriptions to their appropriate use capacity.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use a drawing-lines matching format instead of writing out the category names.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.

teach-mass-extinctions · 60 min · teach

Introduce the geological time scale, highlighting major mass extinctions and the Cambrian explosion. Use a large timeline on the board to point out these events.

Mastery criterion
Students can verbally identify at least one mass extinction and the Cambrian explosion on the timeline.
Materials
Large timeline poster, Markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a smaller, personal timeline for students to follow along.
Time rationale
20 minutes for introduction, 25 minutes for timeline exploration, 15 minutes for Q&A.

prac1-mass-extinctions · 75 min · practice

Students are given a blank geological time scale and a set of event cards (mass extinctions, Cambrian explosion). They must place the events in the correct periods on the timeline.

Mastery criterion
All event cards are placed in the correct geological periods.
Materials
Blank timelines, Event cards, Glue
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Color-code the eras to help students narrow down where events belong.
Time rationale
15 minutes for instructions, 45 minutes for sorting and gluing, 15 minutes for review.

assess-mass-extinctions · 45 min · assessment

Identify the periods of mass extinctions and the Cambrian explosion on a provided geological time scale.

Mastery criterion
Correctly points out the extinction events and the Cambrian explosion.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Use a simplified timeline with fewer distractors.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for independent completion.

Limitations: The unit simplifies the complexities of absolute dating and advanced tectonic mechanisms to suit a primary school cognitive level.; Soil classification focuses on basic physical properties and broad land-use categories, omitting detailed chemical analysis and complex taxonomy.; Safety constraints prevent direct observation of active geological hazards, relying heavily on models, simulations, and historical data.; The distinction between magnitude and intensity is introduced conceptually without requiring complex logarithmic calculations.

Grade 6

Fluids

Students begin by understanding density as a property of matter, which is a prerequisite for understanding buoyancy. They then explore pressure in solids, extending this to fluids at rest (hydrostatic pressure and Pascal's principle). Finally, they transition to fluids in motion, learning about flow rate and Bernoulli's principle, applying these concepts to real-world phenomena like flight. The progression moves from static properties to dynamic interactions.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 4 planning weeks.

Analyze properties and behaviors of fluids at rest

Understanding fluids at rest establishes the foundational concepts of density, buoyancy, and pressure, which are essential for explaining everyday phenomena and preparing students for fluid dynamics.

calculate the density of solid objects using mass and volume measurements
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide students with the mass and volume of three different irregular objects. Ask them to calculate the density of each and identify which two are made of the same material.
Expected response
Students divide mass by volume for each object, state the calculated densities with correct units, and match the two objects with identical densities.
Scoring rule
1 point for correct calculation of each density; 1 point for correctly identifying the matching materials based on density.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly calculate density given mass and volume, and identify it as an intensive property.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Density depends on the size or amount of the material.; Heavy objects are always more dense than light objects.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Density is a specific property for each substance that relates mass and volume. · Source page 10 · paragraph p10-paragraph-4
explain the relationship between displaced fluid volume and buoyant force
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Ask students to explain what determines the magnitude of the buoyant force on a submerged object.
Expected response
The buoyant force is equivalent to the weight of the fluid that the object displaces.
Scoring rule
1 point for mentioning displaced fluid; 1 point for equating its weight to buoyant force.
Mastery evidence
Students state that the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Displaced fluid has no relation to the object's weight.
Local prerequisites
m-density
Scientific support
  • The buoyant force is equivalent to the weight of the displaced fluid. · Source page 13 · paragraph p13-paragraph-9
predict the buoyancy of objects based on their density and the displaced fluid
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Present a scenario where a solid block is placed in two different liquids (water and oil). Ask students to predict and justify in which liquid the block will experience a greater buoyant force if it sinks in both.
Expected response
Students predict the buoyant force is greater in water because water is denser than oil, meaning the displaced volume of water weighs more than the same volume of oil.
Scoring rule
1 point for predicting water; 1 point for justifying based on the weight of the displaced fluid.
Mastery evidence
Students predict whether an object will float or sink by comparing its density to the fluid and explaining the role of displaced fluid.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Objects float because they are light, regardless of volume.; Buoyancy is a property of the object, not the fluid.
Local prerequisites
m-archimedes
Scientific support
  • Submerging an object displaces a quantity of water related to its volume. · Source page 14 · paragraph p14-paragraph-4
compare the pressure exerted by solid objects on different surface areas
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Show a rectangular brick resting on its widest face and its narrowest face. Ask students to decide which orientation exerts more pressure on the ground and justify their choice.
Expected response
Students state that the narrowest face exerts more pressure because the same force (weight) is distributed over a smaller contact area.
Scoring rule
1 point for selecting the narrowest face; 1 point for explaining the inverse relationship between pressure and area.
Mastery evidence
Students determine which orientation of an object exerts more pressure based on the contact area.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Pressure and force are the exact same concept.; A larger object always exerts more pressure regardless of its contact area.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Pressure increases when the contact surface area decreases. · Source page 17 · paragraph p17-paragraph-6
describe the dependence of hydrostatic pressure on fluid density and depth
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Ask students to describe how the pressure on a submarine changes as it dives deeper into the ocean and why.
Expected response
Students describe that the pressure increases as the submarine dives deeper because hydrostatic pressure depends on the depth of the fluid above it.
Scoring rule
1 point for stating pressure increases; 1 point for linking it to the depth of the fluid.
Mastery evidence
Students state that hydrostatic pressure increases with depth and fluid density.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Pressure in a liquid only pushes downwards.; The shape of the container affects the hydrostatic pressure at a given depth.
Local prerequisites
m-density
Scientific support
  • Hydrostatic pressure depends on density, gravity, and depth (referred to as height in the formula). · Source page 18 · paragraph p18-paragraph-4
explain the transmission of pressure in enclosed fluids using Pascal's principle
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Provide a diagram of a simple hydraulic press. Ask students to explain how pushing down on the small piston can lift a heavy load on the large piston.
Expected response
Students explain that the pressure applied to the enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions, allowing a small force over a small area to create a larger force over a larger area.
Scoring rule
1 point for mentioning pressure is transmitted equally; 1 point for applying this to the lifting of the load.
Mastery evidence
Students explain how a force applied to one part of an enclosed fluid results in pressure transmitted to all parts.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Pressure applied to a fluid only affects the area directly pushed.; Fluids compress easily to absorb applied pressure.
Local prerequisites
m-pressure-solid
Scientific support
  • Pressure on an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. · Source page 19 · paragraph p19-paragraph-6
differentiate surface tension and capillarity based on cohesion and adhesion forces
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Present two scenarios: an insect walking on water and water rising in a narrow glass tube. Ask students to identify which property and which intermolecular force is responsible for each.
Expected response
Students identify the insect scenario as surface tension due to cohesion, and the rising water as capillarity due to adhesion.
Scoring rule
1 point for linking surface tension to cohesion; 1 point for linking capillarity to adhesion.
Mastery evidence
Students correctly attribute surface tension to cohesion and capillarity to adhesion.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Surface tension and capillarity are the same phenomenon.; Water climbs up tubes because it is pushed by air pressure.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Surface tension is related to cohesive forces. · Source page 24 · paragraph p24-paragraph-5

Analyze properties and behaviors of fluids in motion

Transitioning from static to dynamic fluids allows students to understand flow rates and pressure changes in moving fluids, connecting theoretical principles to real-world applications like plumbing and flight.

calculate the flow rate of a fluid given volume and time data
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Provide data showing a tap fills a 1500 ml container in 30 seconds. Ask students to calculate the flow rate.
Expected response
Students divide 1500 ml by 30 seconds to get a flow rate of 50 ml/s.
Scoring rule
1 point for the correct numerical value (50); 1 point for the correct units (ml/s).
Mastery evidence
Students calculate flow rate by dividing volume by time and use appropriate units.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Flow rate is the same as the speed of the fluid.; A larger container always means a higher flow rate.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Flow rate is expressed as volume over time. · Source page 26 · paragraph p26-paragraph-7
relate changes in pipe diameter to the speed of fluid flow
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Show a diagram of a pipe that narrows from a large diameter to a small diameter. Ask students to predict where the water moves fastest and justify their answer.
Expected response
Students predict the water moves fastest in the narrow section because the same volume of water must pass through a smaller area in the same amount of time.
Scoring rule
1 point for identifying the narrow section; 1 point for justifying based on constant flow rate or volume conservation.
Mastery evidence
Students predict that fluid speed increases when the diameter of the conduit decreases to maintain a constant flow rate.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Fluid slows down when a pipe gets narrower because it gets squeezed.; Pipe diameter has no effect on fluid speed if the source is constant.
Local prerequisites
m-flow-rate
Scientific support
  • The textbook prompts an investigation into the relationship between pipe section and flow characteristics. · Source page 29 · paragraph p29-paragraph-6
predict pressure changes in moving fluids using Bernoulli's principle
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Describe a scenario where air is blown rapidly between two suspended balloons. Ask students to predict what the balloons will do and justify using Bernoulli's principle.
Expected response
Students predict the balloons will move toward each other because the fast-moving air between them creates an area of low pressure, and the higher pressure outside pushes them together.
Scoring rule
1 point for predicting they move together; 1 point for explaining the pressure drop due to increased air speed.
Mastery evidence
Students predict that an increase in fluid speed results in a decrease in internal fluid pressure.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Faster moving fluids exert more pressure because they hit harder.; Pressure in a fluid is constant regardless of its speed.
Local prerequisites
m-flow-diameter
Scientific support
  • Increasing the speed of a fluid decreases its pressure, though the text's application to drones contradicts this. · Source page 28 · paragraph p28-paragraph-10
identify applications of Bernoulli's principle in everyday phenomena like flight
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Ask students to name one technological application that relies on the pressure differences described by Bernoulli's principle to achieve lift.
Expected response
Students identify airplane wings or drone propellers as an application.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly identifying a valid application of lift via pressure difference.
Mastery evidence
Students identify flight and drone propellers as applications of Bernoulli's principle.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Airplanes fly because the engines push them up.; Bernoulli's principle only applies to liquids, not gases.
Local prerequisites
m-bernoulli-pressure
Scientific support
  • The textbook states that high fluid speed over a propeller generates high pressure below it, allowing ascent. · Source page 32 · paragraph p32-paragraph-5
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

act-teach-density · 60 min · teach

Students measure the mass of different solid blocks using a balance and calculate their volume by water displacement in a graduated cylinder. They record data in a table, calculate the density for each block, and compare their results to identify materials. The teacher reviews the data tables to ensure correct calculations and units.

Mastery criterion
Accurate measurement recording and correct calculation of density using the mass/volume formula.
Materials
Balances, Graduated cylinders, Water, Assorted solid blocks (wood, metal, plastic)
Safety
Ensure any spilled water is wiped up immediately to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-measured mass values for students who struggle with using the balance, allowing them to focus on the volume measurement and calculation.
Time rationale
15 mins introduction and setup, 30 mins for hands-on measurement and calculation, 15 mins for discussion and review.

act-teach-buoyancy · 60 min · teach

Students submerge objects of known density into water and measure the displaced volume. They calculate the weight of the displaced water and compare it to the object's weight to predict and observe floating or sinking. They write a short justification for each object's behavior.

Mastery criterion
Written justifications correctly link the object's behavior to the weight of the displaced fluid compared to the object's weight.
Materials
Spring scales (dinamómetros), Catch basins, Graduated cylinders, Various objects (some that float, some that sink)
Safety
Use plastic containers instead of glass to prevent breakage if heavy objects are dropped.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual chart showing the relationship between displaced fluid weight and buoyant force.
Time rationale
20 mins for data collection, 20 mins for calculations, 20 mins for writing justifications.

act-teach-pressure-solid · 60 min · teach

Students place a rectangular wooden block on a bed of sand in three different orientations (flat, side, upright). They measure the depth of the indentation left in the sand for each orientation. They write a conclusion relating the contact area to the pressure exerted (depth of indentation).

Mastery criterion
Conclusions explicitly state that smaller contact areas result in greater pressure for the same force.
Materials
Rectangular wooden blocks, Trays of fine sand, Rulers
Safety
Ensure sand is not thrown or blown into eyes.
Access and differentiation
Use blocks with highly contrasting side areas to make the differences in indentation very obvious.
Time rationale
15 mins setup, 30 mins experimentation and measurement, 15 mins writing conclusions.

act-teach-hydrostatic · 45 min · teach

Students observe a demonstration or simulation of a tall water container with holes at different heights. They draw the trajectory of the water streams and write a description of how the distance the water shoots out relates to the depth of the hole.

Mastery criterion
Drawings and descriptions correctly show that water from lower holes shoots further due to higher hydrostatic pressure at greater depth.
Materials
Tall plastic bottle with holes at different heights, Tape, Water, Catch basin
Safety
Teacher prepares the bottle with holes beforehand to avoid students using sharp tools.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-drawn outline of the bottle for students to trace the water streams onto.
Time rationale
15 mins observation, 15 mins drawing, 15 mins writing descriptions.

act-teach-pascal · 60 min · teach

Students connect two syringes of different sizes with plastic tubing filled with water. They push the small plunger and observe the force required and the movement of the large plunger. They write an explanation of how pressure is transmitted through the fluid to create a larger force.

Mastery criterion
Explanations correctly apply Pascal's principle, noting that pressure is transmitted equally, resulting in a larger force on the larger area.
Materials
Syringes of different sizes (e.g., 10ml and 50ml), Plastic tubing, Water
Safety
Ensure tubing is securely attached to prevent water spraying under pressure.
Access and differentiation
Provide a fill-in-the-blank template for the explanation to guide students in using the correct terminology.
Time rationale
20 mins assembly and exploration, 20 mins guided questioning, 20 mins writing explanations.

act-teach-surface-capillary · 60 min · teach

Students perform two mini-experiments: dropping water onto a coin until it spills (surface tension) and placing a celery stalk in colored water (capillarity). They create a T-chart comparing the two phenomena, identifying the dominant force (cohesion or adhesion) for each.

Mastery criterion
T-charts accurately distinguish between surface tension (cohesion) and capillarity (adhesion).
Materials
Coins, Droppers, Water, Food coloring, Celery stalks, Small cups
Safety
Use food-safe coloring and ensure students do not ingest the materials.
Access and differentiation
Provide definitions of cohesion and adhesion on the board for quick reference during the activity.
Time rationale
30 mins for the two mini-experiments, 30 mins for creating and reviewing the T-charts.

act-teach-flow-rate · 60 min · teach

Students use a stopwatch and a graduated cylinder to measure the volume of water collected from a tap at different valve openings over 10 seconds. They calculate the flow rate for each setting and graph flow rate vs. valve opening.

Mastery criterion
Accurate calculation of flow rate (volume/time) and correct plotting of data points on the graph.
Materials
Graduated cylinders, Stopwatches, Access to water taps
Safety
Wipe up any spills immediately.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-labeled graph axes for students who need support with data visualization.
Time rationale
20 mins data collection, 20 mins calculations, 20 mins graphing.

act-teach-flow-diameter · 30 min · teach

Teacher demonstrates water flowing through a clear plastic tube that has a wide section and a narrow section, injecting food coloring to show speed changes. Students observe and write a justification for why the speed changes.

Mastery criterion
Justifications correctly state that speed increases in the narrow section to maintain a constant flow rate.
Materials
Clear plastic tubing with varying diameters, Water source, Food coloring, Syringe
Safety
Teacher handles the injection of food coloring to avoid messes.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to verbally explain their reasoning to the teacher before writing it down.
Time rationale
15 mins demonstration, 15 mins writing justifications.

act-teach-bernoulli-pressure · 60 min · teach

Students blow air between two empty aluminum cans suspended on strings. They observe the cans moving together. They draw a diagram showing the air speed and pressure areas, and write a prediction of what would happen if they blew harder.

Mastery criterion
Diagrams correctly label the area between the cans as high speed/low pressure, and predictions state the cans would move together more forcefully.
Materials
Empty aluminum cans, String, Tape, Straws (for blowing air)
Safety
Ensure students take breaks from blowing to avoid dizziness.
Access and differentiation
Provide a partially completed diagram where students only need to add the labels for 'high' and 'low' pressure.
Time rationale
20 mins experimentation, 20 mins drawing diagrams, 20 mins writing predictions.

act-teach-bernoulli-flight · 45 min · teach

Students examine images of drone propellers and read the textbook explanation of how moving air creates pressure differences that allow the drone to ascend.

Mastery criterion
Descriptions correctly identify that the interaction of the propeller with the air generates pressure differences resulting in upward lift.
Materials
Images of drone propellers, Textbook excerpts
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank including terms like 'lift', 'pressure', 'speed', and 'propeller'.
Time rationale
15 mins examining models, 30 mins writing descriptions.

act-practice-statics · 60 min · practice

Students complete a structured problem set calculating densities of various objects, determining which face of a block exerts the most pressure, and ranking containers based on hydrostatic pressure at the bottom. They peer-review their answers using a rubric.

Mastery criterion
Correct calculations and logical rankings based on the principles of statics.
Materials
Problem sets, Calculators, Peer-review rubrics
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide formula sheets and step-by-step calculation guides for the density problems.
Time rationale
40 mins independent work, 20 mins peer review.

act-practice-dynamics · 60 min · practice

Students analyze three real-world scenarios and calculate specific fluid speeds in narrow vs wide sections, then predict the outcome of pressure changes.

Mastery criterion
Accurate calculation of fluid speeds and logical predictions based on fluid dynamics.
Materials
Scenario worksheets
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to work in pairs to discuss the scenarios before writing their individual answers.
Time rationale
45 mins scenario analysis, 15 mins class discussion.

act-inquiry-boat-design · 90 min · practice

Students design and build a small boat out of aluminum foil that can hold the maximum number of metal washers without sinking. They must calculate the density of their boat before adding washers and justify their design choices based on buoyancy and displaced fluid.

Mastery criterion
Designs maximize displaced volume, and justifications correctly reference Archimedes' principle.
Materials
Aluminum foil, Metal washers, Basins of water, Balances
Safety
Ensure spilled water is cleaned up.
Access and differentiation
Provide a basic template for a boat shape for students who struggle with the initial design phase.
Time rationale
30 mins design and calculation, 40 mins testing and modifying, 20 mins final justification.

act-assessment-unit · 60 min · assessment

Students complete an autonomous written assessment featuring calculation problems (density, flow rate) and short-essay questions requiring them to predict and justify outcomes in novel fluid scenarios.

Mastery criterion
Correctly calculating flow rate and buoyant force, and accurately predicting outcomes in 3 out of 4 fluid dynamics scenarios with evidence-based justifications.
Materials
Assessment papers
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide extra time and allow oral responses for the short-essay questions for students with writing difficulties.
Time rationale
60 mins for independent completion of the assessment.

act-retrieval-density-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given cards with mass and volume data for various unknown materials. They must quickly calculate the densities and sort the cards into groups of identical materials.

Mastery criterion
Correct grouping of cards based on accurate mental or scratchpad density calculations.
Materials
Data cards
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Use simple numbers (e.g., mass 10, volume 2) to reduce cognitive load on arithmetic and focus on the concept.
Time rationale
10 mins explanation, 15 mins sorting activity, 5 mins review.

act-retrieval-density-2 · 30 min · retrieval

Students receive a 'mystery object' profile with its mass and volume. They calculate its density and use a provided reference table of material densities to identify what the object is made of.

Mastery criterion
Accurate calculation and correct identification of the material from the table.
Materials
Mystery profiles, Density reference tables
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide calculators to ensure arithmetic errors do not mask conceptual understanding.
Time rationale
20 mins calculation and identification, 10 mins sharing results.

act-retrieval-bernoulli-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given three blank diagrams of fluid flow scenarios. They must quickly draw arrows indicating fluid speed and write 'H' or 'L' to indicate high or low pressure areas.

Mastery criterion
Correct placement of speed arrows and pressure labels according to Bernoulli's principle.
Materials
Blank diagrams
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Review the inverse relationship between speed and pressure verbally before starting the timer.
Time rationale
20 mins drawing and labeling, 10 mins peer correction.

act-retrieval-bernoulli-2 · 30 min · retrieval

The teacher performs a quick demonstration (e.g., blowing over a strip of paper so it rises). Before the demonstration, students write a prediction of what will happen and why. After, they compare their prediction to the result.

Mastery criterion
Predictions correctly anticipate the outcome based on the creation of a low-pressure zone by fast-moving air.
Materials
Strips of paper
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence starters for the prediction (e.g., 'I predict the paper will... because the fast air creates...').
Time rationale
10 mins prediction, 5 mins demonstration, 15 mins discussion.

act-practice-buoyancy · 60 min · practice

Students solve a series of word problems calculating the buoyant force on different objects submerged in various fluids, determining if they will float or sink.

Mastery criterion
Correct calculation of buoyant force and accurate prediction of floating or sinking.
Materials
Worksheets, Calculators
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a step-by-step formula guide for students who need help structuring their calculations.
Time rationale
15 mins review, 30 mins independent practice, 15 mins peer review.

act-practice-pascal · 60 min · practice

Students calculate the force output of various hydraulic press systems given the input force and the areas of the pistons.

Mastery criterion
Accurate application of Pascal's principle to find the correct output force.
Materials
Problem sets, Calculators
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Use simple ratios for piston areas to reduce mathematical complexity for struggling students.
Time rationale
20 mins guided practice, 40 mins independent problem solving.

act-practice-flow-rate · 60 min · practice

Students analyze different scenarios (e.g., filling a pool, water flowing through a pipe) and calculate the flow rate or the time required to move a specific volume of fluid.

Mastery criterion
Correct use of the flow rate formula and appropriate units in all answers.
Materials
Worksheets, Calculators
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a conversion chart for units (e.g., liters to milliliters, minutes to seconds).
Time rationale
15 mins introduction, 35 mins practice, 10 mins review.

act-practice-bernoulli · 60 min · practice

Students read descriptions of real-world phenomena (e.g., a roof lifting off during a hurricane, a curveball in baseball) and write explanations using Bernoulli's principle.

Mastery criterion
Explanations correctly identify areas of high and low fluid speed and the resulting pressure differences.
Materials
Scenario cards, Notebooks
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw diagrams to support their written explanations.
Time rationale
20 mins reading scenarios, 40 mins writing explanations.

act-bridge-statics-dynamics · 60 min · bridge

Students investigate how the hydrostatic pressure (depth of water in a container) affects the flow rate of water exiting a hole at the bottom.

Mastery criterion
Conclusions correctly state that higher hydrostatic pressure results in a faster flow rate.
Materials
Large water containers with a hole at the bottom, Stopwatches, Graduated cylinders, Water
Safety

Limitations: The unit simplifies fluid dynamics by assuming ideal fluids in most cases.; Activities rely on macroscopic observations to infer microscopic properties like cohesion and adhesion.; Safety constraints prevent the use of high-pressure systems or hazardous liquids, limiting experiments to water and safe household materials.; Calculations are kept to basic arithmetic to suit the grade level, avoiding complex algebraic manipulations of fluid equations.

Heat and temperature

Students enter Grade 6 with a basic sensory understanding of hot and cold and the macroscopic states of matter (solid, liquid, gas). In this unit, they progress to a microscopic particle model to explain these phenomena. Understanding the relationship between kinetic energy and temperature (relate-temp-kinetic-energy) is a crucial prerequisite for explaining phase changes (identify-phase-changes) and thermal expansion (explain-thermal-expansion). Similarly, distinguishing heat from temperature (differentiate-heat-temp) is required before analyzing how heat transfers (classify-heat-transfer) or how different materials respond to heat (compare-heat-capacity). In future grades, students will revisit these concepts with quantitative thermodynamics, calculating specific heat and exact thermal expansion coefficients.

Review: panel_passed · optimizer revisions: 2. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Applying the particle model to explain temperature, phase changes, and thermal expansion.

Students transition from macroscopic observations of states of matter to microscopic explanations using the kinetic particle model, laying the foundation for thermodynamics. The relationship between pressure and particle escape bridges phase identification and altitude prediction.

describe the relationship between temperature and the average kinetic energy of particles
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given diagrams of particles in two identical containers at different temperatures, select the diagram representing the higher temperature and state the rule connecting temperature to particle speed.
Expected response
The diagram with longer motion arrows represents the higher temperature because temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy (movement) of the particles.
Scoring rule
1 point for selecting the correct diagram; 1 point for explicitly linking temperature to particle movement/kinetic energy.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies that higher temperatures correspond to faster particle movement.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Temperature is a measure of how much 'heat substance' an object contains.; Particles in cold objects do not move at all.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Temperature is related to the movement of atoms and molecules. · Source page 36 · paragraph p36-paragraph-14
classify macroscopic phase changes (melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, sublimation) from everyday examples
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Read three scenarios (e.g., dew forming on leaves, dry ice disappearing, a puddle drying up) and classify each with the correct scientific term for the phase change.
Expected response
Dew forming is condensation; dry ice disappearing is sublimation; a puddle drying up is evaporation.
Scoring rule
1 point per correctly classified scenario using the exact scientific term.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately names the phase change occurring in a given real-world scenario.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Condensation on a cold glass comes from water leaking through the glass.; Boiling water turns into air rather than water vapor.
Local prerequisites
relate-temp-kinetic-energy
Scientific support
  • Clouds form through the condensation of water vapor and the sublimation of ice crystals. · Source page 41 · paragraph p41-paragraph-22
predict the boiling point of water based on changes in atmospheric pressure or altitude
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Predict whether water will boil at a higher or lower temperature on top of the San Salvador volcano compared to the port of La Libertad. Justify your answer using the concept of atmospheric pressure.
Expected response
Water will boil at a lower temperature on the volcano because the altitude is higher, which means the atmospheric pressure is lower.
Scoring rule
1 point for predicting a lower boiling point; 1 point for justifying it with lower atmospheric pressure at higher altitudes.
Mastery evidence
Student predicts whether the boiling point will be higher or lower than 100°C based on altitude and justifies it using atmospheric pressure.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Water always boils at exactly 100 degrees Celsius regardless of location.; Higher altitudes make water boil at higher temperatures because it is closer to the sun.
Local prerequisites
identify-phase-changes
Scientific support
  • Lower atmospheric pressure causes water to boil at temperatures below 100 °C. · Source page 43 · paragraph p43-paragraph-10
explain the thermal expansion of solids, liquids, and gases using macroscopic evidence
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain why a balloon placed over the mouth of a bottle inflates when the bottle is placed in hot water, using the particle model.
Expected response
The hot water transfers thermal energy to the air inside the bottle. The air particles move faster, collide more forcefully, and spread further apart, causing the gas to expand and inflate the balloon.
Scoring rule
1 point for mentioning heat transfer to the gas; 1 point for explaining that particles move faster and spread apart (expansion).
Mastery evidence
Student explains macroscopic expansion by referencing the increased separation of particles due to thermal energy.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Objects get bigger when heated because the particles themselves swell and grow in size.; Only metals expand when heated.
Local prerequisites
relate-temp-kinetic-energy
Scientific support
  • An increase in temperature leads to an increase in gas pressure inside a container. · Source page 39 · paragraph p39-paragraph-5

Analyzing heat transfer mechanisms and thermal properties of materials.

Students distinguish between heat and temperature, and analyze how thermal energy moves and affects different materials, applying these concepts to everyday phenomena.

distinguish between heat as transferred energy and temperature as a measure of average kinetic energy
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Sort a list of statements and units into two categories: 'Heat' and 'Temperature'.
Expected response
Heat: measured in Joules, is energy in transit. Temperature: measured in Celsius/Kelvin, is average kinetic energy.
Scoring rule
1 point for correctly sorting the units; 1 point for correctly sorting the conceptual definitions.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies definitions and units for heat versus temperature.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Heat and temperature are exactly the same thing.; Cold is a substance that can be transferred to cool things down.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Heat and thermal energy are measured in Joules. · Source page 60 · paragraph p60-paragraph-18
classify everyday scenarios into conduction, convection, or radiation mechanisms
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given three images (a metal spoon in hot soup, a pot of boiling water, and hands warming near a fire), label each with the primary heat transfer mechanism.
Expected response
Spoon in soup: Conduction. Boiling water: Convection. Hands near fire: Radiation.
Scoring rule
1 point for each correctly labeled mechanism.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately identifies the primary heat transfer mechanism in given scenarios.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Heat only travels upwards.; Radiation requires a medium to travel through.
Local prerequisites
differentiate-heat-temp
Scientific support
  • Heat is transferred through three mechanisms: conduction, convection, and radiation. · Source page 45 · paragraph p45-paragraph-10
compare the heat capacity of different substances based on their temperature change when exposed to the same heat source
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
If 100g of water and 100g of sand receive the same amount of thermal energy, the sand's temperature increases much more than the water's. Decide which substance has the higher heat capacity and justify your answer.
Expected response
Water has a higher heat capacity because it requires more heat to change its temperature, which is why its temperature increased less than the sand's.
Scoring rule
1 point for identifying water; 1 point for justifying that a smaller temperature change indicates a higher heat capacity.
Mastery evidence
Student deduces which material has a higher heat capacity based on temperature change data.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All materials heat up at the exact same rate if given the same amount of heat.; Larger objects always heat up faster than smaller ones.
Local prerequisites
differentiate-heat-temp
Scientific support
  • A higher heat capacity means more heat is required to change the substance's temperature. · Source page 53 · paragraph p53-paragraph-12
predict the direction of heat flow between two objects until thermal equilibrium is reached
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
An ice cube is placed in a glass of warm water. Predict the direction of heat flow and describe what the final temperature state of the system will be.
Expected response
Heat will flow from the warm water to the ice cube until both the melted ice and the water reach the same final temperature (thermal equilibrium).
Scoring rule
1 point for stating heat flows from warm water to ice; 1 point for stating they will eventually reach the same temperature.
Mastery evidence
Student predicts heat flow from hotter to colder objects and identifies when equilibrium is reached.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Cold flows from a cold object into a warm object.; Objects stop exchanging energy completely once they reach the same temperature.
Local prerequisites
differentiate-heat-temp
Scientific support
  • The human body eventually adapts by reaching thermal equilibrium with the ambient temperature. · Source page 35 · paragraph p35-paragraph-5

Students place equal masses of water and cooking oil in identical cups in a sunny spot. They measure the temperature every 10 minutes and deduce which has a higher heat capacity.

Mastery criterion
Students deduce that water has a higher heat capacity because its temperature increased less than the oil's.
Materials
Cups, Water, Cooking oil, Thermometers
Safety
Clean up any oil spills immediately to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-drawn graph for students to plot their data points.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup, 20 minutes observation and recording, 10 minutes conclusion.

prac3-heat-capacity · 40 min · practice

Students read a scenario about a hot day at the beach, comparing the temperature of the sand and the ocean water. They write an explanation using the concept of heat capacity.

Mastery criterion
Students explain that the ocean is cooler than the sand because water has a higher heat capacity and requires more energy to change temperature.
Materials
Scenario worksheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide guiding questions to help structure the written explanation.
Time rationale
10 minutes reading, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes sharing.

assess-heat-capacity · 35 min · assessment

If 100g of water and 100g of sand receive the same amount of thermal energy, the sand's temperature increases much more than the water's. Decide which substance has the higher heat capacity and justify your answer.

Mastery criterion
1 point for identifying water; 1 point for justifying that a smaller temperature change indicates a higher heat capacity.
Materials
Assessment worksheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use a diagram to support their written justification.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.

teach-thermal-eq · 40 min · teach

Demonstrate thermal equilibrium by mixing equal amounts of hot and cold water. Measure the initial temperatures and the final mixed temperature. Explain that heat flows from hot to cold until temperatures are equal.

Mastery criterion
Students can state that heat flows from hotter to colder objects until they reach the same temperature.
Materials
Hot tap water, Cold water, Thermometers, Beakers
Safety
Use hot tap water, not boiling, to prevent scalds.
Access and differentiation
Write the initial and final temperatures on the board for visual reference.
Time rationale
15 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes explanation, 10 minutes discussion.

prac1-thermal-eq · 40 min · practice

Students are given scenarios (e.g., hot metal dropped in cold water) and must draw arrows indicating the direction of heat flow and state the final condition (equilibrium).

Mastery criterion
Students correctly draw arrows from hot to cold and state that the final temperatures will be equal.
Materials
Worksheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a color-coding system (red for hot, blue for cold) to help visualize heat flow.
Time rationale
10 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 10 minutes review.

prac2-thermal-eq · 40 min · practice

Students place an ice cube in a cup of warm water and measure the temperature every 2 minutes until the ice melts and the temperature stabilizes. They graph the results.

Mastery criterion
Students graph the temperature change and identify the flat part of the graph as thermal equilibrium.
Materials
Ice cubes, Warm water, Thermometers, Graph paper
Safety
Wipe up any spilled water.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-labeled axes on the graph paper.
Time rationale
10 minutes setup, 20 minutes data collection and graphing, 10 minutes discussion.

prac3-thermal-eq · 40 min · practice

Students write a short story from the perspective of a heat particle moving from a hot cup of coffee to a cold room, ending when equilibrium is reached.

Mastery criterion
The story accurately describes heat moving from the hotter object to the colder environment until temperatures are equal.
Materials
Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a story outline or comic strip template for students who prefer drawing.
Time rationale
10 minutes brainstorming, 20 minutes writing, 10 minutes sharing.

assess-thermal-eq · 40 min · assessment

An ice cube is placed in a glass of warm water. Predict the direction of heat flow and describe what the final temperature state of the system will be.

Mastery criterion
1 point for stating heat flows from warm water to ice; 1 point for stating they will eventually reach the same temperature.
Materials
Assessment worksheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw a diagram with arrows to supplement their written answer.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent work, 10 minutes collection.

Limitations: The particle model is highly abstract for 6th graders; activities rely heavily on analogies and macroscopic evidence to infer microscopic behavior.; Heat capacity and specific heat are treated qualitatively. Mathematical formulas (Q=mcΔT) are excluded to maintain grade-level appropriateness.; Safety constraints prevent the use of open flames by students; teacher demonstrations or safe alternatives (like hot tap water) are required for several heat transfer and expansion activities.

Electricity and magnetism

Students enter with basic qualitative experiences of magnets and simple circuits. This unit formalizes these concepts into measurable quantities (voltage, resistance) and introduces the domain model of magnetism. In future grades, this foundation will support the study of electromagnetic induction, AC/DC differences, and complex circuit analysis using Ohm's Law.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 4 planning weeks.

Electrical Circuit Analysis

Students transition from qualitative observations of electricity to quantitative measurements, understanding how components interact in different circuit configurations. Measurement serves as the primary vehicle for reasoning about parallel circuits, allowing students to empirically discover and justify voltage constancy across branches.

measure direct voltage of a battery using a multimeter
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a multimeter and a AA battery, measure and record its voltage.
Expected response
The multimeter reads approximately 1.5V when the red probe is on the positive terminal and black on the negative.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student selects the 20V DC scale and obtains a reading between 1.2V and 1.6V.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly sets the multimeter to DC voltage and places probes on the correct battery terminals to read the value.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Voltage is the same as current; Multimeter probes can be placed anywhere without regard to polarity
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • To measure battery voltage, the multimeter is set to DC voltage and probes are placed on the respective terminals. · Source page 66 · paragraph p66-paragraph-5
measure electrical current in a circuit using a multimeter
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a simple circuit, correctly use a multimeter to measure the current flowing through it.
Expected response
The student breaks the circuit and places the multimeter probes in series, obtaining a valid current reading.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly connects the multimeter in series and reads the current.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly opens the circuit and connects the multimeter in series to measure current.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Current is measured in parallel like voltage; Opening the circuit is not necessary to measure current
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • To measure current, the circuit must be opened and the multimeter connected in series. · Source page 68 · paragraph p68-paragraph-10
calculate electrical resistance using the standard color code
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Calculate the resistance of a resistor with brown, black, and brown bands.
Expected response
100 ohms.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly identifies 1, 0, and multiplier x10 to get 100.
Mastery evidence
Student decodes the colored bands on a resistor to determine its resistance value in ohms.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Colors represent random numbers; The tolerance band is read first
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The color code is used to calculate the theoretical resistance value. · Source page 67 · paragraph p67-paragraph-3
predict the effect of removing a component in a series circuit
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain what happens to a second LED in a series circuit if the first LED is removed, and why.
Expected response
The second LED will turn off because removing a component breaks the single path for the electrical current.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student states the LED turns off and justifies it by the interruption of the single current path.
Mastery evidence
Student deduces that breaking a series circuit stops the current flow for all components.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Current will bypass the removed component; Only components after the removed one will turn off
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Disconnecting a component in a series circuit stops the current flow through all components. · Source page 73 · paragraph p73-paragraph-13
compare voltage distribution across components in a parallel circuit
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Predict the voltage across two resistors in parallel, then measure to verify, justifying why they are the same.
Expected response
The student predicts 3V for both, measures approximately 3V, and explains that parallel branches connect directly to the source.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student predicts equal voltages, verifies with measurement, and justifies using parallel circuit principles.
Mastery evidence
Student concludes that voltage remains constant across all parallel branches.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Voltage is divided equally among parallel branches; Adding more parallel branches increases total voltage
Local prerequisites
measure-voltage
Scientific support
  • Components in a parallel circuit share the same voltage as the power source. · Source page 78 · paragraph p78-paragraph-9
analyze equivalent resistance in a mixed circuit
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Build a mixed circuit with three resistors and measure the total equivalent resistance.
Expected response
The student correctly assembles the circuit and uses the multimeter to find the equivalent resistance.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly builds the mixed circuit and measures a resistance value close to the theoretical equivalent.
Mastery evidence
Student builds a mixed circuit and measures its equivalent resistance.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Mixed circuits are analyzed exactly like simple series circuits; Parallel and series parts cannot be combined
Local prerequisites
measure-voltage, calculate-resistance
Scientific support
  • The equivalent resistance of a mixed circuit can be measured by connecting a multimeter across the entire disconnected circuit. · Source page 77 · paragraph p77-paragraph-9

Magnetic Interactions and Electromagnetism

Students explore invisible magnetic forces and their relationship with electricity, building foundational models of fields and domains.

draw magnetic field lines around a bar magnet using a compass
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Use a compass to trace three magnetic field lines on one side of a bar magnet.
Expected response
A drawing showing curved lines originating from one pole and ending at the opposite pole.
Scoring rule
Pass if the lines are curved, connect the poles, and do not intersect.
Mastery evidence
Student uses a compass to trace continuous lines from the north pole to the south pole of a magnet.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Magnetic fields only exist at the poles; Field lines cross each other
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Magnetic field lines exit the north pole and enter the south pole. · Source page 81 · paragraph p81-paragraph-3
justify the attraction of ferromagnetic materials using magnetic domains
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Why is a steel paperclip always attracted to a magnet and never repelled?
Expected response
The paperclip's internal magnetic domains align so that their opposite poles face the magnet, causing attraction.
Scoring rule
Pass if the explanation includes the alignment of internal magnetic domains in response to the external magnet.
Mastery evidence
Student explains that materials like iron are attracted because their internal magnetic domains align with the external magnet.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All metals are attracted to magnets; Magnets pull things by creating a vacuum
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Ferromagnetic materials are attracted because their internal magnetic domains align with the external magnetic field. · Source page 83 · paragraph p83-paragraph-9
build an electromagnet using a nail, copper wire, and a battery
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Assemble an electromagnet and demonstrate its ability to attract at least two paperclips.
Expected response
The student coils the wire tightly around the nail, connects the stripped ends to the battery, and lifts paperclips.
Scoring rule
Pass if the device successfully attracts paperclips when connected and drops them when disconnected.
Mastery evidence
Student successfully coils wire around a nail and connects it to a battery to pick up paperclips.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The nail itself generates the electricity; The wire must be bare (uninsulated) everywhere to work
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • An electromagnet is built by coiling wire around a core and stripping the ends for electrical connection. · Source page 82 · paragraph p82-paragraph-2
predict the loss of magnetic properties when an electromagnet is disconnected
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
What will happen to the paperclips attached to your electromagnet if you disconnect one wire from the battery? Justify your answer.
Expected response
The paperclips will fall because the magnetic field is only generated while the electric current is flowing.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student states the paperclips fall and links this to the cessation of electric current.
Mastery evidence
Student predicts that disconnecting the circuit will cause the electromagnet to drop attracted objects.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The nail remains permanently magnetized forever; The battery stores magnetism
Local prerequisites
construct-electromagnet, explain-magnetic-domains
Scientific support
  • Electromagnets rely on electric current to align domains and are not permanent. · Source page 81 · paragraph p81-paragraph-5
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-measure-voltage · 30 min · teach

Introduce the multimeter, demonstrate setting it to the 20V DC scale, and show how to place the red probe on the positive terminal and black on the negative terminal of a AA battery to read the voltage.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly sets the multimeter to DC voltage and places probes on the correct battery terminals to read the value.
Materials
multimeter, AA battery
Safety
Ensure batteries are low voltage (1.5V) and not leaking. Do not short-circuit the battery.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual diagram of the multimeter dial for students who need help identifying the DC voltage section.
Time rationale
10 minutes for introduction and demonstration, 20 minutes for guided student practice in pairs.

prac1-measure-voltage · 45 min · practice

Students test a variety of household batteries (AAA, AA, C, D) using a multimeter, recording the voltage of each and comparing it to the labeled voltage.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately records the voltage of at least three different batteries using the correct multimeter settings.
Materials
multimeter, AAA battery, AA battery, C battery, D battery
Safety
Use only standard low-voltage alkaline batteries. Inspect for leaks before use.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to work in mixed-ability pairs to support reading the digital display.
Time rationale
15 minutes setup and instruction, 20 minutes testing multiple batteries, 10 minutes sharing results.

prac2-measure-voltage · 45 min · practice

Students connect two AA batteries end-to-end (positive to negative) and measure the combined voltage, noting how it differs from a single battery.

Mastery criterion
Student successfully measures and records the combined voltage of approximately 3V.
Materials
multimeter, two AA batteries, battery holder or tape
Safety
Ensure batteries are connected correctly to avoid short circuits and overheating.
Access and differentiation
Provide battery holders to assist students with fine motor difficulties.
Time rationale
15 minutes for setup, 20 minutes for measurement and recording, 10 minutes for cleanup and discussion.

prac3-measure-voltage · 30 min · practice

Students are given a multimeter with the probes intentionally placed in the wrong ports or the dial set incorrectly, and must correct the setup before measuring a battery.

Mastery criterion
Student identifies the setup error, corrects it, and obtains a valid voltage reading.
Materials
multimeter, AA battery
Safety
Standard low-voltage battery safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist of correct multimeter settings for reference.
Time rationale
10 minutes explanation, 15 minutes troubleshooting, 5 minutes review.

assess-measure-voltage · 30 min · assessment

Given a multimeter and a AA battery, measure and record its voltage independently.

Mastery criterion
Pass if the student selects the 20V DC scale and obtains a reading between 1.2V and 1.6V.
Materials
multimeter, AA battery, recording sheet
Safety
Standard low-voltage battery safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Read instructions aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes individual assessment, 5 minutes collection.

bridge-measure-voltage · 30 min · bridge

Students measure the voltage of new versus heavily used batteries and calculate the hypothetical replacement cost in US dollars for a household device.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly measures voltages and calculates the hypothetical cost of replacing the dead batteries.
Materials
multimeter, new AA batteries, used AA batteries, calculator
Safety
Standard low-voltage battery safety applies.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-set prices for the batteries to simplify the math.
Time rationale
15 minutes measuring, 15 minutes calculating costs.

teach-calculate-resistance · 30 min · teach

Explain the standard resistor color code system, demonstrating how to read the first two bands as digits and the third as a multiplier to find the resistance in ohms.

Mastery criterion
Student decodes the colored bands on a resistor to determine its resistance value in ohms.
Materials
resistor color code chart, large model of a resistor, whiteboard
Safety
No safety hazards for this theoretical activity.
Access and differentiation
Provide a simplified chart with only the most common colors used in class.

15 minutes direct instruction, 15 minutes guided practice with examples on the board.

prac1-calculate-resistance · 45 min · practice

Students receive a set of 5 different physical resistors and use a color code chart to calculate and record the theoretical resistance of each.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly calculates the resistance for at least 4 out of 5 resistors.
Materials
5 different resistors per group, color code charts, magnifying glasses
Safety
Ensure wire ends of resistors do not poke skin.
Access and differentiation
Provide magnifying glasses for students who have trouble seeing small bands.

10 minutes setup, 25 minutes decoding, 10 minutes reviewing answers.

prac2-calculate-resistance · 45 min · practice

Students are given target resistance values and must draw and color their own paper resistors with the correct band sequences.

Mastery criterion
Student accurately colors the bands to match the assigned target resistance values.
Materials
paper, colored pencils or markers, target value cards
Safety
No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use a digital drawing tool if fine motor skills are a barrier.

10 minutes instruction, 25 minutes drawing and coloring, 10 minutes peer review.

assess-calculate-resistance · 30 min · assessment

Calculate the resistance of a resistor with brown, black, and brown bands using the provided chart.

Mastery criterion
Pass if the student correctly identifies 1, 0, and multiplier x10 to get 100 ohms.

assessment worksheet, color code chart
Safety
No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a large-print version of the assessment.

5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes independent work, 5 minutes collection.

ret1-calculate-resistance · 20 min · retrieval

Students use flashcards with resistor colors on one side and values on the other to test each other in pairs.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly recalls or calculates the values for the flashcards presented.
Materials
pre-made flashcards
Safety
No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Pair students strategically for peer support.

5 minutes setup, 15 minutes paired practice.

ret2-calculate-resistance · 20 min · retrieval

A short written quiz where students must write the resistance value for three given color sequences from memory or using a blank chart they fill in.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly calculates the resistance for the three sequences.
Materials
quiz paper
Safety
No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow extra time for students who need it.

5 minutes distribution, 15 minutes quiz time.

bridge-calculate-resistance · 30 min · bridge

Students calculate the resistance of various components and determine the hypothetical cost in US dollars to purchase a set of 100 ohm resistors for a school project.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly identifies the 100 ohm resistor by color and calculates the total hypothetical cost.
Materials
resistor catalogs with hypothetical US dollar prices, color code chart

No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide calculators for the cost multiplication.

15 minutes identifying resistors, 15 minutes calculating costs.

teach-analyze-series-circuit · 45 min · teach

Build a series circuit with a battery and two LEDs. Remove one LED to demonstrate that the other turns off, explaining that the single path for current is broken.

Mastery criterion
Student deduces that breaking a series circuit stops the current flow for all components.

AA battery, battery holder, wires, two LEDs, breadboard
Safety
Use low-voltage batteries. Ensure LEDs have appropriate built-in or external resistors to prevent popping.
Access and differentiation
Use oversized components for better visibility during the demonstration.

prac1-analyze-series-circuit · 45 min · practice

Students build their own series circuits with three LEDs and predict, then test, what happens when the middle LED is removed.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly predicts the outcome and verifies that all LEDs turn off when one is removed.

AA batteries, wires, three LEDs per group, breadboards
Safety
Use low-voltage batteries. Handle components gently to avoid sharp wire ends.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-wired breadboards where students only need to insert the LEDs.

20 minutes building, 15 minutes testing and predicting, 10 minutes recording results.

prac2-analyze-series-circuit · 45 min · practice

Students add a mechanical switch to their series circuit and explain how the switch acts like removing a component to control the flow of current.

Mastery criterion
Student explains that an open switch breaks the single path, stopping current just like removing an LED.
Materials
AA batteries, wires, LEDs, switches
Safety
Use low-voltage batteries.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual analogy of a drawbridge for the switch concept.

15 minutes building, 15 minutes testing, 15 minutes writing explanations.

assess-analyze-series-circuit · 30 min · assessment

Explain what happens to a second LED in a series circuit if the first LED is removed, and why.

Mastery criterion
Pass if the student states the LED turns off and justifies it by the interruption of the single current path.
Materials
assessment worksheet
Safety
No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow verbal explanations for students who struggle with writing.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent writing.

bridge-analyze-series-circuit · 30 min · bridge

Students analyze a hypothetical series circuit used for a volcano warning siren system in San Miguel, identifying why a series design is a bad idea for emergency alerts if one siren breaks.

Mastery criterion
Student reasons that a series circuit is unreliable for emergencies because one broken component disables the entire system.

circuit diagrams, worksheet

No safety hazards.

15 minutes analyzing the diagram, 15 minutes writing the justification.

Student concludes that voltage remains constant across all parallel branches.

3V battery source, three resistors, multimeter, wires, breadboards

Use low-voltage batteries.

Provide pre-drawn circuit maps where students only need to fill in the measured values.

Use low-voltage batteries.

15 minutes setup, 20 minutes experimenting, 10 minutes discussion.

Predict the voltage across two resistors connected in parallel to a 3V battery, then measure to verify, and justify why they share the same voltage.

Provide a checklist of steps for using the multimeter.

assess-explain-magnetic-domains · 30 min · assessment

Why is a steel paperclip always attracted to a magnet and never repelled? Write a short explanation using the concept of magnetic domains.

Mastery criterion
Pass if the explanation includes the alignment of internal magnetic domains in response to the external magnet.

assessment worksheet
Safety
No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to include a drawing to support their written explanation.

5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent writing.

ret1-explain-magnetic-domains · 20 min · retrieval

Students are asked to recall the definition of a magnetic domain and explain to a partner how it relates to a paperclip being attracted to a magnet.

Mastery criterion
Student correctly recalls that domains are tiny magnetic regions that align to cause attraction.

Safety
No safety hazards.

Students are given a scenario of a new metallic alloy that does not attract to a magnet. They must deduce and draw its internal domain structure compared to a piece of iron, justifying their drawing.

bridge-explain-magnetic-domains · 30 min · bridge

Students read about magnetic minerals in lava from Salvadoran volcanoes (like Izalco) aligning with Earth's magnetic field before cooling, and relate this to the alignment of domains in a paperclip.

No safety hazards.

Student successfully coils wire around a nail, connects it to a battery, and picks up at least two paperclips.
Materials
iron nails, insulated copper wire, AA batteries, paperclips
Safety

Access and differentiation

25 minutes assembly, 15 minutes testing, 5 minutes cleanup.

prac2-construct-electromagnet · 45 min · practice

Students rebuild their electromagnets with half the number of wire coils and test if it changes the number of paperclips they can lift.

Mastery criterion
Student successfully alters the number of coils and records the new lifting capacity.
Materials
iron nails, insulated copper wire, AA batteries, paperclips
Safety
Only connect the battery for a few seconds at a time to prevent overheating.
Access and differentiation
Have students work in pairs to count coils accurately.
Time rationale
20 minutes rebuilding, 15 minutes testing, 10 minutes comparing results.

assess-construct-electromagnet · 30 min · assessment

Assemble an electromagnet using the provided materials and demonstrate its ability to attract at least two paperclips to the teacher.

Mastery criterion
Pass if the device successfully attracts paperclips when connected and drops them when disconnected.
Materials
iron nail, insulated copper wire, AA battery, paperclips
Safety
Only connect the battery briefly during the demonstration.
Access and differentiation

5 minutes instructions, 20 minutes assembly and demonstration, 5 minutes cleanup.

bridge-construct-electromagnet · 30 min · bridge

Students design a hypothetical crane system on paper that uses an electromagnet to move scrap metal, labeling the battery, coil, and core.

paper, pencils, rulers
Safety
No safety hazards.

Provide a basic crane outline for students to complete.

10 minutes introduction, 20 minutes drawing and labeling.

teach-predict-electromagnet-behavior · 30 min · teach

Demonstrate an electromagnet holding paperclips, then disconnect one wire to show the paperclips falling. Explain that the magnetic field depends entirely on the flow of electric current.

Student understands that disconnecting the circuit stops the current, which eliminates the magnetic field.

Repeat the demonstration multiple times so all students can observe the immediate effect.

prac1-predict-electromagnet-behavior · 45 min · practice

Students integrate a switch into their electromagnet circuit and predict how the switch will control the magnetic field, then test their prediction.

Mastery criterion
Student predicts and verifies that opening the switch stops the current and drops the paperclips.
Materials
student-built electromagnets, switches, AA batteries, paperclips
Safety

Access and differentiation
Provide clear diagrams showing how to wire the switch in series with the coil.

20 minutes wiring the switch, 15 minutes testing predictions, 10 minutes recording.

prac2-predict-electromagnet-behavior · 45 min · practice

Students disconnect their electromagnets and test if the iron nail retains any slight magnetism by trying to pick up a single iron filing, then justify why it is mostly non-magnetic.

Mastery criterion
Student reasons that without current, the domains in the soft iron nail randomize again, losing the strong magnetic field.
Materials
student-built electromagnets, iron filings in sealed clear containers
Safety
Keep iron filings sealed to prevent eye contact.
Access and differentiation
Provide a review of the magnetic domains concept to help with the justification.
