15 minutes testing, 30 minutes writing the justification linking current to domain alignment.

assess-predict-electromagnet-behavior · 30 min · assessment

What will happen to the paperclips attached to your electromagnet if you disconnect one wire from the battery? Justify your answer.

Mastery criterion
Pass if the student states the paperclips fall and links this to the cessation of electric current.
Materials
assessment worksheet
Safety
No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use bullet points for their justification instead of full paragraphs.
Time rationale
5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes independent writing.

bridge-predict-electromagnet-behavior · 30 min · bridge

Students compare an electromagnet controlled by a switch to a water valve controlled by a handle, justifying how both require an active flow (current or water) to perform work.

Mastery criterion
Student justifies the analogy, explaining that stopping the flow stops the action in both systems.
Materials
diagrams of water valves and electromagnets
Safety
No safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a matching activity for the components of the analogy before writing.
Time rationale
15 minutes analyzing the analogy, 15 minutes writing the justification.

teach-measure-current · 45 min · teach

Demonstrate how to open a simple circuit and connect a multimeter in series to measure the electrical current, ensuring students understand the difference between series and parallel connections for measurement.

Mastery criterion
Student understands that the circuit must be broken to insert the multimeter in series.
Materials
multimeter, AA battery, resistor, wires
Safety
Ensure the multimeter is set to the correct current scale to avoid blowing the internal fuse.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual diagram showing the difference between parallel (voltage) and series (current) connections.
Time rationale
15 minutes demonstration, 30 minutes guided practice.

prac1-measure-current · 45 min · practice

Students build a simple circuit with a resistor and battery, then open the circuit to measure the current with a multimeter.

Mastery criterion
Student successfully measures and records the current without short-circuiting the battery.
Materials
multimeter, AA battery, resistor, wires, breadboard
Safety
Do not measure current directly across the battery without a resistor.
Access and differentiation
Pair students to double-check multimeter settings before connecting.
Time rationale
15 minutes setup, 20 minutes measuring, 10 minutes review.

assess-measure-current · 30 min · assessment

Given a functioning simple circuit, the student must correctly measure the current flowing through it.

Mastery criterion
Pass if the student opens the circuit, connects the multimeter in series, and gets a valid reading.
Materials
multimeter, AA battery, resistor, wires
Safety
Standard low-voltage safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist of steps for using the multimeter.

5 minutes instructions, 25 minutes assessment.

teach-analyze-mixed-circuit · 45 min · teach

Demonstrate how to build a mixed circuit (one resistor in series with two in parallel) on a breadboard and measure its equivalent resistance.

breadboard, resistors, multimeter, wires

prac1-analyze-mixed-circuit · 45 min · practice

breadboard, resistors (100 ohm, 330 ohm, 120 ohm), multimeter, wires

Limitations: The unit simplifies the atomic model of magnetic domains to a level appropriate for primary education, avoiding quantum mechanical explanations of electron spin.; Safety constraints prevent the use of high-voltage sources, limiting circuit experiments to low-voltage DC batteries.; The concept of internal resistance of batteries is omitted to simplify circuit analysis.

Chemical interactions

The unit begins by establishing the foundational concept of valence electrons, which dictates how atoms interact. This naturally progresses into modeling these interactions via Lewis structures and predicting bond types. Once students understand 2D representations, they move to 3D molecular geometries (VSEPR) and use this to deduce molecular polarity. The second half of the unit shifts from static molecules to dynamic interactions (chemical reactions). Students first learn to distinguish chemical changes from physical ones using macroscopic evidence. They then learn to represent these changes symbolically (chemical equations), classify them by type, and analyze their energy dynamics (endothermic/exothermic).

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 7 planning weeks.

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Understanding how atoms interact to form molecules is fundamental to chemistry. This skill progresses from identifying valence electrons to modeling 3D molecular geometries and predicting polarity, laying the groundwork for understanding macroscopic properties of matter.

identify valence electrons of representative elements using the periodic table
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Given a periodic table, state the number of valence electrons for Carbon, Oxygen, and Sodium.
Expected response
Carbon has 4, Oxygen has 6, and Sodium has 1 valence electron.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct element. Must correctly identify all three to demonstrate mastery.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly state the number of valence electrons for a given representative element.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All electrons in an atom participate in chemical bonding.; The group number has no relation to the number of valence electrons.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Valence electrons are those found in the outermost energy level of an atom. · Source page 88 · paragraph p88-paragraph-10
construct Lewis structures for atoms and simple molecules to satisfy the octet rule
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Draw the Lewis structure for a water molecule (H2O), showing all bonding and non-bonding electron pairs.
Expected response
Oxygen is the central atom with two single bonds to Hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs of electrons.
Scoring rule
Must show 8 electrons around Oxygen and 2 around each Hydrogen, with correct bonding pairs.
Mastery evidence
Students can draw Lewis structures showing correct electron pairing and octet satisfaction (or duet for Hydrogen).
Diagnostic hypotheses
Hydrogen requires eight electrons to be stable.; Electrons are lost when shared in a covalent bond.
Local prerequisites
g6-u4-micro-valence
Scientific support
  • Atoms seek to have eight electrons in their valence shell to achieve stability. · Source page 90 · paragraph p90-paragraph-12
predict the type of chemical bond (ionic, covalent, metallic) formed between specific atoms
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Predict and justify the type of bond that will form between Sodium (Na) and Chlorine (Cl), and between two Oxygen (O) atoms.
Expected response
Na and Cl form an ionic bond because electrons are transferred from the metal to the non-metal. Two O atoms form a covalent bond because they are both non-metals and share electrons.
Scoring rule
Must correctly identify both bond types and provide a justification based on electron transfer or sharing.
Mastery evidence
Students can justify whether a bond will be ionic, covalent, or metallic based on the types of interacting atoms.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Ionic bonds involve sharing electrons.; Metals bond by transferring electrons to other metals.
Local prerequisites
g6-u4-micro-valence
Scientific support
  • Covalent bonds involve the sharing of electron pairs between atoms. · Source page 98 · paragraph p98-paragraph-11
model the 3D geometry of molecules using VSEPR principles
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Using clay and toothpicks, build a model of a molecule with a central atom bonded to four other atoms (AB4) and state its geometry.
Expected response
A tetrahedral model with atoms spaced as far apart as possible in 3D space.
Scoring rule
Model must be 3D (not planar) and correctly identified as tetrahedral.
Mastery evidence
Students can build or draw 3D models of molecules reflecting the correct repulsion of electron pairs.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Molecules are always flat (2D) as drawn on paper.; Lone pairs do not affect the shape of the molecule.
Local prerequisites
g6-u4-micro-lewis
Scientific support
  • Molecular geometry is determined by minimizing the repulsion between electron pairs around the central atom. · Source page 105 · paragraph p105-paragraph-9
justify the overall polarity of a molecule based on bond dipoles and molecular geometry
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain why carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) is a non-polar molecule even though the C-Cl bonds are polar.
Expected response
The molecule has a symmetrical tetrahedral geometry, so the individual bond dipoles cancel each other out, resulting in no net dipole moment.
Scoring rule
Must mention both the polar nature of the bonds and the cancellation due to symmetrical geometry.
Mastery evidence
Students can explain how symmetrical geometries can cancel out polar bonds, resulting in a non-polar molecule.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Any molecule with polar bonds is a polar molecule.; Non-polar molecules cannot contain polar bonds.
Local prerequisites
g6-u4-micro-geometry
Scientific support
  • Opposing dipoles of equal magnitude cancel each other out, affecting overall molecular polarity. · Source page 110 · paragraph p110-paragraph-14

Chemical Reactions and Equations

This skill transitions students from understanding static molecular structures to dynamic chemical changes. It emphasizes distinguishing physical from chemical changes, interpreting chemical equations, and classifying reactions based on observable evidence and energy transfer.

distinguish physical changes from chemical changes using macroscopic evidence
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Read the scenario: 'An iron nail is left outside and turns reddish-brown.' Decide if this is a physical or chemical change and justify your answer.
Expected response
It is a chemical change because a new substance with a different color (rust) was formed, indicating a change in chemical composition.
Scoring rule
Must correctly identify it as a chemical change and cite the color change/new substance as evidence.
Mastery evidence
Students can evaluate a scenario and decide if a chemical reaction occurred based on evidence like color change, gas production, or precipitate formation.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Boiling water is a chemical change because a gas is produced.; Dissolving salt in water creates a new chemical substance.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Physical changes alter appearance but not the essential chemical composition of matter. · Source page 114 · paragraph p114-paragraph-7
identify reactants, products, and state symbols in a chemical equation
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
In the equation CaCO3(s) + heat -> CaO(s) + CO2(g), identify the reactants, products, and the state of CO2.
Expected response
Reactant: CaCO3. Products: CaO and CO2. State of CO2: gas.
Scoring rule
Must correctly identify all three components without error.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly label the parts of a given chemical equation.
Diagnostic hypotheses
The arrow in a chemical equation means 'equals'.; Subscripts and coefficients mean the same thing.
Local prerequisites
g6-u4-micro-phys-chem
Scientific support
  • In a chemical equation, reactants are on the left and products are on the right, separated by an arrow. · Source page 115 · paragraph p115-paragraph-5
classify chemical reactions into precipitation, neutralization, or displacement categories
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
A student mixes an acid and a base, producing water and a salt. Classify this reaction.
Expected response
Neutralization reaction.
Scoring rule
Must state 'neutralization'.
Mastery evidence
Students can categorize a described chemical reaction into the correct type based on its reactants and products.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All reactions that produce a liquid are neutralization reactions.; Precipitation reactions only happen with water.
Local prerequisites
g6-u4-micro-equations
Scientific support
  • A neutralization reaction occurs between an acid and a base. · Source page 119 · paragraph p119-paragraph-10
determine if a reaction is endothermic or exothermic based on temperature changes
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
When baking soda is mixed with vinegar, the container feels cold to the touch. Determine if this reaction is endothermic or exothermic and justify your answer.
Expected response
It is an endothermic reaction because it absorbs heat from its surroundings, making the container feel cold.
Scoring rule
Must identify it as endothermic and justify it by stating that heat is absorbed from the surroundings.
Mastery evidence
Students can deduce the energy flow of a reaction by analyzing temperature changes in the surroundings.
Diagnostic hypotheses
If a reaction gets cold, it is releasing cold energy (rather than absorbing heat).; All chemical reactions require heat to start.
Local prerequisites
g6-u4-micro-phys-chem
Scientific support
  • Reactions that absorb heat from their surroundings are called endothermic. · Source page 121 · paragraph p121-paragraph-28

act-phc-prac-2 · 90 min · practice

Students read 15 short scenarios describing changes in matter and write a justification for whether each is physical or chemical.

Students are given a scenario about an iron nail rusting and must write a short essay deciding if it is a physical or chemical change, justifying with evidence.

Teacher reads quick scenarios aloud; students move to the left side of the room for 'physical' and the right side for 'chemical', then one student is randomly called to justify.

Mastery criterion

Allow students with mobility issues to use hand signals instead of moving.

act-phc-ret-2 · 30 min · retrieval

Students complete a 10-question multiple-choice quiz where they evaluate novel, brief scenarios and deduce if a physical or chemical change occurred based on evidence.

Materials
Printed quizzes, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation

act-equ-teach-1 · 45 min · teach

Introduce the parts of a chemical equation. Show how to identify reactants, products, the yield arrow, and state symbols (s, l, g, aq).

act-equ-prac-1 · 90 min · practice

Students dissect 20 different chemical equations on a worksheet, circling reactants, underlining products, and listing the state symbols present.

act-equ-prac-2 · 90 min · practice

Students translate written descriptions of chemical reactions into symbolic chemical equations, identifying the reactants, products, and states from the text.

Text descriptions, Notebooks

act-equ-assess-1 · 45 min · assessment

Given the equation CaCO3(s) + heat -> CaO(s) + CO2(g), students must write out the reactants, products, and the state of CO2 without reference materials.

Standard classroom safety.

act-cla-teach-1 · 60 min · teach

Teach the patterns for classifying reactions into precipitation, neutralization, and displacement. Show generic formulas (e.g., Acid + Base -> Salt + Water).

Safety
Standard classroom safety.

act-cla-prac-1 · 90 min · practice

Students analyze a set of 15 chemical equations and sort them into categories (precipitation, neutralization, displacement), providing a reason for each classification.

Materials
Equation cards, Sorting mats
Safety
Standard classroom safety.

15 minutes instructions, 50 minutes sorting activity, 25 minutes review.

act-cla-prac-2 · 90 min · practice

Students read descriptions of industrial and everyday chemical processes, write the basic equation, and classify the reaction type.

Mastery criterion

Materials
Process descriptions, Worksheets
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the reactants and products in the text descriptions.

15 minutes instructions, 60 minutes reading and classifying, 15 minutes wrap-up.

act-cla-assess-1 · 60 min · assessment

Students are given 5 novel chemical equations and 5 text descriptions of reactions. They must classify all 10 into the correct categories.

Mastery criterion

Materials
Assessment papers, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow extra time for completion.

10 minutes instructions, 50 minutes assessment.

act-ene-teach-1 · 60 min · teach

Explain endothermic and exothermic reactions based on heat transfer. Demonstrate an exothermic reaction (safe hand warmers) and an endothermic one (baking soda and vinegar with a thermometer).

Mastery criterion
Students can define both terms and explain the direction of heat flow for each.
Materials
Hand warmers, Baking soda, Vinegar, Thermometers, Beakers
Safety
Goggles required. Ensure thermometers are handled carefully to prevent breakage.
Access and differentiation
Provide a graphic organizer showing heat arrows pointing in or out of a system.

30 minutes demonstrations and data logging, 20 minutes theory explanation, 10 minutes summary.

act-ene-prac-1 · 90 min · practice

Students perform safe micro-scale reactions in cups, measure temperature changes over 5 minutes, graph the data, and deduce if the reaction is endothermic or exothermic.

Mastery criterion
Accurate graphs and correct deduction of energy flow based on temperature data.
Materials
Small cups, Thermometers, Safe reactants (citric acid, baking soda, water, calcium chloride), Graph paper
Safety
Goggles required. Wash hands after handling chemicals. No ingestion.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-labeled graph axes for students who struggle with graphing.

20 minutes safety and setup, 40 minutes data collection, 30 minutes graphing and deduction.

act-ene-prac-2 · 90 min · practice

Students analyze provided temperature-time graphs of various unknown reactions, determine the energy type, and write a justification for each based on the graph's slope.

Mastery criterion
Correct identification of reaction type and logical justification referencing the temperature change shown on the graph.
Materials
Worksheets with graphs, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.

15 minutes instructions, 50 minutes analysis, 25 minutes class review.

act-ene-assess-1 · 60 min · assessment

Students read a scenario about mixing baking soda and vinegar where the container feels cold. They must determine if it is endothermic or exothermic and justify their answer in writing.

Mastery criterion
Correctly identifies the reaction as endothermic and justifies it by stating heat is absorbed from the surroundings.

Assessment prompts, Lined paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
