10 minutes instructions, 50 minutes writing.

Limitations: The VSEPR model is simplified for 6th grade; complex geometries involving d-orbitals are excluded.; Bond polarity is treated qualitatively based on general electronegativity differences rather than exact numerical calculations.; The distinction between physical and chemical changes can sometimes be ambiguous in real life (e.g., dissolving salt), which requires careful teacher guidance.; Safety constraints prevent students from performing highly exothermic or toxic reactions; simulations or safe household alternatives (like vinegar and baking soda) are used instead.

Cells

The unit begins by establishing the chemical foundation of life (biomolecules and enzymes), moving to how these molecules organize into cells (prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic, plant vs. animal) and higher levels of organization. Once the structural foundation is laid, the unit shifts to dynamic cellular processes: how cells obtain and use energy (ATP, photosynthesis, respiration) and how they interact with their environment (membrane transport, endomembrane system). Prerequisites ensure students understand the components before analyzing the processes.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 7 planning weeks.

Biomolecules and Cellular Organization

Understanding the chemical basis of life and how these molecules organize into cells and higher structures is fundamental for comprehending biological systems.

identify major groups of biomolecules in food samples
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Classify a list of common food components into carbohydrates, lipids, or proteins.
Expected response
Glucose and starch are carbohydrates; oils are lipids; enzymes and muscle fibers are proteins.
Scoring rule
1 point per correct classification; requires 3/3 for mastery.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly identifies carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins based on their primary characteristics.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All fats are bad for health; Vitamins provide cellular energy directly
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Carbohydrates are also known as sugars. · Source page 130 · paragraph p130-paragraph-4
describe the function of enzymes as biological catalysts
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Write a brief description of what an enzyme does when it encounters its substrate.
Expected response
The enzyme binds to the substrate and accelerates the chemical reaction to form products.
Scoring rule
Must mention acceleration of reaction and interaction with substrate.
Mastery evidence
Student describes enzymes as proteins that speed up chemical reactions without being consumed.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Enzymes are consumed during chemical reactions; Enzymes are living organisms
Local prerequisites
micro-identify-biomolecules
Scientific support
  • The reactants that enzymes work on are called substrates. · Source page 133 · paragraph p133-paragraph-20
compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells using structural features
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Create a Venn diagram comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
Expected response
Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have them; both have a cell membrane and genetic material.
Scoring rule
Must include at least two accurate differences and one similarity.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately compares the presence of a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles between the two cell types.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Prokaryotic cells have no genetic material; Only eukaryotic cells have a cell membrane
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have fundamental characteristics that can be investigated and compared. · Source page 137 · paragraph p137-paragraph-6
classify biological structures into levels of organization
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Sort the following terms from simplest to most complex: cell, atom, tissue, molecule, organ.
Expected response
Atom, molecule, cell, tissue, organ.
Scoring rule
Exact correct sequence required for mastery.
Mastery evidence
Student correctly orders biological structures from subatomic to organism level.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Tissues are smaller than cells; Atoms are only found in non-living things
Local prerequisites
micro-compare-cell-types
Scientific support
  • Tissues represent a specific level of biological organization. · Source page 139 · paragraph p139-paragraph-16
differentiate animal and plant cells based on organelle presence
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Identify whether a described cell with chloroplasts and a cell wall is plant or animal.
Expected response
It is a plant cell because animal cells lack chloroplasts and cell walls.
Scoring rule
Must correctly identify the cell type and justify using specific organelles.
Mastery evidence
Student identifies chloroplasts and cell walls as unique to plant cells in this context.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plant cells do not have mitochondria; Animal cells have cell walls
Local prerequisites
micro-compare-cell-types
Scientific support
  • Plastids, such as chloroplasts, have a double membrane. · Source page 150 · paragraph p150-paragraph-13

Cellular Processes and Energy

Understanding how cells obtain, transform, and utilize energy, as well as how they transport materials, is crucial for grasping the dynamic nature of life.

identify ATP and gradients as forms of biologically useful energy
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Name the two basic forms of biologically useful energy mentioned in the text.
Expected response
ATP (nucleoside triphosphates) and gradients.
Scoring rule
Must name both forms correctly.
Mastery evidence
Student identifies ATP and chemical gradients as the primary energy currencies of the cell.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Energy in cells is the same as electricity in wires; Cells create energy from nothing
Local prerequisites
micro-identify-biomolecules
Scientific support
  • Biologically useful energy drives cellular work. · Source page 142 · paragraph p142-paragraph-8
distinguish passive and active transport mechanisms across membranes
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Categorize a scenario where a cell uses ATP to move sodium out of the cell.
Expected response
Active transport, because it requires energy (ATP).
Scoring rule
Must identify as active transport and cite the use of energy.
Mastery evidence
Student distinguishes between transport that requires ATP and transport that occurs down a gradient.
Diagnostic hypotheses
All transport requires energy; Molecules stop moving once equilibrium is reached
Local prerequisites
micro-identify-energy
Scientific support
  • There are specific mechanisms that exemplify passive transport. · Source page 145 · paragraph p145-paragraph-21
predict the physical changes of cells in hypertonic and hypotonic solutions
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Predict what will happen to a red blood cell placed in a hypotonic solution and justify your answer.
Expected response
The cell will swell and possibly burst because water will move into the cell where solute concentration is higher.
Scoring rule
Must predict swelling/bursting and justify with water movement direction.
Mastery evidence
Student accurately predicts cell swelling or shrinking based on solution tonicity.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Cells swell in hypertonic solutions; Water only moves in one direction during osmosis
Local prerequisites
micro-distinguish-transport
Scientific support
  • Cells swell when placed in a hypotonic medium. · Source page 146 · paragraph p146-paragraph-6
describe the transformation of energy during aerobic respiration
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Describe the main purpose of aerobic cellular respiration and the organelle where it primarily occurs.
Expected response
The purpose is to produce ATP from food molecules using oxygen, and it occurs in the mitochondria.
Scoring rule
Must mention ATP production and mitochondria.
Mastery evidence
Student describes aerobic respiration as the process of converting food energy into ATP using oxygen.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Respiration is just breathing in oxygen and exhaling carbon dioxide; Plants do not perform cellular respiration
Local prerequisites
micro-identify-energy
Scientific support
  • Mitochondria are necessary for aerobic cellular respiration. · Source page 153 · paragraph p153-paragraph-10
explain the role of light and water in producing glucose
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Explain why plants need light and water to produce their own food.
Expected response
Light provides the energy needed to split water molecules, which provide electrons to convert carbon dioxide into sugars.
Scoring rule
Must connect light to energy and water to the production of sugars/electrons.
Mastery evidence
Student explains that light provides energy to split water and reduce CO2 to form sugars.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Plants get their food from the soil; Photosynthesis happens at night
Local prerequisites
micro-identify-energy
Scientific support
  • Plants produce sugars through the process of photosynthesis. · Source page 156 · paragraph p156-paragraph-17
trace the pathway of vesicles in the endomembrane system
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Trace the pathway of a protein destined for secretion, starting from the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Expected response
Rough ER to transport vesicle, to Golgi apparatus, to secretory vesicle, to cell membrane (exocytosis).
Scoring rule
Must include ER, Golgi, and cell membrane in the correct order.
Mastery evidence
Student traces the path of a secreted protein from the ER to the Golgi and out of the cell.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Organelles float freely and do not interact; Proteins are teleported out of the cell
Local prerequisites
micro-differentiate-eukaryotes
Scientific support
  • The Golgi apparatus is a structural component of the cell. · Source page 161 · paragraph p161-paragraph-5
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

teach-biomolecules · 90 min · teach

Students will observe physical samples of common foods (e.g., oil, sugar, egg white) and read short texts describing their primary biomolecule components. They will create a three-column chart in their notebooks to list the characteristics of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins, and classify the observed foods into these categories. The teacher will review the charts for accuracy.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly classify at least 3 out of 4 provided food examples into their primary biomolecule group.
Materials
Samples of cooking oil, sugar, and cooked egg white, Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
Ensure students do not consume the food samples. Check for severe food allergies before bringing samples to class.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-filled chart with sentence starters for students who need writing support.
Time rationale
15 mins introduction, 45 mins observation and reading, 30 mins chart creation and review.

teach-enzymes · 90 min · teach

Students will watch a teacher-led demonstration using a physical model (lock and key puzzle) to represent enzymes and substrates. They will then draw a comic strip in their notebooks illustrating an enzyme binding to a substrate, accelerating a reaction, and releasing products without being changed. The teacher will circulate to check the comic strips.

Mastery criterion
Comic strip accurately depicts the enzyme remaining unchanged after the reaction.
Materials
Lock and key puzzle or similar interlocking toys, Paper, Colored pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a template with blank panels and captions for the comic strip.
Time rationale
20 mins demonstration, 50 mins drawing comic strips, 20 mins sharing and feedback.

teach-cell-types · 90 min · teach

Students will examine large printed diagrams of a bacterium and an animal cell. Working in pairs, they will use a checklist to identify which structures (nucleus, cell membrane, organelles) are present in each diagram. They will then construct a Venn diagram on poster paper comparing the two cell types. Posters will be displayed for a gallery walk.

Mastery criterion
Venn diagram correctly places the nucleus and membrane-bound organelles in the eukaryotic section only.
Materials
Printed diagrams of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, Poster paper, Markers
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide word banks with the names of structures to be placed in the Venn diagram.
Time rationale
20 mins diagram examination, 40 mins Venn diagram creation, 30 mins gallery walk.

teach-levels · 90 min · teach

Students will receive a set of cards with images and names of different biological levels (e.g., carbon atom, protein, red blood cell, muscle tissue, heart). They will work in small groups to physically arrange the cards in order of increasing complexity. They will then glue the sorted cards into their notebooks and write a one-sentence justification for the placement of the 'tissue' card.

Mastery criterion
Cards are glued in the correct hierarchical order from atom to organ.
Materials
Sets of organization level cards, Glue, Notebooks
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Number the backs of the cards so students can self-check their sequence if they struggle.
Time rationale
15 mins instruction, 45 mins sorting and gluing, 30 mins writing justifications and review.

teach-eukaryotes · 90 min · teach

Students will analyze micrographic images of plant leaves and human cheek cells provided by the teacher. They will complete a guided worksheet where they circle the cell wall and chloroplasts in the plant cell images and note their absence in the animal cell images. Finally, they will write a summary paragraph differentiating the two.

Mastery criterion
Worksheet correctly identifies chloroplasts and cell walls as exclusive to the plant cell images.
Materials
Printed micrographic images of plant and animal cells, Guided worksheets, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the cell wall and chloroplasts in the plant cell images for visually impaired students.
Time rationale
20 mins image analysis, 40 mins worksheet completion, 30 mins summary writing.

teach-energy · 90 min · teach

Students will participate in a role-play activity where 'ATP tokens' are exchanged for 'cellular work' (e.g., moving a desk, lifting a book). The teacher will explain how breaking a bond in ATP releases energy. Students will then draw a diagram in their notebooks showing ATP converting to ADP to release energy, and a separate diagram showing a concentration gradient.

Mastery criterion
Diagrams correctly label ATP as an energy source and show a gradient as a difference in concentration.
Materials
Paper tokens representing ATP, Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
Ensure physical tasks during role-play are safe and do not involve heavy lifting.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn outlines of the ATP molecule for students to label.
Time rationale
30 mins role-play, 40 mins drawing diagrams, 20 mins review.

teach-transport · 90 min · teach

Students will model passive and active transport using a cardboard box with a slit (membrane) and ping-pong balls (molecules). They will push balls through the slit from high to low concentration (passive) and then use 'energy' (a designated student pushing back) to move them from low to high concentration (active). They will record their observations and definitions in a graphic organizer.

Mastery criterion
Graphic organizer correctly states that active transport requires energy and moves against the gradient.
Materials
Cardboard boxes with slits, Ping-pong balls or crumpled paper, Graphic organizers
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Use different colored balls to represent different concentrations clearly.
Time rationale
40 mins modeling activity, 30 mins graphic organizer, 20 mins class discussion.

teach-osmosis · 90 min · teach

Students will observe a teacher demonstration of potato slices placed in pure water (hypotonic) and very salty water (hypertonic) prepared the day before. They will measure the flexibility and size of the slices, record the data, and write a conclusion predicting what would happen to a human cell in similar conditions based on the evidence.

Mastery criterion
Conclusion accurately predicts cell shrinking in hypertonic and swelling in hypotonic solutions, citing the potato evidence.
Materials
Potato slices, Salt, Water, Cups, Rulers
Safety
Ensure students do not eat the potato slices.
Access and differentiation
Provide a structured conclusion paragraph with blanks for key terms.
Time rationale
20 mins observation and measurement, 40 mins data recording, 30 mins writing conclusions.

teach-respiration · 90 min · teach

Students will create a flowchart using cut-out shapes representing glucose, oxygen, mitochondria, ATP, water, and carbon dioxide. They will arrange the shapes to show the inputs and outputs of aerobic respiration. Once approved by the teacher, they will glue the flowchart into their notebooks and write a descriptive caption.

Mastery criterion
Flowchart correctly shows glucose and oxygen entering the mitochondria, and ATP, water, and CO2 exiting.
Materials
Cut-out shapes of molecules and organelles, Glue, Notebooks
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a partially completed flowchart template.
Time rationale
20 mins instruction, 40 mins flowchart assembly, 30 mins gluing and caption writing.

teach-photosynthesis · 90 min · teach

Students will analyze a diagram of a chloroplast showing light hitting it, water entering, and oxygen and glucose being produced. They will work in pairs to answer a set of guided questions about the diagram, focusing on the role of light as an energy source to split water. They will then write a short explanatory paragraph.

Mastery criterion
Paragraph explicitly states that light provides energy to split water for glucose production.
Materials
Printed diagrams of chloroplasts, Guided question sheets, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a vocabulary bank (light, energy, water, split, glucose) for the paragraph.
Time rationale
30 mins diagram analysis, 30 mins guided questions, 30 mins paragraph writing.

teach-endomembrane · 90 min · teach

Students will draw a large map of a cell on poster paper, labeling the nucleus, rough ER, Golgi apparatus, and cell membrane. They will use a small token (representing a protein) and physically move it along the pathway, drawing arrows to trace its route. They will present their map to another group, explaining the journey.

Mastery criterion
Map and explanation correctly sequence the pathway: Rough ER -> Golgi -> Cell Membrane.
Materials
Poster paper, Markers, Small tokens (e.g., buttons or coins)
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a numbered list of the organelles for students to follow as a guide.
Time rationale
40 mins drawing the map, 20 mins tracing the pathway, 30 mins peer presentations.

practice-biomolecules-levels · 90 min · practice

Students will complete a matching activity where they link specific biomolecules (e.g., a specific protein) to the cellular structures they form, and then place those structures into the correct level of organization. They will record their matches in a structured table.

Mastery criterion
Table correctly links biomolecules to structures and assigns the correct organizational level.
Materials
Matching worksheets, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Reduce the number of matching items for students who need more time.
Time rationale
15 mins instructions, 50 mins matching activity, 25 mins review and correction.

inquiry-osmosis · 120 min · practice

Students will design a simple experiment using gummy bears placed in tap water and salt water. They will write a hypothesis predicting the outcome based on osmosis, leave the setup overnight (time not counted in minutes), and analyze the results the next day, writing a formal lab report.

Mastery criterion
Lab report correctly identifies the tap water as hypotonic (causing swelling) and salt water as hypertonic.
Materials
Gummy bears, Water, Salt, Cups, Rulers, Scales (optional)
Safety
Do not eat the gummy bears used in the experiment.
Access and differentiation
Provide a lab report template with sentence starters for the hypothesis and conclusion.
Time rationale
45 mins experimental design and setup, 45 mins data collection (next day), 30 mins report writing.

retrieval-biomolecules-1 · 60 min · retrieval

Students will play a flashcard game in pairs. One student reads the characteristics of a biomolecule, and the other must name the group (carbohydrate, lipid, or protein). They will track their correct answers and review any missed cards.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the biomolecule group for at least 80% of the flashcards.
Materials
Pre-made flashcards with biomolecule characteristics
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Include pictures of food examples on the flashcards as hints.
Time rationale
10 mins setup, 40 mins gameplay, 10 mins review.

retrieval-biomolecules-2 · 60 min · retrieval

Students will complete a short written quiz where they must list three foods they ate recently and identify the primary biomolecule in each, justifying their choice based on the characteristics learned.

Mastery criterion
Quiz correctly identifies the primary biomolecule for at least two of the three foods.
Materials
Quiz paper, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to choose from a provided list of foods if they cannot recall their own meals.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 40 mins quiz completion, 10 mins collection.

retrieval-osmosis-1 · 60 min · retrieval

Students will be given three scenarios on a worksheet (e.g., a plant wilting, a slug with salt on it, a red blood cell in pure water). They must predict the direction of water movement and state whether the environment is hypertonic or hypotonic.

Mastery criterion
Correctly predicts water movement and tonicity for at least two of the three scenarios.
Materials
Worksheets, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide diagrams alongside the text scenarios to aid visualization.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 40 mins worksheet completion, 10 mins review.

retrieval-osmosis-2 · 60 min · retrieval

Students will participate in a 'think-pair-share' activity. The teacher will project an image of a shriveled cell. Students will individually write down their prediction of what type of solution caused this, pair up to discuss their reasoning, and then share with the class.

Mastery criterion
Student's written response correctly identifies a hypertonic solution and justifies it with water leaving the cell.
Materials
Projector or printed image of a shriveled cell, Notebooks
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide sentence frames for the written response.
Time rationale
15 mins individual writing, 20 mins pair discussion, 25 mins class sharing.

assessment-unit-5 · 120 min · assessment

Students will complete a comprehensive written exam covering biomolecules, cell types, and energy processes. The exam includes multiple-choice questions, diagram labeling, and short essay responses requiring them to connect photosynthesis and respiration.

Mastery criterion
Scores at least 70% overall, with correct responses on the core essay connecting photosynthesis products to respiration inputs.
Materials
Exam papers, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide extra time and allow oral responses for the essay portion for students with writing difficulties.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 90 mins exam completion, 20 mins collection and buffer time.

bridge-energy-ecosystems · 90 min · bridge

Students will create a conceptual model showing how the outputs of photosynthesis (glucose, oxygen) become the inputs for cellular respiration, and vice versa. They will write a paragraph explaining how this cycle sustains life on Earth, bridging cellular processes to ecosystem dynamics.

Mastery criterion
Model accurately depicts the cyclical relationship between the two processes.
Materials
Large paper, Markers
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a partially drawn cycle for students to complete.
Time rationale
20 mins introduction, 40 mins model creation, 30 mins writing and sharing.

practice-enzymes · 90 min · practice

Students will work in small groups to analyze three different scenarios where enzymes are used in everyday life (e.g., digestion, laundry detergents, fruit browning). They will create a poster for one scenario, illustrating the specific substrate, the enzyme's role, and the resulting products, emphasizing that the enzyme is reusable.

Mastery criterion
Posters accurately identify the substrate and products, and explicitly state that the enzyme is not consumed in the reaction.
Materials
Scenario cards, Poster paper, Markers
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn enzyme-substrate templates for students who need visual support.
Time rationale
15 mins reading scenarios, 45 mins creating posters, 30 mins presenting to the class.

practice-cell-types · 90 min · practice

Students will be given a set of 'mystery cell' profile cards containing descriptions of cellular structures. They must sort the cards into 'Prokaryotic', 'Eukaryotic', or 'Both' categories, and then write a short justification for each placement in their notebooks.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly categorize at least 80% of the mystery cell cards and provide accurate structural justifications.
Materials
Mystery cell profile cards, Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Highlight key terms like 'nucleus' and 'membrane' on the cards for students who need reading assistance.
Time rationale
15 mins instructions, 45 mins sorting and writing, 30 mins class review.

practice-eukaryotes · 90 min · practice

Students will use modeling clay to build 3D models of either a plant or an animal cell. They must include and label the specific organelles that differentiate their chosen cell type from the other, and then pair up with a student who built the opposite type to compare models.

Mastery criterion
Models accurately include chloroplasts and cell walls for plant cells, or omit them for animal cells, with correct labels.
Materials
Modeling clay in various colors, Toothpicks, Sticky labels
Safety
Ensure students wash their hands after using modeling clay.
Access and differentiation
Provide a checklist of required organelles for each cell type.
Time rationale
10 mins planning, 50 mins building models, 30 mins peer comparison.

practice-energy · 90 min · practice

Students will complete a worksheet featuring analogies for cellular energy (e.g., a charged battery vs. a dead battery, water behind a dam vs. flowing water). They must map these analogies to ATP/ADP cycles and chemical gradients, explaining how each represents biologically useful energy.

Mastery criterion
Worksheets correctly map the analogies to ATP and gradients, demonstrating an understanding of stored vs. released energy.
Materials
Analogy worksheets, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw their own analogies instead of writing explanations if they struggle with written expression.
Time rationale
20 mins introduction, 40 mins worksheet completion, 30 mins sharing analogies.

practice-transport · 90 min · practice

Students will participate in a sorting relay race. They will be given cards describing various cellular transport scenarios (e.g., oxygen entering a cell, a pump moving sodium out). They must run to the board and place their card under the correct heading: 'Active Transport' or 'Passive Transport'.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly sort the scenarios and can verbally explain that active transport requires ATP while passive does not.
Materials
Transport scenario cards, Tape or magnets, Whiteboard
Safety
Ensure the classroom is clear of tripping hazards for the relay race.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to walk instead of run, or sort the cards at their desks.
Time rationale
15 mins setup, 45 mins relay race, 30 mins review and correction of the board.

practice-respiration · 90 min · practice

Students will write a creative short story from the perspective of a glucose molecule entering a cell. The story must describe the molecule's journey to the mitochondria, its interaction with oxygen, and its ultimate transformation into ATP, water, and carbon dioxide.

Mastery criterion
Stories accurately include the mitochondria, oxygen, and the production of ATP as the main goal of the process.
Materials
Notebooks, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a storyboard template with key scenes outlined for students who need help structuring their narrative.
Time rationale
15 mins brainstorming, 50 mins writing, 25 mins reading stories aloud.

practice-photosynthesis · 90 min · practice

Students will create a comic strip illustrating the process of photosynthesis. The comic must clearly show light energy being used to split water molecules, and the subsequent use of those components to build glucose from carbon dioxide.

Mastery criterion
Comic strips accurately depict light as the energy source for splitting water and producing sugars.
Materials
Blank comic strip templates, Colored pencils, Markers
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn characters (e.g., 'Sun', 'Water Drop') for students to use in their panels.
Time rationale
15 mins planning, 55 mins drawing and coloring, 20 mins gallery walk.

practice-endomembrane · 90 min · practice

Students will play a board game designed by the teacher where they act as 'cellular delivery drivers'. They must roll dice to move their protein cargo from the rough ER, through the Golgi apparatus, and out of the cell membrane, answering review questions to advance.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully navigate the board game pathway (ER -> Golgi -> Membrane) and answer pathway-related questions correctly.
Materials
Custom board games, Dice, Game pieces, Question cards
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Pair students up so they can consult each other on the review questions.
Time rationale
15 mins explaining rules, 60 mins playing the game, 15 mins wrap-up.

retrieval-enzymes · 60 min · retrieval

Students will complete a quick-fire quiz where they must define an enzyme, identify its target (substrate), and state whether it is consumed in a reaction. They will then swap papers and grade each other's work based on a teacher-provided rubric.

Mastery criterion
Quizzes correctly define enzymes as reusable biological catalysts that act on substrates.
Materials
Quiz sheets, Red pens for grading
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Read the quiz questions aloud for students with reading difficulties.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 30 mins quiz, 20 mins peer grading and review.

retrieval-levels · 60 min · retrieval

Students will participate in a 'whiteboard shootout'. The teacher will call out a biological structure (e.g., 'heart', 'carbon', 'red blood cell'), and students must quickly write the correct level of organization on their mini-whiteboards and hold them up.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the level of organization for at least 80% of the called-out structures.
Materials
Mini-whiteboards, Dry erase markers, Erasers
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a reference list of the levels on the main board for students to choose from.
Time rationale
10 mins setup, 40 mins game, 10 mins review.

retrieval-transport · 60 min · retrieval

Students will complete a 'fill-in-the-blanks' paragraph summarizing the differences between active and passive transport, focusing on the use of ATP and the direction of movement relative to the concentration gradient.

Mastery criterion
Paragraphs correctly use the terms 'ATP', 'active', 'passive', and 'gradient' in the proper context.
Materials
Fill-in-the-blanks worksheets, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank for the fill-in-the-blanks exercise.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 35 mins independent work, 15 mins class review.

retrieval-respiration · 60 min · retrieval

Students will draw a simple diagram from memory showing a mitochondrion, with arrows indicating what goes in (glucose, oxygen) and what comes out (ATP, water, carbon dioxide).

Mastery criterion
Diagrams accurately show the correct inputs and outputs of aerobic respiration in the mitochondria.
Materials
Blank paper, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide a partially drawn mitochondrion outline.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 30 mins drawing, 20 mins comparing with a partner.

assessment-mid-unit · 90 min · assessment

Students will complete a mid-unit written assessment covering biomolecules, enzymes, cell types, and levels of organization. The test will include multiple-choice questions, matching sections, and short-answer questions requiring them to apply their knowledge to new examples.

Mastery criterion
Students score at least 70% on the assessment, demonstrating solid foundational knowledge before moving to complex cellular processes.
Materials
Printed assessments, Pencils
Safety
No specific safety hazards.
Access and differentiation
Provide extended time and a quiet testing environment for students who require accommodations.
Time rationale
10 mins instructions, 70 mins testing, 10 mins collection.

Limitations: The distinction between different types of plastids is simplified to focus primarily on chloroplasts for primary level understanding.; The complexities of the electron transport chain and Krebs cycle are omitted; respiration is treated as a general process of energy transformation.; Enzyme kinetics and specific cofactors are simplified to a basic lock-and-key model.; The endomembrane system focuses only on the primary secretory pathway, omitting retrograde transport details.

Developmental biology

Students enter Grade 6 with basic knowledge of plant and animal life cycles and general cell structure from previous grades. In this unit, they dive deeper into the cellular mechanisms of heredity (DNA, mitosis, meiosis) and how these microscopic processes drive macroscopic reproduction and embryonic development. This establishes a critical foundation for Grade 7, where they will revisit genetics to explore Mendelian inheritance, Punnett squares, and genetic mutations, requiring a solid grasp of how chromosomes segregate during meiosis.

Review: needs_human_review · optimizer revisions: 3. Unit allocation: 5 planning weeks.

Cellular Basis of Heredity and Division

Students must first understand the molecular and cellular foundations of genetic material before they can grasp how traits are passed on and how organisms grow and reproduce. This skill moves from the structural components of DNA to the cellular processes of mitosis and meiosis.

identify the three molecular components of a DNA nucleotide using structural diagrams
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Label a provided diagram of a single DNA nucleotide with its three main chemical components.
Expected response
The student labels the circular part as phosphate, the pentagon as deoxyribose sugar, and the rectangle as the nitrogenous base.
Scoring rule
Full credit for correctly identifying all three components; partial credit if only two are correct.
Mastery evidence
Students can correctly label the phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, and nitrogenous base on a blank diagram of a nucleotide.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think DNA is a single solid structure rather than a polymer made of repeating nucleotide units.; Students might confuse the sugar in DNA with the sugar in RNA.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • DNA is composed of structural units called nucleotides, which consist of three molecules: a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. · Source page 191 · paragraph p191-paragraph-4
contrast the cellular location of DNA in prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Sort descriptions of DNA storage into 'Prokaryotic' or 'Eukaryotic' categories.
Expected response
Eukaryotic: DNA enclosed in a nucleus. Prokaryotic: DNA located in a nucleoid region without a membrane.
Scoring rule
Pass if both descriptions are correctly categorized.
Mastery evidence
Students can state that eukaryotic DNA is enclosed in a nucleus while prokaryotic DNA is in a nucleoid region.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may believe all cells have a nucleus.; Students might think prokaryotes do not have DNA because they lack a nucleus.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • In prokaryotes, DNA is located in the nucleoid region. · Source page 169 · paragraph p169-paragraph-12
justify the use of detergent to disrupt cell membranes during a DNA extraction procedure
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Explain why a DNA extraction protocol would fail if the detergent step were omitted, based on cell structure.
Expected response
Without detergent, the cell and nuclear membranes would remain intact, trapping the DNA inside the cell and preventing it from precipitating in the alcohol.
Scoring rule
Pass if the response explicitly connects the detergent to the breakdown or destabilization of cell membranes.
Mastery evidence
Students can explain that detergent is necessary to break down the lipid membranes of the cell and nucleus to release the DNA.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think the detergent cleans the DNA.; Students might believe DNA can be extracted without breaking the cell membrane.
Local prerequisites
g6-u6-m1-dna-components, g6-u6-m2-dna-location
Scientific support
  • Soap destabilizes cell membranes to release cellular contents. · Source page 167 · paragraph p167-paragraph-14
sequence the stages of mitosis using micrographs or physical models
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Arrange four provided micrographs of an onion root tip cell undergoing mitosis into the correct sequence from prophase to telophase.
Expected response
The student places the images in order: chromosomes condensing, chromosomes aligning in the middle, sister chromatids separating, and two new nuclei forming.
Scoring rule
Pass if all four images are in the exact correct sequence.
Mastery evidence
Students can arrange images of mitosis in the correct chronological order.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think cells divide instantly without intermediate steps.; Students might confuse the alignment of chromosomes with their separation.
Local prerequisites
g6-u6-m2-dna-location
Scientific support
  • Mitosis stages can be described using micrographs, samples, or schemes. · Source page 165 · paragraph p165-paragraph-6
explain how meiosis and fertilization maintain the species' chromosome number across generations
Cognitive demand
reasoning
Assessment task
Predict what would happen to the chromosome number of a human offspring if gametes were produced by mitosis instead of meiosis, and justify your answer.
Expected response
If gametes were produced by mitosis, they would have 46 chromosomes. Upon fertilization, the offspring would have 92 chromosomes, doubling every generation. Meiosis prevents this by halving the number to 23.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly predicts the doubling effect and justifies it by contrasting the outcomes of mitosis and meiosis.
Mastery evidence
Students can articulate that meiosis halves the chromosome number to create gametes, so that fertilization restores the original diploid number.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think meiosis produces identical diploid cells like mitosis.; Students might believe fertilization doubles the normal chromosome number permanently.
Local prerequisites
g6-u6-m4-mitosis-sequence
Scientific support
  • Fertilization combines two haploid gametes into a diploid cell with a double set of chromosomes. · Source page 174 · paragraph p174-paragraph-2
  • Meiosis produces haploid cells from a diploid cell. · Source page 179 · paragraph p179-paragraph-20

Reproduction and Development in Organisms

Building on cellular division, this skill scales up to organism-level reproduction and development. It covers the diversity of reproductive strategies (asexual vs. sexual, internal vs. external) and the early stages of embryonic development, providing a holistic view of life cycles.

classify organism reproduction scenarios as asexual or sexual based on the presence of genetic exchange
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Read three short scenarios of organism reproduction (e.g., yeast budding, human fertilization, bacterial fission) and classify each as sexual or asexual.
Expected response
Yeast budding: Asexual. Human fertilization: Sexual. Bacterial fission: Asexual.
Scoring rule
Pass if all scenarios are correctly classified based on genetic exchange.
Mastery evidence
Students can read a scenario and correctly identify it as sexual or asexual based on whether one or two parents contribute genetic material.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think plants only reproduce asexually and animals only sexually.; Students might confuse physical contact with sexual reproduction, ignoring the genetic definition.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • Asexual reproduction requires only one parent and involves no genetic exchange. · Source page 180 · paragraph p180-paragraph-17
categorize plant propagation methods into sexual (seeds) and asexual (cuttings, tubers, bulbs)
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Sort a list of plant propagation methods (planting a bean seed, planting a potato tuber, grafting a fruit tree branch) into sexual and asexual categories.
Expected response
Sexual: planting a bean seed. Asexual: planting a potato tuber, grafting a fruit tree branch.
Scoring rule
Pass if all methods are correctly categorized.
Mastery evidence
Students can distinguish between plant reproduction via seeds and vegetative propagation methods.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think seeds are a form of asexual reproduction.; Students might believe a plant grown from a cutting is a completely new genetic individual.
Local prerequisites
g6-u6-m6-reproduction-types
Scientific support
  • Plant reproduction via seeds is sexual, while other forms like tubers or cuttings are asexual. · Source page 181 · paragraph p181-paragraph-12
differentiate internal and external fertilization based on the environment where gametes meet
Cognitive demand
applying
Assessment task
Given a description of a frog releasing eggs into a pond where a male releases sperm, determine if this is internal or external fertilization and state why.
Expected response
External fertilization, because the sperm and egg meet in the aquatic environment outside the mother's body.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student correctly identifies external fertilization and cites the meeting of gametes outside the body as the reason.
Mastery evidence
Students can identify whether fertilization occurs inside or outside the maternal body based on environmental descriptions.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think all aquatic animals use external fertilization.; Students might believe external fertilization involves physical mating behaviors similar to internal fertilization.
Local prerequisites
g6-u6-m6-reproduction-types
Scientific support
  • External fertilization occurs outside the mother's body, typically in an aquatic environment. · Source page 190 · paragraph p190-paragraph-9
identify the macroscopic structures of an amniotic egg and their protective and nutritional functions for the embryo
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
State the specific survival function of the yolk and the shell for a developing bird embryo.
Expected response
The yolk provides essential nutrients and energy for the embryo to grow, while the shell provides physical protection from the outside environment.
Scoring rule
Pass if both the nutritional role of the yolk and the protective role of the shell are correctly stated.
Mastery evidence
Students can state how specific parts of the egg (shell, yolk) support the survival and growth of the embryo.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think the yolk is the embryo itself rather than its food source.; Students might believe the shell is completely solid and impermeable to air.
Local prerequisites
No dependency asserted within this unit
Scientific support
  • The structure of the egg provides protection and maintenance for the embryo, and its contents provide enormous nutritional value for the new living being. · Source page 189 · paragraph p189-paragraph-3
identify the early stages of vertebrate embryonic development (blastula, gastrula)
Cognitive demand
knowing
Assessment task
Identify the blastula stage and the gastrula stage of an embryo from models or drawings.
Expected response
The student identifies the blastula as a hollow sphere of cells and the gastrula as a sphere with an inward fold (invagination) forming layers.
Scoring rule
Pass if the student clearly distinguishes the hollow structure of the blastula from the layered/folded structure of the gastrula.
Mastery evidence
Students can identify the transition from a single cell to a blastula and then a gastrula.
Diagnostic hypotheses
Students may think an embryo starts as a miniature version of the adult rather than going through cellular stages.; Students might confuse the blastula (hollow ball) with the gastrula (invaginated structure).
Local prerequisites
g6-u6-m4-mitosis-sequence
Scientific support
  • Vertebrate embryonic development can be represented using models or simulations. · Source page 165 · paragraph p165-paragraph-10
Activity bank: materials, safety and differentiation

a-m1-teach · 45 min · teach

Introduce the three components of a DNA nucleotide using a large board diagram. Students draw their own nucleotide in their notebooks, color-coding the phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, and nitrogenous base, and write a one-sentence definition for each part.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly draw and label the three components of a nucleotide with appropriate color-coding.
Materials
Whiteboard, Markers, Notebooks, Colored pencils
Safety
Ensure students remain seated while using colored pencils to avoid accidental pokes.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-drawn outline of the nucleotide for students who struggle with fine motor skills, allowing them to focus on labeling and coloring.
Time rationale
15 minutes for teacher explanation and board diagram, 20 minutes for student drawing and color-coding, 10 minutes for peer review and correction.

a-m1-practice · 45 min · practice

Students use modeling clay to build a 3D model of a single nucleotide. They must select three different colors to represent the phosphate, sugar, and base, assemble them in the correct structural arrangement, and present their model to a partner.

Mastery criterion
The 3D model accurately reflects the structural connection between the phosphate, sugar, and base.
Materials
Modeling clay in various colors, Cardboard bases, Toothpicks
Safety
Remind students not to ingest the modeling clay and to wash hands after the activity.
Access and differentiation
Offer a reference card showing the 2D structure to help students translate it into a 3D model.
Time rationale
10 minutes for material distribution and instructions, 25 minutes for building the model, 10 minutes for partner presentations.

a-m1-assessment · 30 min · assessment

Students receive a worksheet with three different blank diagrams of nucleotides in various orientations. They must correctly label the phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, and nitrogenous base on all three diagrams.

Mastery criterion
All three components are correctly identified on at least two of the three diagrams regardless of orientation.
Materials
Printed worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety; no specific hazards.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use a word bank if they struggle with spelling the scientific terms.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for independent completion of the worksheet, 5 minutes for collection.

a-m2-teach · 45 min · teach

Present side-by-side diagrams of a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell. Explain the difference between a nucleus and a nucleoid region. Students create a Venn diagram comparing where DNA is stored in both cell types.

Mastery criterion
The Venn diagram correctly places 'nucleus' under eukaryotic, 'nucleoid region' under prokaryotic, and 'contains DNA' in the overlapping section.
Materials
Projector or large posters, Notebooks, Rulers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide partially filled Venn diagrams for students who need structural support.
Time rationale
20 minutes for direct instruction and visual comparison, 20 minutes for Venn diagram creation, 5 minutes for review.

a-m2-practice · 45 min · practice

Students are given 10 cards with descriptions of different cells (e.g., 'A human skin cell', 'A bacterium found in soil'). They must sort the cards into 'Eukaryotic (Nucleus)' and 'Prokaryotic (Nucleoid)' categories based on prior knowledge of organisms and the new DNA location rules.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 cards into the proper DNA location categories.
Materials
Sets of 10 cell description cards per group
Safety
Ensure clear pathways when students move to form groups.
Access and differentiation
Include visual icons on the cards (e.g., a simple animal icon or bacteria icon) to assist with organism identification.
Time rationale
10 minutes for group setup and instructions, 25 minutes for sorting and discussion, 10 minutes for class-wide verification.

a-m2-assessment · 30 min · assessment

Students write a short paragraph answering the prompt: 'If you were a scientist looking for DNA in a plant cell versus a bacterial cell, where exactly would you look in each, and why?'

Mastery criterion
The response explicitly states that plant cell DNA is in the nucleus and bacterial DNA is in the nucleoid region.
Materials
Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow oral responses for students with severe writing difficulties.
Time rationale
5 minutes to explain the prompt, 20 minutes for writing, 5 minutes for collection.

a-m3-teach · 60 min · teach

Demonstrate a virtual or video-based plant DNA extraction. Pause the video before the detergent step. Explain the lipid nature of cell membranes and how soap interacts with lipids. Students write a hypothesis about what would happen if this step were skipped.

Mastery criterion
Students hypothesize that without detergent, the membranes will not break, and DNA will remain trapped inside the cell.
Materials
Projector, Video of DNA extraction, Notebooks
Safety
No physical chemicals used; standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a visual analogy of washing greasy hands with and without soap to help conceptualize membrane breakdown.
Time rationale
20 minutes for video and explanation, 20 minutes for guided discussion on lipids and soap, 20 minutes for writing the hypothesis.

a-m3-practice · 60 min · practice

Students perform a safe, hands-on DNA extraction using strawberries (or bananas), salt, dish soap, and cold rubbing alcohol. They mash the fruit, mix it with the soap/salt solution to break down lipid membranes, filter it, and add cold alcohol to precipitate the DNA, documenting how the soap was necessary.

Mastery criterion
Students successfully document that the soap was required to break down the lipid membrane to access the DNA.
Materials
Strawberries or bananas, Ziplock bags, Dish soap, Salt, Water, Coffee filters, Clear cups, Cold rubbing alcohol, Stirrers
Safety
Ensure students do not ingest any materials. Handle rubbing alcohol with care and ensure good ventilation.
Access and differentiation
Pair students so that one can handle the wet materials while the other records observations.
Time rationale
15 minutes for setup and safety briefing, 30 minutes for the extraction and cleanup, 15 minutes for documenting findings.

a-m3-assessment · 45 min · assessment

Students are given a flawed protocol for DNA extraction that omits the detergent step. They must write a critical review of the protocol, identifying the missing step, explaining its purpose based on cell structure, and predicting the outcome of the flawed protocol.

Mastery criterion
The review identifies the missing detergent, explains its role in breaking lipid membranes, and predicts that no DNA will be extracted.
Materials
Printed flawed protocols, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the steps in the protocol to help students focus on the sequence and identify what is missing.
Time rationale
10 minutes reading the protocol, 25 minutes writing the review, 10 minutes for final review and submission.

a-m4-teach · 60 min · teach

The teacher performs a live demonstration of preparing an onion root tip squash, explaining the process of staining and pressing to see cells. Then, introduce the four main stages of mitosis using large printed micrographs of onion root tip cells on the board. Explain the visual hallmarks of each stage (condensing, aligning, separating, dividing). Students create a four-panel comic strip illustrating these stages in order.

Mastery criterion
The comic strip shows the four stages in the correct chronological order with accurate visual representations of the chromosomes.
Materials
Onion root tips, Microscope, Slides and coverslips, Safe stain (e.g., iodine or food coloring), Large printed micrographs, Blank comic strip templates, Pencils, Erasers
Safety
Standard classroom safety. Ensure safe handling of glass slides and coverslips.
Access and differentiation
Provide templates with the written descriptions already in place, requiring the student only to draw the corresponding visuals.
Time rationale
25 minutes for direct instruction, demonstration, and micrograph analysis, 30 minutes for comic strip creation, 5 minutes for cleanup.

a-m4-practice · 60 min · practice

Students are given a mixed set of 12 micrographs showing various cells in different stages of mitosis. Working in pairs, they must identify the stage of each cell and arrange them into three complete, sequential timelines of mitosis.

Mastery criterion
Pairs successfully create at least two complete, correctly ordered timelines from prophase to telophase.
Materials
Sets of 12 micrograph cards per pair
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Limit the set to 4 clear cards for students who are overwhelmed by the larger set.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 40 minutes for sorting and arranging, 10 minutes for teacher verification.

a-m4-assessment · 45 min · assessment

Students receive an assessment sheet with four out-of-order micrographs of mitosis. They must cut them out, paste them in the correct sequence on a new sheet, and write a one-sentence justification for the placement of each image.

Mastery criterion
All four images are pasted in the exact correct sequence, and justifications match the visual evidence.
Materials
Assessment sheets, Scissors, Glue sticks, Blank paper
Safety
Instruct students on the safe use of scissors.
Access and differentiation
Pre-cut the images for students with fine motor difficulties.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 10 minutes for cutting, 30 minutes for sequencing, pasting, and writing.

a-m4-retrieval-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Flashcard speed-sort: Students receive a shuffled deck of mitosis stage images and must arrange them in the correct order as quickly as possible, repeating the process three times to improve their speed.

Mastery criterion
Students can arrange the four stages in the correct order without hesitation.
Materials
Small decks of mitosis image cards
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to work with a partner if they need collaborative support during retrieval.
Time rationale
5 minutes setup, 20 minutes for repeated sorting rounds, 5 minutes for packing up.

a-m5-teach · 60 min · teach

Use a bead model to demonstrate chromosome numbers. Show a cell with 46 beads dividing by mitosis (resulting in 46) versus meiosis (resulting in 23). Walk through a hypothetical scenario on the board showing what happens if two 46-chromosome gametes fuse. Students calculate the resulting chromosome numbers for three generations under this hypothetical scenario.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly calculate that the chromosome number would double each generation (92, 184, 368) if mitosis produced gametes.
Materials
Beads, Cups, Whiteboard, Notebooks
Safety
Ensure beads are not swallowed or left on the floor to prevent slipping.
Access and differentiation
Provide calculators for students who struggle with mental math during the doubling calculations.
Time rationale
25 minutes for bead demonstration and explanation, 25 minutes for student calculations, 10 minutes for class discussion.

a-m5-practice · 60 min · practice

Students work in groups to create a poster explaining 'The Meiosis Solution'. They must visually depict the problem of chromosome doubling and how meiosis solves it by halving the number before fertilization. They must include a written justification.

Mastery criterion
The poster clearly contrasts the outcome of fertilization with diploid vs. haploid gametes and justifies meiosis as the mechanism for maintaining species chromosome numbers.
Materials
Large poster paper, Markers, Rulers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a structured template on the poster paper with designated areas for 'The Problem' and 'The Solution'.
Time rationale
10 minutes for group planning, 40 minutes for poster creation, 10 minutes for gallery walk.

a-m5-assessment · 45 min · assessment

Students answer a written prompt: 'Predict what would happen to the chromosome number of a human offspring if gametes were produced by mitosis instead of meiosis. Justify your answer using the concepts of fertilization and chromosome sets.'

Mastery criterion
The response predicts the doubling of chromosomes (to 92) and justifies this by explaining that mitosis does not halve the chromosome number like meiosis does.
Materials
Assessment paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw a diagram to support their written explanation if they struggle with expressive writing.
Time rationale
5 minutes for prompt explanation, 35 minutes for writing and diagramming, 5 minutes for collection.

a-m6-teach · 60 min · teach

Define sexual and asexual reproduction focusing on genetic exchange. Read three distinct scenarios aloud (yeast budding, human fertilization, bacterial fission). For each, students hold up a 'Sexual' or 'Asexual' card and write down the key phrase from the scenario that justifies their choice.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the reproduction type for all three scenarios and cite the presence or absence of two parents/genetic exchange.
Materials
Scenario scripts, Sexual/Asexual voting cards, Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide printed copies of the scenarios so students can highlight the key phrases instead of writing them down.
Time rationale
20 minutes for definitions, 30 minutes for the scenario reading and voting activity, 10 minutes for debriefing.

a-m6-practice · 60 min · practice

Students are given a set of 15 short case studies of different organisms reproducing. They must classify each case into a T-chart (Sexual vs. Asexual) and underline the evidence in the text that led to their decision.

Mastery criterion
At least 13 out of 15 case studies are correctly classified with appropriate evidence underlined.
Materials
Printed case study sheets, Highlighters or pens
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Reduce the number of case studies to 8 for students who need more time to process text.
Time rationale
10 minutes for instructions, 40 minutes for reading and classifying, 10 minutes for peer review.

a-m6-assessment · 45 min · assessment

Students read three new, unseen scenarios of organism reproduction. They must write a short paragraph for each, classifying it as sexual or asexual and explaining why based on genetic exchange.

Mastery criterion
All three scenarios are correctly classified with a valid explanation referencing genetic exchange or parent number.
Materials
Assessment sheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a sentence starter: 'This is [sexual/asexual] reproduction because...'
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for reading and writing, 5 minutes for collection.

a-m7-teach · 60 min · teach

Explain the difference between growing plants from seeds (sexual) and vegetative parts (asexual). Show physical examples or high-quality images of a bean seed, a potato tuber, and a grafted branch. Students draw each method and label it as sexual or asexual.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly label the seed as sexual and the tuber/graft as asexual in their drawings.
Materials
Bean seeds, Potatoes with eyes, Images of grafting, Notebooks, Colored pencils
Safety
Ensure students do not eat the raw beans or potatoes. Wash hands after handling.
Access and differentiation
Provide pre-drawn outlines of the plants for students to label if drawing is a barrier.
Time rationale
25 minutes for explanation and observation of physical items, 25 minutes for drawing and labeling, 10 minutes for review.

a-m7-practice · 60 min · practice

Using the local-crops context, students analyze agricultural fact sheets about how maize (grown from seed) and potatoes (grown from tubers) are propagated in El Salvador. They must categorize the methods described in the fact sheets into sexual and asexual reproduction.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly categorize maize propagation as sexual and potato tubers as asexual based on the text.
Materials
Printed agricultural fact sheets on maize and potatoes, Highlighters, Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Highlight the specific sentences in the fact sheets that describe the propagation method to guide reading.
Time rationale
15 minutes for reading the fact sheets, 30 minutes for analysis and categorization, 15 minutes for class discussion.

a-m7-assessment · 45 min · assessment

Students are given a list of five plant propagation actions (e.g., planting a sunflower seed, burying a piece of ginger rhizome, planting a mango pit, taking a rose cutting, planting a bulb). They must sort them into a table under 'Sexual' or 'Asexual'.

Mastery criterion
All five actions are correctly sorted into the sexual (seeds/pits) and asexual (rhizomes, cuttings, bulbs) categories.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Include small illustrations next to each action description to aid comprehension.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for sorting and completing the table, 5 minutes for collection.

a-m8-teach · 60 min · teach

Define internal and external fertilization based on where gametes meet. Use a diagram of a fish spawning in water versus a mammal. Students write a rule in their notebooks for determining the type of fertilization based on the environment described.

Mastery criterion
The written rule accurately states that if gametes meet outside the body (usually in water), it is external; if inside, it is internal.
Materials
Projector or posters, Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a fill-in-the-blank version of the rule for students who need language support.
Time rationale
25 minutes for direct instruction and diagram analysis, 20 minutes for writing and refining the rule, 15 minutes for sharing rules.

a-m8-practice · 60 min · practice

Using the protected-areas context, students read fact sheets about three animals found in San Salvador volcano protected areas (e.g., a specific tree frog, a snake, a bird). They must determine if each uses internal or external fertilization based on clues about where the eggs and sperm meet, and write a justification.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify the fertilization type for all three animals and cite the environmental meeting place of gametes as evidence.
Materials
Printed fact sheets about the reproductive habits of specific fauna from the San Salvador volcano area, Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Bold the sentences in the descriptions that indicate where the gametes are released.
Time rationale
15 minutes for reading, 30 minutes for determining and writing justifications, 15 minutes for group sharing.

a-m8-assessment · 45 min · assessment

Students read a short paragraph about a newly discovered aquatic species that releases thousands of eggs into a river, followed by a male releasing sperm over them. They must state whether this is internal or external fertilization and explain why.

Mastery criterion
The student identifies external fertilization and explains that it is because the sperm and egg meet in the river water, outside the mother's body.
Materials
Assessment prompt, Paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to draw the scenario and label the meeting point of the gametes to support their written answer.
Time rationale
5 minutes for reading the prompt, 35 minutes for writing the response, 5 minutes for collection.

a-m9-teach · 60 min · teach

Crack open an unfertilized chicken egg into a petri dish (teacher demonstration). Identify the shell, yolk, and albumen. Explain the function of each for a developing embryo. Students draw the egg and write the survival function next to the shell and yolk.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly label the shell as protection and the yolk as the nutrient/energy source.
Materials
Unfertilized chicken egg, Petri dish, Document camera or gather students around, Notebooks, Colored pencils
Safety
Teacher handles the raw egg. Ensure hands are washed and surfaces sanitized after the demonstration to prevent salmonella exposure.
Access and differentiation
Provide a pre-labeled diagram where students only need to write the functions.
Time rationale
20 minutes for the demonstration and explanation, 30 minutes for drawing and writing functions, 10 minutes for cleanup and review.

a-m9-practice · 60 min · practice

Students are given a design challenge: 'Design a synthetic egg for a robotic embryo.' They must draw their design, explicitly including a structure that acts like a shell and a structure that acts like a yolk, and write a paragraph explaining how their synthetic parts perform the same survival functions as the biological ones.

Mastery criterion
The design includes a protective outer layer (shell equivalent) and an internal energy source (yolk equivalent), with a logical explanation of their functions.
Materials
Drawing paper, Markers, Rulers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a list of possible synthetic materials (e.g., titanium, battery) to help spark ideas for students who struggle with open-ended design.
Time rationale
15 minutes for explaining the challenge, 35 minutes for designing and writing, 10 minutes for sharing designs.

a-m9-assessment · 45 min · assessment

Students answer two questions: 1) What is the function of the yolk for a bird embryo? 2) What is the function of the shell? They must state their answers based on the functions of these structures.

Mastery criterion
The student states that the yolk provides energy to grow, and the shell provides protection.
Materials
Assessment paper, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Allow oral assessment for students who have difficulty expressing complex reasoning in writing.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for writing responses, 5 minutes for collection.

a-m10-teach · 60 min · teach

Explain the transition from a single cell to a blastula (hollow ball) and then a gastrula (folded/layered ball). Demonstrate this using a deflated rubber ball: show it round (blastula), then push one side in (gastrula). Students sketch the two stages and label the key difference (hollow vs. folded).

Mastery criterion
Sketches clearly show the blastula as a simple hollow circle of cells and the gastrula with an inward fold.
Materials
Deflated rubber ball or soft foam ball, Whiteboard, Notebooks
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a cross-section diagram for students to trace if they struggle with 3D visualization.
Time rationale
25 minutes for demonstration and explanation, 25 minutes for sketching and labeling, 10 minutes for checking understanding.

a-m10-practice · 60 min · practice

Students use modeling clay to create a physical model of a blastula and a gastrula. They must slice their models in half (using a plastic safe knife or string) to reveal the cross-section, proving that the blastula is hollow and the gastrula has an invagination.

Mastery criterion
The physical clay models, when cut, accurately display a hollow center for the blastula and an inward fold for the gastrula.
Materials
Modeling clay, Plastic safe knives or dental floss for cutting, Paper plates
Safety
Ensure students use only the provided safe plastic knives or string for cutting the clay. Do not ingest clay.
Access and differentiation
Work in pairs so one student can mold while the other assists with the cutting process.
Time rationale
10 minutes for material distribution, 40 minutes for modeling and cutting, 10 minutes for teacher inspection.

a-m10-assessment · 45 min · assessment

Students are given two blank circles on a page. They must draw the cellular cross-section of a blastula in the first circle and a gastrula in the second circle, then write one sentence stating the physical difference between the two.

Mastery criterion
The drawings correctly depict the hollow blastula and the invaginated gastrula, and the sentence describes the folding/layering process.
Materials
Assessment worksheets, Pencils
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a word bank (e.g., hollow, fold, layers, cells) to assist with the written explanation.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 35 minutes for drawing and writing, 5 minutes for collection.

a-m10-retrieval-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Whiteboard quick-draw: The teacher calls out either 'Blastula' or 'Gastrula'. Students have 30 seconds to draw the correct cross-section on their mini-whiteboards and hold them up. Repeat for several rounds to build speed and accuracy.

Mastery criterion
Students consistently draw the correct structure (hollow vs. folded) within the time limit.
Materials
Mini-whiteboards, Dry erase markers, Erasers
Safety
Ensure markers are used properly and caps are replaced to avoid drying out or fumes.
Access and differentiation
Allow students to use hand gestures (making a hollow ball with hands vs. pushing a fist into a cupped hand) if drawing quickly is stressful.
Time rationale
5 minutes for distributing materials, 20 minutes for quick-draw rounds, 5 minutes for cleanup.

a-m10-retrieval-2 · 30 min · retrieval

Students are given a mixed set of clay models (some blastulas, some gastrulas, some incorrect shapes) prepared by the teacher. They must quickly sort them into 'Blastula', 'Gastrula', and 'Incorrect' piles based on their structural features.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly identify and sort the models based on the presence of a hollow center or an invagination.
Materials
Pre-made clay models (cut in half)
Safety
Standard classroom safety. Do not ingest clay.
Access and differentiation
Provide a reference poster showing the correct cross-sections for students to check against if they get stuck.
Time rationale
5 minutes for instructions, 20 minutes for sorting, 5 minutes for review.

a-m1-practice-2 · 60 min · practice

Students use recycled materials (bottle caps, straws, cardboard) to construct a large-scale model of a nucleotide, labeling the phosphate, sugar, and base.

Mastery criterion
The model accurately represents the three components and their connections.
Materials
Recycled materials, Tape, Markers
Safety
Ensure no sharp edges on recycled materials.
Access and differentiation
Provide a template for the connections.
Time rationale
15 mins planning, 35 mins building, 10 mins sharing.

a-m2-retrieval-1 · 30 min · retrieval

Students play a rapid-fire sorting game on the board, categorizing cell descriptions into 'Nucleus' or 'Nucleoid'.

Mastery criterion
Students correctly categorize 90% of the descriptions.
Materials
Whiteboard, Sticky notes
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Read descriptions aloud for auditory learners.
Time rationale
10 mins setup, 20 mins gameplay.

a-m5-practice-2 · 60 min · practice

Students analyze a hypothetical alien species that reproduces using mitosis for gametes. They must calculate the chromosome number over 5 generations and write a scientific report on why this species would face genetic instability.

Mastery criterion
The report correctly calculates the exponential growth of chromosomes and justifies why meiosis is necessary.
Materials
Paper, Calculators
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a table template for the calculations.
Time rationale
15 mins introduction, 30 mins calculation and writing, 15 mins peer review.

a-m7-practice-2 · 60 min · practice

Students design a community garden plan using the local-crops context, selecting specific propagation methods (seeds for maize, tubers for potatoes) and justifying their choices as sexual or asexual.

Mastery criterion
The garden plan correctly identifies the propagation method for each plant and categorizes it accurately.
Materials
Large paper, Markers
Safety
Standard classroom safety.
Access and differentiation
Provide a list of local plants and their propagation methods.
Time rationale
20 mins research/planning, 30 mins drawing, 10 mins presenting.

Limitations: The curriculum simplifies DNA extraction by not requiring pure isolation; the resulting precipitate includes proteins and RNA, which requires human review to clarify for students.; Microscopic observation of mitosis in onion roots depends heavily on the quality of the stain and the squash technique; failure to see clear phases is common and should be supplemented with prepared slides or digital micrographs.; Embryogenesis is highly simplified to the blastula and gastrula stages, omitting complex organogenesis to fit the primary education abstraction level.; The distinction between sexual and asexual reproduction in plants (e.g., spores vs. seeds) is simplified; the alternation of generations in mosses and ferns may require careful teacher guidance to avoid confusing haploid/diploid life stages.
